Urged by faith, we are obliged to believe and to maintain that the Church is one, holy, catholic, and also apostolic. We believe in her firmly and we confess with simplicity that outside of her there is neither salvation nor the remission of sins, as the Spouse in the Canticles [Sgs 6:8] proclaims: ‘One is my dove, my perfect one. She is the only one, the chosen of her who bore her,‘ and she represents one sole mystical body whose Head is Christ and the head of Christ is God [1 Cor 11:3]. In her then is one Lord, one faith, one baptism [Eph 4:5]. There had been at the time of the deluge only one ark of Noah, prefiguring the one Church, which ark, having been finished to a single cubit, had only one pilot and guide, i.e., Noah, and we read that, outside of this ark, all that subsisted on the earth was destroyed.
We venerate this Church as one, the Lord having said by the mouth of the prophet: ‘Deliver, O God, my soul from the sword and my only one from the hand of the dog.’ [Ps 21:20] He has prayed for his soul, that is for himself, heart and body; and this body, that is to say, the Church, He has called one because of the unity of the Spouse, of the faith, of the sacraments, and of the charity of the Church. This is the tunic of the Lord, the seamless tunic, which was not rent but which was cast by lot [Jn 19:23- 24]. Therefore, of the one and only Church there is one body and one head, not two heads like a monster; that is, Christ and the Vicar of Christ, Peter and the successor of Peter, since the Lord speaking to Peter Himself said: ‘Feed my sheep‘ [Jn 21:17], meaning, my sheep in general, not these, nor those in particular, whence we understand that He entrusted all to him [Peter]. Therefore, if the Greeks or others should say that they are not confided to Peter and to his successors, they must confess not being the sheep of Christ, since Our Lord says in John ‘there is one sheepfold and one shepherd.’ We are informed by the texts of the gospels that in this Church and in its power are two swords; namely, the spiritual and the temporal. For when the Apostles say: ‘Behold, here are two swords‘ [Lk 22:38] that is to say, in the Church, since the Apostles were speaking, the Lord did not reply that there were too many, but sufficient. Certainly the one who denies that the temporal sword is in the power of Peter has not listened well to the word of the Lord commanding: ‘Put up thy sword into thy scabbard‘ [Mt 26:52]. Therefore, both are in the power of the Church, namely, the spiritual sword and the material. But indeed, the latter is to be exercised on behalf of the Church; and truly, the former is to be exercised by the Church. The former is of the priest; the latter is by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the will and sufferance of the priest.

However, one sword ought to be subordinated to the other and temporal authority, subjected to spiritual power. For since the Apostle said: ‘There is no power except from God and the things that are, are ordained of God‘ [Rom 13:1-2], but they would not be ordained if one sword were not subordinated to the other and if the inferior one, as it were, were not led upwards by the other.

For, according to the Blessed Dionysius, it is a law of the divinity that the lowest things reach the highest place by intermediaries. Then, according to the order of the universe, all things are not led back to order equally and immediately, but the lowest by the intermediary, and the inferior by the superior. Hence we must recognize the more clearly that spiritual power surpasses in dignity and in nobility any temporal power whatever, as spiritual things surpass the temporal. This we see very clearly also by the payment, benediction, and consecration of the tithes, but the acceptance of power itself and by the government even of things. For with truth as our witness, it belongs to spiritual power to establish the terrestrial power and to pass judgement if it has not been good. Thus is accomplished the prophecy of Jeremias concerning the Church and the ecclesiastical power: ‘Behold to-day I have placed you over nations, and over kingdoms‘ and the rest. Therefore, if the terrestrial power err, it will be judged by the spiritual power; but if a minor spiritual power err, it will be judged by a superior spiritual power; but if the highest power of all err, it can be judged only by God, and not by man, according to the testimony of the Apostle: ‘The spiritual man judgeth of all things and he himself is judged by no man‘ [1 Cor 2:15]. This authority, however, (though it has been given to man and is exercised by man), is not human but rather divine, granted to Peter by a divine word and reaffirmed to him (Peter) and his successors by the One Whom Peter confessed, the Lord saying to Peter himself, ‘Whatsoever you shall bind on earth, shall be bound also in Heaven‘ etc., [Mt 16:19]. Therefore whoever resists this power thus ordained by God, resists the ordinance of God [Rom 13:2], unless he invent like Manicheus two beginnings, which is false and judged by us heretical, since according to the testimony of Moses, it is not in the beginnings but in the beginning that God created heaven and earth [Gen 1:1]. Furthermore, we declare, we proclaim, we define that it is absolutely necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff.

The History and Legend of Scottish Rite Origins
What We Know

In 1754, near Paris, Chevalier de Bonneville established the Chapter of Clermont. The Chapter resided in the College of Jesuits of Clermont, hence the name. It is said to have been created to honor the Duc de Clermont, then Grand Master of the English Grand Lodge of France.

The Chapter of Clermont was a “Chapter of the Advanced Degrees” and initially entailed six degrees and was later extended to 25 known degrees. The six initial degrees were 1˚, 2˚ and 3˚ St John’s Masonry, 4˚ Knight of the Eagle, 5˚ Illustrious Knight or Templar, 6˚ Sublime Illustrious Knight.

Interestingly enough historically, prior to the time of the Rite’s creation, James II had been in residence at Clermont in exile from Britain from 1688 to his death in 1701. As noted by German Masonic historian, Lenning… “whilst in exile, James II residing at the Jesuit College of Clermont in France, allowed his closest associates to fabricate certain degrees in order to extend their political views.” Lenning believed this to have been an attempt on the part of James and his associates to regain control of the British throne for the House of Stuart. If Lenning is right, this places the origins of the “Rite of Perfection” in the hands of James II and the Jacobite (Stuart) Freemasons who at the time were in exile from Great Britain throughout France and Italy. Lenning also contends that these degrees were introduced into French Freemasonry under the name of the Clermont System.

James II died in exile in 1701. His son James III is said to have continued his father’s Masonic legacy and later created further higher degrees.

Perhaps James II saw in the Jesuit morality plays of the College of Clermont a vessel for passing on a set of moral lessons. Some of the world’s greatest playwrights had emerged from Clermont. Jesuit tutelage had previously produced great writers such as Lope de Vega, Moliere, Racine, and the Corneille brothers. Ensconced in exile, I believe James II did find the inspiration and the training to help produce what would later become the first six degrees. From out of the darkness… comes light.

Louis William Valentine DuBourg PSS (French: Louis-Guillaume-Valentin DuBourg; 10 January 1766 – 12 December 1833) was a French Catholic prelate and Sulpician missionary to the United States. He built up the church in the vast new Louisiana Territory as the Bishop of Louisiana and the Two Floridas and later became the Bishop of Montauban and finally the Archbishop of Besançon in France.

Born in the colony of Saint-Domingue, DuBourg was sent to France at a young age to be educated and entered the Society of Saint Sulpice. As a cleric and son of a noble family, the French Revolution forced him into exile in Spain. In 1794, DuBourg sailed to the United States and began teaching and ministering in Baltimore, becoming the president of Georgetown College in Washington in 1795. He significantly improved the quality of the institution, but mounted a substantial debt and was ousted by the Jesuit owners of the college in 1798. DuBourg then founded a lay collegiate counterpart to St. Mary's Seminary in Baltimore. He also selected the site of Baltimore's first cathedral and became the ecclesiastical superior to Elizabeth Ann Seton's newly founded Sisters of Charity.

In 1812, DuBourg was made the apostolic administrator of the Diocese of Louisiana and the Two Floridas, and three years later, its bishop. Catholic New Orleanians rejected his authority and he was forced to move his episcopal seat to St. Louis, Missouri. There, he built the first cathedral west of the Mississippi River and established missions to the American Indians, dozens of churches, and numerous schools, including St. Mary's of the Barrens Seminary and Saint Louis University. He also recruited the Sisters of Loretto and Rose Philippine Duchesne's Sisters of the Sacred Heart to found several academies.

Never able to establish his seat in New Orleans, DuBourg returned to France in 1826, where he was made the Bishop of Montauban. Just months before his death in 1833, he became the Archbishop of Besançon.

Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

LOUIS Raphaël I Sako (Arabic: لويس روفائيل ساكو;[2] born 4 July 1948) is a Chaldean Catholic prelate who served as Patriarch of Baghdad from 2013 to 2026. Pope Francis made him a cardinal in 2018.

Biography
Early life
Sako was born in the city of Zakho, Iraq, on 4 July 1948.[3] He comes from an ethnic Assyrian family of the Chaldean Catholic Church that has roots in a religious community that has had a presence in the city of his birth since the 5th century AD.[4]

He completed his early studies in Mosul and then attended the Dominican-run Saint Jean’s Seminary there. He was ordained a priest on 1 June 1974 and filled his first pastoral assignment at the Cathedral of Mosul until 1979. He then earned a doctorate in Eastern patrology at the Pontifical Oriental Institute. When denied a license to teach because he was only qualified for religious instruction, he earned a second doctorate in history from the Sorbonne in Paris.[5] With this he secured his teaching license and was able to provide religious instruction. From 1997 to 2002 he was rector of the Patriarchal Seminary in Baghdad. He then returned to Mosul and guided the parish of Perpetual HELP for a year.[6][7]

Sako speaks Neo-Aramaic, German, French, English, Italian, Kurdish and Arabic.[3]

pickled beans aldi vitamins

Pickled beans (like the green snap beans or kidney beans from Aldi's own brand King's Crown) contain valuable nutrients despite the heating process during preservation, above all vitamin K, B vitamins (such as folic acid/B9 and B6) as well as beta-carotene (a precursor of vitamin A).

Since the vegetables are processed directly after harvest for canning, a large part of the vitamins remains well protected, even though heat-sensitive vitamins like vitamin C are partly lost during boiling.

Vitamin content by bean type

Green beans / snap beans in jar/can: They are particularly rich in vitamin K (important for blood clotting and bones). They also provide beta-carotene and vitamin B6. Since they consist largely of water, they are very low in calories (approx. 20–26 kcal per 100 g).

Broad beans, kidney beans & white beans: These legumes score above all with B vitamins (especially folic acid, which is important for cell division). Besides vitamins they provide considerably more plant protein and filling fibre than green beans.

Advantages and disadvantages of Aldi canned beans

Advantage / Disadvantage: Long shelf life and quick preparation / Vitamin C loss through heating during filling. Stable nutrients: minerals (magnesium, iron) and fat-soluble vitamins (A, K) are fully retained / Additives: salt, sugar or citric acid as an acidifier is often added to the liquid.

Tip: Drain the beans in a sieve before further processing and rinse them briefly with cold water. This significantly reduces the often elevated salt or sugar content from the canning liquid.

To give you more precise information, feel free to tell me: Do you mean green snap beans or legumes like kidney/white beans? Are you looking for figures for a specific product from Aldi Nord or Aldi Süd? Is this about a specific health goal (e.g. muscle building, weight loss or pregnancy)?

are pickled kidney beans healthier or pickled chickpeas

Both pickled kidney beans and chickpeas are absolute nutrient bombs and are among the healthiest foods there are. There is no clear "better" here, rather it depends on which health goals you are pursuing.

In direct comparison, each type has its own strengths:

Nutrient comparison (per 100 g canned, drained)

Calories: approx. 100–115 kcal (kidney) / approx. 120–140 kcal (chickpeas) — winner: kidney beans (better for weight loss) Protein: higher, approx. 7.5–8.5 g / somewhat less, approx. 6.5–7.5 g — kidney beans (better for muscle building) Fibre: higher, approx. 7–8 g / somewhat less, approx. 5–6 g — kidney beans (better for digestion) Healthy fats: almost fat-free (0.5 g) / higher, approx. 2–3 g unsaturated fats — chickpeas (better long-lasting satiety) Iron & potassium: very high / moderate — kidney beans (important for vegan/vegetarian diets) Folic acid (B9) & magnesium: moderate / very high — chickpeas (ideal in pregnancy & for nerves) Glycaemic index: lower / somewhat higher — kidney beans (better for stable blood sugar)

When is which healthier?

Kidney beans are the winners for fitness & diets: If you want to save calories, build muscle or keep your blood sugar extremely stable (e.g. with diabetes), kidney beans offer a marginally better ratio of high protein and fibre to fewer calories. They also provide considerably more plant-based iron.
Chickpeas are the winners for nerves, brain & pregnancy: They score with an enormous amount of folic acid (B9) and magnesium. The healthy fats they contain, together with the proteins, provide a very pleasant, long-lasting feeling of fullness.
The "can disadvantage" with both
Since both products are pickled, they often float in a brine. Always rinse the legumes thoroughly in a sieve with cold water before eating. This washes away up to 35–40% of the excess sodium (salt) as well as gas-producing sugars.
Conclusion: Variety is healthiest. Both feed your good gut bacteria perfectly.
Would you like to know how best to combine the beans to make optimal use of the protein source (biological value)? Or are you looking for a recipe idea for one of the two types?
the pickling water is rubbish

That is absolutely right: The pickling water (the pouring liquid) from normal kidney beans contains above all a lot of salt, preservatives and dissolved gas-producing sugars — that's why it belongs down the drain.

There is however one important exception with chickpeas:

The secret of chickpea water (aquafaba)

The water from the chickpea can is not rubbish in the kitchen, but a valuable protein substitute. It is called aquafaba.

The vegan egg white: If you whip the chickpea water with a hand mixer, it becomes stiff like real egg white.

What is it used for? It is perfect for vegan chocolate mousse, meringue, macarons or for baking.

Why the kidney bean water had to go

With kidney beans the whipping theoretically works too, but the water has two big disadvantages:

Colour and taste: It tastes extremely earthy and dyes everything dark red.

Digestive problems: The so-called oligosaccharides collect in this water. These are the multiple sugars that the human gut cannot digest and which cause the typical bloating.

Conclusion: Always pour away kidney bean water and rinse the beans. Chickpea water you can collect and freeze for baking or desserts if you don't use it immediately.

Your logic is completely correct: If chickpeas and kidney beans are preserved by the same manufacturer in the same way in cans or jars, they basically contain the same technological additives in the pouring liquid.

Here is the correction, where the error in reasoning lay and what is actually the case:

1. Preservatives: none in either

Cans and jars (whether from Aldi Nord or Aldi Süd) are made shelf-stable by pure heating (autoclaving). Neither kidney beans nor chickpeas contain artificial preservatives, because they simply don't need any. With both products the liquid almost always consists only of water and salt, sometimes a little antioxidant (like ascorbic acid) or citric acid. On this point the liquids therefore do not differ.

2. Why chickpea water can still be whipped (and kidney water cannot)

The actual difference lies not in added substances, but in the natural properties of the bean itself, which pass into the water during cooking:

The protein structure (aquafaba): Chickpeas release a very particular combination of soluble starches and plant proteins (saponins and albumins) into the water during cooking. Only this specific protein composition behaves like egg white when whipped and traps air.

The kidney bean water: The proteins and starches of the kidney bean have a different molecular structure. If you try to whip the dark red kidney water, no stable, airy foam forms. It also tastes extremely earthy-bitter.

In summary

From a chemical point of view the water is equally "unhealthy" in both products due to the added salt. The only reason you don't pour away chickpea water is a purely culinary trick (egg white substitute) — health-wise the salty water gains no plus points from this.

1. One Body Means That Their Wounds Belong to Us

Hebrews 13:3 does not offer a sentimental suggestion. It issues a command: “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.” The verse does not tell us to remember prisoners only when their stories become popular, when a television network notices them, or when their suffering fits the political interests of the moment. We are to remember them as though the chain were fastened around our own wrist. We are to think about the believer inside the prison as if we were sitting beside him on the concrete floor. We are to remember the widow as if the grave in front of her held our own husband. We are to remember the orphan as if the burned house had been ours. That is not emotional manipulation; that is spiritual identification. The Holy Ghost does not allow a Christian in safety to shrug at a Christian in chains. The distance between the two may be thousands of miles, but there is no distance inside the Body of Christ. A chain placed upon one member ought to be felt by all the others.

First Corinthians 12:26 declares, “And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.” That verse exposes the shallow, nationalized Christianity that recognizes only what happens inside its own neighborhood. The Body of Christ is not an American body, an African body, an Asian body, or a European body. It is one spiritual Body composed of every saved believer who has been baptized by the Spirit into Jesus Christ. The Christian hiding in North Korea belongs to the same Body as the Christian sitting freely in an air-conditioned church in Florida. The widow in Nigeria belongs to the same Body as the family eating lunch after Sunday service in Ohio. The imprisoned house-church pastor in China belongs to the same Body as the preacher who can livestream his sermon without expecting the police to break down the door. Geography may separate us, language may challenge us, and political borders may divide nations, but Calvary has joined every blood-bought believer to the same Head. If we can hear that one part of the Body is being cut and feel nothing, something is terribly numb in the parts that remain comfortable.

The persecuted Church does not primarily need our pity. Those believers are not spiritual museum pieces to be stared at from a safe distance. Many of them possess a depth of faith, courage, prayer, and spiritual endurance that would make the average prosperous church blush. They need our remembrance, our prayer, our practical support, and our willingness to tell the truth about what is happening. They need to know that when the world treats them as forgotten people, the Body of Christ has not forgotten them. The brother who wrote from Africa was not begging strangers to manufacture concern. He was reminding family members of their responsibility. His plea crossed an ocean, but it came from inside the same Body. The question is not whether we heard the words. The question is whether those words will reach farther than our ears and disturb the comfortable machinery of our daily lives.

text:
Apparently some people think consequences are optional.

A woman is found slumped behind the wheel of a RUNNING Porsche outside a Florida restaurant.

The deputy explains that being parked doesn’t magically make everything disappear when you’re sitting in the driver’s seat with the engine running.

Her response?

Basically: “But I’m not driving.”

Then she’s repeatedly asked for her license.

She refuses.

She’s given warnings.

Still refuses.

She’s even offered the opportunity to call someone for a ride.

Still keeps arguing.

Because apparently when life gives you an off-ramp, the logical choice is to drive straight past it and find out where the consequences live.

Backup arrives.

She’s taken into custody.

And suddenly the situation she insisted wasn’t a problem… became a much bigger problem.

The DUI charge was later reduced to reckless driving, she pleaded no contest, adjudication was withheld, and the resisting charge was dismissed.

But the bigger lesson is almost painfully simple:

Your choices have consequences.

You don’t get to make decision after decision, ignore every warning, refuse every opportunity to change course… and then act surprised when life finally hands you the receipt.

text:
Whiskey Jug Genie by Sultonna Nadine is a lighthearted and charming paranormal fantasy that mixes magic, humor, and a touch of romance for pure escapist fun.

When quiet London apothecary shop owner Martin buys an old whiskey jug on vacation, he has no idea he’s about to release Bubba, a genie who’s been trapped inside for 200 years and is thoroughly out of touch with the modern world. Chaos, spells, cultural clashes, and plenty of laughs ensue as the unlikely pair (along with a very annoyed cat) try to navigate the mess. Set against the backdrop of contemporary London with elements of white magic and everyday wonder, the story balances humorous situations with warmer moments. Readers appreciate its playful tone, quirky characters, and the perfect blend of paranormal fantasy, magic, and comedy—it’s the kind of book that delivers smiles and a welcome dose of whimsy.

text:
Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

🇺🇦 Ukraine may legalize porn to fund the war

Producing or possessing pornography in Ukraine carries up to 7 years in prison. 

It hasn't stopped the industry. Tax authorities got data from OnlyFans showing 7,900 Ukrainians earned over $131 million on the platform in 2023 alone.

So Kyiv started sending tax letters. Anyone who filed confessed to a crime in the process, and police followed with raids. One model had $200,000 seized and was offered the standard arrangement: hand over half, keep the rest. 

She refused, filed a petition on Zelensky's website, and cleared the 25,000 signatures needed to force a response.

A bill to legalize passed its first reading in July. Its author, Yaroslav Zhelezniak, estimates $25 million a year in tax, against defense needs of $120 billion. 

Or, put the way it's being sold in Kyiv: 30,000 drones.

Meanwhile hundreds of models have relocated to Georgia and elsewhere, paying tax to somebody else's treasury.

Source: The Wall Street Journal / Writer: Oliver

text:
Actually, you're the one who's being misleading here. The new CBA's EPIC provision gives her an opportunity to replace the fourth year of her rookie contract with a maximum level contract. It is an eligibility pathway, not an automatic raise or a completed extension.

Clark's original contract covers the 2024 to 2027 seasons. Without a new agreement, she would generally reach restricted free agency after the 2027 season, in 2028.

The new CBA allows certain players still on rookie contracts to renegotiate the fourth year of that contract and sign a three year extension. Clark qualifies because she made the 2024 All WNBA First Team. Players who make All WNBA First or Second Team on a rookie contract can qualify for the standard maximum, while a rookie contract MVP can qualify for the supermax.

The CBA therefore gives Clark an earlier negotiating opportunity, but it does not force Indiana to offer the deal or require Clark to accept it. The first practical example came when Aliyah Boston signed the WNBA's first reported EPIC agreement after qualifying through her 2025 All WNBA Second Team selection.

text:
The first and most honest reason The Perils of Gwendoline in the Land of the Yik Yak still punches through the noise of every other adventure picture, every other late night cable relic, every other European erotic romp of its decade is simple and physical and unapologetic. Two beautiful women, Tawny Kitaen as the wide eyed Gwendoline and Zabou as her sharper maid Beth, spend a startling amount of the running time in clothing that barely qualifies as clothing, or in the rumor and then the fact of nudity, and the film treats that fact not as a side dish but as the weather of the story. Kitaen, in her feature debut, arrives looking like she was assembled specifically for the camera to fall in love with her: the hair, the body, the combination of convent innocence and instant heat. Zabou matches her as the worldly counterpart who already knows the score. Then the movie multiplies the idea until an entire lost city of warrior women appears in thongs, breastplates, helmets, and almost nothing else. That is the gravitational center. Everything else orbits it. You can pretend you came for the butterfly or the jungle or the mercenary with the hat. You stayed because the film understood that looking, and being looked at, can be both the danger and the point.

That surface is not empty. The movie is loosely adapted from John Willie’s Sweet Gwendoline, the bondage and peril comic that lived in the pages of Bizarre magazine from the late 1940s into the 1950s, a heroine who was always being tied, sold, rescued, and posed. Just Jaeckin, the man who had already given the world Emmanuelle and The Story of O, took that fetish DNA and dropped it into a pulp adventure that wants to be Raiders of the Lost Ark if Indiana Jones had been directed by someone who also directed Lady Chatterley’s Lover. The result is a hybrid no other film quite managed: comic book peril, colonial travelogue, softcore gaze, and a lost city that looks like it was designed by a Belgian graphic novelist because it was. François Schuiten, later famous for Les Cités Obscures, worked on the look of Pikaho. Pierre Bachelet, who scored Emmanuelle, wrote the music. The picture was shot across the Philippines, Morocco, and French studios over eighteen weeks. It exists in a 106 minute French cut and a leaner American version that lost roughly a quarter hour. It made a little over a million dollars. Critics were not kind. Cable and home video turned it into a secret handshake.

The basic plot is a quest that keeps changing its object. Gwendoline, raised in a convent, ships herself and Beth across the ocean inside a crate because she cannot afford a cabin. She is looking for her father, a scientist who vanished in the legendary Land of the Yik Yak while hunting a rare black butterfly on which he had staked his entire reputation. At a Chinese port thieves find her in the crate, sell her toward a casino brothel, and the same men later snatch Beth. Willard, a mercenary river man who is in it for money and not much else, crashes into the situation, extracts what he is owed, and leaves bodies behind. Gwendoline is immediately, ridiculously, sincerely in love with the violence and the competence. Beth withholds information Willard needs until he agrees to guide them. Gwendoline offers two thousand dollars. The three of them push upriver, through jungle and the Kiops, across desert, toward the butterfly and the rumor of a father. They find the insect. Beth is taken. The trail leads underground into Pikaho, a diamond city swallowed by a twelfth century volcano, its men later wiped out by disease, leaving an all female society of workers, warriors, and a queen who keeps the bloodline going by allowing a victor among her women the right to mate with any captured man. Gwendoline, disguised, wins that right. What follows is escape, eruption, and the butterfly finally taken. The father is already gone. The name she wanted for him becomes something she has to carry herself.

What you are supposed to take away is not a moral so much as a collision. Innocence is not purity; it is a starting velocity. Gwendoline leaves the convent the way a person leaves a locked room, and the world answers with thieves, heat, knives, and desire. The lesson inside the crate scene is that desperation will put you in a box and call it travel. The lesson inside the rescue is that the person who saves you may not be good, only effective, and that the difference can feel identical when you are young and burning. The lesson inside the jungle and the desert is that a quest inherited from a father can outlive the father; finishing the work is how you stop being the daughter and start being the one who names the specimen. The lesson inside Pikaho is stranger and more interesting than most adventure films ever attempt. A society of women that has survived by erasing men still needs a man to continue, and the ritual around that need is both grotesque and honest about power. Gwendoline does not simply endure the gaze of that city. She puts on its armor, wins its contest, and uses the rules against the queen. Beth, who began as the knowing servant, becomes the co conspirator who actually understands the machinery. Willard, who began as the man who would sell anyone, ends up capturing the butterfly because the women made the journey matter more than the cargo. Desire and danger keep trading clothes. Loyalty between the two women is the one contract that does not get rewritten by money or sex or a volcano.

That is why the film stands apart from the rest of its field. Most erotic pictures of the era stay indoors, in apartments and country houses, letting the camera do the traveling. Most adventure pictures of the early eighties after Raiders keep the heroine clothed and the sexuality as a wink. Gwendoline does both at once and refuses to apologize for the contradiction. It is Barbarella if Barbarella had a maid and a mercenary and a scientific MacGuffin. It is a serial queen cliffhanger if the cliffs were also an excuse to undress. It is a fetish comic that suddenly had a budget, locations, and a rock video body before the rock videos existed. Kitaen would, a few years later, roll across the hoods of Jaguars for Whitesnake and become one of the defining images of the decade. This is the raw version of that image, before the styling, before the fame, when the camera still seemed surprised by her. Zabou gives the film its sly intelligence. Bernadette Lafont, a veteran of the French New Wave, plays the queen as if she is having the time of her life chewing scenery in robes while everyone else wears almost nothing. The production design of the underground city, built from one or two studio rooms with walls that rolled away and were redressed between setups, looks more expensive and more invented than the budget should have allowed. The lip sync is often wrong because the production was multilingual and the English track was laid later. That slight unreality is part of the spell. You are watching a dream of pulp, not a documentary of it.

Call it a masterpiece only if you accept that some masterpieces are made of sweat, camp, excellent shoulders, and a sincere belief that a butterfly and a body can be equally worth crossing a continent for. Call it a cultural icon because late night HBO and Cinemax in the mid eighties turned it into the movie you found when you were not supposed to be awake, the one that taught a generation that adventure and appetite could share the same frame. It is a must watch because it is a complete object from a moment that no longer exists: European softcore prestige colliding with American pulp timing, a comic book underground crossing into theaters just as that whole tradition was about to be replaced by home video and then by something coarser. It is a classic legend the way certain midnight movies are legends. Not because every line is well written (many are not) and not because every fight is well staged (some are charmingly clumsy) but because the whole thing coheres as a mood. Heat. Silk and leather and almost nothing. A woman who does not know how to make love asking her friend how, then learning in public. A mercenary who keeps saying he does not say those kinds of things and then saying them. A city of women that looks like a fever and collapses like one.

The deeper current is about what happens when a sheltered person decides the sheltered life is no longer large enough. Gwendoline’s father went looking for a rare thing and disappeared into the looking. She goes looking for him and finds that the rare thing was never only the insect. It was the willingness to be seen, to be at risk, to finish a story that someone else started and then write your name on it anyway. The film does not lecture. It just keeps putting bodies in peril and in light until the viewer understands that the perils were the point and the land of the Yik Yak was always a state of mind as much as a place on a map.

Behind the scenes came last because the dream should arrive before the scaffolding. Jaeckin put a serious amount of his own money into the picture. The shoot ran eighteen weeks. Philippines for the ports and jungle, Morocco for the desert (they used an airplane engine to fake a sandstorm), Les Baux de Provence and the Billancourt studios for the rest. The entire underground city of Pikaho was essentially one stage whose walls were dressed, rolled, and redressed so that a handful of rooms could pretend to be a civilization. A boa constrictor intended for a scene died from lack of oxygen; they used the body anyway and moved it with cables. The American distributors cut the film down, trimming dialogue and some of the Willard and Gwendoline material so the picture would sprint faster toward the warrior women. Jaeckin never directed another theatrical feature. Kitaen went on to Bachelor Party the same year and then to the videos that made her face unavoidable. Willie, the original artist, had already been dead for years; his heroine survived him in this strange, sweaty, gorgeous translation. The movie remains what it always was: an object that knows why you are watching and is not ashamed to give you that reason while also smuggling in a quest, a friendship, a collapse of a city, and a butterfly that finally gets caught because three people refused to turn around.

text:
This post was my most viral content of the past week—as you can verify with a simple web search—and Margaret Elaine Foster’s story is now known to everyone, despite X’s preemptive censorship:

“This was filmed last Wednesday morning at Animal Shelter in Lexington, Kentucky.
The woman is Margaret Elaine Foster. She's 76 years old.
The dog is a small golden mixed-breed named Teddy.
Eight years old. Margaret has had him since he was ten weeks old.
Margaret's health has been declining for several months. Her daughter and son-in-law live in Lexington and have been helping with her care, but the level of support Margaret now needs has made living alone difficult. Last month, her doctor recommended a transition to an assisted living facility.
Margaret toured three facilities in Lexington. The one that felt right - Sycamore Gardens - is clean, kind, and close to her daughter. It does not allow pets.
Margaret spent two weeks trying to find an alternative. Called everyone she could think of. Her daughter asked neighbors. Her son-in-law asked coworkers. Nobody was in a position to take Teddy long-term and give him the care he needed.
Margaret drove to shelter on a Wednesday morning. Her daughter offered to come. Margaret said she needed to do it herself.
She walked in carrying Teddy's bed, his food bowl, and a ziplock bag of his favorite treats with a handwritten note attached listing everything about him. What he likes. What scares him. That he needs to sleep with a blanket even in summer. That he likes to sit near a window in the afternoon.
Shelter coordinator Janet sat with Margaret at the front desk to complete the paperwork. Teddy stayed pressed against Margaret's legs the entire time. Both front paws wrapped around her ankle. Every time Margaret shifted in her chair, Teddy shifted with her. Not whining. Not pulling. Just staying as close as he could possibly get.
Margaret signed each page slowly. Her hand was shaking. Tears dropped onto the desk.
At one point she reached down and stroked Teddy's head without looking at him. Teddy pressed further into her legs.
Janet told us: "I've been doing intake for six years. l've sat with a lot of people at that desk. Margaret was trying so hard to be composed. She'd clearly rehearsed staying calm. But when Teddy wrapped around her ankle and wouldn't move, she just couldn't hold it anymore. And honestly, neither could I."
Margaret stood up when the paperwork was complete. She knelt down on the shelter floor with some difficulty and held Teddy for a long time. She whispered something to him that Janet couldn't hear.
Then Margaret stood up, handed the leash to Janet, and walked to the door.
She paused at the door for a moment. Didn't turn around.
Then she left.
Janet stood in the lobby holding Teddy's leash.
Teddy watched the door.
Margaret's daughter called Shelter that same evening to check that Teddy had settled in. She told Janet: "Mom hasn't stopped crying since she got home. She keeps saying she's sorry. Like she has something to be sorry for."
Janet said: "Please tell your mother that Teddy is safe and warm and he finished his dinner. And tell her that leaving him here when it was the only option left
- that's one of the most loving things a person can do for a dog they love. That's not abandonment.
That's sacrifice."
*Loving something deeply sometimes means making the decision that breaks your heart so it doesn't break theirs.* “

text:
Harvesting Grace, A Forty-Day Devotional by C.S. McDonald is a warm, reflective Christian devotional that invites readers to slow down and reconnect with God’s grace, especially during the beauty of autumn.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. Each entry includes a daily Bible verse, a peaceful and thought-provoking observation, and soft reflections designed to refresh faith and cultivate joy. McDonald encourages readers to pause amid life’s busyness, sit quietly or take a walk, and intentionally harvest God’s steadfast love and boundless grace. It serves as a humble, encouraging guide that can be used in autumn or anytime throughout the year. Readers looking for a calming, faith-centered companion will find it uplifting and accessible.

C.S. McDonald taught dance and choreographed shows for twenty-six years before turning to writing. She lives with her husband Bill and their dogs on a Thoroughbred farm near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. She is the author of the popular clean Fiona Quinn Mysteries (cozy mysteries featuring a kindergarten teacher turned sleuth) and the Owl’s Nest Mysteries, as well as children’s books inspired by farm life. In recent years she has added devotionals, including *Harvesting Grace*, as part of her spiritual writing. She is a wife, mom, grandma, dog lover, and self-described helpless chocoholic.

text:
Israel and Ireland’s Inextricable History

The Irish have forgotten how deeply Jewish people helped shape their state.    ByMasada Siegel

On  a flight from Queenstown, New Zealand, to Sydney in July, I sat next to  Niall, an Irishman who had lived in Australia for 15 years and was  considering moving home. I’ve never met an Irish person I didn’t connect  with, and Niall was no exception. Somewhere over the Tasman Sea, our  conversation turned to Ireland’s relationship with the Jewish people.

Niall  was shocked when I blurted out: “I love Ireland, but I doubt I will  ever visit the Emerald Isle again. Your government hates people like  me.”

Growing  up, my Israeli mother’s best friend, Anita Leeman, was Irish, and from  age 5, I considered her my best friend, too. Our families were so  connected that her family connected with ours in Israel to meet my grandparents. She would invite us for Christmas in Valley  Stream, N.Y., where I can still remember the scent of the tree and the  dancing flames that lit up the fireplace. Years later, in 2010, the  Irish government invited me to visit as a travel writer. I was excited,  knowing I would receive a warm welcome.

Dublin  has since drifted away from Israel, in both antagonistic speeches and  the law. Ireland recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. In July  2026, the Dáil, Irish parliament’s lower house, passed the Occupied  Territories Bill to ban trade tied to Israeli settlements, making  Ireland the first European Union nation to enact a commercial blockade  on Israeli goods. The Jewish state no longer even has an embassy in  Dublin.

Ireland  is moving in the wrong direction, and in doing so it seems to have  forgotten how deeply Jewish people helped shape the modern Irish state.

Robert  Briscoe, an Orthodox Jew, procured arms for Irish Republican Army  leader Michael Collins during the War of Independence. Briscoe served in  the Dáil for 38 years. In 1956 he became Dublin’s Lord Mayor.

Rabbi  Isaac Herzog, the first chief rabbi of Ireland and the first Ashkenazi  chief rabbi of Israel, learned fluent Irish. He supported independence  so strongly that people called him the “Sinn Féin rabbi.” His son Chaim  grew up in Dublin, boxed as the country’s youth bantamweight champion,  then became Israel’s sixth president. Chaim’s son Isaac is Israel’s  current president. I wonder if the Dublin city councillors trying to  strip Chaim’s name off a local park know their own history.

Ireland  has a history of antisemitism, too. A boycott started in Limerick in  1904 drove out most of the Jewish families there. In the 1930s, Dublin  largely turned away Jewish refugees fleeing the Nazis. Days after  Hitler’s suicide, in May 1945, Ireland’s head of government, Éamon de  Valera, visited the German envoy in Dublin, Eduard Hempel, to offer his  condolences.

Ireland has a history of antisemitism, too. A boycott started in  Limerick in 1904 drove out most of the Jewish families there. In the  1930s, Dublin largely turned away Jewish refugees fleeing the Nazis.  Days after Hitler’s suicide, in May 1945, Ireland’s head of government,  Éamon de Valera, visited the German envoy in Dublin, Eduard Hempel, to  offer his condolences.

This  legacy continues in the form of the baseless hatred flowing toward  Ireland’s 2,200 Jewish residents. The Jewish Representative Council  recorded 143 antisemitic incidents from July 2025 to January 2026,  ranging from “Jew Rat” graffiti to direct harassment of students on  university campuses and Holocaust denial.

I  told Niall I’d faced hostility for speaking out against antisemitism  and anti-Zionism. He listened, then said that he’d seen many antisemitic  conspiracy theories spreading on Irish social media.

“If  Jewish people controlled the world,” I said, “why would we allow  everyone to hate us? It makes no sense. And I clearly didn’t get the  memo, because my hometown of Phoenix wouldn’t be 115 degrees every July  if I had any say in the matter.”

He  burst out laughing. A difficult conversation didn’t end a connection;  it forged a friendship. If only Ireland’s leaders would reflect on their  history and remember who helped build their nation in the first place.

text:
Is it better to always fight to the end or survive another day and be present for any at all waiting possibility?

I always think of this.

I really still have never determined whether or not I would have sided with Michael Collins or De Valera and the anti-Anglo-Irish Treaty IRA.

I want to share a comparable moral dilemma that is extremely relatable to Irish historians and political activists in dissident republican spheres.

The Melian Dialogue.

Athenian historian Thucydides recorded the events of the Peloponnesian war between Athens and Sparts.

He was notable, though not so popular, for his impartiality in recording current events in politics. 

He achieved knowledge of the stances of many relevant figures involved by
attending their speeches or interviewing others who had.

The level of overall long-term significance of the war is debated and commentary is made on the political parties involved and their agenda in either overplaying or downplaying it respectively. 

The impartiality is difficult to achieve but vital, even if it loses favor with all sides by being so.

Thucydides alongside Herodotus embarked on their most ambitious journalistic project yet when sixteen years into the war, Athens raided and pillaged the islands of Argos and then even neutral Melos. 

Negotiations between delegates  take place of which the transcripts are recorded by Thucydides with contribution from Herodutus. 

A perspective and rationale is given from both sides with equal attention and no bias demanded.

The Athenians offer justification for imperial expansion. 

The Melians, for resistance and independence. 

These negotiations are not held in good faith, neither from the Athenians as their minds of conquest were
already made up nor from the Melians who only invited elites to attend in a private group, not allowing the
envoys to meet a more public audience.

A clear contrast of mentality is displayed.

Reason vs emotion. 

Hope vs reality. 

The Athenian’s have a much more practical and “Realpolitik” approach, encouraging the enemy to swallow their pride for the sake of their people’s security. 

The Melians view honor and integrity as paramountand the defiance is key to showing loyalty to their country and their people. 

Fighting for that is
something that is worth doing. 

Athens is much more concerned with the short and medium term, the immediate survival of Melos. 

The Melians are considering the long-lasting implications of giving up their sovereignty and becoming part of the Athenian state. 

There is also a notion among
the Athenians that the disparity of strength between the two compels them incorporate Melos for the sake of providing them with prosperity and to an extent, security from Sparta.

Athens and Melos soon enter a state of war. 

By the next wintert, an invasion had been attempted by the Lacedaemonians on Argive territory and was unsuccessful. 

Athens defeats the Melians in a battle that follows a siege near Athenian lines and a mass Melian surrender is achieved.

Much of Melos is later sacked and destroyed.

Thucydides very much laments this, views it as a great avoidable tragedy, a shame that the Melians were so prideful and that such
destruction and loss of life had to occur because of that.

He viewed retreating and surrender when necessary to be less shameful than dying for the sake of denial of any type of life that is not truly living.

What is the opinion of any reader?

I saw one of those too, but she gave no basis for her claim. If I may, I’ll tell you what I think. 

When I started watching the trial, I expected to see someone depicted who reminded me of my mother: a psychopath. But I didn’t. 

My mother had no lifelong friends. She could be incredibly charming and made new friends very easily. Some stuck with her for a time but all moved on within a period of time. It was usually not pleasant when they did. My father said that if she was left alone in a room with herself for long enough, she’d start arguing with the nails on her toes. 

She even alienated her own family members, except her poor mother who despised her, but depended on her. If she could have, my grandmother would have gladly testified AGAINST my mother. She was as terrified of her as I was. 

Lindsay Clancy had lifelong friends and people who genuinely care about her, even now — including her former mother-in-law, who would have EVERY reason to despise her. 

Dora was 5. Everyone described Lindsay as an incredible mother. 

By the time I was 5 (although times were different and no one helped me), all the mothers in my neighbourhood knew that I was terrified of my mother. So much so, that if I played with other kids at their houses, they washed and dried the white dresses my mother dressed me in before I went home because they could feel my tension. I’d be severely punished if I went home with a speck of dirt on my white dress. Wise mothers offered me a change of clothes so I could get dirty. 

The only person who ever knew my mother and thought she was a wonderful mother was herself. She bragged about it nonstop. 

As an adult, after I came to America, we had an Irish client who went back to Ireland for a visit and unbeknownst to me, decided to look up my mother. She came from a town not far from my mother. Back then, dropping in on a stranger in Ireland was not uncommon. 

My mother spent the whole visit talking about how upset she was that I didn’t speak to her. And she showed this woman all the trophies I won and my report cards to prove what an amazing mother she had always been. But her only proof of her amazing motherhood were my accomplishments. 

When I spoke to the woman afterwards, she gave me a guilt trip for not speaking to my mother. Trying not to involve the woman in my disgusting family, I simply said it was complicated. The woman made some inquiries in my home town in Ireland and was able to discern that no one liked my mother and she was a problem to many people. Not one person ever praised her mothering skills. They simply wondered why I’d disappeared and talked about what a sweet well behaved child I’d been. 

My mother never showed any genuine emotion. Those who met her often remarked on how she could switch from anger or upset to calm and composed in a literal heartbeat. 

I watched Lindsay Clancy genuinely sob in court. I saw her bloodshot eyes. The only time my mother had bloodshot eyes was when she was drunk. My father always called her “crocodile tears.”  

I read Lindsay Clancy’s journal entries which some claim seem self-obsessed. But the theme was clear: she believed she was failing her children.  My mother never once thought she was failing her children. She wouldn’t have cared if she did. 

I listened to testimony from all of Lindsay Clancy’s treating mental health providers. Not one of them suggested a personality disorder. I listened to the testimony of 5 mental health experts — 3 of whom were experts from the prosecution. Not one of them suggested a personality disorder. In fact, they described her as honest and genuine. Those 3 had an actual incentive to find a personality disorder. 

The only mental health provider who I know of who ever saw my mother was one who was evaluating me when I was 13 and my mother had me committed to a psychiatric hospital after she tried to kill me. He was alarmed when he met her and feared for my safety. 

So my conclusion is Lindsay Clancy is not like Mum.

text:
Within days of listing, the trust commanded roughly 445,000 ZEC—representing over $460 million in market value.

The implications reach far beyond pricing efficiency. Every coin absorbed into ZCSH is a coin anchored within the institutional fence. It ceases to be purely a private token floating across sovereign-less networks; it becomes the balance-sheet foundation of an American security.

Even ZCSH’s 2.5% management fee takes on a different function here.

 While steep by passive equity standards, Grayscale’s commitment to direct those fee revenues toward Zcash ecosystem development and product marketing turns structural friction into institutional reinforcement. For a privacy network whose primary scarcity has never been cryptographic math, but rather regulated room to breathe, that mechanism has real utility.

ZCSH secured the one asset Zcash historically lacked: institutional entanglement. Entanglement is an effective political shield because unwinding it guarantees collateral damage.

The Russian ADR Precedent

The immediate objection is obvious: exchange listings do not guarantee survival when geopolitics turns hostile.
Russian American Depositary Receipts made that painfully clear.

Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, U.S. exchanges suspended trading in Russia-linked securities within days. Listings vanished, depositary programs froze, and clearing corridors broke down. The ticker offered no shelter from sanctions.

Yet something critical survived the wreckage: the underlying legal claims did not simply vanish.

An ADR represents a beneficial ownership stake in an underlying asset. When domestic trading stopped, the underlying property claim remained legally active. OFAC even maintained explicit conversion guidelines allowing unsanctioned foreign investors to redeem ADRs into underlying ordinary shares.

The crisis wasn’t that the property disappeared; it was that the bridge connecting ownership to market liquidity had collapsed. Russia blocked foreign withdrawals, Western sanctions choked settlement pipelines, and depositary receipts were stranded.

The Russian precedent defines the limits of the thesis: an exchange listing can vanish overnight, even while the legal property interest lingers.

ZCSH Has No Moscow

Yet the mechanical differences between a Russian ADR and ZCSH are decisive.

An ADR is an inherently fragile cross-border construct. On one side sits an American depositary bank; on the other sits a foreign enterprise, an overseas registrar, foreign securities depositories, and a hostile foreign state. The bridge survives only as long as both sovereign jurisdictions tolerate it.

Moscow could sever its end—and did.

ZCSH possesses a completely different topology:
 * The vehicle is a Delaware statutory trust.
 * The underlying asset is ZEC secured via Coinbase Custody.
 * The administrator is an American trust bank.
 * The exchange is NYSE Arca.
 * The beneficial owners are predominantly American citizens.

There is no Gazprom board in Moscow to terminate the custodian program. There is no foreign ministry that can nationalize the entity underlying the receipt. There is no overseas registrar required to prove the shares exist.
The controversial asset is already sitting on American soil.

That does not disable state power. It changes where that power must fall, and who absorbs the shock.

If a decentralized exchange drops ZEC, non-custodial users take custody and route around it. But if federal policy intentionally impairs the ZEC backing ZCSH, the state must address an outstanding domestic security:

 * What happens to the Delaware trust?
 * Can the institutional custodian legally retain the coins?
 * Can the trust liquidate the collateral—and to whom?
 * If market access is eliminated, who absorbs the hundreds of millions in stranded capital?
The moment regulatory action inflicts that loss, investors don’t need an intricate legal brief to appeal to Congress:
>

Through Ebony, I was introduced to towering figures such as Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall. Their courage, moral clarity and commitment to justice shaped how I thought leadership and service.
King is rightly remembered for his leadership in the civil rights movement but far less attention is paid to his views on health and justice. He once observed, "Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health is the most shocking and inhuman."

text:
A genetically modified pig kidney functioned inside a human for a record 271 days before the patient successfully received a human kidney transplant, marking a major milestone in transplant medicine.

Tim Andrews, a 66 year old man with end stage kidney disease, received the pig kidney at Massachusetts General Hospital in January 2025. The organ kept him alive and free from dialysis for 271 days, the longest time a pig kidney has successfully functioned in a living human.

The donor pig had been genetically modified with multiple DNA edits to reduce immune rejection and improve compatibility with the human body. Although the pig kidney eventually began to fail and was removed, Andrews later underwent a successful human kidney transplant, becoming the first person to transition from a pig organ to a human donor kidney.

Researchers say this breakthrough brings xenotransplantation, the use of animal organs for human transplants, one step closer to becoming a practical solution for the global shortage of donor organs. While more research is needed, the results offer hope to thousands of patients waiting for life saving transplants.

Would you be willing to accept a genetically modified pig organ if it could save your life? Let me know in the comments section.

text:
You’re mixing a trial tactic with a confession. Her plea stayed not guilty. Facts and Massachusetts law below:

-The DA charged first-degree murder and stayed there. 
-A grand jury later indicted three first-degree murders. That proceeding is secret and one-sided: only the prosecution presents evidence. 
-After the grand jury indicted her, she pleaded not guilty. Massachusetts has no “I plead NGRI” box. You plead not guilty, then raise lack of criminal responsibility at trial.
-She stayed not guilty at trial and raised lack of criminal responsibility. That puts the burden on the Commonwealth: prove the crime and prove she was responsible.
-With the DA refusing to move off murder 1, LCR (lack of criminal responsibility) was the only workable route left to beat that charge.
-Reddington motioned to bifurcate: acts first, responsibility second.
-The judge denied the motion.
-Then Reddington offered a stipulation: we will not fight that her alleged actions caused the deaths if the case can focus on responsibility.
-That is not a guilty plea to murder. It is conceding alleged causation, not first-degree guilt.
-He asked for a Bowden instruction (bad police work can create reasonable doubt). Prosecutors objected. There is no clear public report that the judge gave the formal Bowden charge.
-Reddington could still argue the investigation was deficient, and he did so in the defense closing.
-Under the law, she never pleaded guilty and never formally admitted that she committed the act of murder. 

In the eyes of the law, Lindsay did not confess to the murders. The law does not treat “what she reported remembering” and “I am guilty of murder” as the same thing. They are treated differently because a crime is not just a physical event. Murder requires proof that she did the act and that the law can blame her for it. Once LCR was raised, that burden stayed on the Commonwealth.
Sources: G.L. c. 265, § 1: https://t.co/NtxAjOpPlu Mass. R. Crim. P. 5: https://t.co/jzWai7u2X1 How a Mass. grand jury works: https://t.co/Qv7FTBSMXv Mass. R. Crim. P. 12: https://t.co/xJhnL3szy7 Homicide LCR instructions / criminal responsibility / LCR burden: https://t.co/W5GLEYHeUg District Court LCR instruction 9.200: https://t.co/bTyD081O4V Bowden / Mass. text:
ALNYLAM $ALNY CUT ITS OWN FORECAST WITH 160,000 PATIENTS STILL UNTREATED:

The Hypergrowth Len5 is watching Alnylam Pharmaceuticals ALNY at $266.11, +$1.61 / +0.61% on Friday. The Cambridge, Massachusetts company makes RNA interference medicines - drugs that switch off a single gene so the body stops producing one harmful protein. Its biggest, AMVUTTRA, treats a disease in which a misfolded protein stiffens the heart.

The verdict: Alnylam grew 74% and made real money, then lost more than a quarter of its value in one session for saying its year would be smaller. That cut was not weak demand. It was a waiting room emptying - and the trial evidence quietly agrees.

The quarter, reported before the open on July 30 for the three months ended June 30:

- Net product revenue $1.17B vs $672M, +74%
- AMVUTTRA $1.01B vs $492M, +106% - the drug's first billion-dollar quarter
- Profit $164.5M, or $1.21 a share, against a $72.2M loss a year earlier
- Cash and securities $3.3B against $1.01B of convertible borrowings

Then the line that did the damage: 2026 net product revenue guided to $4.7B-$5.1B, cut from $4.9B-$5.3B. July 29's $286.62 became $205.48 the next day, -$81.14 / -28.3%, on 9.8M shares against about 1.3M the session before - the lowest close of the past twelve months.

Here is what that $200M came off. Patients arrive two ways. First-line means AMVUTTRA is the first treatment they get. Second-line means they were already on an older drug, a stabilizer, and add this one on top. When the heart approval landed in 2025, years of waiting second-line patients all showed up at once. That queue is now spent, and management called the growth it produced pent-up demand that has since normalized. What is left is arguably the better half: roughly 80% of new treatment starts are now first-line, and the company estimates 200,000 people have this disease with about 160,000 on nothing at all.

Now the part that ties the forecast to the science. On July 9, Ionis Pharmaceuticals at $58.09, -$0.04 / -0.07% on Friday, said its rival drug eplontersen missed the main goal of a 1,432-patient heart trial, with full results presented in Munich at the European Society of Cardiology congress, August 28-31. One finding matters most: among patients already on a stabilizer, it added nothing measurable.

Alnylam's own trial says something uncomfortably close. In HELIOS-B, AMVUTTRA cut the risk of death and heart events 28% overall and 33% among the 395 patients not on a stabilizer - but in the roughly 40% who were on one, the result pointed the same way without clearing the statistical bar. Two drugs, two different technologies, one thin spot: adding either on top of a stabilizer. That is precisely the second-line business whose growth just stopped. Alnylam says the cut is timing; the trials offer a second reading of the same $200M, and nobody can yet separate them.

Since July 30 the shares have recovered 29.5%, including +$21.29 / +8.65% on September 2 as the Munich data was digested. At about 47 times the roughly $5.60 a share earned across the last four reported quarters, none of this is cheap.

One company, six ways of looking:

- HYPERGROWTH - STRONG, and why it sits here. Wants a business still early as well as still fast. Fast is settled at +74%. Early belongs to the market rather than the maker - the company dates to 2002, but the heart use opened only in 2025 and four fifths of it is untouched. CHANGE IT: first-line starts flattening.

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - PARTIAL. Wants a good business priced under what it looks worth after something visible went wrong. Visible is textbook: -28.3% in one session, and Friday sits $225.11 / 45.8% under the $491.22 of October 20 last year. Priced under is missing at 47 times profit. CHANGE IT: earnings growing into that number faster than the price climbs back to it.

- QUALITY-VALUE - NOT A FIT, and the closest miss. Wants a hard-to-copy business at a fair price. Hard to copy is real - nobody else sells RNA interference medicine at this scale. Durable is not: one profitable year and a profitable half follow two decades of losses. CHANGE IT: profit holding through a setback, not only a launch.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Wants expansion nobody is overpaying for. Expanding is not in dispute; cheap growth needs an earnings record to be cheap against, and this one is two years old. CHANGE IT: the multiple falling while the company's own 25%-a-year target for this franchise holds.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Wants a price near its twelve-month best with the short and long stretches agreeing. They contradict: +21.5% from the $219.00 of August 4, against -12.4% from the $303.64 of June 4 and -18.7% from the $327.30 of March 4. CHANGE IT: a close above $286.62, where this sat the evening before the cut.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT, furthest from it. Wants cash genuinely reaching owners and funded by the business. Nothing reaches owners - no dividend, no buyback - against $2.7B-$2.8B of research and selling costs guided this year. CHANGE IT: nothing realistic while a 1,200-patient trial runs toward a decision around 2030.

Ionis is the other side of the same week: from August 27, the session before Munich opened, it has fallen 7.0% while Alnylam rose 12.5%. It fits none of the six Len5es - a missed Phase 3 is a live event, not a discount.

What settles Alnylam is the first-line share of new starts against that 80%, with the total count of new starts beside it, so nobody mistakes a better mix for a bigger market. The risk is that fact inverted: if the second-line thinness is scientific rather than seasonal, 160,000 untreated people are a market only on paper. Alnylam has not dated the third quarter; last year's landed October 30, and Huntington's disease results are set for October 23.

A queue can only be spent once. Alnylam spent its in about eighteen months, marked down what was left, and got repriced as a broken growth story for doing that arithmetic out loud.

Main framing hit: The article asserts, as fact, that “Republicans in Congress have largely moved in lockstep with President Donald Trump,” then presents Deaton as the exception. •  Deaton’s own shot at Republicans (“they complained about Obamacare but never offered a real solution”) is quoted without pushback—useful if the goal is “GOP has no answers.”
What’s not there: no similar unattributed slam on Markey as lockstep with the left, no equivalent “slogans vs. solutions” framing of Democrats as the default. @ArthurMacwaters 
Food is obviously the most basic need of a human being.
We work to put food on the table.

Our first thought in the morning is a tea, coffee, green tea, warm lemon juice, fruit juice...

Our next big concern is breakfast... Cereals, milk, toast, eggs, beans, whatever the person likes...

Three hours later, the next question follows... Lunch, high tea (evening coffee, snacks), dinner...

Yes, I know you must have got bored reading this...

But, poverty affects a person's mental health severely because when the person wakes up, the first thought is not what beverage to have, but is there any coffee in the coffee jar...

Is there any milk, is there any sugar, is there any leftover food in the fridge, is there some stale bread to eat???

These questions of provisions hit the person on an empty stomach...

Now, just imagine the person has nothing much for breakfast either?!?

Poverty doesn't cause crimes...
Not being able to afford food is the problem...

If a person has a wife, he has to share the food with her...
Even if a man can afford a loaf of bread and butter, it has to be shared with his wife...

If the wife is pregnant, she needs to eat properly for the baby.

If the food is not affordable, how much can a family share... How much can they buy...?!

A couple with two kids have to buy two loaves of bread. Can they afford it, if the man is the sole bread winner? 

It is not that people are criminals, but they have a family to feed. Sleeping on an empty stomach is going to create a disgruntled person. A person cannot be taught philosophy on an empty stomach when his wife and children are starving.

In India, most temples have free food. The food is distributed daily... Some kitchens are run 24 hours. 

You can see these documentaries...
The Mega Kitchens of India. 
https://t.co/jMc3keqqSB

All over India, there are Gurudwaras that offer food called langar seva.

People donate for food.

If a country like India did not have these mega kitchens, the poverty levels would have been appalling. 

There are daily labourers who eat food at these places. They cannot afford a tiffin or go home!

My point being... No one can sleep on a growling empty stomach...

These are the figures for our Mega Kitchens... Of India...

The Akshaya Patra Foundation: Runs 78 locations and centralized kitchens across 16 states and 3 union territories to serve mid-day meals to school children. 

The Golden Temple (Amritsar, Punjab): Operates one of the world's largest community kitchens (langar), serving 50,000 to 100,000 free meals daily. 

Tirumala Venkateswara Temple (Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh): Feeds over 150,000 pilgrims every day through its massive Annaprasadam complex.

Jagannath Temple (Puri, Odisha): Features a historic mega kitchen with over 270 earthen ovens feeding more than 100,000 devotees daily. 

Shirdi Sai Baba Prasadalaya (Shirdi, Maharashtra): Serves free meals to over 50,000 devotees daily. 

Just calculate these massive numbers...

Besides these there are many other medium and small organizations arranging subsidized and free food for all...

So, the testable hypothesis has been already tested in India.

text:
Pedri just represents class.

I used to get genuinely angry whenever Barcelona fans called him the best midfielder in the world. But the more I actually watched Pedri, the more I realised the class was always there.

I've looked at the midfielders football currently has to offer, and the only midfielder I can clearly say is better than Pedri right now is Rodri.

After Rodri, you're talking about the likes of Pedri, Vitinha, Bellingham, Bruno Fernandes, João Neves and Declan Rice.

And amongst those midfielders, you can genuinely make a case for Pedri being better than every single one of them.

My point is simple: Pedri is world-class and generational.

People constantly ask why Barcelona dominate La Liga with so much ease and then use the quality of the opposition as an excuse.

Yes, the league has its financial limitations, but at some point you have to give Barcelona credit.

They're simply that good at what they do.

And Pedri is arguably the main catalyst behind what makes Barcelona so good. The way he controls the tempo, progresses the ball, finds spaces and keeps everything flowing is beautiful to watch.

Since I chose to become a football analyst, I've decided to look at the game from a different angle. I want to appreciate what I see on the pitch without letting club rivalries and bias cloud my judgement.

With that said...

Cristiano Ronaldo is still the greatest of all time.

But jokes aside, Pedri is just class.

text:
@Arsenal 2-1 @ChelseaFC: How Arteta's Champions Weathered an Early Storm

The Emirates Stadium had barely settled into its Sunday rhythm when the afternoon turned on its head. Seventy seconds. That was all Chelsea needed to silence a ground that had arrived expecting a coronation, not a contest. Morgan Rogers, released by a clever ball from Jorrel Hato, finished with the composure of a man who had rehearsed the moment a hundred times. For a few minutes, Xabi Alonso's Chelsea looked like the team writing the script for this fixture, not the visitors trying to spoil someone else's party.

Arsenal, winners of each of the last three meetings between these two sides, needed an answer. They found two and the manner in which they found them told you almost everything about why Mikel Arteta's side remain champions.

A shock to the system

Chelsea's opener was not a fluke. It was a statement of intent from Alonso, whose reshaped side pressed with real conviction from the opening whistle. Hato's pass split a defence still finding its bearings, and Rogers did the rest with a first time finish that will have delighted a Chelsea bench desperate to prove this was no longer the same soft touch of recent seasons.

What followed, though, was a lesson in how champions absorb a blow without losing their shape. Arteta did not send his players chasing the game in a panic. Arsenal simply kept doing what they do, patient in possession, probing for the gaps that a high press inevitably leaves behind it.

Havertz finds the seam

The equaliser, when it came in the twenty fifth minute, had Declan Rice's fingerprints all over it. Rice carried the ball forward through the space Chelsea's midfield had vacated in their eagerness to win it back high and delivered a ball into the box that Kai Havertz met with the sort of conviction only a player who knows this fixture intimately could summon.

There is a story within the story here. Havertz spent three years at Stamford Bridge before crossing London to join Arteta's project and there was something fitting about him being the man to drag his new side level against his old one.

Odegaard turns the tide

Five minutes into the second half, the captain finished off a flowing move that swept through Chelsea's lines with rehearsed precision. Odegaard found the pocket of space nobody else notices and arrived there half a second before the defender realised it existed. Arsenal did not need to force anything. They simply waited for Chelsea's structure to bend and then they broke it.

Holding firm

The final half hour was where this match earned its billing as a genuine title fight preview. Chelsea pushed men forward and came desperately close to a leveller when a rapid counter released Neto down the right, his curled effort beating Raya only to cannon back off the post. Arsenal defended with the calm organisation that has become their trademark, the back line snuffing out crosses and second balls with the sort of understanding that comes from repetition and trust. Raya was alert when called upon.

The verdict

Nine points from three matches keeps Arteta's side perfect and sends an early message to the rest of the division. For Alonso, there will be encouragement in how his team started the game, even in defeat. But in a fixture defined for years now by Arsenal's composure under pressure, Sunday offered yet another example of why that reputation remains intact.
