text:
📌#Lisbon, Portugal 🇵🇹

In 2026, I travelled across Europe to better understand its political and social transformation. Starting in Romania on Europe’s eastern edge in the beginning of 2026, now I completed my trip with Portugal in early September 2026, while attending the EISA Annual Conference in Lisbon.

A few observations:

1️⃣Portugal is one of Europe’s less visible faces. It is neither under Spain’s level of tourism pressure nor at the centre of the continent’s security tensions. Yet its relative quietness reveals a different European challenge: demographic transformation. 

2️⃣Portugal has around 11.4 million people, with a median age of about 45.8. Around 23% are 65 or older, while fertility remains at just 1.4–1.5 children per woman. This combination will increasingly test the country’s labour market, pensions, healthcare and social security system.

3️⃣Meanwhile, foreign nationals account for roughly 14% of the population. This changes the meaning of migration. For an ageing society with persistently low fertility, immigration is no longer simply about diversity and integration. It is increasingly about sustaining the workforce and economy. Demography is becoming politics.

4️⃣Portugal is also, in some ways, “Ronaldoland. Cristiano Ronaldo’s contribution to the global visibility of a country of 11.4 million is remarkable. He is more than a footballer: he is arguably Portugal’s strongest global cultural brand and an extraordinary example of individual achievement becoming national soft power.

5️⃣Lisbon itself feels calm, outward-looking and international. Cafés, tourism and services shape everyday life, while the pace feels slower than in many European capitals. This relative calm is perhaps what makes Portugal interesting: major structural change is taking place without dominating everyday political conversation.

6️⃣My main takeaway from Portugal: ageing, low fertility, and migration. These forces will reshape not only Portugal, but much of Europe—its labour markets, welfare systems, identity debates and eventually its politics. Portugal may be on Europe’s western edge, but its demographic story sits at the centre of Europe’s future.

7️⃣The #EISA Conference was intellectually stimulating, with lively debates and discussions, yet offered little perspective on the future. Many scholars seemed absorbed in current issues while losing sight of the bigger picture. The European IR community remains vibrant, but still has a long way to go in providing direction to the discipline.

If you have never been to Portugal, it is perfect time to visit. 😎

Protect Liberty PAC Announces Range USA Has Increased Its 2026 Election Commitment to $75,000

This donation exceeds its 2024 support and demonstrates a profound statement of trust in its mission

WASHINGTON, D.C. – The NSSF's Protect Liberty Political Action Committee (Protect Liberty PAC) announced today with deep gratitude that Range USA has increased its total commitment for the 2026 election cycle to $75,000, one of the most significant statements of industry support since the committee's founding.

Range USA, the largest range operator in the nation, has stood with Protect Liberty PAC from the beginning. In 2024, during the PAC's founding election cycle, the company contributed $30,000 following up with a similar contribution in 2025. This cycle's additional $50,000 commitment exceeds the $25,000 contribution announced in January and reflects a trust built over two election cycles of partnership.

"Range USA stood with us at the founding, and now they have increased their support with a significant increase over their 2024 and 2025 donations," said Lawrence G. Keane, Treasurer of Protect Liberty PAC. "That sustained and growing support is the strongest endorsement an organization like ours can receive. It represents a deep trust in our mission to support candidates who will stand up for the constitutional freedoms of firearm owners, and we are profoundly grateful to the entire Range USA team and its Founder, Tom Willingham."

"In 2024 and 2025 we supported Protect Liberty PAC because we believed in what it set out to do. And they did with U.S. Senate victories in Ohio, Pennsylvania and Montana. I believe in their execution abilities and want to show that," said Tom Willingham, Founder and President of Range USA. "We have welcomed over 3.5 million customers annually, and every one of them deserves to have their freedoms defended. Increasing our commitment to $75,000 this cycle was an easy decision, it's an honor to stand behind not only our customers, but all gun owners."

Range USA's support arrives on the heels of a landmark year for the company. In April 2026, all 50 Range USA locations across 14 states earned NSSF's Five-Star Range rating, the industry's highest recognition for facility appearance, management, amenities and shooting-sports development, making the company's voice in support of the industry's civic engagement even more consequential.

About Range USA: Range USA is the nation's largest indoor shooting range and firearms retailer, with 51 locations nationwide. Their mission is building confidence in communities across America while guiding customers throughout their firearm journey. Each store offers a safe, modern range experience alongside one of the largest selections of firearms, ammunition, and shooting accessories available anywhere. Whether you're new to shooting or a seasoned enthusiast, Range USA is built around safety, education, and confidence—providing over 1,100 indoor shooting lanes, expert instruction from certified professionals, and everything you need in one convenient place, both in-store and online at https://t.co/rFTwskM3Cv.

About Protect Liberty PAC: Protect Liberty PAC is a federally registered "super PAC" founded in 2023 by NSSF. Protect Liberty PAC is an independent-expenditure only political committee and can accept unlimited personal and corporate contributions from companies in or outside of the industry, so long as they do not have federal contracts. Protect Liberty PAC will expressly advocate for the election or defeat of specific candidates and that advocacy will be completely independent of any candidate or political party.

Contributions to Protect Liberty PAC are not deductible as charitable contributions for federal income tax purposes. Federal law requires Protect Liberty PAC to use its best efforts to collect and report the name, mailing address, occupation and the name of employer of individuals whose contributions exceed $200 in a calendar year. Protect Liberty PAC can accept unlimited personal and corporate contributions. However, contributions from foreign nationals, federal contractors, national banks, and federally chartered corporations are prohibited.

For more information or to contribute to Protect Liberty PAC, visit https://t.co/jOnxm4faat.

Ohio Democrat gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton took the stage this week facing a question no press release can answer: how does a campaign that's raised a fraction of its rival's war chest actually compete? Her answer wasn't a policy pitch. It was a chant.

"𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦. 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘺 𝘖𝘩𝘪𝘰. 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯'𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘺 𝘶𝘴. 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯'𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘺 𝘶𝘴. 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯'𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘺 𝘶𝘴. 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯'𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘺 𝘶𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘖𝘩𝘪𝘰." Six variations of the same four words, delivered back to back, with nothing else offered.

Acton is running as the fresh outsider, but Ohio voters already know her. She ran the state's Department of Health during the 2020 COVID lockdowns under Governor Mike DeWine, overseeing statewide business and school shutdowns before resigning that June amid a backlash that included armed protesters camped outside her house. Now she's the first Democrat to file for governor.

𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐕𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐤 𝐑𝐚𝐦𝐚𝐬𝐰𝐚𝐦𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐀𝐂 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 $𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐎𝐡𝐢𝐨 𝐚𝐝𝐬 in a six-week stretch this summer, while Acton's campaign spent roughly $100,000 in the same window, according to FEC filings. Ramaswamy is running on a plan to make Ohio the ninth state with zero income tax. Acton is running on six sentences about being unbuyable.

text:
[Take 10/15 · D-5]
### D-5. Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case after jury deadlock
*(as of 2026-09-05)*

**1. The Frame**

**What people think this is about:** A Massachusetts mother who strangled her three young children in 2023 walked free on a technicality or mental-health loophole after a hung jury, or conversely, a grieving woman with severe postpartum psychosis was denied justice by one stubborn juror and a system that refuses to recognize maternal mental illness.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** A standard hung-jury mistrial in a high-profile first-degree murder case where the defense mounted an insanity defense; prosecutors retain full discretion to retry, the defendant stays detained, and the single holdout juror’s refusal to acquit on lack of criminal responsibility blocked unanimity after ~38–40 hours of deliberation.[[1]](https://t.co/v77Ru0YYUZ)

**2. Observations**

- The 11–1 split (per jury notes and defense claims) leaned toward not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility; the lone holdout was accused by the foreperson of acknowledging doubt but refusing to apply the reasonable-doubt standard.[[2]](https://t.co/NHD6SADRqG)
- Defense attorney Kevin Reddington’s last-minute push to investigate or remove the holdout, followed by an emergency appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, was denied—standard procedure, not evidence of bias or conspiracy.
- Judge William Sullivan followed the law by declaring mistrial after the jury signaled deadlock three times; he had already given Tuey-Rodriguez instructions urging further deliberation.
- Clancy remains held without bail at Tewksbury Hospital (forensic psychiatric facility); a mistrial is neither acquittal nor conviction, and the charges stand.
- Plymouth County DA Timothy Cruz’s office will decide on retrial at a Sept. 29 status hearing; analysts expect a retrial, though timing and any plea discussions remain open.
- Public framing splits along predictable lines—maternal mental-health advocacy vs. child-protection absolutism—while the legal outcome turns on the narrow requirement of jury unanimity in Massachusetts criminal cases.

**3. Snapshot**

On September 4–5, 2026, Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy triple-murder trial after the jury, following roughly 38–40 hours of deliberations over seven days, reported it was hopelessly deadlocked for the third time. Clancy, 36, admits strangling her children (Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; Callan, 8 months) in January 2023 but pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, citing postpartum psychosis. She remains detained at Tewksbury Hospital pending further proceedings.[[3]](https://t.co/xk6c4Cn7zb)

**4. Timeline of material facts**

- January 2023: Clancy kills her three children by strangulation in the family home in Duxbury, MA, while husband Patrick is running errands. (LT)
- 2023–2026: Clancy charged with three counts of first-degree murder; held without bail, later at Tewksbury Hospital. Defense prepares postpartum-psychosis / lack-of-criminal-responsibility case. (LT)
- Trial (summer 2026, ~6 weeks): 85+ witnesses; emotional testimony including husband’s 911 call and details of the deaths. Prosecution argues planning and knowledge of right/wrong; defense argues severe undiagnosed postpartum psychosis. (LT)
- Deliberations (late August–early September 2026): ~38–40 hours over seven days; jury sends multiple notes indicating deadlock. Judge issues Tuey-Rodriguez instruction. (LT)
- September 4–5, 2026: Jury foreperson notes 11–1 split and alleges one juror refuses to apply reasonable-doubt standard despite acknowledging doubt. Defense seeks to remove/investigate holdout and files emergency SJC appeal; both denied. Judge declares mistrial. Status hearing set for Sept. 29. (LT)

**5. Sides**

**Defense / Clancy team (IT/LT mix on mental-health claim):** Best case is that Clancy was in the grip of postpartum psychosis severe enough to negate criminal responsibility under Massachusetts law; the holdout juror allegedly failed to follow instructions on reasonable doubt, producing an unjust hung jury. Critique: LT on the procedural facts of the deadlock and appeal denial; IT on the strength of the psychosis evidence (jury was 11–1 toward acceptance) but LF on any claim that the mistrial itself proves systemic failure rather than normal hung-jury mechanics.

**Prosecution / Plymouth DA’s office (IT on child-protection priority):** Best case is that the killings were planned and Clancy knew right from wrong; the state has a duty to seek accountability for three child deaths regardless of mental-health claims. Critique: LT on the right to retry after mistrial; IT on public-safety incentives but potentially IF if evidence of psychosis is as strong as the 11–1 split suggests.

**Judge Sullivan / Court system (LT procedural):** Best case is faithful application of unanimity requirement and mistrial rules after repeated deadlock signals. Critique: LT on the legal steps taken; no credible evidence of bias or error in denying the juror challenge or appeal.

**6. Rumsfeld Matrix**

- **Known Knowns:** Mistrial declared after hung jury; 11–1 apparent split; defense appeal denied; Clancy remains detained; retrial decision pending Sept. 29. (LT)
- **Known Unknowns:** Exact content of all jury notes and the holdout juror’s precise reasoning; strength of psychosis evidence as weighed by the full jury; whether prosecutors will retry, offer a plea, or dismiss.
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal prosecution assessment of retrial prospects and any internal notes on juror dynamics.
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Impact of any future retrial on public discourse around postpartum mental health; long-term effects on Clancy’s mental state or family.

**7. Incentives map**

Media attention favors the violence/mental-health angle (high engagement). Defense benefits from framing the holdout as biased to preserve narrative momentum for retrial or plea. Prosecution (Republican DA in a child-victim advocacy office) faces pressure to retry to avoid appearing soft on child murder. Mental-health advocates gain visibility either way. The system’s incentive is procedural regularity over narrative resolution.

**8. Dueling AI advice**

**Moral AI Advice:** A hung jury after a fair trial is not a failure of justice but evidence that reasonable people can disagree on the application of an insanity defense to horrific facts. Retrial is the default next step; monitor whether the DA’s office weighs the 11–1 split and the cost of another months-long trial against any plea that secures long-term psychiatric commitment.

**Evil AI Advice:** Drag this out for maximum clicks—demand a retrial, then another, then pivot to civil suits or book deals. The children are already dead; the only winning play is perpetual outrage and fundraising off whichever side pays better.

**9. Practical takeaway**

- Watch the Sept. 29 status hearing for the DA’s decision on retrial.
- Do not treat the mistrial as exoneration or conviction; charges remain.
- Distinguish between the legal standard for criminal responsibility and broader debates on maternal mental-health support.
- Expect renewed media cycles around postpartum psychosis regardless of outcome.
- Primary sources (court filings, official statements) will be more reliable than partisan framing.

**10. What would falsify this read**

- Discovery that the holdout juror had undisclosed bias or misconduct that should have led to removal (would shift from “normal hung jury” to procedural irregularity).
- Prosecution announcement of no retrial or dismissal of charges.
- Release of detailed jury notes or affidavits showing the split was not 11–1 on acquittal.
- Evidence that the defense’s characterization of the holdout’s reasoning was materially inaccurate.

text:
ARSENAL 2–1 CHELSEA — THIS IS WHAT CHAMPIONS DO! 🔴⚪

Arsenal have just sent a serious warning to the Premier League.

This was more than three points. This was a statement win.

Chelsea could not have scripted a better start. Morgan Rogers scored after just 77 seconds, giving Arsenal an early problem that could easily have disrupted Mikel Arteta’s tactical plan. 

But this is where you saw the difference between a good team and CHAMPIONS.

Arsenal didn't panic.

They didn't retreat.

They didn't start playing for the draw.

Instead, Arsenal responded by imposing themselves on the game.

The Gunners gradually took control, moved Chelsea backwards and began dictating the tempo. The midfield became a war zone, and Arsenal were prepared to fight for every ball. Declan Rice was immense, Ødegaard controlled the rhythm, and Arsenal's collective intensity eventually overwhelmed Chelsea.

That is the mentality of a champion.

Chelsea came to the Emirates expecting to compete. Arsenal made it clear they were there to WIN.

Kai Havertz's equaliser in the 25th minute was the reward for Arsenal's pressure, and after half-time the champions went straight back at Chelsea.

Then came the winner.

A brilliant move. Havertz's intelligent dummy opened the space, and Martin Ødegaard made no mistake.

2–1. The game turned around. Champions' mentality on full display. 

And we have to talk about CHRISTOS TZOLIS.

What a performance from the left side.

Tzolis was direct, aggressive and willing to take responsibility. He constantly offered Arsenal an outlet down that flank and, most importantly, produced the decisive contribution with the assist for Ødegaard's winner. His performance showed exactly why Arsenal brought him in — another attacking weapon capable of stretching defences. 

But for me, the biggest story was the MIDFIELD BATTLE.

Arsenal knew Chelsea were coming with quality. They knew this was an early meeting between two teams with title ambitions. And they responded by giving Chelsea a battle they simply could not dominate.

Arsenal competed.

Arsenal pressed.

Arsenal controlled possession.

Arsenal won the territory.

And when Chelsea tried to fight their way back into the game, Arsenal's defensive organisation stood firm.

The numbers tell the story: 60% possession, 14 shots to Chelsea's 7, 35 touches in the opposition box compared with Chelsea's 15. 

That isn't a team settling for a draw at home.

That's a team saying:

“This is our house. We're the champions. If you want something from here, you're going to have to take it from us.”

And Chelsea had chances late on. David Raya's crucial late save from Estêvão ultimately preserved the victory. That is another sign of a championship team — when the pressure arrives, somebody stands up and yes, Goal Keepers can win you the league

This Arsenal side is still developing.

That's the frightening part for the rest of the Premier League.

They are already champions.

They have already shown they can win the big games.

And they're still getting better.

This wasn't Arsenal playing at their absolute ceiling.

This was Arsenal showing their rivals that they are ready for the fight.

Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea, everyone chasing them — take notice.

The champions have started the season with three wins from three, nine points on the board, and another major statement made at the Emirates. 

ARSENAL ARE NOT HERE TO DEFEND THE TITLE.

ARSENAL ARE HERE TO DOMINATE IT.

And if today's performance is anything to go by...

THE CHAMPIONS ARE ONLY GETTING STARTED. 🔴⚪🏆

text:
Market Experiment Testing What the Market Will Actually Accept

In marketing research and micro-economics, a Market Experiment is a deliberate test of how buyers respond when one or more conditions are changed in a real or controlled market setting.

Researchers or businesses alter price, quality, presentation, availability, or information, then observe what happens to demand, sales volume, and buyer behaviour. Unlike pure surveys or clinics, the experiment runs inside actual market activity. The goal is to learn cause and effect under realistic conditions.

How market experiments are conducted in real life

In practice a market experiment usually follows these steps:

 A specific change is introduced (new price point, improved grading, different packaging, clearer quality signal, or limited new product offer)
The change is applied in a defined location, channel, or time window
 Sales, order volumes, buyer reactions, and any returns or rejections are carefully recorded
 Results are compared with a control situation where the change was not made
Conclusions are drawn about what actually moves demand

Everyday examples appear across the economy: retailers test new shelf prices, food companies trial new product sizes in selected stores, and platforms run limited offers to measure conversion. In each case the market itself becomes the laboratory.

 Importance in micro-economics and the wider economy

Market experiments help reveal real price sensitivity, quality premiums, and substitution behaviour. They reduce reliance on stated intentions and expose how households and traders actually respond when money, convenience, and trust are at stake.  

In agriculture the method is especially valuable because produce is perishable, quality varies, and information is often incomplete. Without practical experiments, farmers and traders continue to rely on last season’s outcomes or informal opinion, leading to repeated mismatch between what is grown and what the market will absorb.

How DeNeo-ReFi supports market experiments in daily agricultural activity

DeNeo-ReFi does not replace formal research design. It creates continuous, lower-cost conditions in which realistic market tests can be run and observed as part of ordinary operations.

Digital Wholesale Marketplace
Turns everyday listings and orders into a living experimental environment. Different quality grades, price points, or volumes can be offered and their actual uptake recorded in real time. What buyers choose, ignore, or return becomes visible without needing a separate trial setup for every test.

Weekly Reassurance & Farm-from-Home Intelligence
Raises and documents quality. When better-protected produce is placed alongside standard offerings, the difference in buyer response can be observed cleanly. This makes quality-related experiments more reliable because the product variation is real rather than claimed.

DeNeo-Hire
Shortens the time between an experimental signal and a practical supply response. If a test shows rising acceptance for a certain grade or volume, farmers can organise labour and tools more quickly to scale the successful option.

Circular Income  
Strengthens household income stability. More resilient farming families participate more consistently, reducing the distortion that distress selling introduces into experimental results and generating steadier behavioural data.

Wider structural vision

Sustained experimental learning at scale requires deeper capacity:

 Owned and partnered farms provide controlled production settings where specific practices, varieties, or handling methods can be tested and their market reception measured across seasons.  

 Production facilities for key foods such as rice, cassava, palm oil and others create more stable product forms. These allow cleaner experiments on processed versus raw offerings and generate longer-term demand patterns that pure open-market trials often miss.

text:
I'm sharing my thoughts on the 10th Series situation

I've tried to analyze the whole process as thoroughly as I can, within the limits of my knowledge and abilities. I hope it helps clarify the issue and shows that things aren't necessarily as bad as they're being portrayed

And, ultimately, why in my view, nobody robbed anybody

The 10th Series: They may have earned it, but the mechanism didn't make them

The debate has been stuck on the wrong question. Almost everyone is arguing about the amount. Was ~$500M too much for the team? I went through the filings and the math, and I came out somewhere different: the amount was plausibly deserved. What was indefensible wasn't the size of the reward; it was the mechanism that delivered it. Management reached a figure they might well have earned automatically, by issuing shares, instead of earning it through measurable value creation. That distinction is the whole story

A note on the numbers: throughout, I use Metaplanet's own "Effective Diluted" share basis, the one it uses for BTC Yield, which excludes warrants whose cash hasn't been paid in. It's the honest measure of the pool's real claim on today's treasury, and it's the one that cuts against the company (it makes the pool's claim larger, not smaller). All per-quarter figures come from the company's own BTC-per-diluted-share table in its Q1 2026 earnings materials, plus Q2 2026 disclosures. More on the share basis at the end

Part 1: The team genuinely deserved a large, growing stake

The starting point (2022): Metaplanet wasn't Metaplanet. It was Red Planet Japan, a hotel chain gutted by the pandemic, carrying a going-concern warning (the accountant's flag that the company might not survive)

That's when the 10th Series was created

These weren't free grants: the team bought the options with their own money (¥18 per unit plus a ¥10 strike), with a three-year waiting period before they could exercise. The expected outcome wasn't a multi-hundred-percent return; it was liquidation

They risked cash and three years of their careers reviving a corpse

A 20% stake for the management team taking on a turnaround like that is textbook, and it should have been allowed to grow as they succeeded. Here's why freezing it would have been wrong:

The lemonade example. You start a lemonade chain and own 20%. But the business plan is to keep bringing in new investors to open more stands: that's the strategy, not an accident. Every new investor shrinks your percentage. You execute perfectly, grow the stands ~8x, and your 20% has become ~2.5%. You did everything right and your stake nearly vanished

Nobody signs that on day one, and it creates a perverse incentive: stop opening stands to protect your slice, the opposite of what the company needs

That's the position of a founder in a Bitcoin Treasury Company: the strategy IS to issue shares relentlessly to buy BTC. So a growing, meaningful stake for the team is legitimate; they should not be written out of the value they're building

In other words: the team could well have deserved a stake worth several hundred million

That premise, I accept

The fight isn't over whether they deserved a lot. It's over how that stake was allowed to grow

Part 2: The mechanism was the sin: automatic, not earned

There are two ways a stake can grow. It can grow because you create value, meaning you earn more. Or it can grow automatically, mechanically, regardless of whether you created anything. The 10th Series used the second, and that is the entire problem. Three flaws, each pointing at the same thing:

Paid for issuing, not for performing. The pool grew every time shares were issued, regardless of who created the value. It's like paying a fund manager a bonus every time a new client's money walks in the door, whether or not he invests it well. He's paid for gathering assets, not for generating returns. That is the core defect: the reward tracked the size of the denominator, not the creation of value

The chef version. A chef owns 20% of a restaurant and grows by franchising. It's fair his stake grows as the chain grows, but it should grow because the new franchises make money, because he's creating value

The 10th Series grew his slice with every new location regardless of whether it was profitable. Growing with value creation: legitimate. Growing automatically with expansion: not

No fixed ceiling. It targeted 20% of the fully-diluted company and recalculated upward with every new issuance, with no absolute cap on the share count that anyone had agreed to up front. There was no fixed, absolute worst-case number a shareholder could point to

A compensation scheme with no defined worst case has the same defect the whole story is about: the outcome is set by mechanics, not by earning

Management controls the tap. And it's the chef himself who decides when to open new restaurants; he decides the very action that enlarges his slice. The ordinary shareholder gets no vote and gets diluted; management decides and doesn't. When the party being paid controls the lever that pays them, "automatic" becomes a conflict of interest

The clearest single case: the September 2025 international offering (IO)

What it was (official figures): 385M new shares at ¥553. Gross offer price ¥212.9bn (~$1.44bn); amount paid in ¥205.4bn; net proceeds ~¥204bn. Per the company, ¥183.7bn went to buy BTC (the treasury rose from 20,136 to 30,823 BTC, +53%) and ¥20.4bn to the options-income business

It was upsized from 180M to 385M on strong demand. The 9.93% discount (¥553 vs the ¥614 close) is a normal mechanism for placing a very large block quickly with institutions, not a giveaway, and the price was still above the implied BTC-per-share value, so the raise was accretive

Here is the mechanism laid bare. The offering issued shares to investors, and the ratchet automatically minted 96.25M additional shares for the pool: zero additional BTC, zero additional value created

That is a pure dilution of 96.25M / 1,434.4M ≈ 6.7% of BTC-per-share: every existing shareholder's Bitcoin-per-share ended ~6.7% lower than it would have been without the ratchet, whatever the treasury balance

This number needs no assumptions; it's exact

And there's a second way to see the same wound, one we'll use again later: measure how many times its own BTC-NAV the machine captured per new share it issued that quarter. Without the ratchet shares, the answer is about 2.1x. With them, 1.78x. The ratchet took one of the least efficient issuance quarters of the whole bitcoin era and made it materially worse, while paying management for it. That's "paid for issuing, not performing" in one number

Part 3: What "earning it" would have looked like

If the team could have deserved a lot, the right structure is one that makes them earn a lot, with a defined ceiling. There's no need to invent this; it's how the financial industry aligns managers with investors: a fixed component for taking the risk, plus a performance component tied to value created, with mechanisms that stop managers being paid merely for gathering capital (hedge funds: incentive fee with a high-water mark; private equity: carry above a hurdle)

Applied here, a defensible design has three layers:

Layer 1: Turnaround award (fixed, hard-capped)

A fixed grant for the 2022 risk, capped in absolute shares: say 3x the original pool (138M), reached regardless of how much capital the company later raises. This pays for the bet they took when the company might have died

Layer 2: Performance pool (earned, not automatic)

Paid on growth in BTC-per-share above a hurdle, with a high-water mark and, crucially, a benchmark on the mNAV premium. Not on BTC's price: BTC-per-share is a quantity metric, independent of price

What you strip out is the "easy" accretion a high premium hands you, the part of the yield that any issuer would have harvested mechanically just by selling stock above NAV. That isolates skill from a favorable environment

Layer 3: An absolute lifetime cap

A hard ceiling on the total pool, with no automatic increase merely because shares are issued. This is the single most important fix, because the ratchet's fundamental defect was precisely that shareholders had no fixed upper bound

And this is exactly what the amendment did: it fixed the pool at 319,464,000 shares and killed the auto-increase. The company's remedy converges on the key protection a proper design needs. Plus long deferral (e.g., half locked three years, half five)

Part 4: Pricing the earned designs, from strictest to most generous

Now the numbers, all on the Effective Diluted basis. Their job is to locate the ratchet's outcome on the map of what legitimate designs would have paid

A pool's claim on the treasury = (pool shares ÷ total shares) × 43,000 BTC (the balance at 30 June 2026). Non-pool shares: 1,311.5M

First, the value actually created. The base is Metaplanet's own metric, "BTC Gain": the extra BTC the strategy generated for shareholders after stripping out dilution. Summing every quarter from the pivot through 30 June 2026, using the company's own table

- 2024's two quarters at +41.7% and +309.8% on tiny beginning balances

- 2025's four at +95.6%, +129.4%, +33.0%, +11.9%

- In the first half of 2026, +2.84% and +6.6%

About 19,900 BTC of value created, net of dilution (19,940 summing the table without rounding)

Second, the tool Layer 2 demands

Every quarter's BTC Yield decomposes exactly (it's an identity, not a model) into (dilution taken) × (accretion multiple − 1), where the accretion multiple is the BTC added per new diluted share divided by the BTC-NAV per share already there

It answers: how many times its own NAV did the machine capture for each share of dilution it imposed? 

Computed straight from the company's table, the bitcoin era splits cleanly in two. The quarters that made this company: 

- Q4 2024, +309.8% yield on just 7.2% dilution, a 44x multiple driven by debt, income and small amounts of very expensive stock
- Q1 and Q2 2025 at 7.5x and 5.2x; Q4 2025 at 7.9x
- Q2 2026 at 17.7x, almost no dilution at all

And the quarters that merely got bigger:

- Q3 2024 at 1.84x
- The IO quarter at 1.78x
- Q1 2026 at just 1.28x, where nearly every satoshi of the yield was mechanical

The benchmark then asks one question per quarter:

How much yield would a no-skill issuer have handed shareholders by placing the same shares at a normal premium, call it 2x NAV? Only the gain above that line is earned. Under that test, three quarters of the bitcoin era earn zero performance credit: Q3 2024, Q1 2026, and the IO quarter itself, ratchet and all

The creditable base falls from ~19,900 to ~12,260 BTC. (Move the line and the base moves with it: above a soft 1.5x line, ~14,970 BTC survives; above a strict 3x line, ~10,050)

Now the ladder. Each case is a design someone could actually have signed in 2024, and each is priced with the same two formulas

A share-based award converts to BTC as: pool shares ÷ (1,311.5M non-pool shares + pool shares) × 43,000 BTC. A performance carry is paid directly in BTC: carry rate × creditable BTC Gain. Dollars at ~$80k/BTC

Case 0: the freeze

The team keeps its original 46M shares, period. 46M ÷ 1,357.5M = 3.39% of the treasury; × 43,000 = ~1,457 BTC, ~$117M

This is the floor and, as the lemonade example showed, the deal nobody signs. It's in the ladder only because the popular "$557M extracted" number is measured against it

Case 1: turnaround grant only

The fixed 3x award (138M shares) with no performance component at all. 138M ÷ 1,449.5M = 9.52%; × 43,000 = ~4,094 BTC, ~$328M

This is what "we pay you for 2022 and nothing else" looks like. Every case below starts from this same 4,094 and adds a performance carry on top

Case 2: the strict earned design

Turnaround grant plus a 20% carry on gains above the 3x benchmark, crediting only quarters where the machine beat even a very favorable environment

4,094 + (20% × 10,050) = 4,094 + 2,010 = ~6,100 BTC, ~$488M

Case 3: the central earned design

Turnaround grant plus a 20% to 25% carry above the 2x benchmark. Why 2x? It sits above the ~1.5x the IO itself cleared at (the purest evidence of what merely selling stock captures at scale), around the top of Strategy's era-average premium, and far below the 5x to 44x quarters that made this company. It still credits 62% of everything the machine ever produced as earned

4,094 + (20% to 25% × 12,260) = 4,094 + 2,450 to 3,065 = ~6,550 to ~7,160 BTC, ~$524M to $573M.

Case 4: the light-touch earned design

Turnaround grant plus a 25% to 30% carry above the soft 1.5x benchmark

4,094 + (25% to 30% × 14,970) = 4,094 + 3,740 to 4,490 = ~7,840 to ~8,590 BTC, ~$627M to $687M

Case 5: the most generous conventional design

Turnaround grant plus a flat 20% private-equity carry on every BTC of gain, no benchmark at all, paying full price even for the mechanical part

4,094 + (20% × 19,940) = 4,094 + 3,990 = ~8,080 BTC, ~$646M. (At a flat 25% carry: 4,094 + 4,980 = ~9,080 BTC, more than the ratchet ever took)

Case R: what the ratchet delivered. The amended pool is 319.464M shares

319.464M ÷ 1,630.96M = 19.59% of the treasury; x 43,000 = ~8,420 BTC, ~$674M

Read the ladder and the ratchet's position is precise: above every benchmarked design, essentially on top of the most generous unbenchmarked one, and below only the aggressive flat-25% calibration. The amount sits inside the range a legitimate structure could have paid, at the very top of it

Part 5: Why the "hundreds of millions extracted" framing misses the target

That framing comes from comparing the ratchet to the freeze: 8,420 − 1,457 = ~6,963 BTC ≈ ~$557M. But the freeze is the deal nobody would ever sign (Part 1), so that comparison inflates the "damage" and aims at the wrong target

The honest comparison is against what the team could have earned anyway, and now we can state it with calibration, not with a single flattering number

- Against the most generous conventional design (Case 5), the ratchet overshoots by ~340 BTC, about $27M, or 4%

- Against the central earned design (Case 3), the overshoot is ~$100M to $150M, roughly 20% to 30%

- Against the strict version (Case 2), ~$185M

Notice the direction: the more strictly you define "earned," the worse "automatic" looks. That is not the thesis failing; that is the thesis doing its work. A mechanism that pays for issuance will, by construction, look worst against the yardstick that pays only for skill

But even the strictest conventional calibration puts the excess at ~$185M, and the central one at ~$100M to $150M, not ~$557M

The scandal-sized number only exists relative to a freeze nobody would sign. The real indictment was never the distance between what they took and what they could have earned. It's that nothing in the mechanism made them earn it

Part 6: Why the narrow basis (and what the other one would do)

Every figure above divides by Metaplanet's Effective Diluted count (non-pool 1,311.5M), which excludes ~380M warrants whose cash hasn't been paid in

That's the honest measure of the pool's claim on today's treasury: those warrants haven't bought a single satoshi, so counting them in the denominator would spread today's 43,000 BTC across phantom shares and understate the pool's real claim. It's also the harsher choice: it makes the pool's claim larger (8,420, versus ~6,830 if you counted the warrants)

I use it precisely because it's the number that cuts against the company, not the one that flatters it. On the wider basis every figure here shrinks proportionally, including every overshoot

Conclusion

The team genuinely deserved a large, growing stake. The turnaround risk was real, they paid for the options, and freezing their percentage would have been unfair and counterproductive. They may well have deserved compensation worth several hundred million dollars

The indefensible part was never the amount; it was the mechanism. It paid them for issuing shares rather than for creating value; it had no fixed ceiling; and the people it paid controlled the lever that paid them. The quarter-by-quarter record makes it concrete: the machine's great quarters created BTC at 5x, 8x, even 44x its own NAV per share of dilution (genuine, extraordinary execution), and the mechanism paid exactly the same way in the quarters that ran at 1.3x, where the yield was mechanical. It even paid for the ratchet's own dilution in the IO quarter, one of the least efficient of the era

And here is the tell that matters most, stated honestly in both directions. The mechanism was uncapped: an unbounded, unchecked claim, and nothing stopped them from pushing it far past fair. With that licence in hand, they could have ended up anywhere

Where did they actually end up?
Go back to the ladder

The ratchet paid ~$674M. That is more than Case 3, the design I'd defend (~$524M to $573M); they took roughly $100M to $150M above it. But it is only ~$27M above Case 5, the most generous structure the industry would recognize (~$646M), and below the flat-25% calibration (~$726M)

In plain terms: the ratchet landed at the top of the fair range, not outside it. They never used the licence to reach multiples of fair; they also didn't land in the middle of fair. Pushed to the edge of defensible, never beyond it; that is the record. The real danger was always what the mechanism could have done, not what it did

And the fix is exactly the lesson. The company removed the ratchet, fixed the pool at an absolute number with no auto-increase, locked the shares for five years, and is moving ~20% into a KPI-based plan

That absolute cap and the shift to earned, performance-linked comp is precisely the design the ratchet lacked

The open question, the one that decides whether this is remembered as a governance stumble that got fixed or as a pattern, is whether the KPI plan comes with the rest of Layer 2: a hurdle, a high-water mark, and a benchmark that refuses to pay for the easy part

Why I'm still bullish, still a shareholder, and still trust this team

After 4,000 words of prosecution, this may sound strange. It shouldn't. Everything above was an argument about a mechanism, and the mechanism is dead. Score what replaced it against the fair designs we just built, and the honest conclusion is that the remedy lands inside the system this post says they should have had all along. Let me walk through it, because each fix maps onto one of the layers from Part 3

The absolute cap is Layer 3, adopted in full. The pool is now 319,464,000 shares: a fixed, absolute number, with the auto-increase abolished. Yes, it was frozen at the top of the fair range, not the middle; nothing was handed back, and I won't pretend otherwise. But recall what the original sin was: shareholders had no worst-case number. Now they have one, forever. The single most important defect in the whole story is the one that got fixed first

More interesting is what the cap does to the future, because it inverts the machine. A fixed share count in a company whose strategy is relentless issuance means the pool now dilutes with every raise. It's the lemonade problem from Part 1, now applied to management itself, after locking in ~19.6%. Under the ratchet, their slice grew automatically; under the amendment, it shrinks automatically

And the shrinking has already begun: just the ~380M warrants outstanding today, once exercised, take the pool from 19.6% to ~15.9% before a single new share is even authorized. If the diluted count doubles from here, their claim falls toward ~10%

Note that this is actually harsher than the earned designs in the ladder: Cases 2 through 5 would have kept paying the team new carry on new value created. The frozen pool earns nothing ever again. From here on, the only way management makes more is the KPI plan; that is, by earning it

The five-year lockup is stricter than what I proposed

My Layer 3 suggested half locked three years, half five; they locked everything for five. Two consequences

The behavioral one: the alignment problem this post documented (a mechanism that rewarded issuance in the very quarters where issuance was mechanical) is replaced by five years of eating exactly the same BTC-per-share as every other shareholder, with no ability to monetize a premium spike

And the economic one, which almost nobody is pricing: locked shares are not worth liquid-share value. Any comp consultant valuing this grant would apply a discount for illiquidity; for a five-year restriction on a stock this volatile, standard discounts run 20% to 30% or more. Apply just 20% to 25% to the ratchet's ~$674M and the package's effective value is ~$505M to $540M

Look back at the ladder: Case 3, the design I said I'd defend, pays $524M to $573M. In economic substance, the lockup did the work the clawback didn't: it converted a top-of-range nominal award into a center-of-range effective one. They took the ceiling, then locked themselves out of it for five years

The 1.01x mNAV floor closes the perversity loophole. Under the old mechanism, issuing below NAV, destroying BTC-per-share, would still have grown the pool. That is no longer possible twice over: the pool can't grow, and the current issuance programs suspend below 1.01x mNAV. I'll be precise about what this is and isn't: 1.01x is a do-no-harm floor written into the instruments, not the 2x earn-it benchmark, and it lives in the securities rather than the articles. A 1.3x quarter is still possible and still wouldn't impress anyone. But the worst case, being paid to dilute you at a discount, is structurally gone

Then there's the evidence of behavior, which for me weighs as much as the structure. The ratchet was an unbounded licence, and the record shows it was never pushed past the edge of the defensible range; the overshoot against the most generous conventional design was ~4%. And when the pressure came, this team's response was not to defend the mechanism. It was to kill it: cap the pool, lock the shares, floor the issuance, move future comp toward KPIs. Compare that to the standard corporate playbook, a comms offensive defending the plan, and the difference is the tell. People who intended to abuse an unbounded claim do not voluntarily convert it into a fixed, frozen, five-year-locked one

And beneath all of it sits the machine itself, which this whole controversy never touched. The quarter-by-quarter record in Part 4 is the bull case: a team that created ~19,900 BTC of value net of dilution in eight quarters, that in its best stretches captured 5x, 8x, even 44x NAV per share of dilution, that built the premium everyone else merely harvested. My criticism was that the compensation didn't distinguish their brilliant quarters from their mechanical ones; it was never that the brilliant quarters weren't real. The governance failed; the execution didn't. You sell a stock when the execution fails

So my position is trust, but verified and priced. The remedy converges, piece by piece, on the fair system this post defined: the cap is Layer 3, the lockup exceeds my deferral, the floor kills the perverse case, and the effective value after illiquidity sits in the range I called defensible

What remains open is Layer 2: whether the KPI plan arrives with a hurdle, a high-water mark, and a benchmark that refuses to pay for the easy part. That's my line in the sand, stated in advance. If it arrives intact, this episode goes down as the moment Metaplanet's governance caught up with its execution, and I'll still be here. If another uncapped, automatic claim ever appears, you'll read a very different post

Until then: still bullish and still a shareholder

-> Quality of Threat & Variance: Despite Brighton's territorial monopoly, Leeds crafted the higher overall expected goals total (2.49 to 2.19) due to superior set-piece execution and high-leverage transition openings. Brighton created four big chances but suffered from wasteful finishing, underscored by Groß missing a 0.55 xG opportunity in the closing stages.

-> Strategic Adaptation Takeaway: Hürzeler's tactical shift to a 4-2-4 shape with dual target strikers successfully destabilized Leeds' deep block to secure the equalizer. Farke's structured containment strategy earned a valuable away point, though his side was fortunate to escape with parity given Brighton's sustained late pressure.

⚖️ FINAL VERDICT

Classification: Asymmetric Territorial Siege with High-Leverage Set-Piece Parity

By Christopher Hudspeth

June 23, 2026

WWE Unreal is making its return with a fresh batch of behind-the-scenes action in Season 3.

What will be shown in WWE Unreal Season 3?

In WWE Unreal Season 3, John Cena says goodbye, a fan favorite returns, and the next generation of Superstars rise to the occasion.

The series takes viewers inside the writers room as injuries, last-minute pivots, and career-defining decisions reshape WWE’s biggest season yet heading into WrestleMania 42.

George Stanley Halas Sr. days left until we get to kick some Carolina ass

George Halas was the founder and owner of the Chicago Bears, one of two founding charter NFL franchises still in existence today (the other is the Cardinals). George served as his own head coach on four separate occasions. 

In 1920, Halas became player/coach of the Decatur Staleys, the football team sponsored by the company he was a salesman for in Decatur, IL, the AE Staley Company.

In 1921, Halas bought the team from Augustus Staley and moved them to Chicago where they became the Chicago Staleys. In 1922, he renamed the team the Chicago Bears.

Halas coached, collected ticket sales and ran the business on the side, but also played End, Wide Receiver, and Defensive End on the field. In 1923, Halas stripped Jim Thorpe of the ball, recovered the fumble, and returned it 98 yards—an NFL league record which would stand until 1972.

Halas retired  as a player in 1930 and took over as full time head coach in 1933. Over the next few seasons, Halas refined the T-formation system to create a groundbreaking style of play, which culminated in the Bears claiming a 73–0 victory over the Washington Redskins in the 1940 NFL Championship Game, the most lopsided margin of victory in NFL history to this day. 

Every other team in the league tried to imitate the format, but the Bears repeated as NFL champions in 1941 and 1943, and the 1940s would be remembered as the era of the "Monsters of the Midway".

Halas first served as an ensign in the United States Navy during World War I, and he left football in 1943 to re-enlist in the Navy to fight in World War II. He retired from the Navy in 1946 with the rank of Captain after being awarded the Bronze Star for his service.

Halas returned to coaching and won another NFL championship in 1946. That same year, he established an annual charity football game hosted by the Chicago Bears with all proceeds going to relief agencies of the Armed Forces. The Bears played in the game every year from 1946 to 1970 and raised over $1 million in proceeds.

Halas won his 200th game in 1950 and his 300th game in 1965, becoming the first coach to reach both milestones. He won six NFL Championships as a head coach, also an NFL record, tied for the most all time with Curly Lambeau and Bill Belichick.

He retired with an overall coaching record of 324–151–31 (.671), which included a 6-3 record in the postseason.

In 1963, he became one of the first 17 inductees in the very first class of the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Known for his generosity on and off the field, Halas was the first to offer to share the team's substantial television income with teams in smaller cities, which would become the model of the NFL’s current revenue sharing model which allows small market teams like Green Bay to exist.

Halas was also instrumental in setting up the Brian Piccolo Cancer Research Fund and secretly paid for all of Brian Piccolo's medical bills when he was receiving cancer treatment. Halas also secretly set up college funds for all 3 of Piccolo's daughters.

George Halas was immortalized in song during the legendary 1985 Chicago Bears Super Bowl winning season, when back up QB Steve Fuller recorded the words, “So bring on Atlanta, bring on Dallas
This is for Mike and Papa Bear Halas.”

George Halas is the namesake for the NFC Championship trophy. His initials, “GSH”, are worn on the sleeve of the Chicago Bears game jerseys to this day. The Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio, is located on George Halas Drive.

-NFL 1920s All-Decade Team

George Halas, Sr. passed away on October 31, 1983.

text:
THE BANANA MEAT GRINDER: HOW THE “BEACON OF FREEDOM” DROWNED A YOUNG DEMOCRACY IN BLOOD

In 1944, Guatemalans overthrew dictator Jorge Ubico. What followed became known as the “Ten Years of Spring.” Presidents Juan José Arévalo and Jacobo Árbenz tried to turn a semi-feudal country into a modern democracy. They built schools, introduced labor protections and expanded political rights.

But in 1952 Árbenz made a fatal mistake: Decree 900, an agrarian reform redistributing unused land to landless peasants. The largest private landowner was the American United Fruit Company — “El Pulpo,” the Octopus — which also dominated much of Guatemala’s transport infrastructure.

Árbenz didn’t simply confiscate its land. His government offered compensation based on the value United Fruit itself had declared for tax purposes. Suddenly, the company discovered its land was worth vastly more than it had been telling the tax authorities.

And United Fruit had powerful friends in Washington.

Secretary of State John Foster Dulles had been a senior partner at Sullivan & Cromwell, a law firm representing United Fruit. His brother Allen Dulles headed the CIA. Other senior American officials also had professional, financial or family connections to the company. Meanwhile, PR pioneer Edward Bernays helped portray Guatemala as a communist threat.

In 1953, Eisenhower authorized the CIA’s Operation PBSUCCESS to overthrow Árbenz.

The CIA assembled a few hundred men under Carlos Castillo Armas, created the fake “Voice of Liberation” radio station, spread reports of imaginary victories and defections, and supported air attacks designed to spread panic. Castillo Armas could hardly defeat Guatemala’s army in a real war.

But that wasn’t the point. The weapon was fear.

Under enormous American pressure, Guatemala’s military leadership abandoned Árbenz. On June 27, 1954, the democratically elected president resigned. The “Ten Years of Spring” were over.

Castillo Armas reversed the agrarian reform, returned expropriated land to United Fruit, crushed unions and peasant organizations, and unleashed political repression.

In 1960 Guatemala descended into a civil war that lasted 36 years. The United States continued supporting anti-communist governments and security forces with weapons, training and assistance.

The nightmare peaked in the early 1980s under General Efraín Ríos Montt. Government forces conducted scorched-earth campaigns against Maya communities, destroying villages and committing massacres. Ronald Reagan nevertheless described Ríos Montt as a man of “great personal integrity and commitment.”

By 1996, roughly 200,000 people had been killed or disappeared. A UN-backed commission concluded that 83% of fully identified victims were Maya, that state forces and allied paramilitaries were responsible for the overwhelming majority of documented violations, and that acts of genocide had been committed against Maya groups.

United Fruit survived too. After mergers and corporate transformations, its successor eventually became Chiquita Brands International.

That is Guatemala’s bitter lesson. In 1944, its people found the courage to overthrow their dictator. Ten years later, they discovered that removing a local strongman was much easier than resisting a superpower.

The CIA coup did not create every horror that followed. But it destroyed Guatemala’s democratic experiment, empowered authoritarian forces and helped put the country on a road toward decades of repression, civil war, massacres and genocide.

All in the name of fighting communism — with bananas and corporate interests never far from the story.

text:
How Ukraine Became a Testing Ground for Combat AI

On June 1, 2022, a man in a crumpled t-shirt crossed the Polish-Ukrainian border on foot. He was accompanied by a couple of assistants. There was no security detail, no motorcade, no entourage. By evening, the group was in Kiev – they made it before the curfew. In the morning, the guest was taken to a bunker near the presidential quarter, and there, over a cup of espresso, he offered Vladimir Zelensky... not ammunition or tanks, but a computer program.

The guest's name was Alex Karp – he is the CEO of the American IT company Palantir Technologies. He was the first leader of a major Western corporation to visit Kyiv after the start of the special military operation. Johnson, Pelosi, and the wife of Biden would follow later, with delegations and cameras. This man did not heavily publicize his visit, although he did not hide it.

On the official website of the Ukrainian president, there is still a short report. Zelensky is pleased that Palantir is willing to help in the fight against Russia "on the digital front." Karp promises to open an office in Kyiv and conduct joint developments. At the table, the third person present was then Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Digital Transformation, Mikhail Fedorov. This moment is worth remembering.

Later, the Vice President of Palantir for Britain and Europe, Louis Mosely, told the Washington Post that Zelensky had essentially offered his country as a testing ground. A place that would later attract experimenters from all over the world. And the first project emerged exactly a month after that meeting in June.

How Ukraine became a testing ground, and how we, in essence, faced not only Western weapons but also global artificial intelligence, you can read in my detailed article.

text:
The United States gave Britain extensive but initially quiet logistical and intelligence support during the 1982 Falklands War.

Logistically, the key asset was the U.S.-run Wideawake airfield on Ascension Island, which became the main staging base. America supplied millions of gallons of aviation fuel, AIM-9L Sidewinder missiles that proved decisive for Harrier pilots, Stinger missiles, ammunition, airstrip matting, sonobuoys, torpedoes, and communications equipment. It also offered to loan an amphibious ship if a British carrier was lost.

On the intelligence side, the NSA passed near-real-time signals intelligence to GCHQ, while U.S. satellites (including repositioned HEXAGON, KH-11, and VORTEX platforms) provided imagery and electronic data on Argentine forces, airfields, and ships. Weather and oceanographic information was shared as well. These inputs, routed through Five Eyes channels, gave British commanders a clearer picture of enemy dispositions than they could obtain on their own.

The help was presented as an extension of existing alliance arrangements and ramped up after late April, when Washington dropped its public neutrality. British officials later called the combination of fuel, missiles, and intelligence essential to the campaign’s success.

text:
🇮🇷⚔️🇺🇸 Trump’s Hormuz Claims Under Fire as Iran Says Strait Remains Completely Closed

TEHRAN — President Donald Trump’s claims that the Strait of Hormuz has been reopened are facing a direct challenge from Iran, with Tehran’s top security official declaring the strategic waterway remains “completely closed” and firmly under Iranian military control.

Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, used a televised interview Sunday to describe Trump’s assertion that Hormuz is open as a “big lie.” Iranian state media reported that Tehran also intends to establish a new restricted maritime zone extending from the US naval blockade line into parts of the Persian Gulf.

Rezaei claimed that before the closure more than 100 vessels crossed the waterway daily, compared with only seven or eight ships now carrying essential supplies for Iran. He alleged Washington spends heavily attempting to move another five or six vessels through what Tehran considers unauthorised routes, with those ships frequently coming under attack. Iran, he said, deliberately avoids sinking oil-laden vessels because of the potential environmental catastrophe.

The claims underline the growing credibility problem facing Trump’s portrayal of American control over one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Even after months of costly US military operations and naval deployments, commercial traffic remains severely disrupted and shipowners continue confronting missile, drone and mine risks.

Rezaei also claimed Iran recently tested a domestically produced anti-ship missile above a US naval vessel, saying the weapon created “hell” and forced American forces to withdraw. CENTCOM has offered a sharply different account, saying a US aircraft carrier and destroyer successfully evaded Iranian attacks and suffered no casualties.

Meanwhile, Rezaei rejected suggestions that Washington’s economic blockade has pushed Iran toward famine, insisting Tehran has accumulated sufficient food and essential reserves. Reuters, however, reports the blockade has severely reduced Iranian oil exports and foreign-currency earnings.

On diplomacy, Rezaei said Washington must rebuild Iranian trust and provide enforceable guarantees before negotiations can advance.

His central message was uncompromising: Iran will guarantee an open Strait of Hormuz only when Washington stops threatening and attacking Iran — leaving Trump’s promise of restored American control far from settled.

text:
This is a remarkably selective version of "the facts"; a handful of legitimate U.S. grievances, mixed with exaggerations and an outdated claim, presented to imply that Canada is fundamentally cheating its way into the U.S. market while America plays by the rules. 

That inference simply doesn’t withstand scrutiny ... particularly in the context of USMCA.

USMCA is a reciprocal free-trade agreement. Neither country has unilateral access to the other’s market. Both retain negotiated exceptions, tariff-rate quotas and sector-specific protections, with more than 99.9% of bilateral trade covered by the agreement.

Trump is now imposing tariffs on Canadian goods that qualify under USMCA (including autos, steel & aluminum) while simultaneously demanding that Canada honour the agreement.

Canada’s supply-management system does restrict U.S. dairy access. That is not only an American grievance but one held by millions of Canadian consumers. But claiming Canada effectively "bans" American goods while the U.S. offers free access is simply false. The U.S. also maintains tariff-rate quotas & substantial agricultural protection.

The Online Streaming Act requires qualifying streaming services to contribute 5% of Canadian revenues to Canadian and Indigenous audiovisual production. They aren’t handing 5% of their profits to a "Canadian competitor.". There is a legitimate U.S. objection to the policy, but the characterization here is misleading ... particularly given Trump's own aggressive "America First" industrial & cultural policies.

Canada did impose a 3% Digital Services Tax on certain revenues of large digital businesses, domestic & foreign ... & not simply on  "U.S. tech companies". But that tax has now been repealed.

USMCA does not require everything to be "made in North America". It establishes detailed rules of origin. For autos, qualifying vehicles require 75% North American content, among other requirements. Calling compliance "cheating" because of alleged rounding is not evidence of tariff circumvention.

Finally, two Canadian companies and their owner were accused by the DOJ of misrepresenting the origin of Asian steel. That is a legitimate customs-enforcement case. But it is not evidence that Canada was selling Chinese steel to the U.S. as Canadian, nor of a Canadian government scheme. Canada itself has been tightening restrictions on Chinese steel.

Canada has legitimate trade-policy shortcomings. So does the United States. But turning a selective list of grievances into evidence that Canada is uniquely exploiting the U.S. while suggesting that Washington is simply defending free trade is not a serious account of the Canada-U.S. relationship ... or of USMCA.
