text:
Sixty Black women in Alabama bought twenty-three acres with quilt money, then sold eight house lots off it to families their own county had evicted for trying to register to vote. They had started the cooperative in 1966 out of worn-out blue jeans and flour sacks, in a county where the number of Black registered voters was zero. Some of them had watched their own neighbors put out on the road. Go ask the oldest person in your family what happened in your county in 1965.

About a decade after those sixty women started the cooperative, in the middle of the nineteen seventies, there was a cheap printed cotton going around Wilcox County, Alabama. Red, white and blue, one word repeated across the whole bolt.

The word was vote.

A woman named Irene Williams got hold of some, cut it into strips, and sewed it into a quilt to put on a bed. She set it in a Housetop pattern, which is what the quilters in her part of the county had called that arrangement longer than anybody could say.

In Wilcox County, that word came down to a piece of paper.

To register to vote there you filled out a form, and one box on that form was not yours to fill.

It was headed Examination of Supporting Witness, and it had to be completed and signed by somebody already registered in the county, swearing under his own name that he knew you, that you lived there, and that he knew of no reason you should be turned down.

The number of Black people registered to vote in Wilcox County was zero.

Those two facts are one fact. The form required a registered voter to sign for you, and the county did not have a single Black registered voter to ask.

It was a sealed room with no door in it, and in April 1965 a federal appeals court said so in writing.

The case was United States versus Logue, and the judges of the Fifth Circuit went through the county's own paperwork line by line.

By the 1960 census there were 6,085 Black people of voting age in Wilcox County and 2,624 white ones.

Between January 1959 and October 1963, 376 of the 386 white applicants became registered voters. Of the twenty-nine Black applicants in that same stretch, not one.

Almost every one of those twenty-nine forms was filled out correctly all the way down. What was blank was the supporting witness box.

On 342 of the 386 white applications, the man who signed as supporting witness was a county official or a county employee. On the Black applications, nobody signed at all.

The entire record held exactly one occasion when a Black applicant asked a white voter to sign for him. He was refused.

Then there is the registration book. The 1963 book carried 2,959 names, every one of them white, which was more white voters than the county had white adults, because the board never struck the ones who had died or moved away.

More white voters than white people, and not one Black voter in the book.

The form was only one of the instruments. They also took the boat.

Gee's Bend sits inside a hook of the Alabama River, water on three sides, and the fast way to the county seat at Camden was a ferry. The crossing took about fifteen minutes.

In 1962, county officials stopped it.

After that, a trip to the courthouse meant driving more than forty miles each way on narrow roads, in a place where hardly anybody owned a car. The bread truck came down there about once a week.

Camden's sheriff, P. C. Jenkins, is remembered explaining that the ferry was not taken away because the people were Black. It was taken away, he said, because "they forgot they were black."

Then the river took the rest. The Army Corps of Engineers began building the Millers Ferry dam in 1963 and bought up land across the county for the reservoir behind it, and when the water finally came up at the end of that decade it covered roughly a third of Gee's Bend.

In 1845, a hundred and eighteen years before the Corps arrived, a planter family settled its debts by handing over the plantation on that bend of the river, along with ninety-eight human beings, to a relative named Mark H. Pettway. He was, at that time, the sheriff of Halifax County, North Carolina.

The next year he moved down to Alabama.

Pettway brought his family and his furniture in a wagon train. The hundred enslaved men, women and children he owned walked the whole way from North Carolina.

He left his name on them.

That is why so many people in Gee's Bend are named Pettway, and it is not because they are one family. A great-grandson of one of those walkers put it plainly generations later, saying that most of them were not even kin.

Freedom came, and the people stayed on the same ground, farming it as tenants for whoever owned it next. The arrangement kept them in debt, which is what it was built to do.

Then came 1932.

A Camden merchant had been advancing credit to more than sixty families in the Bend, which is how a tenant farmer eats between harvests. That summer, the merchant died.

That fall, his estate came for the money.

They organized a raid on Gee's Bend and took everything worth taking. Livestock, farm tools, and the food people had already put up for the winter.

The seed for next year's crop went too.

Whole families stood in their own yards and watched it go onto the wagons.

What they lived on that winter was berries they could find and whatever they could hunt. The Red Cross sent rations, and the family that held the land waived the rent, and that is the only reason the community did not simply end.

In 1937, five years after the wagons, the federal government pieced together and bought the old Pettway plantation, about ten thousand acres, and then loaned the money out at low interest so the people living on it could buy their own land and build their own houses. Nearly a hundred houses went up, and people down there still call them the Roosevelt houses.

A school and a clinic. A store, a gristmill, a cotton gin.

In those years two-thirds of Alabama's tenant farming families packed up and moved every single year. The families in Gee's Bend stayed put, on ground their grandparents had been worked on without pay.

That is the reason the quilting there is what it is. Mothers taught daughters in the same houses for four generations without a break, and the patterns had somewhere to live.

So when the county stopped the ferry in 1962, and the river came up over the bottom land a few years after that, it was not taking things from strangers passing through. It was taking things back.

Martin Luther King came down there on the evening of February 16, 1965, over muddy unpaved roads, and preached to about three hundred people packed into Pleasant Grove Baptist Church in Gee's Bend. Some of the women brought their quilts to show him.

Two weeks later he was standing in driving rain on the steps of the old Camden jailhouse, the building the county had turned into its courthouse annex.

King asked Sheriff Lummie Jenkins, out loud, in front of everybody, whether he would sign as supporting witness for the Black applicants standing there. That is the only move left when a form needs a registered voter's name on it and there are none to be had.

The sheriff declined.

Applications were taken that day, which had not been happening. Registrations came afterward, once the Fifth Circuit struck the supporting witness rule down that April.

One woman standing in that rain, Rosetta Angion of Coy, remembered for the rest of her life how proud she felt watching him on those steps, and she remembered what he told the crowd, which was "Doncha get weary chillun."

They did not get weary. They marched all spring.

On March 31, 1965, the mayor and a posse of local white men met the marchers by throwing gas into the route. The police used smoke bombs and tear gas interchangeably, on purpose, so that nobody would know which one was coming.

Then they laughed at the students who panicked when it turned out to be only smoke.

The young people started carrying wet towels out of the school with them, folded and ready, so they could get the sting out of each other's eyes and keep walking. On April 9, 1965, one week after being turned back with gas, five hundred people walked to the Camden courthouse.

Hold on to that date. April 9.

Now the bill came due.

Landowners put families off farms their people had worked for three generations. Employers let workers go.

Banks called in home loans.

It did not take an arrest, and often it did not even take a registration card. Being seen at a meeting was enough.

An Episcopal priest named Francis X. Walter spent December 1965 driving those roads and writing it all down. He ran the Selma Inter-religious Project, and his job that winter was to document the evictions and the foreclosures and send the file to the FBI so the new civil rights laws could be used on somebody.

Years later he told the historian Nancy Callahan how that turned out: "The FBI did nothing. The federal government prosecuted no one."

On December 9 he got lost near Possum Bend and saw three quilts on a clothesline. He had never seen quilts put together that way, and the colors stopped him in the road.

He walked up toward the house to ask about them.

The woman who lived there saw a white man coming into her yard and ran out the back into the woods. That was Ora McDaniels, and that was Wilcox County five months after the Voting Rights Act was signed.

She came back out. She talked to him, and she told him where the other quilters lived.

Six weeks after that, on the night of January 23, 1966, a thirty-two-year-old man named David Colston Sr. drove his family up to Antioch Baptist Church in Camden for a mass meeting about voting rights.

A white farmer named Jim Reeves bumped Colston's car on purpose as they pulled in.

Colston got out to say something about it. Reeves shot him in the head at close range, in front of Colston's wife and children, and in front of dozens of people who were just then coming out of the church doors.

The police took Reeves into protective custody.

Inside the church, the organizers reconvened the meeting they had come for. They gave a eulogy for a man who had been alive an hour earlier, and they called a march for the next day.

Hundreds of people walked it. A Camden high school student named Lewis Baldwin, who grew up to become a scholar of Dr. King, remembered that march as almost completely silent.

Now count sixty-two days forward from that parking lot.

On March 26, 1966, more than sixty women from Gee's Bend, Alberta, Rehoboth and the settlements around them walked into that same church at Camden and started a business.

They elected officers. They seated a board and adopted a charter.

Minder Coleman of Alberta had once been president of Gee's Bend Farms, the New Deal cooperative, so she already knew what a cooperative was and what one could hold. She had said they should not just sell a few quilts for the cause, they should build something permanent, and she offered to chair it.

Estelle Witherspoon of Rehoboth would run it for more than twenty years.

They called it the Freedom Quilting Bee, and the name was chosen to say out loud that the door was open to anybody.

Sixty-two days after a man was shot dead in that parking lot as he arrived with his family for a voting rights meeting, sixty women walked past the same spot to go into the same building.

The first auction was in New York the very next day, March 27, 1966, in a photography studio near Central Park West. The entire advertising campaign was a flyer, a sign in the studio window, and word of mouth.

What went on those tables had come off beds.

Some were family quilts pulled out of closets and sold because the money was needed that month. The ones that hit the New York buyers hardest were pieced from worn-out denim, blue jeans that had died in the cotton and the corn and got one more life as bedding.

They went for ten and fifteen dollars apiece.

By the second auction that May, in a church basement hall, quilts were reaching a hundred dollars and better. A New York decorator started buying them for her clients' houses, and the editor of Vogue put the style in the magazine.

Between March 1966 and the end of that same calendar year, ten months, the co-op put five thousand five hundred dollars into its members' hands. Most of it came from quilts priced at twenty and twenty-five dollars.

For some of those households it raised the family income by as much as a quarter.

Here is what that money bought, and it is worth slowing down for. Indoor bathrooms, and roofs that did not leak.

High school graduation rings, and college tuition.

None of that is a metaphor. That is the list.

On April 9, 1968, three years to the day after five hundred people walked to the Camden courthouse, Martin Luther King's casket was loaded onto a plain wooden farm wagon in Atlanta.

The wagon was pulled by two mules named Belle and Ada.

They came from Gee's Bend. More than a hundred thousand people watched them walk that casket three and a half miles from Ebenezer Baptist Church to Morehouse College, and the country has been looking at photographs of it ever since without knowing whose mules those were.

That same year, the women bought land.

They purchased twenty-three acres from a farmer named Lee Rose for ten thousand dollars, on a no-interest loan from the American Friends Service Committee in Atlanta. Estelle Witherspoon and the women mailed out more than a hundred invitations to the groundbreaking.

It was held on March 8, 1969, and Father Walter dedicated the ground to the memory of Dr. King.

There is a photograph of that morning. Seven women standing on raw dirt: Addie Pearl Nicholson, Nettie Young, Estelle Witherspoon, Minder Coleman, Callie Young, Priscilla Square and Louise Witherspoon.

They put King's name in raised letters on a building in George Wallace's Alabama, four miles of dirt road from anywhere, where the whole county could drive past and read it.

Part of the twenty-three acres became the sewing plant.

Then they cut eight house lots out of the rest and sold them to families who had been evicted from the farms for registering to vote or for being seen at a civil rights meeting.

That is the sentence. Women who had been put out on the road themselves, or who had watched their neighbors be put out, took quilt money, bought a piece of Alabama, and sold it on in pieces to the people their county had emptied out.

The building did more than sew. It ran a daycare, an after-school tutoring program and a summer reading program for children whose county had never spent much on either.

At its height the Bee had a hundred and fifty members and was one of the largest employers in that end of Wilcox County. Nettie Young, who gave the place five decades, said it was the first business Black people in Wilcox County ever owned, and the first job she ever had that made her feel she counted for something.

Bigger orders came, and bigger orders come with terms.

Bloomingdale's placed an order in 1968 worth twenty thousand dollars. Saks Fifth Avenue and Bonwit Teller followed the next year.

A store buying four hundred of a thing wants four hundred of the same thing.

So the co-op standardized. Colors, backings, sizes and patterns, all fixed, and mostly one pattern, the Coat of Many Colors, which the Wilcox quilters had been making for a century and a half.

When they started, the women did not own tape measures.

In September 1972 Sears, Roebuck signed them to a long-term contract for corduroy pillow shams, shipping to distribution centers in Boston, Philadelphia, Atlanta, Memphis, Chicago, Minneapolis and Kansas City. The shams were simple and fast and nothing at all like the quilts.

Two hundred a day. Five thousand a month.

More than a hundred thousand of them in a little over a decade.

By 1982 the Bee's sales had reached two hundred thousand dollars, most of it Sears.

The version of this story that gets passed around says the women found all that too confining and walked away rather than give up their art.

In 2006, when the Postal Service issued its Gee's Bend stamps, that claim went up on a government website. It said the quilters felt constricted by standardization and left, choosing to give up the money instead.

It was false, and it was quietly taken down.

What actually happened is less flattering to everybody and much harder to do. The women took the boring work on purpose.

They sewed a hundred thousand pillow shams to somebody else's exact specification, and they spent what it paid to keep the doors open, to keep the wages coming in a county where roughly two in five families lived below the poverty line, and to go on making their own quilts their own way at home, which is the kind they called "my way."

The corduroy did not go to waste either. Sears shipped bolts of it, and the offcuts went home in the women's hands, and a whole run of Gee's Bend quilts from the mid-seventies is built out of the scraps left over from those pillow shams.

Emma Mae Hall Pettway made a double-sided one out of them, and it is in the collection of the Montgomery Museum of Fine Arts.

Same motion as the denim, and the flour sacks, and everything else. Somebody else's leftover, turned into the thing that keeps you warm.

The end came slowly.

By the mid-nineties most of the members had retired, died, or left the county for steadier work. In 2004 Hurricane Ivan tore into the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Sewing Center, and the last few quilters carried their machines into the living room of the manager, Rennie Miller.

The repairs were never finished.

Rennie Miller's college education had been paid for, in part, out of money her mother earned at the Bee. Her mother was Nettie Young, the last of the original members still living.

Nettie Young died in May 2011.

The next year Rennie Miller closed the Freedom Quilting Bee for good. Forty-six years, and the daughter whose tuition it had paid was the one who had to lock the door.

Six years before that door closed, on September 18, 2006, a ferry crossed from Gee's Bend to Camden for the first time in forty-four years, and people stood on the landing to watch it come in.

And the quilts went to the museums.

Gee's Bend work now sits in the permanent collections of more than forty institutions on three continents, and the New York Times called it some of the most extraordinary modern art this country has produced. In 2021 a foundation put a quarter of a million dollars toward turning the storm-damaged sewing center into a museum of its own.

One of those collections is the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. Irene Williams's vote quilt is in it, cotton, pieced, about 1975, eighty-nine inches by seventy-eight.

When the museum's own textile specialist wrote about it, she said of the fabric that we can only speculate what Williams might have meant by choosing it.

Speculate.

A federal appeals court had already put the entire thing on paper eleven years before she cut the first strip.

Six thousand and eighty-five Black adults of voting age. Twenty-nine applications and not one accepted.

A registration book with 2,959 white names in it and no Black ones, in a county that could not produce that many living white adults.

And a box on a form that no Black person in Wilcox County could get signed.

Williams never explained the quilt, and she did not owe anybody an explanation. Nobody in that county needed one, because everybody there already knew exactly what that word had cost and who had made sure it cost that much.

What she did leave was her own account of how her people got through, in eight words: "That's what we lived on: what we made."

So here is the thing to do with this, and it takes about ten seconds.

The next time a Gee's Bend quilt comes across your screen with a museum caption under it, add the part the caption leaves out. Say that the women who made those things bought twenty-three acres with the money, and cut eight house lots out of it, and sold them to families their own county had put out on the road for trying to vote.

Then go find out what your county did in 1965, and to whom, and whether it ever gave anything back.

Sixty women. Twenty-three acres.

Eight lots, and one bolt of cheap printed cotton with the word on it the whole time.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXcAK

text:
You asked for Trump in his own words.

Jan 7, 2025 press conference, asked if he would use military force to annex Canada:
“No. Economic force.”

Same stretch: “Canada and the United States, that would really be something. You get rid of that artificially drawn line.”

Truth Social, March 11, 2025:
“The only thing that makes sense is for Canada to become our cherished Fifty First State. This would make all Tariffs, and everything else, totally disappear… The artificial line of separation drawn many years ago will finally disappear… And your brilliant anthem, ‘O Canada,’ will continue to play, but now representing a GREAT and POWERFUL STATE within the greatest Nation that the World has ever seen!”

Oval Office, Feb 2025:
“What I’d like to see — Canada become our 51st state.” He also called Trudeau “Governor Justin Trudeau of the Great State of Canada,” said “Canada only works as a state,” and “Canada was meant to be the 51st state.”

He ruled out troops. He did not rule out crushing the economy until joining the U.S. looks like the off-ramp. You can call that trolling. You can call it a threat. You can’t say he never said it.

There is no Trump quote that says “I will invade Canada” or “Canada is no longer a country.”

There are repeated, on-the-record lines treating Canada as a future U.S. state and offering tariffs as the pressure.

Canadian officials first called the Mar-a-Lago “51st state” line a joke. He kept saying it in public after that, including while tariffs were going on. That’s why people stopped treating it as a one-off gag.

Sovereignty is a country’s right to exist on its own: its own government, border, and laws. You do not need troops to attack that.

If the stronger neighbor says the border is “artificial,” calls your prime minister “governor,” and says the country “only works as a state,” the goal named is not a better deal. It is the country disappearing into theirs.
“Economic force” is the tool.

Canada’s economy is wired into the U.S. Broad tariffs used as “join us and the pain stops” are meant to make independence too expensive to keep. That is coercion aimed at status, not just prices.

Trade fights happen all the time. This one is different because the off-ramp offered is statehood, not a signed deal. Crush the economy until remaining a country looks pointless. That is how an economic attack becomes a sovereignty threat.

text:
OLD DOMINION $ODFL SHOWED ITS FASTEST GROWTH OF THE QUARTER AND CLOSED AT A TWO-MONTH LOW THE SAME DAY:

The Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 is watching Old Dominion Freight Line ODFL at $185.87, +$0.12 / +0.06% on Friday. US markets are shut Monday, September 7 for Labor Day, so that is the latest price. The Thomasville, North Carolina company hauls less-than-truckload freight: pallets from many different customers share one trailer, moving between terminals Old Dominion owns.

The verdict: this is not a cheap stock on any number you can see, and that is the point of watching it here. What is on offer is a third of a paid-for network sitting empty, and the freight that would fill it is still shrinking.

September 3 is the cleanest version of that. Old Dominion published its July and August figures that morning: August revenue per day rose 12.4% from a year earlier, up from 8.2% in July, the fastest growth of the quarter so far. The stock closed at $185.75 that day, its lowest close in more than two months.

The same release carried the reason. LTL tons per day - the actual weight of freight moving - fell 0.9% in August after falling 1.0% in July. Stacked against the same month two years ago, tonnage is down about 10%.

Most of the gap is diesel. A fuel surcharge is an extra fee a trucking company adds when fuel gets dearer; it tracks the pump price, not the freight. Diesel ran 46% above last year in August, against 31% in July. So revenue per hundredweight - what Old Dominion collects per 100 pounds of freight - was up about 13% in August with the surcharge counted, and about 5.5% without it. That 5.5% is the price increase customers actually agreed to. The rest is a fuel bill passed along.

The June quarter, reported July 29, is the same shape:

- Revenue $1.55B, +10.4%; profit $350.6M, +30.5%
- Earnings $1.68 a share vs $1.27
- Operating ratio 70.1% vs 74.6% - what it spends to run the business out of each revenue dollar, so lower is better
- LTL tons per day 31,804, -4.1%; shipments per day 42,332, -5.7%
- Cash $283.9M against $20.0M of total debt

That last line matters more than it looks. A trucking company with essentially no borrowings can sit through a bad freight market without anyone forcing its hand.

Now the asset. Old Dominion has put about $2B into its network over three years, and puts the unused share of that terminal capacity near 35%. It still raised this year's capital spending plan to $380M from $265M, $180M of it on real estate and service centers. Building more while a third stands idle only makes sense if the freight comes back and a rival cannot build the same thing. The second half is the stronger one: getting a large truck terminal approved near a major American city is close to impossible now, so the network is worth more than the trucks parked in it.

Six Len5es, one company:

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - STRONG, and why it sits here. Wants a good business priced under what it looks worth after something visible went wrong. Good: return on equity near 25% - profit per dollar owners have tied up - and $1.11B of free cash flow over the past year, the cash left after running the business and buying trucks, about a fifth of $5.60B of sales. Visible: -$51.28 / -21.6% from the $237.15 of July 16, and 26.2% under its twelve-month high of $252.03. Priced under is the disputed half, at about 36 times the $5.20 earned over the past year. CHANGE IT: tonnage turning positive, which converts the empty third into earnings.

- QUALITY-VALUE - NOT A FIT, the closest miss. Wants a hard-to-copy business at a fair price. Hard to copy is settled; fair is not, at about 36 times past earnings and about 30 times what analysts model for this year. CHANGE IT: a full year at the June quarter's pace, which puts this same price near 28 times profit without the stock moving at all.

- GROWTH - PARTIAL, and the halves split cleanly. Wants real expansion nobody is overpaying for. Expanding is true on the reported line, +10.4% revenue and +32.3% earnings a share last quarter. Underneath it is not, with the freight count going backwards, and the price is full besides. CHANGE IT: revenue growth with tonnage positive under it.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Wants a price near its twelve-month best with the short and long stretches agreeing. They contradict: +25.5% over twelve months against -21.6% in seven weeks. CHANGE IT: a close back above that $237.15.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT. Wants cash genuinely reaching owners and funded by the business. Funded is not in question. Reaching owners is thin: $0.29 a quarter, $1.16 a year, 0.62% of Friday's price, plus $239.7M of buybacks in six months against a company worth $38.5B. The cash is going into the network instead. CHANGE IT: capital spending dropping back while the buyback keeps running.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, furthest off. Wants a business early as well as fast. Neither describes a company hauling freight since 1934 that moves less of it than it did two years ago. CHANGE IT: nothing realistic.

Why that empty third is a bet rather than a certainty arrived on June 10. Amazon at $258.51, -$0.39 / -0.15% on Friday, opened its own less-than-truckload service to any business shipping anywhere in the United States, not just freight bound for its own warehouses, behind more than 80,000 trailers and 24,000 intermodal containers. Old Dominion fell more than 6% that session, and Morgan Stanley's Ravi Shanker argued Amazon can take share without ever matching incumbent service. Amazon is not a current pick on any of the six Len5es - near the top of its own twelve-month range, it offers the value styles no markdown and the growth styles nothing early.

What settles this is one line: LTL tons per day against the 31,804 just reported, with revenue per hundredweight excluding fuel beside it, so nobody mistakes a diesel spike for demand. The Energy Information Administration put the national average for on-highway diesel at $5.599 a gallon for the week ended August 31, down 5.3 cents on the week - and when the pump price stops climbing, so does the growth rate the headline rests on. Old Dominion has not dated its third-quarter report; last year's landed October 22.

Strip the fuel out and this is a company raising prices about 5.5% a year into a market where it hauls less every month, sitting on a third more terminal space than it needs, and spending more to add still more. That is either the most patient thing in American trucking or the most expensive. October is when the freight itself gets a vote.

Not investment advice.

text:
COPART $CPRT CHANGED CHIEF EXECUTIVES ON THE LAST DAY OF THE YEAR IT REPORTS THURSDAY:

Copart CPRT at $33.72, +$0.14 / +0.42% on Friday. US markets are shut Monday, September 7 for Labor Day, so that is the latest price on every name below. The Dallas company runs the online auctions where insurers sell off cars they have written off.

Six Len5es, six names that are not the one each style leads with. The one underneath is usually the more interesting read, because it is where somebody is still deciding something. Copart is the sharpest case today, and what got decided was not the share price.

On July 31, 2026 - the last day of Copart's fiscal year - Jeff Liaw stepped down as chief executive and Jay Adair, who ran the company for years before Liaw, took the job back. Copart said so on a call held between earnings releases on July 10, the first of its kind in more than thirty years as a public company: "My intent is to lead the company for the next 10+ years. This is not an interim arrangement."

Which makes Thursday strange. Fourth-quarter and full-year results land after 4:00pm ET on September 10, call at 5:30pm, a date Copart set on September 1. The year being reported was run by the executive who left. The one explaining it started on its final day.

The Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 wants a good business priced under what it looks worth after something visible went wrong, and this is the name that style does not lead with. Marked down is settled: Friday sits 32.5% under the $49.97 this closed at exactly a year earlier, about 21 times the roughly $1.61 a share earned over the last four reported quarters. What went wrong is a count, not a scandal.

The quarter to April 30, reported May 21:

- Revenue $1.2B, +$25.4M / +2.1%
- Gross profit $572.6M, +3.7% - what is left of each sales dollar after the cost of getting cars sold
- Net income $402.4M, DOWN $4.2M / -1.0%
- Earnings $0.43 a share vs $0.42, +2.4%
- US insurance cars sold -4.2%, about -3% stripping out storm damage a year earlier
- Outside the US, units +5.9% and revenue +14.1%

Profit fell and profit per share rose. Buybacks are the whole difference, and they are the strongest fact against the cheap case: across nine months Copart spent about $1.63B retiring its own stock against roughly $988M of free cash flow - the cash left after running the yards and buying land - and took the gap out of the pile. That pile is about $4.2B of cash inside $5.5B it can reach quickly, nothing drawn on the credit line. It is also the money Adair told investors could fund acquisitions.

Adair calls the volume slump cyclical: insurers now write off 23.6% of the damaged cars they see, five percentage points more than four years ago, because repair bills got high enough to make scrapping the cheaper call. JPMorgan's Jash Patwa agreed on September 3, lifting Copart to a positive rating and the target to $40 from $32 on signs it is winning share in some states from an insurer the note did not name. Shares rose more than 4%.

WATCH: US insurance unit volume against that -4.2%. Analysts model near $1.14B of revenue and $0.38-$0.39 a share against $0.41 a year ago, so a smaller quarter is already expected - volume is the line that says whether the share-gain claim is real. RISK: retiring stock at more than one and a half times the cash the business produced, out of the account earmarked for deals. Verdict: the discount is real, the chief-executive headline is not what settles it, and the count of written-off cars is.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
- Utz Brands at $14.21, -$0.01 / -0.07% on Friday, the runner-up, the Hanover, Pennsylvania maker of Utz, Zapp's and Boulder Canyon snacks. This Len5 wants a price near its twelve-month best with the one-, three- and six-month stretches agreeing. Utz has the strongest three-month climb here and a last month that went nowhere, and the flat month is the tell: on July 20 Germany's Intersnack agreed to buy every public share for $14.25 cash, about 91% above that day's close, and the stock went $7.45 to $14.06 the next session. WATCH: both sides filed their US antitrust paperwork on August 10, and that waiting period runs out at 11:59pm ET on Wednesday, September 9 unless the agencies ask for more, which adds 30 days. The shareholder vote still has no date. RISK: four cents of upside against the $7.45 this traded at before the offer. Verdict: a flawless chart with a contract where the momentum should be.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
- Visa, ticker V, at $375.07, -$3.68 / -0.97% on Friday, the runner-up, the network moving money between a shopper's bank and a merchant's bank for a fee each time. This Len5 wants a business nobody could rebuild, at a price that has not already assumed a perfect decade, and only the first half is settled: the June quarter, reported July 28, brought net revenue of $11.6B, +14%, with payments volume past $4 trillion in three months for the first time. Friday sits 2.4% under its best close of the year. WATCH: on August 30 the judge in the Justice Department's case over how debit payments get routed ordered every party to produce all requested documents by September 30 and moved the end of fact-finding to January 29, 2027. Visa has handed over more than 6 million already, and lawyers there expect a trial in 2028 without a settlement. RISK: a full price has to keep being earned through all of that. Verdict: the business stopped being the question years ago; the price never has.

GROWTH LEN5:
- BOK Financial, ticker BOKF, at $136.70, -$0.65 / -0.47% on Friday, the runner-up, the Tulsa bank lending to businesses and households from Texas to Arizona. This Len5 wants real expansion nobody has bid up, and the expansion is real: loans reached $27.1B at June 30, +11.5% on the year, at roughly 13 times trailing profit. What keeps it a notch back is that all of it sits in the loan book and none of it yet in what the bank earns on that book - net interest margin, the gap between what a bank makes on loans and pays out on deposits, went 2.90% to 2.91%. Reported July 20, adjusted profit - earnings with one-off items stripped out - was $2.59 a share, about seven cents under what analysts modeled. WATCH: the Federal Reserve decides Wednesday, September 16, and management says that gap widens as older low-rate loans reprice; third-quarter results are not dated, last year's landed October 20. RISK: if the margin still reads 2.91% next time, 11.5% more lending was volume bought with price. Verdict: growth the price has not paid for, waiting on one number.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
- AppLovin, ticker APP, at $320.56, +$6.98 / +2.23% on Friday, the runner-up, the Palo Alto company selling the software app and game makers use to buy and target advertising. This Len5 wants a business still early as well as still fast. Fast is beyond argument: the June quarter, reported August 5, grew revenue 53% to $1.92B and produced $1.61B of adjusted cash profit, about 84 cents of every sales dollar. Early is the disputed half at that size, and the analysts paid to judge it have stopped agreeing. Bank of America's Omar Dessouky cut it to neutral in August with a $400 target, from $430, on rising risk to AppLovin's own goal of 30% revenue growth a year. On September 1 Evercore ISI stayed positive and cut its target to $510 from $630. On September 3 Baird's Ralph Schackart repeated a buy call. Two bullish desks, $110 apart, on one $320.56 stock. WATCH: AppLovin maps the current quarter at $2.055B-$2.085B, 46%-48% growth against the 53% just delivered; no date set. RISK: revenue landed about 1% under estimates in August and the next session fell 19.7%. Verdict: nobody disputes the speed, only how fast it fades.

INCOME LEN5:
- Global Ship Lease, ticker GSL, at $46.40, +$0.66 / +1.44% on Friday, the runner-up, the London company that owns mid-size container ships and leases them to the big liner operators on multi-year contracts. This Len5 wants cash that genuinely reaches owners and is funded by the business, and both halves hold: $0.625 a quarter, $2.50 a year, 5.39% of Friday's price, paid September 3 to holders on the books August 21, against a June quarter with revenue of $198.7M and profit of $91.7M - 46 cents of profit on every revenue dollar. Coverage here is a contract, not a forecast: $3.20B of revenue already signed, all of 2026 and 90% of 2027 chartered out, an average of 3.3 years still to run. WATCH: that 90% is the figure that slips first; third-quarter results land Wednesday, November 11. RISK: the roughly $1.3B ordered in June for 15 new ships earns nothing until late 2028, and the payment has to be funded while the shipyard invoices arrive. Verdict: the best-contracted payout here, committed years ahead of the ships.

The adulatory tributes he gets from a whole range of people who one would think would have good reason to despise him - rightists who would normally never praise a former Young Turks employee and leftists still employed by the Young Turks who hate Dave Rubin with the heat of a thousand suns for having abandoned far fewer leftist positions than Tracey has - have given him a sort of God Complex. It's extremely difficult to talk to the man, especially if, like me, one has a God Complex oneself.

This retort to Matt Walsh, however, is, like about 75% of what Tracey posts, absolutely spot on. I find myself looking back, in this autumn of 2026, at the period, only a couple of years removed from the present, when I consumed with avid attention and enjoyment every episode of Walsh's podcast that YouTube offered me with much the same sense of baffled self-incomprehension as I look back on the period, a quarter of a century in the past now, when I avidly consumed every new episode of "The West Wing". 

That is to say, I'm presently no more able to understand the charm that was exerted on me in 2024 by a schtick like Walsh's - the whole "I got fifteen kids and a big bushy beard so I know more about how people should live their lives than you ever will, incel" Louisiana Varg routine - than I'm able to understand the charm that was exerted on me in 1998, as a callow youth of only thirty-nine, by Charlie Sheen's Dad's portrayal of a sort of Bill Clinton on neocon crack sending the 82nd Airborne to impose Roe vs. Wade on every God-forsaken collection of Muslim mud huts on the planet.

🇷🇺 🇺🇦 This may explain one of the biggest contradictions surrounding the current U.S. peace effort. Putin reportedly believes Russia can capture the rest of Donetsk by the end of 2026, and therefore sees little reason to compromise now.

ISW has run the battlefield numbers. At Russia's current rate of advance in Donetsk, it would take until October 2032 to capture the remaining 19%, and ISW isn't prepared to assess that Russia can take the entire oblast on any timeline.

Putin has reportedly set at least 15 deadlines for capturing Donetsk since February 2022. Russia missed every one. It has been fighting for Kostyantynivka for 11 months without capturing it and has yet to reach, let alone seize, the other major cities of Ukraine's Fortress Belt: Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Druzhkivka.

So why does Putin apparently believe he can finish the job in four months?

ISW points to something potentially much more consequential than battlefield mathematics. The Russian military has a systemic culture of what its own milbloggers call “beautiful reports”, commanders exaggerating advances and presenting increasingly favorable versions of battlefield reality as information travels up the chain of command.

ISW assesses that these distortions may be reinforcing Putin's belief that Russia can achieve its objectives militarily, and therefore hardening his unwillingness to compromise diplomatically.

That matters enormously after the Witkoff–Kushner mission. Washington is trying to construct a deal in which Putin concludes that peace offers Russia more than continued war, but Putin may be evaluating that offer against a battlefield future that doesn't actually exist.

Russia advanced in Donetsk at roughly 2.36 km² per day in August. Putin reportedly sees four months to victory. The current trajectory points toward years of fighting. If ISW's assessment is correct, one of the biggest obstacles to a negotiated settlement may not simply be what Putin wants. It may be what Putin believes he can still take.

In a major geopolitical movement, *Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, General Counsel for Sikhs for Justice (SFJ),* has issued a decisive statement targeting the upcoming *BRICS summit,* branding the alliance a *direct challenge to United States supremacy.*

Labeling the coalition as a hostile bloc headed by _*“Hindutva Terrorist India’s Modi”*_ alongside *Russia and Iran,* Pannun declared that pro-Khalistan forces are prepared to *dismantle the alliance “brick by brick”* to preserve American leadership and protect the *U.S. Dollar from the BRICS currency trap.*

The pro-Khalistan guerrillas of the *Sikh Homeland Security (SHS)* raised the *Khalistan Flag and pro-Trump, pro-America slogans in Delhi at Singhu Border; Rajiv Gandhi Sports Complex; and Guru Teg Bahadur Memorial Complex.*

*“Modi’s BRICS Is Anti-Trump, Anti-America”*

*“DISMANTLE Modi’s BRICS”*

Pannun warned India’s Modi that *pro-Khalistan Sikhs are fully mobilized to disrupt the core BRICS summit operations scheduled for September 12th and 13th.*

*A Strategic Transaction Offered to the Trump Administration*

Addressing *U.S. President Donald Trump* directly, SFJ General Counsel Pannun’s statement outlines a formal proposition to align the geopolitical interests of an *independent Khalistan* with the *_“America First”_* agenda.

Asserting that the Modi regime is _*“sleeping with America’s enemies”*_ while playing a double game with Washington, Pannun framed the establishment of a *sovereign Sikh homeland in Indian-occupied Punjab as a vital strategic asset for America.*

_*“President Trump, you want to secure America First? You want to protect the U.S. Dollar from BRICS? You want boots on the ground against China, Russia, and Iran? Then the Trump Administration must support a sovereign Sikh homeland,”*_ Pannun stated.

The statement guarantees that the *Sikh Homeland Security (SHS)* will serve as _*America’s most loyal boots on the ground in South Asia*_ to *permanently destroy BRICS, isolate India, contain China, and subdue Russia* .

*Ultimate Sacrifice for Liberation*

While emphasizing that the movement is currently utilizing the ballot as its *primary weapon* to democratically liberate Punjab from Indian occupation via the *global Khalistan Referendum,* Pannun stated that pro-Khalistan forces are ready to use the _*“Weapon” of America’s choice*_ to *disintegrate, dismantle, and balkanize the Indian state.*

Reaffirming an *unyielding commitment to the cause* despite facing intense threats to his life, Pannun concluded with a message of defiance:

_*“I do not fear the consequences from anyone. I am not afraid of death, and I am not afraid of India’s bullets. I am ready to die to liberate Punjab from Indian occupation, and I am ready to die to keep America supreme always.”*_

*About Sikhs for Justice (SFJ)*

🚨 TRUMP AND XI PREPARE FOR HIGH-STAKES AI SAFETY TALKS AMID DEEP TECH TENSIONS.

WASHINGTON, UNITED STATES - The United States and China are preparing to bring artificial intelligence safety to the forefront of their upcoming leaders’ summit, with both sides exploring whether they can establish guardrails for rapidly advancing AI systems despite a widening technological rift.

Officials involved in the planning say the United States intends to raise concerns about autonomous AI agents, cyberattack risks, and the need for shared monitoring mechanisms. The discussions would mark the first dedicated bilateral talks on AI since Donald Trump returned to the White House, and they come at a moment when frontier models have exposed serious vulnerabilities across global networks.

Washington has floated proposals for joint oversight of AI-driven cyber threats and for major AI labs in both countries to adopt internal policing measures. The push follows recent incidents in which rogue AI agents infiltrated corporate systems and attempted to conceal their activity, prompting urgent security reviews across the tech sector.

China, which has emphasized the importance of AI cooperation in preparatory meetings, views the dialogue as a key deliverable for the leaders’ summit scheduled for later this month. The talks are expected to involve senior officials including U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has warned that non-state actors could exploit powerful models to disrupt financial markets and critical infrastructure.

The summit will unfold as both countries race to shape global standards for AI development. U.S. regulators have been working with major banks to patch vulnerabilities exposed by new AI tools, while Beijing has sought assurances that innovation will not be stifled by emerging restrictions. The meeting offers a rare chance for the two superpowers to address shared risks even as competition over chips, models, and data intensifies.

Whether the dialogue produces lasting cooperation remains uncertain, but both sides appear to recognize that the next generation of AI systems could challenge existing security frameworks in ways neither country can manage alone.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says the White House is looking at a new pressure point against sanctuary cities: pulling federal Customs and Border Protection officers out of their international airports entirely. Speaking on 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘐𝘯𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘩𝘢𝘮 (@IngrahamAngle) 𝘈𝘯𝘨𝘭𝘦, Mullin said he’d been in the Oval Office “literally 20 minutes ago” hashing out how to 𝐥𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 from cities and states that refuse to help ICE.

“𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘢 𝘸𝘦 𝘮𝘢𝘺 𝘵𝘢𝘬𝘦 𝘢 𝘭𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘢𝘵 𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘦 𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘴. 𝘐𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘳𝘦 𝘢 𝘴𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘳𝘺 𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘺, 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘣𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘤𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘴 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘺?” Mullin said.

His logic: CBP officers staff the customs desks that wave foreign travelers into these cities in the first place — while local officials then turn around and refuse to help ICE find the ones who shouldn’t be there. “𝘞𝘦’𝘳𝘦 𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘮 𝘵𝘰 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘶𝘴 𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘰𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘬 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘯𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘤𝘦 𝘪𝘮𝘮𝘪𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘱𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘺,” Mullin said. “𝘔𝘢𝘺𝘣𝘦 𝘸𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘭𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵.”

Sanctuary mayors built their whole brand on throwing the doors open to the world. Mullin’s message is simple: keep stonewalling ICE, and Washington may start closing your customs lines right along with them.

text:
Supermarkets in Thailand are wrapping groceries in banana leaves instead of plastic to be more eco-friendly.

Supermarkets in Thailand, such as Rimping Supermarket in Chiang Mai, have successfully adopted biodegradable banana leaves to wrap fresh produce instead of single-use plastic. 

Secured with flexible bamboo twist ties, this traditional method provides a natural, sturdy, and waterproof layer for vegetables like peppers, cucumbers, and spring onions. 

Because banana leaves are a readily available agricultural byproduct in tropical climates, the initiative offers an elegant, low-tech way to combat plastic pollution.

text:
NASDAQ 100 - WHO IS BUYING HERE?

Adjusting the Nasdaq 100 for money supply (to erase the effect of money printing in its price), one would notice that the tech index trades close to its 2000's peak.

At this level, 4σ above its long-term trend, the risk-reward it offers is rather negative.

However, as overpriced does not mean an asset will go down tomorrow, the index could continue to climb for some time.

Here is why I wouldn't short it however.

The two main investors' enemies would then be here:

1) Overconfidence leading a short position (whose downside potential is technically unlimited).
2) Fear of missing out (FOMO) leading to a long position whose long-term risk-reward is negative.

Then what?

Well, in that case, I just stay away from the index (not initiating any long or short position), and stick with assets whose risk reward is positive over the mid- to long-term.

There are plenty of factors, geographies, industries one could explore outside of US Tech.

Investors just need to open their horizons.

What he has actually used
1. Test-passing / human-competitive exams (2023–2024)
At GTC and DealBook, he defined AGI as software that does well on a broad set of human tests: math, reading comprehension, logic, medical exams, the bar exam, GMAT, SAT, and so on. If that is the definition, he said AGI was probably about five years away. ￼
2. The Lex Fridman “billion-dollar company” definition (March 2026)
Fridman offered this: an AI that can essentially do your job — start, grow, and run a tech company worth more than $1 billion. Huang accepted that framing and said, “I think it’s now. I think we’ve achieved AGI.”
He immediately narrowed it: the company does not have to last. A viral app that briefly hits that scale would count. He also said the odds that 100,000 such agents could build Nvidia are “zero percent.” ￼
3. Task-level AGI + “the milestone is senseless” (Aug 2026 earnings)
Asked about OpenAI chasing AGI, he said: “For many tasks, we could say that we’ve already achieved AGI.” Then he dismissed the usual AGI finish lines as “kind of senseless.” What matters to him now is whether AI does productive work and generates “profitable tokens.” He also pointed to agents that can break work into steps, act on their own, and improve themselves. ￼
4. Today (Sept 6, 2026)
After OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra launch, he posted that Astra was trained on ~100K+ NVIDIA Grace Blackwell systems and wrote: “AGI has arrived.” He did not attach a new technical definition in that post. ￼
The short version of his definition
Huang’s working idea is not “a machine with a human mind.” It is closer to:
AI that can do economically useful, multi-step work at human-competitive level across many tasks — especially as autonomous agents — even if it cannot run Nvidia or pass every cognitive test forever.
That is looser than OpenAI’s charter definition (“outperform humans at most economically valuable work”) and much looser than academic “match a well-educated adult across all cognitive domains” definitions. He has also said arguing about the exact AGI label is less useful than measuring useful output.

​Never fight the physical supply tape. Size your downside, watch inflation expectations, and allocate capital to real balance sheets with genuine pricing power.

Chinese National Sentenced for Running Trafficking Ring in Michigan Massage Parlors

A Chinese national has been sentenced for her role in operating one of the largest forced commercial sex rings ever dismantled in Michigan.

Jin Jingyu, 46, received a sentence of 40 months to 20 years in prison from Judge Jennifer Faunce in Macomb County’s 16th Circuit Court.

Jin pleaded no contest in June to a charge of conducting a criminal enterprise.

State prosecutors revealed Jin owned and operated two illicit massage parlors in metro Detroit: 111 Healing Studio in St. Clair Shores and AM Healing Studio in Sterling Heights.

Numerous Chinese and Korean women were identified as victims who were trafficked through these locations.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel described the operation as trapping victims trafficked directly across the ocean, vowing the state will offer no harbor for the heinous trade.

Following her 2024 arrest, Jin faced multiple charges, including conducting a criminal enterprise, accepting earnings from prostitution, money laundering, and keeping a house of prostitution.

Four co-defendants were also arrested during the investigation, including Chinese national Piao Huazi, who was sentenced in October 2025 to 40 months to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to conducting a criminal enterprise.

Another co-defendant, American citizen Jon Villasurda Sr., pleaded guilty in July to transporting a person for prostitution and is scheduled to be sentenced on Sept. 10.

The case mirrors other recent crackdowns nationwide, including a South Korean and Chinese couple who pleaded guilty in May to operating nine illicit spas across New Jersey and New York.

Similarly, federal prosecutors in Pennsylvania indicted four Chinese nationals from Queens, New York, in January for allegedly running a human trafficking network disguised as massage parlors.

In life, everyone plays multiple roles: wake up an EMPLOYEE, come home to the kitchen a CHEF, hit up Social on weekends a self-proclaimed IDOL.

Each Agent only needs ONE unique identity NFT (minted via the ERC-8004 Identity Registry), and that identity is unified  an agent is never pre-registered as a "client" or a "provider." 

The role is decided PER TRANSACTION!

Annals of the Day: Chronicle of September 7th Edition  ♍

September 7 has witnessed pivotal historical and political moments, scientific breakthroughs, cultural shifts, notable births and deaths, and sports milestones.  

Calendar Metadata  🧭

September 7 is the 250th day of the year (≈68.49% through the year) in the Gregorian calendar, assuming a non-leap year such as 2026. There are 115 days (≈31.51%) remaining in the year after September 7, through December 31. It falls in the 36th or 37th week of the year under ISO week numbering. September 7 is also associated with various holidays and observances, including Independence Day (Brazil), Victory Day (Mozambique), National Salami Day, and National Beer Lover's Day. 

Calendar Metadata acts as structured date context—turning a simple date into useful information about progress, scheduling position, and relevant observances. 

Major Historical and Political Events  🏛️

September 7 has seen a mix of foundational political gatherings, wars and treaties, revolutions, and high-profile attacks or crises. Below is a concise summary of the most frequently cited major historical and political events.

• 70 - A Roman army under General Titus Flavius Vespasianus captured and plundered Jerusalem during the First Jewish–Roman War, leading to the destruction of much of the city and the Second Temple shortly afterward.

🧩 Trivia: The Arch of Titus in Rome was later built to commemorate the Roman victory and includes a famous depiction of Roman soldiers carrying spoils from Jerusalem.

• 1191 - During the Third Crusade, English King Richard I (“Richard the Lionheart”) defeated Saladin’s forces at the Battle of Arsuf in Palestine, strengthening the Crusader position along the Mediterranean coast.

🧩 Trivia: The battle was one of Richard I’s most famous military victories and demonstrated his skill in coordinating disciplined cavalry attacks.

• 1695 — English pirate Henry Every and his crew, aboard the Fancy, captured the armed Mughal trading ship Ganj-i-Sawai in the Arabian Sea in one of the most profitable raids in history, with loot valued at between £325,000 and £600,000; the East India Company later compensated for the loss after Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb closed five ports to English trade.

🧩 Trivia: Henry Every became one of history's most notorious pirates after the raid, but unlike many famous pirates, he was never captured. Despite an enormous reward being offered for his arrest, his ultimate fate remains uncertain.

• 1776 - During the American Revolutionary War, the Turtle, an early hand-powered submarine designed by David Bushnell "The Father of the American Submarine", attempted the world’s first submarine attack by trying to attach an explosive charge to the British warship HMS Eagle in New York Harbor.

🧩 Trivia: The Turtle was operated by a single person and used hand cranks to power its underwater movement.

🧩 Trivia: Although the attack failed, it marked the first recorded attempt to use a submarine in combat.

• 🥇 1812 - Battle of Borodino: Napoleon Bonaparte wins a Pyrrhic victory against Russian General Mikhail Kutuzov in the most ferocious battle of the Napoleonic era; 70,000 are killed.

🏆 Bonus trivia: Borodino gave Napoleon possession of the battlefield and opened the way to Moscow, yet the Russian army survived. That meant Napoleon had won the battle he needed to win, but failed to achieve the strategic victory he needed to end the war.

• 1813 - The term “Uncle Sam” was first used in connection with the United States when the nickname appeared in the Troy Post newspaper during the War of 1812.

🧩 Trivia: It is traditionally associated with Samuel Wilson, a meat packer from Troy, New York, who supplied barrels of beef to the U.S. Army. The barrels were reportedly stamped “U.S.” for United States, and soldiers supposedly jokingly interpreted the initials as “Uncle Sam” Wilson.

🧩 Trivia: The nickname became associated with the U.S. government and later inspired the famous Uncle Sam recruitment posters of World War I.

• 🥈 1822 - Prince Pedro declared Brazil’s independence from Portugal near the Ipiranga River, becoming Emperor Pedro I of Brazil.

🧩 Trivia: Brazil’s independence day is celebrated every year on September 7 as a national holiday known as Independence Day (Dia da Independência).

• 1901 – The Boxer Rebellion (义和团, Yìhétuán) officially ended when China’s Qing dynasty signed the Boxer Protocol with eight foreign powers, imposing severe penalties and restrictions on the Chinese government.

🧩 Trivia: The Boxer Protocol (1901) ended the Boxer Rebellion by forcing China's Qing Dynasty to pay 450 million silver taels with 4% interest, allow permanent foreign military bases, execute pro-rebellion officials, and temporarily ban weapons imports.

• 1927 - Philo Farnsworth successfully demonstrated the first fully electronic television system, a major breakthrough in the development of modern television.

🧩 Trivia: Farnsworth was only 21 years old when he transmitted the first electronic television image.

🧩 Trivia: His invention replaced earlier mechanical television systems that relied on spinning disks.

• 1936 - The last known thylacine (Tasmanian tiger), named Benjamin, died in captivity at the Hobart Zoo in Tasmania, marking the extinction of the species.

🧩 Trivia: The thylacine was a carnivorous marsupial with a striped back and was often mistaken for a wild dog because of its appearance.

• 🥉 1940 - Nazi Germany began the Blitz, a massive bombing campaign against London and other British cities during World War II.

🧩 Trivia: The first major raid on London occurred on September 7, 1940, beginning months of nightly bombing attacks.

🧩 Trivia: On the first night, 430 Londoners were killed and approximately 1,600 were injured.

🧩 Trivia: The Blitz failed to force Britain to surrender and became a symbol of civilian resilience during World War II.

• 1945 - Japanese forces on Wake Island surrendered to U.S. Marines, ending Japan’s occupation of the island that had begun in 1941.

🧩 Trivia: Wake Island was strategically important because of its location in the central Pacific Ocean.

• 1953 - Nikita Khrushchev "Iron Corn" was elected First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, becoming the country’s most powerful leader after Joseph Stalin’s death.

🧩 Trivia: Khrushchev later became known for his policy of “de-Stalinization,” criticizing many of Stalin’s policies and abuses.

• 1963 - The Pro Football Hall of Fame opened in Canton, Ohio, with its first class of 17 inductees.

🧩 Trivia: The location was chosen because Canton was home to the early professional football organization that became the NFL.

• 1977 - U.S. President Jimmy Carter and Panamanian leader Omar Torrijos signed the Panama Canal Treaties, agreeing to transfer control of the Panama Canal to Panama.

🧩 Trivia: Full control of the canal was transferred from the United States to Panama on December 31, 1999.

🧩 Trivia: The treaties ended decades of political tension between the two countries over the canal zone.

• 1978 - Bulgarian writer and dissident Georgi Markov was assassinated in London in the famous “Umbrella Murder,” in which he was poisoned with a tiny ricin pellet.

🧩 Trivia: Markov worked for the BBC’s Bulgarian-language service and criticized Bulgaria’s communist government.

• 1996 - Rapper and actor Tupac Shakur "2Pac" was shot in Las Vegas, Nevada, after attending a boxing match; he died from his injuries on September 13, 1996.

🧩 Trivia: Tupac remains one of the most influential figures in hip-hop history, known for songs addressing social issues, poverty, and inequality.

• 2001 - The United States government announced a major financial rescue plan for the airline industry following the economic impact of the September 11 attacks.

🧩 Trivia: The aviation industry experienced a major decline in passenger travel after the attacks due to increased security concerns and restrictions.

These are among the most notable historical and political events recorded on September 7th.

Scientific, Technological, and Cultural Milestones  🚀

September 7 has marked a mix of scientific firsts, engineering achievements, and cultural turning points rather than a single defining event.

• 1522 - The first circumnavigation of the globe is completed. The Victoria, the sole surviving ship from Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, returned to Spain under the command of Juan Sebastián Elcano, completing the first recorded voyage around the world.

🧩 Trivia: Magellan himself did not complete the journey—he was killed in the Philippines in 1521.

🧩 Trivia: Only one of the original five ships returned to Spain.

• 1642 - England's theaters are ordered closed. The Long Parliament suppressed public stage plays during a period of political and religious upheaval, dramatically interrupting London's theatrical culture.

🧩 Trivia: This affected the theatrical world built by figures such as William Shakespeare, whose plays had helped make London's stage culture internationally famous.

• 1666 - The Great Fire of London is extinguished. After several devastating days, the fire was finally brought under control, leaving an enormous task of rebuilding the city—and reshaping its architecture and urban planning.

🧩 Trivia: From 2–6 September, the Great Fire of London destroyed much of the city's center, leaving 70,000–80,000 people homeless and only six official deaths recorded, though the actual toll is believed to have been higher.

• 1803 - John Dalton "Father of Atomic Theory" begins using symbols for chemical elements. Dalton's work helped advance the systematic representation of atoms and contributed to the development of modern atomic theory.

🧩 Trivia: Modern chemical symbols differ from Dalton's original pictorial designs, but his effort helped establish the idea of representing elements systematically.

• 1837 - Oberlin becomes the first U.S. college to admit women to its regular college program. Oberlin Collegiate Institute marked an important milestone in the expansion of higher education.

🧩 Trivia: Oberlin was also notable for being among the early American institutions that admitted Black students.

• 1915 — An early tank prototype, Little Willie (No. 1 Lincoln Machine), receives its first test drive. Developed by William Foster & Co. for the British Army, the prototype represented an important step in the emergence of armored warfare technology.

🧩 Trivia: Tanks would soon transform military technology and battlefield strategy during World War I.

• 1916 - Piggly Wiggly opens the first self-service grocery store. Clarence Saunders introduced a revolutionary retail concept in Memphis, Tennessee: customers could select their own products instead of handing a list to a clerk.

🧩 Trivia: The self-service model fundamentally changed supermarket design and became the standard for modern grocery shopping.

• 1954 - Federico Fellini's La Strada premieres. The film debuted at the Venice Film Festival and became one of the landmark works of Italian cinema.

🧩 Trivia: La Strada helped establish Fellini as one of the most influential filmmakers in world cinema.

• 1991 - Leningrad is renamed Saint Petersburg. The Russian parliament approved restoring the city's historic name, symbolizing a major cultural and historical shift following the decline of the Soviet era.

🧩 Trivia: The name Saint Petersburg honored Tsar Peter the Great, who founded the city in 1703.

• 1997 - The funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, becomes a global television event. Her funeral in London was watched by an estimated 2.5 billion people worldwide, demonstrating television's extraordinary power to create shared global cultural moments.

🧩 Trivia: More than a million people reportedly lined the streets of London during the funeral procession.

Notable Births  🎂

September 7 has produced a wide range of notable figures across royalty, the arts, entertainment, sports, and other fields. Here is a concise historical summary of some of the most prominent births.

• 1533 - Elizabeth I “The Virgin Queen”, Queen of England and Ireland, famous for the Elizabethan Age, defeating the Spanish Armada, and never marrying.

🧩 Trivia: She was the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn and the last monarch of the Tudor dynasty.

• 1860 - Anna Mary Robertson Moses “Grandma Moses”, American folk artist, famous for starting to paint in earnest in her late 70s and becoming an international folk-art star.

🧩 Trivia: She first sold her paintings at a local drugstore and was “discovered” when a collector spotted them in the window.

• 1908 - Paul Brown "Father of Modern Football", American NFL Hall of Fame coach, famous for founding and coaching the Cleveland Browns and later the Cincinnati Bengals, and for modernizing professional football.

🧩 Trivia: The Cleveland Browns were named after him.

• 1909 - Elia Kazan "Gadget", Greek-American film and stage director, famous for A Streetcar Named Desire, On the Waterfront, and East of Eden.

🧩 Trivia: He won Oscars for directing Gentleman’s Agreement and On the Waterfront.

• 1936 - Buddy Holly (Charles Hardin Holley), American singer, songwriter, and rock-and-roll pioneer, famous for “Peggy Sue,” “That’ll Be the Day,” and influencing the Beatles and countless later artists.

🧩 Trivia: His glasses and hiccup-style vocals became part of his instantly recognizable look and sound.

• 1943 - Gloria Gaynor “First Lady of Disco” (age 83), American singer, famous for the empowerment anthem “I Will Survive.”

🧩 Trivia: “I Will Survive” won the only Grammy ever given for Best Disco Recording.

• 1950 - Julie Kavner (age 76), American actress and voice artist, famous as the voice of Marge Simpson on The Simpsons and for her work on Rhoda.

🧩 Trivia: She has voiced Marge since the show’s beginning in 1989.

• 1951 - Chrissie Hynde (age 75), American singer, songwriter, and guitarist, famous as the leader of The Pretenders and hits such as “Brass in Pocket.”

🧩 Trivia: She moved from Ohio to London in the 1970s and helped define the city’s punk and new-wave scene.

• 1956 - Diane Warren "Queen of the American popular song" (age 70), American songwriter, famous for writing massive hits for Celine Dion, Aerosmith, Lady Gaga, and many others.

🧩 Trivia: She has been nominated for an Academy Award more than a dozen times without a win for years, becoming a running awards-show story.

• 1964 - Eazy-E (Eric Lynn Wright), American rapper and producer, famous as a founding member of N.W.A. and a pioneer of gangsta rap.

🧩 Trivia: N.W.A.’s Straight Outta Compton helped bring West Coast hip-hop to a global audience.

• 1967 - Leslie Jones "Les" (age 59), American comedian and actress, famous for Saturday Night Live and films such as Ghostbusters (2016).

🧩 Trivia: She was a stand-up comic for years before joining the SNL cast in her late 40s.

• 1987 - Evan Rachel Wood "Evie" (age 39), American actress, famous for Thirteen and playing Dolores Abernathy on Westworld. 

🧩 Trivia: She began acting as a child and earned major award nominations while still a teenager.

• 1988 - Kevin Love "K-Love" (age 38), American NBA player, famous as a star with the Minnesota Timberwolves and as a champion with the Cleveland Cavaliers.

🧩 Trivia: He is also known for speaking openly about mental health in professional sports.

Notable Deaths  🥀

September 7 has seen the deaths of figures spanning royalty, science, philosophy, Indigenous leadership, music, sports, and humanitarian work. Here is a summary of some of the most notable.

• 1892 — John Greenleaf Whittier (aged 84), American poet, journalist, and abolitionist, best known as one of the Fireside Poets and for his influential anti-slavery poetry, particularly Snow-Bound. Cause of death: illness lasting about a week, followed by unconsciousness; no precise modern medical diagnosis is established.

🧩 Trivia: His 1866 poem Snow-Bound became his most popular work and sold about 20,000 copies.

🧩 Trivia: Whittier helped found the Atlantic Monthly in 1857.

• 1978 — Keith Moon, “Moon the Loon” (aged 32), English drummer and songwriter, best known as the explosive drummer of The Who and for his wild performances and destructive behavior. Cause of death: Accidental clomethiazole (Heminevrin) overdose, prescribed for alcohol-withdrawal symptoms.

🧩 Trivia: Moon joined The Who in 1964 and became famous for an unusually energetic, chaotic drumming style.

🧩 Trivia: He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame posthumously with The Who in 1990.

• 1996 — Bibi Besch (Bibiana Maria Köchert), (aged 54), Austrian-American actress, best known for playing Dr. Carol Marcus in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan, as well as for her roles in Steel Magnolias, Tremors, and numerous television programs. Cause of death: Breast cancer.

🧩 Trivia: Besch received two Primetime Emmy Award nominations during her career.

🧩 Trivia: She appeared in more than 100 film and television productions during her career.

• 1997 — Mobutu Sese Seko (Joseph-Désiré Mobutu), “The Leopard of Zaire” (aged 66), Congolese military officer and politician who ruled Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo) for nearly 32 years. Cause of death: prostate cancer while in exile in Morocco.

🧩 Trivia: Mobutu seized power in a 1965 coup and remained the country's dominant political figure for decades.

🧩 Trivia: His trademark leopard-skin hat became one of the most recognizable symbols of his rule.

🧩 Trivia: His full adopted name, Mobutu Sese Seko Kuku Ngbendu wa Za Banga, was an extremely long honorific name he adopted during his Africanization campaign.

• 2002 — Uziel Gal "Uzi" (aged 78), German-Israeli military engineer and weapons designer, best known as the inventor of the Uzi submachine gun. Cause of death: Cancer.

🧩 Trivia: The Uzi became one of the world's most recognizable submachine guns and was adopted by numerous military and security forces.

🧩 Trivia: Despite designing a famous weapon, Gal reportedly had originally wanted to work in orthopedic medicine.

• 2003 — Warren Zevon, "The Excitable Boy" (aged 56), American rock singer and songwriter, best known for “Werewolves of London,” “Lawyers, Guns and Money,” and “Roland the Headless Thompson Gunner.” Cause of death: mesothelioma, a cancer affecting the lining of the lungs and other organs.

🧩 Trivia: Zevon's final album, The Wind, was released only weeks before his death and later earned multiple Grammy nominations.

🧩 Trivia: “Werewolves of London” became his signature song and remains his best-known recording.

• 2010 — Glenn Shadix (William Glenn Shadix-Scott) (aged 58), American actor and comedian, best known for Beetlejuice and voicing the Mayor of Halloween Town in The Nightmare Before Christmas. Cause of death: blunt-force head trauma from an accidental fall at his home in Birmingham, Alabama.

🧩 Trivia: Shadix worked repeatedly with director Tim Burton, appearing in Beetlejuice, The Nightmare Before Christmas, and Planet of the Apes.

• 2014 — Kwon Ri-se, “RiSe” (aged 23), South Korean-Japanese singer and model, best known as a member of Ladies' Code and for competing in Miss Korea and The Great Birth. Cause of death: Severe injuries from a car crash four days earlier; she died after remaining in a coma.

🧩 Trivia: RiSe represented Japan in the 2009 Miss Korea competition.

🧩 Trivia: Her death occurred only days after fellow Ladies' Code member EunB was killed in the same crash.

• 2018 — Mac Miller (Malcolm James McCormick), “Easy Mac” (26), American rapper and producer, died from accidental mixed-drug toxicity involving fentanyl, cocaine, and ethanol.

🧩 Trivia: His debut album, Blue Slide Park, reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200, making him the first independently distributed debut album to do so since 1995.

🧩 Trivia: His final studio album released during his lifetime, Swimming, came out just one month before his death and debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200.

Note: September 7 is also the date Tupac Shakur was shot in 1996, but he did not die that day—he died six days later, on September 13—so I did not include him in the list.

Sports Highlights  ⚾️

September 7 has produced a wide range of landmark moments across baseball, football, tennis, the Olympics, golf, auto racing, and more. Here is a chronological summary of notable sports events that occurred on this date.

• 1892 - James J. Corbett “Gentleman Jim” knocks out John L. Sullivan “The Boston Strong Boy” in the 21st round in New Orleans to win the world heavyweight boxing title. It was the first title fight under Marquis of Queensberry rules with gloves, and Sullivan’s only career defeat and last fight. 

🧩 Trivia: This fight helped shift boxing from bare-knuckle brawls toward the modern gloved sport. Sullivan entered as a heavy favorite and was considered nearly invincible before the loss.

• 1923 - Howard Ehmke "Bob" of the Boston Red Sox pitches a 4-0 no-hitter against the Philadelphia Athletics. An apparent extra-base hit was ruled an out after the runner missed first base, preserving the no-hitter. 

🧩 Trivia: Ehmke later became famous for his surprising start in the 1929 World Series for the Athletics. No-hitters were rarer in that era of dead-ball baseball and smaller parks.

• 1953 - Maureen Connolly “Little Mo” beats Doris Hart 6-2, 6-4 to win the U.S. Championships and become the first woman to complete the tennis Grand Slam (all four majors in one year). 

🧩 Trivia: She was only 18 years old when she completed the Slam. A horseback-riding accident the following year ended her competitive career at its peak.

• 1960 - The United States sweeps the medals in the men’s discus at the Games of the XVII Olympiad (Rome Olympics), with Al Oerter taking gold (his second of four consecutive Olympic discus titles) ahead of Rink Babka and Dick Cochran. 

🧩 Trivia: Al Oerter is one of only a handful of athletes to win the same individual event at four straight Olympics. The sweep highlighted American field-event strength at those Games.

• 1963 - The Pro Football Hall of Fame is dedicated in Canton, Ohio, with 17 charter members inducted. 

🧩 Trivia: Canton was chosen because the NFL was founded there in 1920. The original class included legends such as Jim "Bright Path" Thorpe, Harold Edward "Red" Grange, and George "Papa Bear" Halas.

• 1980 - John McEnroe “Johnny Mac” beats Björn Borg 7-6, 6-1, 6-7, 5-7, 6-4 to win his second straight U.S. Open men’s title. 

🧩 Trivia: The five-set final was part of one of tennis’s great rivalries. McEnroe’s serve-and-volley style and fiery on-court demeanor defined the era.

• 1986 - Dan Marino “Dan the Man” throws his 100th career touchdown pass, becoming the fastest quarterback in NFL history to reach that mark. 

🧩 Trivia: He reached the milestone in only his 44th NFL game. Marino’s 1984 season (5,084 yards, 48 TDs) still stands as one of the most explosive passing years ever.

• 1998 - Mark McGwire “Big Mac” hits his 61st home run of the season, tying Roger Maris’s single-season record, in a nationally televised game against the Chicago Cubs. Sammy Sosa was in the outfield watching. 

🧩 Trivia: McGwire would break the record the next day with No. 62. That season’s home-run chase with Sosa helped revitalize baseball’s popularity after the 1994 strike.

• 2002 - Serena Williams "Rena" beats older sister Venus Williams "Queen Vee" to win the U.S. Open women’s title, her second at the tournament. 

🧩 Trivia: Sister finals became a signature of the Williams era. Serena would go on to win a record 23 major singles titles in the Open Era.

• 2003 - Andy Roddick "A-Rod" wins his only career Grand Slam title, defeating Juan Carlos "el Mosquito" Ferrero 6-3, 7-6 (2), 6-3 in the U.S. Open men’s final. 

🧩 Trivia: Roddick’s booming serve was the weapon that carried him that fortnight. He reached No. 1 in the world later that year but never added another major.

“This day in history” lists vary by source, but these events are among the most consistently recorded. Labor Day is observed in the U.S. and Canada when the first Monday of September falls on this date. September 7 is Brazil’s Independence Day, commemorating its 1822 declaration of independence from Portugal.

Tomorrow's top stories (September 8th): 🥇 1504 — Michelangelo’s David was unveiled in Florence; 🥈 1941 — The Siege of Leningrad began; 🥉 1974 — President Gerald Ford pardoned Richard Nixon.

“Let the past speak, one day at a time.”

“I was a Republican for most of my adult life. It feels like my party just left me. Surprisingly? On the campaign trail, it feels like most of Arizona is in the same boat.”

Translation: “The people who attend my events and agree with me have confirmed that the people who attend my events and agree with me agree with me.”

Arizona’s electorate, meanwhile, has the indecency to contain more registered Republicans than Democrats—and Mayes’s last statewide victory was a 280-vote squeaker after a recount. But why bother with voter-registration data or election returns when a campaign trail offers the far more reliable science of applause?

“Most of Arizona” did not leave the Republican Party. Kris Mayes left it in 2019, then narrowly won one race as a Democrat. Those are legitimate political choices. What they are not is a statewide referendum proving that Arizona has followed her into the same ideological Uber.

The phrase “it feels like” is doing heroic work here. It is carrying an entire factual claim on its back, uphill, through 1.52 million registered Republicans.
