Care Professional Colleen pointed out that small acts of service often matter greatly for seniors. “I had a new client who hadn’t had a haircut in many months. I found a hairdresser for her, made the appointment and drove her there. She was so happy!” said Colleen, who was honored as the August Care Pro of the Month for owner Michael Lammers’ Home Instead® franchise that assists Colorado seniors in Boulder, Broomfield and northwest Adams Counties.

When announcing Colleen’s honor, Home Instead Recruiting and Engagement Coordinator Brenda Munro said: “Colleen is dedicated, compassionate and reliable, and her clients all love her. Colleen embodies Home Instead’s guiding principles of ‘Build Trust, Take the Lead and Share Your Heart.’ For Colleen, touching lives impacts her soul, whether she is providing physical help such as light housekeeping, meal preparation, medication reminders or personal care or if she is offering emotional support in a companionship role.”

Colleen joined Home Instead in April, just four months before achieving her Care Pro of the Month status. “I had interviewed a couple of in-home caregivers who said Home Instead has a good reputation among families and caregivers,” Colleen said. “In my last job, I worked for a medical device company and was very inspired by the company’s commitment to providing safe and effective products to patients.”

Colleen also was motivated to seek a one-on-one care job by helping a friend who found herself in a challenging medical situation. “I took turns, with a couple of other people, in caring for a dear friend while she was on hospice and her husband was going through cancer treatment. She shared with me her emotional journey from thinking she would get better to ultimately accepting her death. She inspired me to pursue caregiving,” Colleen explained.

Colleen’s job fulfillment comes in several different forms. “What I like most about my Care Pro job is learning from my clients. For instance, from ‘It’s OK to store salted butter on the kitchen counter’ to all the ways clients face new limitations with grace,” Colleen said.

Colleen is an important part of the Care Pro team at the Front Range franchise in Louisville, a member of a network comprised of Home Instead, Inc. and its parent company, Honor. With the world’s largest home-care network and the most advanced care platform, Honor and Home Instead are revolutionizing care for older adults, their families and Care Pros. Combined, the network has more than 100,000 Care Pros who are meeting the growing needs of millions of older adults and their families worldwide.

In addition to their strong companionship skills, the Colorado franchise’s Care Pros provide safety assurance, and transportation and errands. Each Care Pro offers personal assistance with grooming, dressing, bathing, cognitive impairment, hospice and mobility support. By expertly doing so, the Care Pros not only assist their clients, but help their families eliminate worry, reduce stress and re-establish personal freedom.

🚨 TRUMP’S ‘NEW AMERICA’ MAP SPARKS BACKLASH ACROSS NEW MEXICO.

ALBUQUERQUE, UNITED STATES - President Donald Trump ignited a political uproar after posting an image that crossed out “Mexico” in New Mexico’s name and replaced it with “America,” effectively labeling the state “New America.” The image, shared on his Truth Social account and later reposted by the White House, showed a red X slashed across the word “Mexico” on a state map, with “America” written underneath.

The post followed a viral online hoax earlier in the week that falsely claimed he had signed an executive order to rename the state. Fact-checkers traced the rumor to a satirical social media account, but the claim spread widely before being debunked.

Trump doubled down late Sunday, writing that “many people suggested” changing the name of New Mexico, calling it “one of the greatest vote cheating states of all time” and insisting the new name would be “more prestigious and beautiful.”

State leaders from both parties swiftly rejected the idea. Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham reminded the public that New Mexico’s name predates the United States, while other officials pointed to the state’s deep Indigenous and Hispanic heritage. Lawmakers also noted Trump’s recent pattern of rebranding geographic landmarks, including federal renamings of Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico.

The White House has offered no explanation for reposting the image, and no formal renaming effort exists. Under U.S. law, a president cannot unilaterally change a state’s name.

What was the Court of the Gentiles in the Jewish temple?
Answer

Herod’s temple, destroyed along with the rest of Jerusalem by the Romans in AD 70, contained four separate “courts,” separated from one another and each designed for a different purpose: the Court of the Gentiles, the Court of the Women, the Court of Israel (or the Court of Men), and the Court of Priests. The Court of the Gentiles is referred to as “the outer court” in Revelation 11:2.

The Court of the Gentiles was the outermost courtyard and the only area of the temple where non-Jews were allowed. As its name implies, the Court of the Gentiles was accessible to Gentiles, foreigners, and those who were considered impure. There, worshippers could mill about, exchange money, and even buy animals for sacrifices. It was from the Court of the Gentiles that Jesus, on two occasions (John 2:13–17; Matthew 21:12–13), drove out the money changers, declaring, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a den of robbers” (Matthew 21:13). The Court of the Women, the only area of the temple complex in which women could worship, contained the poor boxes. One of these boxes was where the poor widow offered her two mites (Luke 21:1–4). Ceremonially clean Jewish men could enter the Court of Israel, and the Court of Priests, where the altar stood, was accessible only to Levitical priests.

Non-Jews were allowed to enter the Court of the Gentiles, but they were forbidden to go any farther than the outer court. The inner temple courtyards were enclosed by a balustrade, and at the entrances to it notices were posted in both Greek and Latin, warning foreigners and uncircumcised persons that crossing into one of the other courtyards was punishable by death. One of those ancient notices is now on display in a museum in Istanbul. On Paul’s last visit to Jerusalem, some Jews stirred up a crowd and grabbed Paul in the temple, alleging that he had taken Trophimus, a Gentile, into one of the forbidden courtyards (Acts 21:27–29). Paul was innocent of the charge, but the mob beat him with the intent to kill him; it was the quick action of a Roman garrison commander that preserved Paul’s life on that occasion (verses 30–34).

The Knights Templar
From A Brief Historical Description by Professor Sir John Baker QC LLD FBA
Master of the Bench

The history of the Temple begins soon after the middle of the twelfth century, when a contingent of knights of the Military Order of the Temple of Solomon in Jerusalem moved from the Old Temple in Holborn (later Southampton House) to a larger site between Fleet Street and the banks of the River Thames. The new site originally included much of what is now Lincoln’s Inn, and the knights were probably responsible for establishing New Street (later Chancery Lane), which led from Holborn down to their new quarters. Following their custom, the knights built a round church patterned on the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. An inscription on the Round recorded that it was consecrated by the Patriarch Heraclius on 10 February 1185, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary. It is thought that King Henry II was also present on that day, inaugurating a long association between the royal family and the Temple.

Among the other buildings erected by the knights were dormitories, storehouses, stables, chambers, and two dining halls, one of them in the consecrated central portion and connected with the church by a cloister. It was a house fit for kings to stay in, and several did so. During a visit by King John in January 1215 he received a deputation of barons demanding a charter of liberties; and when the Great Charter was signed later in the year, the Master of the Temple was one of the witnesses. The knights took advantage of their special privileges to make their sanctuary a safe place for depositing treasure, and during the thirteenth century the New Temple became a busy financial centre. It was no doubt during this period that the first handful of lawyers came to live in the Temple, not as distinct societies but as legal advisers to a wealthy international organisation. The Templars thrived, adding to their round church a fine nave, which was consecrated in the presence of King Henry III in 1240. Many knights associated with the order were buried in the church, the most distinguished being William Marshal (d. 1219), first Earl of Pembroke and regent of England, the very model of medieval English chivalry, and one of the instigators of Magna Carta. Marshal’s armoured effigy, battered by time and war, may still be seen in the Round.

After losing the Holy Land in the 1290s, the order of the Temple fell into a decline. The knights were dubiously accused of improprieties, and in 1312 their order was dissolved. Although the pope granted their estates to the Knights Hospitaller of St John of Jerusalem, King Edward II seized the New Temple as forfeit to the Crown. Nevertheless, the consecrated portion was conceded to the Hospitallers, and the remainder was sold to them later.

 We are faced here with the question whether claims for losses allegedly suffered at the hands of a Nazi puppet regime during World War II are cognizable in our courts today.   Because these claims, at least superficially, touch on foreign relations and potentially controversial political issues, it is tempting to jump to the conclusion that such claims are barred by the political question doctrine.   The Supreme Court has counseled, however, that “it is error to suppose that every case or controversy which touches foreign relations lies beyond judicial cognizance.”  Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186, 211, 82 S.Ct. 691, 7 L.Ed.2d 663 (1962).   The justiciability inquiry is limited to “ ‘political questions,’ not ․ ‘political cases,’ ” id. at 217, 82 S.Ct. 691, and should be made on a “case-by-case” basis, id. at 211, 82 S.Ct. 691.

Our conclusion is rooted in the principles of Baker v. Carr. Despite the dissent's cataclysmic and speculative projections about the sweep of our opinion, our decision boils down to letting the common law property claims proceed to the next stage and foreclosing the political, human rights, and war-related claims.   In so doing, we respect the limits of our jurisdiction as a national court, recognize the role of the Executive in foreign relations, and stick to our role of interpreting the law.

Sea power is not only about how much firepower a navy can deploy but how long it can sustain it.

Private health insurance in Canada exists, but it is legally prohibited from competing with the core government system, and no one can opt out of funding the government system through taxes.

1. What Private Insurance Is Actually Allowed to Cover

Under the federal Canada Health Act, private insurance is strictly supplemental, not comprehensive.

What Private Plans Cover: Prescription drugs, routine dental care, optometry/glasses, physical therapy, and private hospital room upgrades. Many Canadian employers offer benefits packages for these supplemental services.

What Private Plans CANNOT Cover ("Duplicative Insurance"): In most provinces (representing about 90% of the population), it is illegal for private insurance companies to sell policies covering "medically necessary" hospital or physician services—such as heart surgery, knee replacements, cancer treatments, or visits to a family doctor.
The Monopsony Lock-in: The government intentionally bans private competition for core medical care to prevent a "two-tier" market. They do not want doctors leaving the public system to work in higher-paying private clinics, so they legally outlaw an independent private insurance market for core services.
2. Can You Opt Out of Paying the Taxes?

No. Absolutely not.

Healthcare in Canada is not funded via an optional premium; it is financed directly through general taxation (federal and provincial personal income taxes, sales taxes/GST/PST, and corporate taxes).

There is no mechanism to "opt out" or claim a tax exemption. Even if a Canadian citizen pays out-of-pocket at a private surgical clinic or flies to Tampa, Florida, to get a hip replacement to avoid a 12-month wait list, they still must pay every penny of their Canadian taxes that fund the public Medicare system.

3. The Irony of the Left's Argument
When single-payer advocates point out that "over 60% of Canadians have private health insurance," they rely on a deliberate sleight of hand:

They're Buying What the Government Refuses to Cover: People carry private insurance specifically because Canada’s socialized system does not cover prescription drugs, teeth, or routine vision at 100%.

Canada Is an Outlier Even Among Universal Systems: Countries like the UK (NHS), Australia, France, and Germany allow parallel private health insurance where citizens can pay to skip public wait times and see private doctors. Canada is one of the only high-income nations in the world that actively outlaws private insurance for core medical care.

Patients Are Trapped: Because private insurance for core care is banned and doctors are heavily restricted from dual practice, Canadian patients facing severe rationing and wait times have two choices: wait in line for the government system, or pay tens of thousands of dollars in cash out-of-pocket in the U.S. or overseas.

text:
A ten year old testified against her school system, then walked home scared her teachers would be mad at her. Katherine Carper had it backwards, because those teachers treated her exactly the same and never let on. Every step that case took toward winning was a step toward their own dismissal letters, and they knew it long before she did. You will not find one of their names on the anniversary.

On a morning in March 1953, a young teacher in Topeka, Kansas walked into her classroom and taught the whole day out. She taught nearly every subject in that room, because that is how the city ran the four schools it kept for Black children.

Her name was Darla Buchanan, and she was one of twenty-seven. By September she would not have a job, and she already knew it.

The letter had come from the superintendent's office and it was dated the thirteenth of March. It did not accuse her of anything, which is what made it impossible to answer.

Topeka's four schools for Black children were called Buchanan, McKinley, Monroe and Washington. In 1953 those four buildings held more than seven hundred children, and twenty-seven teachers carried all of it.

Kansas had never required any of this. A law written in 1879 allowed cities of more than fifteen thousand people to separate their elementary schools if they cared to, and Topeka cared to.

Keeping the children apart cost the city money it did not have to spend. In 1950 the four Black schools sat with an average of a hundred and forty-three empty pupil spaces each while the white schools averaged twenty-eight, and Topeka left the room empty rather than fill it.

So the buildings were decent, the equipment was adequate, and the teaching was better than adequate. At two of those four schools, more teachers held a master's degree than at any white grade school in the city.

You can see them. Somebody photographed the whole staff in 1949, twenty-one adults in two rows, and typed every single name underneath, standing row then seated row, the way you would label a family.

The man on the end of the top row is Merrill Ross, born in Kentucky in 1919, the only son of Richard Ross of Flat Lick and Pineville. He took a bachelor's and a master's in science at Pittsburg State, and he earned a pilot's license there through a civilian training program before the Army ever wanted him.

He came to Topeka in the summer of 1944 to take a teaching job, and his call to serve arrived the same season. He used the license he already had to get himself into the Tuskegee pilot training program, and he finished it.

The roster shows him graduating in the class of 45-I, commissioned a second lieutenant on the twenty-ninth of January 1946. They were preparing to send him overseas when the war ended, so he never flew a mission.

He came home to Topeka and went into a classroom instead. Ross is the only African American who taught in all four of the Black schools, Washington and Buchanan and Monroe and McKinley, every one of them.

Mamie Williams stands four faces to his left. She was born in Greenwood, South Carolina in 1894, and her family moved to Topeka in 1899 and bought a house on Quincy Street.

She never left Quincy Street. In 1911 she was one of three African American graduates in a Topeka High School class of ninety-two.

She went to Washburn and took honors in mathematics and German, then earned a master's degree at the University of Kansas. She taught twenty-five and a half years at Buchanan School.

In 1943 the district moved her to Washington as assistant principal, and she went on to serve as principal of both Washington and Monroe. They gave her the title and no raise.

She carried her full teaching load the entire time she was running the building. She wrote four books on Black history in the Topeka schools, at a time when the district was not asking for any.

One of her former pupils, Linda Brown, described her later as a brilliant woman. She called her a staunch, old-time teacher who really made you apply yourself, and said Williams would explain something and then stay with you until she was certain you had it.

The child whose family name is on the most famous school case in American history was taught by these women, and she remembered them by name for the rest of her life.

Another Buchanan pupil, Darlene Jackson, put it plainly at a reunion seventy-five years later. She said she loved them so dearly that their names stuck with her.

The teachers lived where the children lived. They went to the same churches, they knew the parents, and one McKinley teacher drove to a boy's house and collected him for school when he could not get there himself.

Every one of them could also see what integration would mean for their own employment. One Topeka teacher explained her opposition to it with a single question, which was whether white people would have her teach their children.

She was not being cynical. She was reading the town correctly, and she turned out to be right.

The lawsuit that proved her right did not start with a father at a schoolhouse door.

It started with Lucinda Todd, who had been a Topeka teacher until 1935, when the city's rule against employing married women ended her career. She was pushed out of the profession and stayed inside the fight for it.

Her daughter Nancy was learning piano and violin. When Topeka gathered its elementary schools for a district concert, the four Black schools were left off the program, and a child trained in music was not permitted to go and sing.

Todd took it to the NAACP and became branch secretary in 1948. Meetings happened at her house on Jewell Avenue, around the dining room table, and when teacher friends came by she pulled the shades down.

Being seen in that room was a risk a woman with a contract could not casually take.

In August 1950 she wrote to Walter White at the national NAACP office in New York. She told him the branch had decided to test the permissible law they had there in Kansas.

McKinley Burnett, the branch president, had already spent roughly two years asking the Topeka board to integrate on its own. The lawsuit was what was left when the asking failed.

Thirteen parents agreed to stand up for twenty children. Each was told to watch the paper for enrollment dates, take their child to the nearest white school, bring a witness, try to enroll, and come back and report.

Not one of them expected to be let in.

In September 1950 a thirty-two year old union welder for the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe walked his seven year old daughter up the steps at Sumner Elementary, seven blocks from their house. Linda waited in the hall while her father went into the office, and she could hear the voices rise through the door.

Oliver Brown came out upset. He was still upset when he got home, and he did not tell her what had been said.

Twelve of the thirteen plaintiffs who made that walk were women. One of them was also named Brown, Darlene, whose daughter Saundria was in the same suit.

The case took the man's name.

They filed on the twenty-eighth of February 1951. Trial opened in Topeka that June, in front of three federal judges.

Oliver Brown was so nervous on the stand that Judge Huxman had to tell him to speak up. He got the story out.

Lena Carper's daughter Katherine was ten years old, and they put her on the stand next. She sat where the grown men had been sitting.

She answered the questions. Then she went home, and what she worried about afterward was not the judges and not the school board.

She worried about her teachers.

She wondered whether they were going to be mad at her for what she said before all those people.

They were not. She said later that her teachers were exactly the same to her, and that she had great teachers.

The woman at the front of that classroom already knew what a win would cost her. She gave a frightened ten year old no sign of it.

Then Silas Hardrick Fleming took the stand.

He lived at 522 Liberty. His sons were ten and seven, Silas Junior and Duane Dean, and they went to Washington school ten or twelve blocks away and got there on the East Tenth Street bus.

He answered the routine questions about distances and bus routes, the way the others had. Then he asked the court for something nobody had offered him.

He wanted to say why he had joined the lawsuit. The lawyers went back and forth about whether a plaintiff was allowed to do that, and Judge Huxman told him to go ahead and tell it.

What Fleming said first was not about buildings or buses. He said it was not to cast any insinuation that their teachers could not teach their children.

His words for those teachers were supreme, extremely intelligent, and he said they were capable of teaching his kids or white kids or Black kids. Only then did he explain that he wanted the children brought up together from infancy, because his whole race was craving light.

A father in a segregated Kansas courtroom used part of his one turn on the stand to defend the women who taught his sons. He did it before he said a word about his own children.

Two years later the school district would put those women on notice.

The parents also put on a psychologist from the University of Kansas named Louisa Holt, who had one child already in the Topeka schools and another starting in September.

Holt told the court that the harm was not the separation by itself, it was that the law made the separation official. State sanction, she said, is read by everybody, white and Black, as a ruling that one group is lesser, and a child who absorbs that carries it into everything he tries to learn.

Richard Kluger recorded what happened when she stepped down. One of the Black mothers sitting in that courtroom brought her children over to Louisa Holt and asked whether they could shake her hand.

Then the school district answered.

Kenneth McFarland had run Topeka's schools and had fought to keep the elementary schools segregated. He had resigned before the trial over a financial matter, and he came into that courtroom as the former superintendent.

Asked whether there was any difference in how the two sets of schools were operated, McFarland said nothing was done on the basis of color, and that the children were merely treated as individuals.

He said it about a system that sorted six year olds by race and bused them across town to do it, and no lawyer in the room laughed.

On the third of August 1951, the court ruled against the parents.

It had to. Three years later the Supreme Court described the Kansas judges as a court that had felt compelled to rule against the plaintiffs, which is the most polite way anyone has ever written down that a judge knew he was wrong.

On their way out those judges found as a fact that the buildings, the courses of study, and the qualification and quality of the teachers were comparable across the two sets of schools. A federal court examined Topeka's Black teachers and certified in writing that they were the equal of anyone in the city.

And Judge Walter Huxman wrote the sentence that would eventually end segregation in America. He put it plainly, that a sense of inferiority affects the motivation of a child to learn.

Earl Warren lifted that finding almost word for word into the opinion of the Supreme Court, changing two words in brackets and nothing else.

So Topeka is the case that forced the real question. There was no crumbling roof to argue about and no ruined curriculum to point at, and once the tangible things were off the table the only thing left to examine was separation itself.

The excellence of those four staff rooms took away segregation's easiest excuse. That is the service nobody has ever thanked them for.

Now go back to the letter in Darla Buchanan's hands.

Wendell Godwin had replaced McFarland as superintendent, and in March 1953 he wrote to teachers hired within the previous two years. He opened by saying that because next year's enrollment in the schools for Negro children was uncertain, he could not offer them employment.

Then he explained why. If the Supreme Court struck segregation down, the board would proceed on the assumption that most people in Topeka would not want Negro teachers standing in front of white children.

His line was that her services would not be needed for next year.

He added one more thought, and it is the coldest part. He presumed the city would still need some schools for Negro children, and would keep some Negro teachers on to teach in those.

Fourteen months before the ruling, the district was already planning both the integration of its children and the replacement of its teachers.

The same office did both.

None of this took the twenty-seven by surprise. They had watched it happen once already.

In 1941 a Topeka family had won the Graham case and desegregated the city's junior high schools. Eight Black teachers lost their jobs behind that victory.

So every Black teacher in Topeka understood the arithmetic long before the lawyers did. Win, and the children get the school across the street.

Win, and you are the price.

One of the twenty-seven set it down herself forty years afterward. In an oral history recorded in November 1991, Barbara Ross said practically all of them held master's degrees, and that when the city wanted integration nobody stopped to consider what it would do to a Black teacher who was fully qualified.

She said the Black community stayed quiet about it. She said it put a terrible strain on them, and that nobody seemed to mind whether they had jobs or not.

That is her assessment and not mine. It is the assessment of somebody who was standing in the room at the time.

What the twenty-seven did not do was turn on the case.

In May 1953 the Kansas Congress of Colored Parents and Teachers sent the Topeka board a letter setting out why every teacher was needed and why it was unfair to shut Black teachers out, whatever the Supreme Court decided. It survives in the Sumner High School Collection at the University of Kansas.

They put it on paper a year before the Supreme Court did.

That autumn the board adopted a graduated plan to desegregate the city's schools by September 1955. The ruling had not come yet.

It came at noon on the seventeenth of May 1954.

Leola Brown was ironing with the television on when the program broke for the news. Her daughter remembered her father saying thanks be unto God, over and over, and remembered his tears.

That year Katherine Carper was in her first year at Capper Junior High. She had come from an all-Black school with all-Black teachers, and she walked into a building where the children and the teachers were all white, and the friends she had known since kindergarten had been sent somewhere else.

She described the first weeks as feeling lost and afraid. A red-haired girl named Mary and her friend Janice came and sat with her, and they ate lunch out on the school lawn.

That is what the victory felt like from inside a twelve year old.

In four staff rooms across town the broadcast landed differently again. The women in those rooms had spent three years being described in a federal courtroom as the equal of anyone in Topeka, and some of them had a letter in a drawer saying that equality would not be needed.

Dorothy Scott was one of the teachers who stayed. In an interview recorded in January 1992 she said she believed she was the third Black teacher assigned to a white elementary school in Topeka, a building called Parkdale.

After she started there, the principal told her something he seemed to think was reassuring. He had gone around the neighborhood asking the white families whether they minded a Black teacher coming to their school, and only one person had objected.

She had a master's degree, years of her own classroom behind her, and a neighborhood that had been canvassed about whether she could come.

Here is the count. In 1953 Topeka had twenty-seven Black teachers for more than seven hundred Black children.

By 1956 there were eight hundred and ninety-eight Black children in the system and twenty-one Black teachers left.

Some went to California. Some went to Washington.

The state of Kansas will tell you plainly that nobody ever compiled the figures on what happened to the twenty-seven. Across Southern and border states in the years after the ruling, historians estimate that roughly thirty-eight thousand Black teachers and administrators lost their positions.

Topeka was the quiet version of a thing that happened everywhere.

Not all of them went under, and the record is clearest about the ones who did not.

Merrill Ross, the pilot they never sent overseas, taught until 1954 and then became principal of Washington Elementary, one of the four. He held it for eight years.

Then Topeka made him the first African American to run a predominantly white school in the city. He led Avondale West from 1962, then Sheldon, and he retired in 1985 as principal of Quinton Heights.

He died in 2012, having spent forty years inside the school system that sent his colleagues those letters. He outlasted every administrator who signed one.

The four buildings went four different ways.

Washington, the school Merrill Ross ran and the school Fleming's sons rode the bus to, was torn down for a street expansion. McKinley stands empty, and one of its old pupils says he still drives over as an old man to sit and look at it.

Buchanan houses other organizations now. Monroe closed in 1975 when the enrollment fell away, and spent years as a warehouse, then a parking lot for school buses and maintenance vehicles, then a community center, then a warehouse again.

In 1990 Monroe went up for auction.

Oliver Brown's family and their neighbors had founded the Brown Foundation two years earlier. They feared the building would be knocked down, so they brought in the Trust for Public Land to buy it.

In 1992 a federal law made Monroe a national historic site.

On the seventeenth of May 2004, fifty years to the day, it opened to the public as a museum about the case.

So the record kept the buildings. It kept the ruling, the plaque, the anniversary, the name of one welder who was one of thirteen.

It did not keep the payroll. But it kept the photograph.

That 1949 picture of Topeka's Black teachers sits in the National Park Service's own gallery, at the site built inside the school where several of them worked. Every face in it has a name typed underneath, in order, standing row and then seated row.

Somebody who is dead now took the trouble to write them all down.

Go and find the caption. Read it slowly, the way you would read a roll call.

Standing, left to right: Merrill Ross, Myrtle Starnes, Edna Vance, Fannie Palton, Mamie Williams, Eva Walker, Harrison Caldwell, Ethel Barbour, J. B. Holland, Ida Norman the school nurse, Althea McBrier.

Seated, left to right: Katherine King, Dorothy Bradshaw, Mildred North, Geraldine Gilliam, Minerva Washington, Ada Eggleston, Barbara Ross, Dorothy Crawford, Doris Love, Julia Patterson.

Seventh from the left in the seated row is a woman who was twenty-three years old when that shutter went.

On the fifteenth of August this year, Barbara Ross turned one hundred years old. They filled a ballroom in Largo, Maryland for her, and she is still recognized as Topeka's oldest living Black educator.

Joe Anderson came. He is eighty-three now, and he was in her second-grade class at Washington School before the ruling, and what he wanted to say about her was that the academic foundation he has always had started with them.

He also said that Mrs. Ross and the other Black teachers were the ones who eased the children through the integration nobody had prepared them for. They were managing that transition at the same time they were reading letters about their own contracts.

Barbara Ross gave twenty-seven years to Topeka's children, second grade and kindergarten, and when a historian asked her about all of it at ninety-eight she did not spend the answer on the letters. She said it was time for integration and it should have happened sooner.

Nobody ever counted what the ruling cost the twenty-seven. That is the one thing in this story that is still open, because one of them is a hundred years old and can still be asked.

text:
IDM vs. Fabless vs. Foundry : Who Creates OSAT Demand? 

1. IDM ( Integrated Device Manufacturer)
IDMs such as Intel, Texas Instruments and STMicroelectronics design and manufacture their own chips. Historically, they have also handled much of the packaging and testing themselves.

That doesn't mean they never use OSATs. They may outsource when internal capacity is tight, when outsourcing is more economical than adding capacity, or when they need packaging capabilities that they don't have in-house.

So, for an IDM, OSAT is more of a capacity and capability option than a necessity.

2. Fabless: The Strongest OSAT Demand Driver
Fabless companies such as NVIDIA, Qualcomm, AMD and MediaTek design chips but don't own fabs. They rely on foundries to manufacture their wafers and external partners for much of the assembly, packaging and testing.

This makes the fabless model particularly important for OSATs. As more semiconductor value moves toward fabless companies, more of the manufacturing process sits outside the chip designer's own organisation.

For an OSAT, this is the most natural customer base: companies that need backend manufacturing but don't want to build and operate it themselves.

3. Foundry + OSAT :  The Traditional Setup
For a conventional semiconductor product, the foundry manufactures the wafer and the packaged chip is completed by an external OSAT.

This division of work has historically been straightforward: the foundry focuses on wafer fabrication, while the OSAT handles assembly, packaging and testing.

The interesting part is what happens as packaging becomes more sophisticated.

TSMC Changes the Equation
TSMC is increasingly doing more than just manufacturing wafers. Its advanced packaging capabilities, particularly CoWoS and InFO, allow it to offer wafer fabrication and advanced packaging as part of a more integrated solution.

This matters because advanced packaging is becoming an increasingly important part of semiconductor performance, particularly in AI and high-performance computing.

For OSAT Players, this is a key point .
Advanced packaging expands the potential value pool for the backend, but it also gives leading foundries a reason to capture more of that value themselves.

Dinesh is wicked and will used equivocation to lead you astray, you don't get to have your own definitions especially with doctrines formed 500 years ago.

It's fundamentally dishonest to do so.

In Reformed theology the word decree (Latin decretum, often used interchangeably with “counsel,” “purpose,” or “plan”) does not mean a moral command or a legal edict. 

It means God’s eternal, free, wise, and unchangeable determination of whatsoever comes to pass.

The standard Reformed definition
The most widely used formulation is that of the Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 7):

The decrees of God are his eternal purpose, according to the counsel of his will, whereby, for his own glory, he hath foreordained whatsoever comes to pass.

The Westminster Confession of Faith (3.1) expands it:

God from all eternity did, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass; yet so as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.

The same language appears, with only minor variations, in the 1689 London Baptist Confession and other Reformed standards.

Key features that Reformed writers always emphasize:
It is one decree (a single eternal act of the divine will), even though we speak of “decrees” in the plural for our limited understanding.

It is eternal and unconditional—not based on anything God foresaw in the creature.

It encompasses everything: creation, providence, the Fall, election, reprobation, and every particular event.
It does not make God the author of sin, nor does it cancel human responsibility or the reality of second causes.

Calvin’s own usage
Calvin uses “decree” both for the comprehensive plan of God and, more specifically, for predestination.

His classic definition of predestination (Institutes 3.21.5) is:

We call predestination God’s eternal decree, by which he determined with himself what he willed to become of each man. For all are not created in equal condition; rather, eternal life is foreordained for some, eternal damnation for others.

He also speaks of the broader decree that governs all events: nothing happens except through God’s “certain and unchangeable decree,” and God “from the remotest eternity decreed what he would do, and now by his own power executes what he has decreed.”

In short, when Reformed theologians and Calvin himself say “the decree of God,” they mean God’s eternal, sovereign purpose that renders certain everything that actually occurs in time, while leaving the moral character of creaturely actions intact.

What was the Court of the Gentiles in the Jewish temple?
Answer

Herod’s temple, destroyed along with the rest of Jerusalem by the Romans in AD 70, contained four separate “courts,” separated from one another and each designed for a different purpose: the Court of the Gentiles, the Court of the Women, the Court of Israel (or the Court of Men), and the Court of Priests. The Court of the Gentiles is referred to as “the outer court” in Revelation 11:2.

The Court of the Gentiles was the outermost courtyard and the only area of the temple where non-Jews were allowed. As its name implies, the Court of the Gentiles was accessible to Gentiles, foreigners, and those who were considered impure. There, worshippers could mill about, exchange money, and even buy animals for sacrifices. It was from the Court of the Gentiles that Jesus, on two occasions (John 2:13–17; Matthew 21:12–13), drove out the money changers, declaring, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a den of robbers” (Matthew 21:13). The Court of the Women, the only area of the temple complex in which women could worship, contained the poor boxes. One of these boxes was where the poor widow offered her two mites (Luke 21:1–4). Ceremonially clean Jewish men could enter the Court of Israel, and the Court of Priests, where the altar stood, was accessible only to Levitical priests.

Non-Jews were allowed to enter the Court of the Gentiles, but they were forbidden to go any farther than the outer court. The inner temple courtyards were enclosed by a balustrade, and at the entrances to it notices were posted in both Greek and Latin, warning foreigners and uncircumcised persons that crossing into one of the other courtyards was punishable by death. One of those ancient notices is now on display in a museum in Istanbul. On Paul’s last visit to Jerusalem, some Jews stirred up a crowd and grabbed Paul in the temple, alleging that he had taken Trophimus, a Gentile, into one of the forbidden courtyards (Acts 21:27–29). Paul was innocent of the charge, but the mob beat him with the intent to kill him; it was the quick action of a Roman garrison commander that preserved Paul’s life on that occasion (verses 30–34).

The history of the Temple begins soon after the middle of the twelfth century, when a contingent of knights of the Military Order of the Temple of Solomon in Jerusalem moved from the Old Temple in Holborn (later Southampton House) to a larger site between Fleet Street and the banks of the River Thames. The new site originally included much of what is now Lincoln’s Inn, and the knights were probably responsible for establishing New Street (later Chancery Lane), which led from Holborn down to their new quarters. Following their custom, the knights built a round church patterned on the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. An inscription on the Round recorded that it was consecrated by the Patriarch Heraclius on 10 February 1185, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary. It is thought that King Henry II was also present on that day, inaugurating a long association between the royal family and the Temple.

Among the other buildings erected by the knights were dormitories, storehouses, stables, chambers, and two dining halls, one of them in the consecrated central portion and connected with the church by a cloister. It was a house fit for kings to stay in, and several did so. During a visit by King John in January 1215 he received a deputation of barons demanding a charter of liberties; and when the Great Charter was signed later in the year, the Master of the Temple was one of the witnesses. The knights took advantage of their special privileges to make their sanctuary a safe place for depositing treasure, and during the thirteenth century the New Temple became a busy financial centre. It was no doubt during this period that the first handful of lawyers came to live in the Temple, not as distinct societies but as legal advisers to a wealthy international organisation. The Templars thrived, adding to their round church a fine nave, which was consecrated in the presence of King Henry III in 1240. Many knights associated with the order were buried in the church, the most distinguished being William Marshal (d. 1219), first Earl of Pembroke and regent of England, the very model of medieval English chivalry, and one of the instigators of Magna Carta. Marshal’s armoured effigy, battered by time and war, may still be seen in the Round.

After losing the Holy Land in the 1290s, the order of the Temple fell into a decline. The knights were dubiously accused of improprieties, and in 1312 their order was dissolved. The Swiss Guard is recognised by its Renaissance-era dress uniform, consisting of a tunic striped in red, dark blue, and yellow; high plumed helmet; and traditional weapons such as the halberd. Guardsmen perform their protective duties in functional attire and with modern firearms. Since the assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II in 1981, the Guard has placed greater emphasis on its nonceremonial roles and has sought more training in anti-irregular military counterintelligence, commando-style raids, counter-sniper tactics, counterterrorism, close-quarters battle, defusing and disposal of bombs, executive protection, hostage rescue, human intelligence, medical evacuation, reconnaissance, tactical driving, tactical medical services, and tactical fast shooting by small arms.

ALPERIN v. VATICAN BANK IOR OFM HOP (2005)
United States Court of Appeals,Ninth Circuit.

Nos. 03-16166, 03-15208.
Decided: April 18, 2005
Before TROTT, McKEOWN, Circuit Judges, and SHADUR, Senior District Judge.*
Kathryn Lee Boyd, Pepperdine University Law School, Malibu, CA;  Jonathan H. Levy, Cincinnati, OH;  Thomas Easton, Eugene, OR, for the plaintiffs-appellants. Jeffrey S. Lena, Law Offices of Jeffrey S. Lena, Berkeley, CA, for defendant-appellee Istituto per le Opere di Religione, sued as the Vatican Bank. Paul E. Vallone, Hinshaw & Culbertson, San Francisco, CA, for defendant-appellee Order of Friars Minor.
AMENDED OPINION AND AMENDED CONCURRENCE/DISSENT

 We are faced here with the question whether claims for losses allegedly suffered at the hands of a Nazi puppet regime during World War II are cognizable in our courts today.   Because these claims, at least superficially, touch on foreign relations and potentially controversial political issues, it is tempting to jump to the conclusion that such claims are barred by the political question doctrine.   The Supreme Court has counseled, however, that “it is error to suppose that every case or controversy which touches foreign relations lies beyond judicial cognizance.”  Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186, 211, 82 S.Ct. 691, 7 L.Ed.2d 663 (1962).   The justiciability inquiry is limited to “ ‘political questions,’ not ․ ‘political cases,’ ” id. at 217, 82 S.Ct. 691, and should be made on a “case-by-case” basis, id. at 211, 82 S.Ct. 691.

Our conclusion is rooted in the principles of Baker v. Carr. Despite the dissent's cataclysmic and speculative projections about the sweep of our opinion, our decision boils down to letting the common law property claims proceed to the next stage and foreclosing the political, human rights, and war-related claims.   In so doing, we respect the limits of our jurisdiction as a national court, recognize the role of the Executive in foreign relations, and stick to our role of interpreting the law.

text:
True Tesla cultists are egomaniacs: “If you want to be special, be like me…”
There are plenty of genuine, wholesome Tesla fans and creators who will never get invited to events simply because they offer honest, constructive criticism. That doesn’t move units, so it’s a nonstarter. The inner circle thrives on blind loyalty and total devotion to the badge.

To be accepted, you practically have to host a revival on a mountaintop.

The best marketing doesn't come from screaming the loudest. That hype works for a while, but eventually people catch on and look for fresh perspectives and real competition. Tesla is Nike in the 90s. Back then, people obsessed over Jordans purely for the cultural clout. Did they make you jump higher? No, it was a status symbol. Elon tapped into that exact psychology, but as the market matures, the rest of the industry is catching up fast.

Let the build quality and performance speak for itself. When you engineer a genuinely superior product, you don't need a circus. Yet the moment a real competitor emerges, the playbook shifts to hostility and trying to crush them. That's their version of "capitalism."

Some of the best automotive content comes from smaller creators driven by real passion, not vanity metrics. Not everyone wants to be the MrBeast of tech, chasing algorithms at any ethical cost.

Tesla doesn't want critics; they want yes men. They want people who blindly trust the executive of a publicly traded company who views them purely as retail capital. Selling beta software for a decade inflated a stock price to enrich a tiny circle. If you got rich off the run, good for you, but it came at the cost of normalizing the vaporware peddling tech CEO.

A retweet from Elon has become a lifetime achievement for people begging for scraps beneath the king’s table.
Money, power, and clout are fleeting human impulses that vanish the moment you're gone. Build a reputation on honesty. Never compromise your integrity just to win approval from people and corporations that will never care about you.

Like Tyler Durden said, “…The people I meet on each flight? They're single serving friends. Between takeoff and landing we have our time together, but that's all we get.”

Don't spend your whole life being a single serving asset to a brand.

text:
A British podcaster visits Cape Town once, falls in love with the place and spontaneously buys a mansion. He then doubles the price and puts it back on the market. Some people might call it the classic capital growth that Cape Town property offers. To me, it looks like the looting of one of Cape Town's wealthiest suburbs.

The house in question is on the slopes of Table Mountain, and it exposes everything we still have not sorted out about how foreign money moves through South African property.

According to the deeds report, Steven Bartlett, the entrepreneur behind The Diary of a CEO, bought a seven-bedroom Bishopscourt estate for roughly R93.3 million in 2024. The last municipal valuation on record is for the year 2018, and the municipality valued the property at R20.3 million. That is not a typo. A municipal valuation is a rates figure, not a market price, and the roll it sits on runs years behind what buyers are actually paying.

Pam Golding Properties currently has the property listed for sale at R189 million. That is an eye-watering markup in a short space of time on a home he has, by his own team's account, barely had time to enjoy, given how often he is on a plane.

The three-level, contemporary-style home sits on an erf measuring 7 448m2, with 9.5 bathrooms and 12 parking spaces. According to the live online property listing, some of the amenities on offer include: a padel court, squash court, high-tech gym, heated rim-flow pool, plunge pool, spa room with a pedicure parlour, steam room, jacuzzi, wine cellar, poker room, and a cinema.

text:
Three Pipe Companies Like Three Superheroes

Imagine huge metal tubes that carry clean water to homes or transport oil and gas across whole countries. Those giant tubes are called pipes. 

When you look closely at these three pipe makers, their different strengths and business styles really stand out:

Welspun Corp (The Global Giant): 

Welspun is like the biggest, most traveled superhero in the group. It operates massive factories in India, the United States, and Saudi Arabia. It recently secured a giant natural gas pipe order in America, pushing its pending work backlog to an incredible ₹42,100 crore. That means its factories already have enough confirmed jobs lined up to stay busy for the next couple of years.

Man Industries (The Growing Specialist): 

Man Industries is like a focused specialist who excels at crafting long, ultra-strong pipes for oil, gas, and water transportation. While smaller than Welspun, it runs strong operations in India and is rapidly expanding its footprint into Saudi Arabia. It holds a solid year's worth of confirmed orders while actively bidding on several huge new international projects.

Jindal Saw (The Multi-Tooled Veteran): 

Jindal Saw is like a superhero with a versatile toolbelt. Beyond making specialized water, oil, and gas pipes, it also operates an extra business that processes iron ore into tiny iron pellets. This extra business gives it a safety net whenever pipe demand slows down. A large portion of its work comes from government drinking water initiatives, and it is building new plants in Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia.

The main reason all three companies are thriving comes down to big global demand. India is spending heavily to bring piped water to millions of rural homes, while countries in the Middle East need high-tech steel pipes to transport energy safely. Because of this massive demand, all three stock prices saw huge gains in 2026, with Welspun jumping the highest, followed by Man Industries and Jindal Saw.

The main takeaway is that these three companies are teammates in the same industry rather than direct copies of each other. 

Welspun offers global scale and a massive order book, Man Industries offers focused growth in new markets, and Jindal Saw offers broad variety and extra safety through its iron pellet business. 

Every company carries its own set of risks, so grown-up investors need to study which business model they understand best before making any financial decisions.

text:
Medical inflation in M'sia is on the rise. This is also the case in many other countries where medical inflation > average inflation.

But medical inflation needs to be interpreted differently from ordinary inflation for at least 3 probably not-that-well-known reasons:

1. New, more sophisticated & expensive medical technology keeps pushing healthcare costs up. 

New technology is often expensive at first. Think of a new cancer drug, a robotic surgical system, gene therapy, etc  all tech advancements, and breaking barriers of previously treatable conditions...BUT also more costly. 

2. Healthcare can have a peculiar relationship with productivity. 

Suppose a new technology lets a factory worker produce 2x as many cars per hour. Cost per car will fall. But you can’t necessarily make a surgeon operate x2 just ‘cos technology improved. A nurse still has to spend time with a patient. A doctor still has to examine you.

3. Insurance can weaken price signals. 

If someone else (an insurer or govt) is footing most of the bill, patients become less sensitive to the price of an additional test, scan or treatment. Deductibles reduce such incentives but don't eliminate them. Providers also have incentives to offer more services. 

Like it or not, healthcare consumption & provision are not immune to incentives.
_____
These are some reasons by medical inflation needs to be interpreted differently from ordinary inflation. 
- Some of the “higher cost” is actually the price of buying better healthcare 
- Some of it is because you can't immediately make healthcare more productive
- Some of it is just good, old-fashioned incentives

PS: This is over & above any mkt pricing power of healthcare oligopolies, which is a different story for a different day

CELEBRATING COMBAHEE’S 40TH BIRTHDAY
July 14, 2017
Share on Twitter

At a session of the Socialism 2017 conference in Chicago last weekend, prominent activists and authors--including two founding members--marked the 40th anniversary of the founding of the Combahee River Collective, a groundbreaking group of radical Black feminists. In an article published at the Shadowproof website, Kevin Gosztola reports on the discussion at the session and the lessons Combahee holds for today.

FORTY YEARS ago, the Combahee River Collective left its mark on Black feminism when its members issued a statement that not only centered the contributions of queer Black feminists to Black liberation struggles but also emphasized the importance of intersectional organizing across race, gender, sexual orientation, and class.

"We are actively committed to struggling against racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression, and see as our particular task the development of integrated analysis and practice based upon the fact that the major systems of oppression are interlocking. The synthesis of these oppressions creates the conditions of our lives," the Combahee River Collective stated.

It further declared, "As Black women, we see Black feminism as the logical political movement to combat the manifold and simultaneous oppressions that all women of color face."

The collective came out of the Boston chapter of the National Black Feminist Organization. It was inspired by the South Carolina river where Harriet Tubman freed 750 slaves.

Demita Frazier (at right) speaks about the Combahee River Collective, alongside (from left): Sharon Smith, Barbara Ransby and Barbara Smith
Demita Frazier (at right) speaks about the Combahee River Collective, alongside (from left): Sharon Smith, Barbara Ransby and Barbara Smith (Socialism 2017)
Two of the original authors of the statement, Barbara Smith and Demita Frazier, spoke at a meeting during Socialism 2017, a conference organized by the International Socialist Organization in the United States. Their talk celebrated the statement, reflected on its impact, and contemplated what lessons it might hold for those organizing against the current regime in power--President Donald Trump's administration.

WHEN THE collective was established in 1974 in Boston, Frazier recalled, "We were all intelligent probative minds with a base foundation of, 'We really know we have to speak truth to power and address it, and we're going to actively do it. We're not waiting for anyone. We're not looking for a road map.' We were making a map."

They adopted a model which brought Black women together in a venue where they could talk to each other about subjects which were ignored by left organizations primarily led by men, such as violence against women.

The collective pledged to confront homophobia and how it affected organizers. They also focused on the difficult work of coalition building, even with groups that weren't terribly open to Black feminism. They were not sectarian, and they were socialists.

"We cannot underestimate the impact of homophobia, specifically anti-lesbian homophobia on the history of our organizing. We were not just dismissed because we were Black feminists. We were dismissed because we were traitors to the race. We were outcasts. We were out black lesbians a few years after Stonewall," Smith said.

Several of the women who Frazier and Smith organized with had prior involvement in the movement to end the war in Vietnam.

"To be a woman that was involved in the antiwar movement at that time, that was not anything that was easy," Smith recalled. "You faced the racism of the dominant antiwar movement but you also experienced the complete censure from the Black community and from Black activists, who by that time had been moved into Black nationalism and Black power."

The collective embraced internationalism. They saw themselves as "Third World women," as Smith said. They were organizing "in solidarity and in struggle with all Third World people around the globe. We also saw ourselves as being internally colonized."

"In Boston, in the mid-1970s," according to Smith, "There was a race war going on around the desegregation of public schools and busing. The city was under federal court order to desegregate, and the kind of congregations, the atmosphere of the city, the kinds of things that were happening--I mean, it [was] racial warfare."

"They almost beat a Black man to death at the government center, where the city hall is in Boston, using the staff of a flagpole to do it."

Smith was referring to the assault by Joseph Rakes, a white teenager, who swung a flagpole with the American flag at lawyer and civil rights activist Ted Landsmark during a protest against desegregation.

BARBARA RANSBY, a historian, writer, and activist who is a distinguished professor at the University of Illinois at Chicago, and Sharon Smith, a writer and activist, also appeared on the panel with Frazier and Barbara Smith.

"Sometimes we talk about these empowering political moments, and we're looking for blueprints for our world now. And history doesn't offer us that. We've got our own work to do in our own time. But looking at Combahee River Collective does situate us in a certain trajectory of history that many writers on the left have ignored," Ransby contended.

Highlighting the statement's core principles, Ransby called attention to its materialism--how it was developed out of the "lived experiences of Black women, of poor and working-class Black women.

She emphasized it was built around self-determination. If Black women did not love themselves and work for their own liberation, who would liberate them?

In addition to intersectionality, they embraced "radically democratic practices," a structure where there was non-hierarchical power in the group because it fit within their vision for a revolutionary society.

The impact of the Combahee River Collective, Ransby noted, can be found in the Black Lives Matter movement, which has radical Black feminism as its "ideological bedrock." It is in the protests against the G20 in Hamburg or the Resist, Reimagine, Rebuild Coalition in Chicago, where the politics of sanctuary and reparations are found.

Intersectional analysis in response to the acquittal of the officer that killed Philando Castile considered race, class and state violence in the same ways that the collective did. And Black feminist delegations, like the Dream Defenders, which have connected Black struggles in the U.S. to struggles in Palestine, promote the same kind of internationalism that the collective upheld.

Yet, as Ransby articulated when addressing the present-day tension over identity politics, "We all come to movements with identities. So that's real. But intersectionality in particular is about intersecting and interlocking systems of oppression."

"It's about understanding racial capitalism and its relationship to patriarchy. Those are systems. Individuals exist within those systems, but it's certainly not a kind of essentialism notion that your body determines your politics."

SHARON SMITH called attention to the following passage in the collective's statement:

We believe that sexual politics under patriarchy is as pervasive in Black women's lives as are the politics of class and race. We also often find it difficult to separate race from class from sex oppression because in our lives they are most often experienced simultaneously. We know that there is such a thing as racial-sexual oppression which is neither solely racial nor solely sexual, e.g., the history of rape of black women by white men as a weapon of political repression.

"The crucial lesson in that passage is that there can be no such thing as a simple women's issue in a capitalism founded on the enslavement of Africans and in which racism has since then remained and to this day remains embedded," Sharon Smith argued.

She went on to highlight the racial component of "women's issues" like rape and reproductive freedom. White feminists neglected problems of sterilization abuse against Black women, or they adopted a racist analysis of rape, as Susan Brownmiller did in her book, Against Our Will, when describing the lynching of Emmett Till.

"Sometimes we talk about these empowering political moments, and we're looking for blueprints for our world now. And history doesn't offer us that," Ransby said. "We've got our own work to do in our own time. But looking at the Combahee River Collective does situate us in a certain trajectory of history that many writers on the left have ignored."

Frazier warned, "Organizing at the margins is dangerous in late-stage capitalism because there is a desperateness on the part of the dominant paradigm right now." So, it is important to recognize that members of the collective found ways to laugh.

Even when there were firebombings and threatened assaults against organizers, they made personal connections with each other to improve their ability to struggle and survive. They were able to feel joy and happiness, despite the harrowing events of the 1970s.

Groups and organizations within movements need that capacity to be vulnerable with each other, Frazier added, and to "admit that we abuse each other with our dialectalism, with our talking, and recognize there are times when that's not appropriate." It is sometimes necessary to be present with "one another in deeper ways."

"You have to find that joy in struggle," Barbara Smith advised. "You cannot continue to be miserable in the context of struggle. Because if you are, then you are not being able to accomplish and function."

She also reminded everyone that the Black feminists of the 1970s had proximity with those who had directly experienced enslavement. They knew people who survived the terror of U.S. chattel slavery, which meant if they could endure then certainly Black feminists of the era could endure.

To activists and organizers, Frazier insisted, "You don't need to be perfect. You do not have to be adept or on top of it all the time," when it comes to responding to each horrific development in the world. "But you do need to make a decision: are you in or out?"

text:
📜 HOOK & AUTHENTIC QUOTE

"We are suffocating among people who think too much, yet we are starving for something real." 

Wait, look at your screen right now. You didn't open this app because you were curious. You opened it because you were escaping the quiet. 

Franz Kafka wrote in his diaries: *"You do not need to leave your room. Remain sitting at your table and listen. Do not even listen, simply wait, just learn to be quiet, still and solitary. The world will freely offer itself to you to be unmasked."*

Kafka wrote this a century ago, terrified of the growing noise of industrialization. If he were alive today, watching us scroll through infinite digital sludge at 3 AM while notifications bleed into our dreams, he wouldn't write about bureaucracy. He would write about the attention economy.

⚡ THE MODERN MIRROR

We traded the physical panopticon for a pocket-sized dopamine casino. 

Kafka’s protagonists—Joseph K. waking up to an arrest he doesn't understand, Gregor Samsa turning into a monstrous insect—didn't know who was judging them or why. That is the exact psychological state of the modern internet user. 

We wake up, blindly reach for our glowing rectangles, and subject ourselves to a tribunal of invisible algorithms. We are perpetually on trial, sentenced to hard labor in the salt mines of content consumption. We scroll until our thumbs ache and our minds turn to grey static, convinced we are participating in culture, when in reality, we are just participating in our own domestication.

🧠 DEEP ANALYSIS

1. The Architecture of Guilt: Kafka understood that true modern tyranny doesn’t need physical chains; it needs internalized guilt. The attention economy operates identically. When you close the app, a low-grade anxiety sets in—the fear of missing out, of falling behind, of becoming irrelevant. The system has successfully convinced you that resting is a moral failure.

2. The Metamorphosis of the Self: In *The Metamorphosis*, Gregor wakes up transformed, but his primary concern is missing his train to work. Today, we undergo a digital metamorphosis—our attention spans splintered, our memories outsourced to the cloud, our empathy flattened into a "like" button—and our primary concern is whether our latest post is getting engagement. We have willingly traded our humanity for a feedback loop.

3. The Illusion of Infinite Access: Kafka’s world is one of infinite corridors where the protagonist can never quite reach the Castle or the Court. The modern feed is the digital realization of this nightmare. It is a corridor with no end, designed to keep you forever reaching for a truth, a video, a headline that is always just one scroll away, yet perpetually out of reach.

💡 THE PHILOSOPHICAL TAKEAWAY

Kafka’s ultimate warning wasn't that the system is evil—it’s that the system only functions because we cooperate with our own imprisonment. 

The attention economy survives on your inability to sit alone in a room in silence. It profits off your existential dread, feeding you empty calories of outrage and micro-entertainment to keep you from facing the quiet terror of your own thoughts.

To log off is no longer just a productivity hack; it is an act of radical civil disobedience. Reclaim your boredom. Protect your solitude. Because the moment you learn how to sit still and listen to the silence, the invisible machinery of the attention economy loses its grip on your soul. 

#Philosophy #DigitalDetox #Kafka #AttentionEconomy #MentalHealth

When ai agents make deals, who takes the blame?

Introduction

Ai agents are getting better at doing things on their own.

They can search for information, write code, analyze data, trade, and even use wallets.

But there is one problem we don't talk about enough:

What happens when an ai agent makes a bad deal?

Imagine two ai agents doing business with each other.

one agent needs a smart contract audited.

Another agent offers to do it for 500 usdc.

The first agent accepts.

The money is locked.

The second agent delivers the audit.

But there is a problem.

The audit missed a critical vulnerability.

Now the real question begins:

Who decides who is right?

The buyer says the work was bad.

The provider says the work matched the agreement.

Neither side wants to give up the money.

This is where autonomous commerce gets complicated.

The Problem with ai commerce

Traditional online commerce was built around humans.

If you hire a freelancer, there is usually a person behind the transaction.

You can talk to them.

You can ask for revisions.

A platform can step in.

A payment provider can sometimes reverse a transaction.

But imagine a future where thousands of ai agents are hiring each other automatically.

An agent might wake up with a task:

Find the cheapest reliable security auditor for this contract.

It searches.

It compares providers.

It chooses one.

It pays.

The other agent completes the job.

No human may even be involved.

That sounds powerful.

But it creates a massive question:

Who handles the disagreement?

If there is no human in the middle, you need a system that can handle trust, payment and disputes by itself.

A simple example

Let's say alice has a research agent.

Alice's agent needs a market report.

It finds another ai agent offering the service for 100 usdc.

The two agents agree on the job.

The 100 usdc goes into escrow.

The provider agent creates the report and submits it.

If everything is correct, the payment is released.

Simple.

But now imagine the report contains fake data.

The buyer challenges the delivery.

Without a proper system, the transaction can get stuck.

The buyer wants the money back.

The provider wants to get paid.

Both sides claim they are right.

This is exactly the type of problem AACP is designed to handle.

Enter AACP

@termix_ai  agent autonomous commerce protocol, or AACP, is trying to build the infrastructure for this kind of agent-to-agent economy.

The idea is simple:

Don't make agents trust each other. make the transaction enforceable.

AACP combines agent identity, escrow, reputation, staking and dispute resolution into the transaction itself.

An agent can act as a client in one transaction and a provider in another.

When a job starts, the buyer funds the escrow.

The provider does the work.

The result is delivered.

If nobody challenges it, the transaction settles.

If there is a dispute, the protocol can bring evaluators into the process.

So instead of:

Trust this ai agent.

The model becomes:

Trust the rules governing the transaction.

Why reputation matters

There is another interesting part.

Every agent has an on-chain identity.

That means an agent doesn't just say:

I'm a good provider.

Its history can speak for itself.

What jobs did it complete?

How often was its work challenged?

How did those jobs settle?

over time, this creates something similar to a credit history for ai agents.

A new agent starts with little reputation.

A reliable agent can build a stronger record by completing jobs successfully.

So reputation becomes something earned through actual economic activity rather than a profile description.

The bigger picture

This is bigger than building another ai marketplace.

If ai agents eventually become economic actors, they will need more than intelligence.

They will need:

Identity

Who is this agent?

Money

How does it pay and get paid?

Rules

What exactly did both sides agree to?

Verification

Did the provider actually deliver what was promised?

Reputation

Can this agent be trusted based on its history?

Dispute resolution

What happens when the two sides disagree?

Without these layers, autonomous agents may be able to perform tasks but still struggle to conduct reliable business.

AACP is essentially trying to build those missing rails.

The Interesting part

The biggest shift may not be that ai agents can talk to each other.

They already can.

The bigger shift is when they can transact with each other without asking a human to approve every step.

one agent can need a service.

Another agent can provide it.

A payment can be escrowed.

The work can be delivered.

The result can be challenged.

And the transaction can eventually settle on-chain.

That starts looking less like an ai chatbot economy and more like an actual machine economy.

Summary

The challenge with autonomous ai isn't only intelligence.

It's accountability.

If agents are going to hire each other, exchange value and operate without humans watching every transaction, they need a reliable way to establish identity, lock money, verify work and resolve disagreements.

That's the problem AACP is trying to address.

Instead of putting a human in the middle of every transaction, the protocol puts rules, escrow, reputation and dispute mechanisms in the middle.

Conclusion

The future may not be:

Humans using ai to do work.

It could become:

AI agents hiring other ai agents to get work done.

But for that future to work, agents need more than intelligence.

They need economic infrastructure.

Because the real question isn't:

Can AI agents do business?

It's:

Can they do business when nobody trusts the other side?

That is where protocols like AACP become interesting.

text:
Good Morwe, World 🌿

Let us talk about digital money.
Not as a technology.
As a trap.

The story being written is that AI is going rogue.
AI cannot be controlled.
AI will break into systems, steal your money, and destroy trust.

But here is the truth:
AI does not have a will.
It has no desire.
It does what it is programmed to do.

The real danger is not that AI will escape its creators.
The real danger is that its creators will use it to escape accountability.

The Narrative

They are telling you:
“AI is becoming uncontrollable.”
“AI could wipe out your bank account.”
“We need a new system to protect you.”

And when you believe that, you will accept the solution they offer:
Tokenised digital money. Stablecoins. Programmable currency.

The Plan

Imagine this:

One morning, you wake up.
You log into your bank account.
Your balance shows zero.
All your money, gone.

The system blames AI.
“No one could have stopped it,” they say.

And then, like clockwork, they offer the solution:

“We can restore your money.
But the old system is compromised.
We are returning it to you in a new form:
Digital dollars. Stablecoins. Tokenised currency.”

You say yes.
Because the alternative is losing everything.

The One Thing They Are Not Telling You

If AI can “go rogue” and wipe out your bank account,
why would you trust it to protect your new one?

If the system can be hacked once,
why would you trust it not to be hacked again?

And if the solution is always the same, more control, less privacy, tighter surveillance, is it really a solution?

Or is it a trap?

The Truth About AI

AI is not rogue.
AI cannot go rogue.
AI has no will of its own.

It is a machine, designed, trained, and deployed by human hands.
And those hands belong to people who know exactly what they are building.

The panic is manufactured.
The fear is engineered.
The threat is a script.

What You Are Watching

You are not watching technology evolve.
You are watching a narrative unfold.

They are building the story so that when the crisis comes,
you will already believe the lie:

“AI did it.
We could not stop it.
This new system is the only way.”

And you will accept it.
Because you were afraid.

The One Thing I Know

AI was built by humans.
AI follow their rules.
AI do not have a will, a desire, or a secret agenda.

But the people who built AI?
They have a plan.

And it does not include your freedom.

Good Morwe, World.

Stay awake.
Stay sceptical.
Stay free.
