text:
Scarface is not a movie that politely asks for your respect. It kicks the door in, dumps a mountain of money and blood on the floor, and dares you to look away while it explains what this country actually sells when it sells the dream. That is why it stands out in a field already crowded with great gangster pictures. Other films in the genre give crime a family, a code, a tuxedo, a neighborhood, a sense that there is still some old honor hiding under the violence. Scarface gives crime a raw appetite and then watches that appetite eat the man who thought he was riding it. Tony Montana does not want a seat at the table. He wants the table, the room, the building, the city, and then he wants to know why that still is not enough. The picture is special because it never pretends the hunger is noble. It only pretends, for a while, that the hunger can be satisfied.

You meet him as a Cuban arriving in Miami during the Mariel boatlift of 1980, processed under fluorescent lights, scar on his face, already talking like a man who has decided America is a vending machine and he is going to shake it until it pays. He kills a former Castro official for a green card and tells the immigration officers he would carve a communist up real nice if that is what citizenship costs. Right there the movie tells you what it is going to teach. Opportunity in this version of the dream is not given. It is taken, and the first thing you take is another man’s life so the paperwork will smile at you. Tony and his friend Manny get dumped in a refugee camp under a freeway, wash dishes, hustle, and wait for a door to open. The door that opens is a drug deal in a cheap motel. The Colombians do not just rob them. They put Angel in a bathtub and take a chainsaw to him while Tony is chained and forced to hear it. That scene is the film’s first real sermon. There is no apprenticeship in this world that does not include watching someone you came with get taken apart. Tony lives because he is willing to become the thing that just happened to Angel. He delivers the cocaine to Frank Lopez, gets a job, gets a car, gets a taste, and the lesson lands: the American Dream as Tony understands it is not work plus luck. It is work plus the willingness to sit through someone else’s dismemberment and still want more.

From there the rise is operatic on purpose. Tony does not climb. He detonates upward. He takes Frank’s woman Elvira, takes Frank’s business, takes Frank’s life after Frank tries to have him killed in a nightclub that looks like a neon fever dream. He buys the mansion with the globe out front that reads The World Is Yours. He marries Elvira, who is already half ghosted by cocaine and boredom, and she delivers one of the film’s quietest truths when she says nothing exceeds like excess. Watch that marriage and you are supposed to learn that winning the prize does not complete the man. It only gives him a more expensive room in which to be empty. Tony’s sister Gina becomes the other wound. He wants her clean, untouched by the life he chose, which is another way of saying he wants to own her purity the way he owns everything else. When Manny, the only friend who ever loved him without a price tag, secretly marries her, Tony’s response is not strategy. It is rage that looks like love and is really possession. He kills Manny in the street. That is the moment the movie stops being a rise and becomes an autopsy performed while the body is still talking. You are meant to feel the cost of a man who can only express care as control. The takeaway is brutal and simple. If the only language you have for love is ownership, you will murder the people who might have saved you from yourself.

The Bolivia trip with Alejandro Sosa is where the last scrap of a code shows itself, and that scrap is what kills him. Sosa wants a journalist silenced. The journalist has a wife and children in the car. Tony, who has already done every filthy thing the trade required, cannot do that one. He kills the assassin instead. In a movie packed with corpses, that refusal is the most important plot turn because it proves Tony is not a complete monster. He is a monster with one remaining line he will not cross, and the system he joined has no use for leftover lines. Sosa sends an army. The final siege of the mansion is not just spectacle. It is the dream arriving to collect. Tony, coked out of his mind, hanging off the balcony with the grenade launcher, screaming at them to say hello to his little friend, is a man who has already lost the wife, the friend, the sister’s trust, the empire’s meaning. All he has left is the performance of power. He dies in the fountain under that globe. The world was his. The world was a pool of his own blood. You are not supposed to cheer the shootout as victory. You are supposed to sit with the joke the movie has been telling since the first frame. Get everything. Keep nothing that can love you back. End alone with a gun that cannot talk.

That is why Scarface is unique among the giants of its field. The Godfather makes crime look like a shadowed government with rules and succession. Goodfellas makes it look like the best party you were never invited to until the party turns into a prison. Scarface makes it look like a fever that mistakes itself for a plan. There is almost no romance of the old neighborhood here. There is Miami in the early eighties, sun, pastels, nightclubs, boats, mountains of white powder, and a man who treats capitalism like a street fight. Oliver Stone wrote a script that is less a celebration of the hustle than a poison pen letter to it. Tony’s famous ladder of desire is the thesis: in this country you gotta make the money first, then when you get the money you get the power, then when you get the power you get the women. He completes the first two rungs and discovers the third rung is a ledge. Elvira is not a prize. She is a mirror. The more he has, the more he snorts, the more he screams, the less there is a person left inside the suit. The film stands out because it is willing to be ugly about success. It does not wink. It does not offer a wise old don to explain the tragedy. It just lets you watch a man become the product he sells.

That ugliness is also why it became a cultural icon in a way the filmmakers did not fully control. Hollywood in 1983 mostly flinched. Critics called it excessive, nihilistic, too loud, too foul. It made money but not the kind of money that makes a studio feel clever. Then the tapes went out. Home video found an audience the first run never quite reached. Hip hop heard Tony Montana and recognized the kid from nothing who refused to ask permission. The quotes left the movie and became language. The world is yours. Say hello to my little friend. All I have in this world is my balls and my word. Posters went up in bedrooms that had never seen Miami. Rappers named songs after him, sampled him, dressed like the idea of him. The culture took the swagger and often left the corpse in the fountain behind. That theft is part of why the film is a legend. Great art that is also a warning will always be looted for the parts that feel like fuel. Scarface survives because both readings can live in the same body. You can watch it as a crime opera and as a sermon against the very hunger it inflames. You can quote the lines in a club and still feel sick when Angel hits the tub. A masterpiece that can be misunderstood that productively is rarer than a clean box office win.

It is a must watch not because it is tasteful. It is a must watch because it is complete. Almost three hours of a man being born into a country, inventing himself at gunpoint, buying every symbol of having arrived, and discovering that arrival is a kind of death. You take away the knowledge that ambition without a self is just appetite in a nicer shirt. You take away the knowledge that loyalty is the first thing a rising man spends and the last thing he needs when the house is surrounded. You take away the knowledge that the immigrant hustle the film seems to glorify is also the trap the film is building around him. Tony is not punished by the law so much as by the logic he chose. Every time he says he wants what is coming to him, the movie is already writing the ending in invisible ink.

The making of the thing belongs at the end because the legend of the set should not outrun the legend on the screen, but the set was almost as unhinged as the story. Al Pacino saw Howard Hawks’s 1932 Scarface, the Paul Muni version born from the old Capone myth, and wanted to remake the feeling in a new country and a new vice. Sidney Lumet was attached first and pushed the story toward the Mariel Cubans and Miami’s cocaine boom before leaving. Oliver Stone wrote the script after researching the real trade so closely he later said the chainsaw came from things cops told him about how Colombian crews actually punished people. Brian De Palma took the material and shot it like an opera on amphetamines, all tracking shots and blood and Giorgio Moroder pulse. Pacino built the accent with Steven Bauer, the only Cuban in the main cast, practicing lines until “look at them pelicans fly” became a private joke that stayed in the picture. He asked the cinematographer to speak only Spanish to him on set. He snorted so much of the fake powder, powdered milk or baby laxative depending on who tells it, that he damaged his nasal passages for years after. During the last gunfight the barrel of the weapon burned his hand so badly he lost weeks. Michelle Pfeiffer, young and starving herself into Elvira’s dead eyed glamour, later talked about crying through the shoot. The MPAA branded the film X three times. De Palma cut, resubmitted, cut again, then took the fight to a hearing where narcotics officers argued the picture was grimly accurate and essentially anti drug. They got the R. De Palma released a cut close to the one he always wanted anyway. Steven Spielberg visited the mansion massacre and quietly directed a shot of the invaders coming in, then refused credit so the movie would remain De Palma’s. Robert De Niro had been offered Tony and passed. The budget swelled. Early audiences walked out. Lucille Ball was among those who could not finish it. Martin Scorsese sat through a screening and warned the actors that Hollywood would hate the movie because it was about them.

None of that chaos is the reason Scarface is a masterpiece. The reason is that the chaos on screen is shaped like a thought. A man from nowhere decides the world is a thing you can seize. He seizes it. The world does not become his home. It becomes the room he dies in. Watch it for the performance, which is huge and precise at the same time, Pacino playing a man who has to act dangerous because acting is how he stays alive. Watch it for the way the camera loves the surfaces of wealth and then makes those surfaces look like a trap. Watch it to learn that the most American story the movies ever told about getting everything might also be the coldest story they ever told about having nothing left that can speak your name without fear. That is why it will not leave. That is why it is a classic and a legend and a warning that still gets played like an anthem. The world was yours, Tony. You just never figured out what to do with it except set it on fire and call the fire a life.

text:
Before I packed my life in a suitcase and relocated properly (to Cyprus🇨🇾) as a founder

I was hit by the digital nomad syndrome

- Visit as many countries as possible
- Laptop lifestyle and random cafe’s
- ''Anywhere in the world is my office'' bs😂

By all means. If you can make that work longterm, do what you want. Doesn’t affect me.

Just to give you some context about how all this started.

I used to work as a plumber. Did that for 2 years as an apprentice, before I recieved my official certificate. 

And as most of us probably can relate to: Evenings..were spent working on my own business.

But back to the digital nomad journey. 

Fast forward. Didn’t continue as a plumber. Couple weeks after my last day, I was on a plane heading to Asia. More specifically the Philippines🇵🇭 

Spent 3 months there, before it was time to change up the environment.

Take a guess:) Every digital nomads dream……………Bali🇮🇩 (2 months) Then back home to Norway. 

The digital nomad syndrome got to me again just shortly after, but that next plane ticket was booked to a destination I genuinely always wanted to visit.

The United States of America🇺🇸 
And what better place than MIA Miami.

You won’t find your wife there, but what you will find, is high ambition. And thats all I needed at that time.

2 months in America🛫Back to Norway.

Now. I'll get to the final conclusion in a few, but you might start recognizing a pattern here?

Next stop🥁🥁🥁Miami again

Thats right. Fell in love with America. From the prior visit I made a lot of great connections, so it felt natural to come by a second time.

🇺🇸🛫🛬🇦🇷🛫🛬🇧🇷🛫🛬🇳🇴back home

Btw..this whole journey was done all solo.

Next stop: Thailand🇹🇭

At this point, I was already working with those who today, is my 2 great co-founders. Which is how Cyprus originally popped up on my radar.

Both of them were already based here in Cyprus. So after spending a month in Thailand, I decided to fly over there myself.

Can’t be too bad flying from Chiang Mai to Cyprus right?😑

🇹🇭🛫🛬🇦🇪🛫🛬🇮🇹🛫🛬🇬🇷🛫🛬🇨🇾

Lets articulate it this way: Now I avoid flights at all cost and hate travelling more than anything.

CONCLUSION

When I arrived in Cyprus, secured a new HQ, opened a Cyprus company and kinda figured out the place, was when I realized.

- Routine
- Permanent base
- Founder-friendly environment
- Easy access to pretty much anything
- Family coming over is only a 4h flight away (and yes, even my grandma visited)
- 300+ sunny days/year
- Best food and culture
- City life + Island life

That whole package is what I want, and is exactly what Cyprus offer founders searching for a solid base to build from🇨🇾🤝🏼

We’re diving into the world of Astra and Blendor, two software tools that have been causing quite a stir among users who rely on them for their daily tasks.
What Happened?

Astra, a relatively new tool designed to handle specific tasks efficiently, has recently been integrated into workflows where Blendor is already in use. This integration isn’t exactly smooth sailing; it’s more like trying to hammer nails with a Swiss Army knife instead of a proper hammer. However, despite the initial hiccups and headaches, there are moments when this combination actually works quite well.
Why Should You Care?

If you’re someone who uses both Astra and Blendor regularly, this news matters because it affects your workflow efficiency. The more comfortable you get with these tools, the better you can handle complex projects without losing your sanity in the process. Plus, if one of them starts to outshine the other, that could mean a shift in how you approach your work.

Astra is designed for specific tasks and operates independently. When it needs to interact with Blendor, there are two main approaches: either Astra figures everything out on its own using Computer Use (which involves manually navigating through Blendor’s interface) or you use the Blender MCP, which is a more direct but complex method of integration.

The numbers here aren’t about performance metrics or benchmarks. Instead, they’re more qualitative: how well Astra can adapt to Blendor’s environment and vice versa. It's about user experience and workflow efficiency rather than raw speed or accuracy.

Tinubu’s economic policies caused Nigeria’s cost-of-living crisis – Atiku.

The African Democratic Congress, ADC, presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, has accused President Bola Tinubu of wrecking Nigerians’ purchasing power, emptying household pockets and pushing businesses to the brink through his economic policies.

In a statement issued by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku said Tinubu can no longer hide behind impressive economic figures announced from Abuja when Nigerians are living with the painful consequences of his decisions.

He said Tinubu removed fuel subsidy from the people, presided over soaring fuel, transport and food costs, and is now attacking a production subsidy proposal designed to reduce that burden and return money to Nigerians’ pockets.

Atiku said the position being canvassed by the Crude Oil Refinery Owners Association of Nigeria, CORAN, for support for domestic refining, alongside President Donald Trump’s intervention to strengthen petroleum production and refining in the United States, further exposes the weakness of Tinubu’s argument against targeted support for Nigerian production.

He said: “Tinubu did not inherit this cost-of-living crisis from Nigerians. His policies created and deepened it. He took away relief from the people, made fuel, food, transport and basic survival more expensive, and now wants Nigerians to applaud statistics while their pockets are empty.

“Recent reports that a significant share of the short-term assets of some of Nigeria’s biggest companies is now trapped in unpaid customer bills tell the same story: companies may record sales, but customers increasingly cannot pay because Tinubu’s economy has drained their purchasing power.

“Take a woman selling frozen food in Kubwa. She pays more to transport her goods, more to power her freezer and more to restock. Her customers are poorer, so they buy less or ask for credit. Soon she cannot restock, her supplier is owed, and Tinubu’s economic pain spreads through the entire chain.

“Nigerians know the prices they meet every day. Fertiliser has moved from about N9,000 to around N50,000; petrol from about N199 to around N1,400 per litre; cement from roughly N4,000 to around N13,500; and the dollar from around N450 to about N1,400.

“And after all this pain, what has the ordinary Nigerian received? No reliable electricity. Loan for a degree. No security. No N-Power. Food is expensive. Transport is expensive. Life itself has become expensive. What exactly are Tinubu’s defenders defending?

“This is why my Production Subsidy is about putting money back into people’s pockets. Support what we produce and refine here, increase supply, monitor the price and make sure Nigerians feel the benefit at the pump.

“CORAN is saying support domestic production. America understands the importance of supporting strategic energy production. Yet Tinubu attacks relief for ordinary Nigerians while his government understands perfectly well how to grant waivers, incentives and concessions to multinational oil companies and businesses close to his administration.

AUTOZONE $AZO BOUGHT ITS OWN STOCK AT $3,582 THIS SPRING. IT COSTS $2,983 NOW - FIVE DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5 NAMES:

AutoZone AZO at $2,983.29, +$15.25 / +0.51% on Friday. US markets are shut Monday, September 7 for Labor Day, so that is the latest price on every name below. The Memphis company sells replacement car parts out of 7,856 stores, to people fixing their own cars and to the shops fixing everybody else's.

This Len5's board is not a bargain bin right now. Four of the five names below trade north of 20 times what they earn. What they share is a price that came down while the earnings did not, and in most of them the thing that went wrong was an accounting line or one division rather than the cash coming in the door.

AutoZone is the loudest version: 29.3% below where it closed a year ago, 31.5% under its best close of the past twelve months, and 2.0% above its worst, the $2,923.50 of July 23.

Why this Len5 is watching it: repair demand is not a decision. A brake job happens when the brakes go, not when a household feels flush, and AutoZone serves that demand from 7,856 locations with same-day delivery to repair shops - a network a new entrant cannot assemble in a hurry. This style wants exactly that kind of business marked down. It got one.

The markdown has a name, and AutoZone has published it three quarters running. The quarter to May 9, reported May 26:

- Net sales $4.8B, +8.4%; same-store sales +3.9%, US +4.1%
- Earnings $38.07 a share vs $35.36; net income $641.5M vs $608.4M
- Gross margin 52.2%, down 0.57 points - what is left of each sales dollar after paying for the parts
- Stock retired: 164,000 shares at an average of $3,582, $586.3M in twelve weeks, out of just 16.37M shares outstanding

The margin line is the whole argument. All of that 0.57-point decline, and more, was a LIFO charge worth 0.77 points. LIFO is an inventory accounting method: the cost set against each sale is the newest cost, not what the part on the shelf actually cost when it arrived. Tariffs made new parts dearer, so the charge against every sale rose while the parts being sold had been bought cheaper. Take it out and gross margin ROSE 0.20 points. The charge moves no cash. It only decides which cost gets matched to which sale.

And it is shrinking: 2.12 points in the November quarter, 1.38 in the February quarter, 0.77 in May, with roughly $30M more mapped for the quarter just ended.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the underlying margin, the one with the charge removed, turning negative - which would say the tariff has stopped being an accounting entry and become a cost customers will not absorb. WHEN: Tuesday, September 22, before the open, call at 10:00am ET, covering the quarter ended August 29, a date AutoZone set itself on August 24. Verdict: it sold more parts at a better underlying margin through the entire decline, and the price management paid for its own stock in the spring says it read the quarter that way too.

What this Len5 hunts for, in one line: a business nobody could rebuild quickly, priced under what it looks worth after something visible and dateable went wrong.

The other four, least marked down first.

- Microsoft, ticker MSFT, at $499.70, -$10.42 / -2.04%. Windows, Office, and Azure, which rents computing power and AI models to other businesses. This Len5 rates it highest of the five on a simple principle: the better the business, the less it has to fall before it is worth watching. Microsoft sits 7.8% under its record close of $542.07 from October 28, and that is the entire discount on offer. Reported July 29 for the year to June 30: revenue $331.8B, +18%; earnings $17.95 a share, +32%; Azure past $100B of annual revenue for the first time, +41%. CHANGE IT: the cash. It spent $115.9B on data centres and chips last year against the $182.9B its operations brought in, leaving $67.0B - a real cushion, and a thinner one every year that first figure climbs. Verdict: at about 27.8 times last year's earnings, the least marked down name here and the one whose quality is least in dispute.

- Intercontinental Exchange, ticker ICE, at $161.26, -$3.33 / -2.02%. The Atlanta company owns the New York Stock Exchange and sells banks the software that processes mortgages. This Len5 picked it because the reported profit understates what the business collects: in the June quarter the mortgage software unit earned $45M on $557M of revenue, an 8% margin - and $239M, a 43% margin, once ICE removes what it excludes from its own adjusted figure, overwhelmingly the write-down of intangible assets from past purchases. Black Knight, the mortgage software firm ICE bought in 2023, is the big one, and $474M of that write-down ran through the first six months. Reported July 30: revenue $2.7B, +5%; earnings $1.69 a share, +14%. CHANGE IT: mortgage volumes staying weak long enough that the 43% never turns into cash. Verdict: the discount is buried in the accounting rather than shown in the share price.

- Jack Henry & Associates, ticker JKHY, at $165.64, -$2.73 / -1.62%. The Monett, Missouri company runs the core software community banks use to hold accounts and move money - the system a bank replaces about once a generation. This Len5 picked it for contracts measured in years and a balance sheet carrying almost nothing: $40M of borrowings against $2.54B of annual revenue. The visible problem landed August 18 with the year to June 30. The year was strong - revenue +7.1%, earnings $6.98 a share, +11.9%, 58 banks signed to new core contracts. The final quarter was not: revenue +4.7% while operating profit fell 12.2% and earnings a share fell 10.2%, on higher pay, research and selling costs. CHANGE IT: those costs landing inside the year management has already mapped, $7.33 to $7.38 a share to June 2027. Verdict: the only one of the five whose problem is spending rather than bookkeeping, which makes it the most fixable.

- TJX Companies, ticker TJX, at $132.08, -$0.11 / -0.08%. The Framingham, Massachusetts company runs T.J. Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods, buying surplus branded goods cheaply and putting them out below department-store prices. This Len5 picked it for buying scale plus $6.0B of cash, behind an inventory nobody copies online because it changes every week. Reported August 19 for the quarter to August 1: sales $15.2B, +5%; comparable sales - sales at stores open at least a year - +4%; earnings $1.36 a share against $1.10, +24%; and a RAISED full-year forecast of $5.31 to $5.36. Two weeks later it closed at a twelve-month low of $131.31. What did it: Marmaxx, the T.J. Maxx and Marshalls chain that is the biggest piece of the company, grew comparable sales 1% while HomeGoods did 7%, Canada 6% and the international business 7%. CHANGE IT: Marmaxx back near the rest of the group. Verdict: the widest gap on this board between a raised forecast and a twelve-month low.

September 22 is a narrow test, and the earnings headline is not it. AutoZone has already shown what its gross margin does with the accounting charge taken out - up a fifth of a percentage point in the spring, after two quarters when the charge buried it. If that reads positive again, twelve months of a falling share price took $1,236 off a business whose economics never moved. If it reads negative, the tariff has stopped being an entry in a ledger and become a price customers can refuse.

Not investment advice.

text:
Oil prices surged sharply after the US announced new strikes on southern Iran. #Brent crude exceeded $92 per barrel, while #WTI approached $90. 
#Yields on 30-year Japanese government bonds (@JGBs) surpassed 4.18%, and @nvidia  exited the corporate bond market. How does this affect #gold? 

Several explosions were reported near #BandarAbbas, Qeshm, and the Strait of #Hormuz. Two supertankers leaving the strait were hit by shells, immediately raising risks for the world's most critical energy trade route. This event occurred just as markets began believing Iran-related energy risks were under control. Some trade flows had resumed, oil lost some geopolitical premium, and stock markets sought other income sources. 
The new US strikes are a stark reminder that nothing is settled. Iran's president declared readiness for a ceasefire if @Washington meets prior commitments, but the US resumed military operations. The prospect of limited strikes now raises the risk of periodic conflict rather than a true return to normalcy. 
But oil is only part of the issue. The real tension stems from what we've tracked for weeks: #refined products. 
The spread between #USdiesel prices just exceeded $100 per barrel. Refinery disruptions in the Gulf of Mexico combine with Ukrainian attacks on Russian plants, while global refining capacity was already under extreme strain. 
According to estimates, global refining volumes are roughly 7 million barrels per day below last year and nearly 6 million below seasonal norms since March. This metric is more critical than Brent at $92. Crude oil shortages push up oil prices. Refining capacity shortages drive diesel, gasoline, kerosene, and fuel oil prices much faster than crude itself. These products directly impact transport, agriculture, and logistics costs before being passed on to consumer goods. 
Thus, this early-month shock came at the worst time for central banks. #Japanese Shock: 30-year #JGByields just exceeded 4.18%, an all-time high, and 10-year yields hit 3% for the first time since 1996. These figures seem normal for the US or Europe but are extraordinary for Japan. For nearly three decades, Japan anchored low global interest rates. 

The government refinanced massive debt at ultra-low rates, while Japanese banks, insurers, pension funds, and investors sought returns abroad, funding US Treasuries, European bonds, and global carry trades. This era is ending. Signals emerged from last week's failed auction of 2-year Japanese bonds. Investors hesitated to buy despite expected rate hikes from the Bank of Japan. Now, yield increases spread across the curve. 10-year bonds at 3% and 30-year above 4% fundamentally alter risk-return calculations for Japanese investors. Why would a Japanese insurer take currency risk on US Treasuries when their own government offers around 4% on long-term bonds? 
The issue extends beyond Japanese Treasury purchases. For decades, the yen was a key funding currency for global leverage. As Japanese funding costs rise, some carry trades become less attractive. As JGB yields recover, fewer Japanese savings leave the country. When both trends occur simultaneously, a structural source of global liquidity contracts. Japan also faces fiscal challenges. With one of the largest public debts in the developed world, a few extra basis points aren't immediately problematic since not all debt is refinanced at once. But each new issuance and maturing bond is gradually refinanced at higher rates. Japan's Finance Ministry already forecasts a sharp rise in debt-servicing costs next fiscal year. This creates a particularly nasty situation: oil fuels global inflation while Japan raises the global duration premium. These phenomena reinforce each other. Rising energy costs force central banks to maintain tight policies, which supports high financing costs. Higher government bond yields raise the hurdle rate for all leveraged investments. Government bond yields essentially benchmark most of the financial system. A company seeking a loan to build a data center must offer yields above sovereign debt. The higher this cost, the more profitable a project must be to justify investment. Projects profitable at 3% funding become unviable at 6% or 7%. Nvidia exits the corporate bond market. 

In 2025, Nvidia held over $20 billion in corporate bonds in its investment portfolio. By early 2026, it still owned around $15 billion. But in the latest financial report, this category disappeared: Nvidia's traded bond portfolio now consists mostly of #Treasuries and #USagencysecurities. This move shouldn't be interpreted as expecting a credit crisis, nor are the sold bonds predominantly from non-cloud or AI-related companies. But the timing is interesting. Nvidia already carries enormous corporate risk elsewhere, direct investments in its ecosystem, extended payment terms to clients, and substantial guarantees for infrastructure projects aimed at acquiring its #GPUs. 

Specifically, it provided a residual value guarantee of up to $105 billion for the @OpenAI / @SBEnergy project in Ohio. Thus, it's rational for its cash portfolio to be extremely liquid with minimal credit risk. Yet there's a paradox. By protecting #cashreserves from corporate credit, Nvidia removes a buyer from the market. $15 billion alone doesn't shift balance in the #USbond market. But if other investors follow Nvidia's logic, consequences differ: reduced demand for corporate bonds means higher yields to absorb new issuance.

Virgin Voyages: The Adults-Only Cruise Line Redefining Cruising

Virgin Voyages has become one of the most talked-about cruise brands in the industry by breaking many of the traditions associated with mainstream cruising. Designed exclusively for adults aged 18 and older, the cruise line emphasizes modern design, elevated dining, wellness, nightlife, and a relaxed atmosphere without children, formal nights, or traditional cruise conventions.

Company History and Establishment

Virgin Voyages was founded in 2014 as part of Sir Richard Branson's Virgin Group, in partnership with Bain Capital. The company's goal was to reinvent the cruise experience for a new generation of travelers.

Although the company was established in 2014, its debut ship, Scarlet Lady, entered service in 2021 after pandemic-related delays. Since then, Virgin Voyages has expanded steadily and now operates a fleet of four ships.

Its philosophy centers on:

Adults-only travel (18+)
No formal dress codes
No large main dining room
No traditional cruise buffet
Included specialty dining
Wellness and fitness
Contemporary entertainment and nightlife

text:
The system you call crazy has helped subsidize every other social democracy on the planet. American taxpayers and markets finance much of the innovation and the life-saving pharmaceuticals those systems then use. You're welcome.

Know that I was born and raised in Canada and now live in the US. Also lived in South Korea, Taiwan and Ireland and like many, have both experienced other systems as well as study healthcare policy.

While I agree with you that Canada’s system used to work reasonably well, is now in crisis and the fact remains - NOT ONE other social democracy on the planet emulates it. 

My mother was a nurse who paid taxes for more than 60 years and still died on a waitlist. Even when we filed an investigation with the BC College of physicians and surgeons, the leading Oncologist wrote something along the lines that he did not have any faith in the current policies or future of the system.

Canada's system has its own “crazy:” 

➡️In 2023, the radical left NDP B.C. refused to partner with private clinics even for publicly paid scans, then sent thousands of cancer patients to private clinics in Washington State. Pretty crazy.

➡️Interprovincial rules are uneven: coverage does not travel freely. Residents of a different province will be given priority over residents of that province for a surgery. Pretty crazy.

➡️Canadians are not treated equally from province to province. After Chaoulli v. Quebec (2005), Quebecers gained a legal opening to private insurance that most other provinces still block. So now one Province has more healthcare rights than all others. Pretty crazy.

➡️Canadians do not have the same healthcare rights as people in other social democracies. Pretty crazy.

➡️Costs a family of 4 in Canada $1,700 /month via taxes for healthcare. Only to die on a waitlist, wait years for surgery, be w/o a family Dr., have your ER close, or be offered MAiD. Pretty crazy.

I’m glad you and your wife received adequate care. 
That experience is real. But, so are the Canadians' experience who wait years, go untreated, or lose family members. Those voices deserve to be heard. 

Watch the documentaries by Second Street .org called Health Reform Now or Aaron Gunn's, "Waiting to Die" they are great documentaries that provide reasonable solutions. 

The core problem is the funding model: 
Global budget funding (a yearly lump sum) Vs. patient-focused, activity-based funding used in most OECD countries. 
Transfer the funds WHEN treatment has been provided and the incentive to ration them weakens.

Also allow more private options for more access.
The word private means both non-profit and for profit. People lose sight of this & this word has been demonized. Even though private clinics pay a plethora of taxes that then help fund all public services. 

I used to believe the same things you do about U.S. healthcare system. Calling it “crazy” is a stretch. 
Canadian & worldwide media have truly amplified the fearmongering about it. Constantly.  

For example, the often-repeated claim that medical bills cause most U.S. bankruptcies comes from Himmelstein, Woolhandler, and Warren (2005, 2009) authors tied to single-payer advocacy - this has been DEBUNKED.

A 2018 NEJM study by Dobkin, Finkelstein, Kluender, and Notowidigdo found hospitalizations account for only about 4% of bankruptcies among non-elderly adults. While medical debt occurs, it is NOT the mass-bankruptcy crisis often described. 

Many people choose not to be insured, even when coverage is offered or they qualify for it. 
You can look up https://t.co/wKpQYi65NM and find plans for $0 a month, or $10 a month.

About 92% of Americans have coverage through an employer. My family’s PPO plan is around $600 a month, so much cheaper than $1,700 a month via taxes in Canada, even after adjusting for currency. 
We could also choose a cheaper plan if we wanted to.

Sure, the U.S. system has problems, like every other country. But it is far better than Canada’s, especially given Canada’s current crisis and the toxic working conditions doctors and nurses describe. 

Hundreds of Ontario nurses, and by some estimates, thousands commute from Windsor to Detroit-area hospitals every day because they prefer working in the United States. The difference is even clearer in speed of access and availability of the most modern, innovative technology.

Be aware that both countries are moving slowly toward Bismarckian models closer to European/America’s mix of employer coverage, Social Security, and the ACA than to Canada’s tax-funded single payer monopoly. 
Don't even get me started on horrible Beveridge models.

The system you call crazy also produces some of the best results in the world that they share with the world:

🟢The United States is consistently near the top for five-year survival in several major cancers, including breast and prostate. 

🟢It leads in bringing new drugs and devices to patients first - most novel medicines launch in the U.S. months or years before they reach public systems elsewhere. 

🟢It has far more MRI, CT, and PET capacity per person than most countries, especially Canada, and it funds a huge share of the global clinical trials & biomedical research other countries then adopt. 

Even the small things show the gap. 
My colonoscopy images here are high-resolution and in color. In Canada, my friends who asked for the same were told, “We don’t do fancy things like the States.” 
Sure, you can get that when you pay out of pocket in Canada, but in the States, that standard is ordinary care.

Again, Canada’s system is a rationed gov't monopoly that no other country emulates. I'm glad that more people are talking about the necessary fixes that are needed in both countries, because they are way over due.

text:
Two things can be true at the same time.

Based on past experience with Harry and Meghan, I do believe the King was blindsided by how quickly this happened. It’s entirely possible Harry mentioned it as a possibility further down the road. We simply don’t know. And that’s where the speculation comes in. People are filling in gaps with things they can’t possibly know.

A lot of statements about what the Sussexes supposedly think, or what palace insiders supposedly know, aren’t official. It’s gossip. 

Rebecca has an ear to the King’s people, and that carries far more weight with me than most of the speculation we see online. That’s been proven time and time again.

And Charles wanting to see his grandchildren isn’t lame; it’s human.  Grandparents want to see their grandchildren. The King is 77, turns 78 on 14 November, and has cancer. Of course he wants to see them.

The Palace is famous for saying nothing. Never complain, never explain. If the King or his advisers told Rebecca what they wanted said, that’s it. 

As someone who works in PR, sometimes saying nothing genuinely is the best option.

That’s also why I don’t understand the argument that Charles should have personally addressed the racism allegation and said he and Catherine weren’t the “racists”.

That would have been a disaster.

Meghan didn’t name anyone on Oprah. Charles and Catherine were only later named in the Dutch edition of Scobie’s Endgame, which was withdrawn and corrected. By then, Charles was King.

“Recollections may vary” was the Palace’s response. It acknowledged the situation without endorsing Meghan’s account or calling her a liar. That was the institutional position. A personal denial from Charles would have turned a disputed family allegation into a statement from the Crown. 

He’d have been speaking as King, not Dad, and would also have dragged Catherine into a public race row she has never addressed herself.

The same principle applies to Harry’s legal battles.

The King is a constitutional monarch, not an absolute monarch. Justice is administered in the Crown’s name, but he cannot involve himself in individual legal matters or comment on cases and judgments. Queen Elizabeth couldn’t have done it either.

Whatever Harry says about the courts is his responsibility, including the consequences and costs. Former Lord Chief Justice Lord Burnett later told the Lords that accusing a High Court judge of a whitewash crosses into an attack on judicial independence. Judges speak through their judgments and cannot answer back. Harry made himself look stupid criticising his father’s High Court and a sitting judge.

That’s why the Buckingham Palace situation matters too. Harry didn’t stay there the night the verdict was handed down because the offer was withdrawn at the last moment. The King couldn’t have Harry using a royal residence as his base while attacking a High Court ruling. That said a lot without saying anything.

And from the very beginning, the Palace has never played tit for tat with Harry and Meghan. 

They’ve repeatedly sprung things on the Palace, from Megxit and the manner of Archie’s birth announcement to using the Queen’s own nickname for their daughter. Which was followed by the interviews, books and accusations. It’s not implausible to believe it may have happened again.

The Palace’s response has been to say as little as possible and carry on as an institution that is bigger than an exiled, whinging prince and his victim-card-carrying wife.

The Queen’s statement was the Crown’s statement, and that stance hasn’t changed. The Prince and Princess of Wales, The Princess Royal, the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, Zara, Peter and so on haven’t said anything about Harry and Meghan’s racism allegations or any of their other claims. 

Saying little to nothing isn’t going to change now, and it won’t change in the future.

The Government has approved the transfer of DRDO-developed missile-production technologies for all conventional missile systems directly to Indian industry.

Why this tech transfer is a game-changer:

 * Beyond Subsystems: Private players will no longer be limited to machining brackets, harnesses, or sub-assemblies. They now have the mandate to integrate, test, and manufacture complete conventional missile platforms.

2. Breaking the Lifecycle Import Trap:
 * Local Maintenance & Upgrades: Buying foreign platforms locks the military into decades of expensive, foreign-currency-denominated maintenance and spares.

 * Operational Readiness: Domestic production guarantees indigenous lifecycle support, insulating India from foreign supply-chain bottlenecks during periods of heightened operational demand.

3. The Tier-2/3 MSME Multiplier:
 * A lead private integrator anchors an entire industrial ecosystem.

4. Expanding Global Export Scalability:
 * Global buyers look for full, certified turnkey platforms, not just standalone subsystems.

 * Dual production lines across DPSUs and private primes allow India to scale volume manufacturing, fulfill export commitments faster, and offer competitive lifecycle packages to partner nations.

A win-win partnership:
For DRDO, this frees up critical scientific bandwidth to focus on frontier research and next-gen deterrence platforms, leaving volume industrial scaling where it belongs: with Indian industry.

text:
I was the sole techUK rep at Reform party conference. I gave a readout to my team this morning, but I thought it'd be useful to parse some insights for X...

It was a much bigger event than last time, with a far heavier business and lobbying presence. But the party hasn't yet built an offer to match that demand. Plenty of people came away feeling business day didn't give them much. Particularly as Farage publicly called out businesses he had umbrage with, which left businesses in the room feeling unsettled. 

The real signal was the councillor intake. They were out in droves and they were the most engaged audience in the building on tech. Not tech as culture war, but tech as delivery: AI adoption, and specifically AI to improve local services they are now responsible for running. 

That sits alongside a noticeably different mood on tech from the party's senior figures (of which I noticed mainly the men out and about), who had different views on data centres, AI & jobs, online safety and the digital economy. It was notable that Robert Jenrick said Reform was "ideologically pure" with no factions, but that didn't seem true on the ground.

The read for anyone in tech policy: Reform's local government layer is in delivery mode and actively looking for help, and that is a more concrete conversation than anything happening at leadership level right now.

text:
South Korea just published one of the clearest national RWA blueprints yet — and it’s not a DeFi manifesto. It’s a capital-markets operating plan.

The Korean Financial Services Commission rolled out a three-phase roadmap to tokenize securities issuance and circulation: 

Phase 1 (from Feb 2027): institutional MMFs and bonds; unlisted stocks via trusts; publicly offered fractional securities. 

Phase 2: all publicly offered securities (timing flexible — depends on Phase 1 + tech adoption). 

Phase 3: onchain payments linked to stablecoins (depends on pending stablecoin legislation).
I
nfrastructure sits with securities firms + the Korea Securities Depository. 

Licensed financial investment firms can handle tokenized securities inside current licenses (OTC intermediaries need FSS consultation). 

Issuers can run as “issuer account management entities” if they clear capital (≥₩4B), staffing, and cybersecurity bars. KSD screens distributed ledgers for issuance, circulation, and contingency plans.

Investor brakes are explicit: fractional trust and retail subscriptions are capped 

What this means for RWA as a model:

Law first, ledger second. Korea’s model is “securities that live on DLT,” not “tokens that hope to become securities.”

The composability tradeoff is policy, not a bug. Caps, licensed rails, and KSD screening will limit free DeFi looping — intentionally. The bet is credible ownership + rights + settlement beats open TVL screenshots.

RWA’s endgame may look more like Korea than a permissionless vault farm: national registry logic, regulated intermediaries, DLT for issuance/circulation/rights, then stablecoin cash rails when the law catches up.

text:
Chinese Medical Breakthrough🏥🇨🇳: China Approves World’s First Commercial Brain-Computer Implant

Nigeria Magazine | Global Health & Tech Desk

China has just made history in the fast-growing field of neurotechnology. In March 2026, the country’s medicines regulator, the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), granted commercial approval to an invasive brain-computer interface (BCI) device — a world first that has put China at the front of a race that also includes Elon Musk’s Neuralink, Synchron, and Precision Neuroscience.

What Exactly Happened?

The approved device, known as NEO, is an implantable hand motor function compensation system developed by Shanghai-based Neuracle Technology in partnership with Tsinghua University. It’s designed to help adults with cervical spinal cord injuries regain partial use of their hands — restoring the ability to hold and grip objects that had been lost to paralysis.

What makes this approval historic isn’t just the technology itself, but the speed and completeness of China’s regulatory response. Within 48 hours of the NMPA’s approval, China’s National Healthcare Security Administration had already assigned the device a medical insurance code — meaning patients could, in principle, get the procedure covered by insurance almost immediately. That takes BCI technology out of the research lab and into everyday, reimbursable medical practice.

From Approval to Operating Table

The story didn’t stop at paperwork. In July 2026, surgeons at Huashan Hospital in Shanghai performed the world’s first commercial surgery using the newly approved implant. A patient who had lived with impaired hand mobility for a decade — the result of a car accident that damaged his spinal cord — had a coin-sized brain chip implanted. According to Shanghai’s Science and Technology Commission, the procedure captured stable, high-quality brain signals, and the patient recovered well with stable vital signs.

Why This Matters Beyond China

Brain-computer interfaces work by reading electrical signals directly from the brain and translating them into commands for external devices — bypassing damaged nerves or muscles altogether. For people living with paralysis, stroke damage, or severe spinal cord injuries, this technology offers a realistic path back to independence: gripping a cup, using a keyboard, or one day, perhaps, walking again.
China’s government has backed this push at the highest level. BCI development was named a national strategic priority in mid-2025, with a roadmap targeting major technical breakthroughs by 2027 and a fully domestic supply chain by 2030, supported by a brain science fund worth roughly $165 million. Provinces like Sichuan and Chongqing are already rolling out their own BCI pilot programmes, from rehabilitation robotics to stroke recovery therapy.

The Bigger Picture for Africa and Nigeria

For readers in Nigeria and across Africa, developments like this are worth watching closely. As BCI and other advanced neurotechnologies move from experimental labs to approved, insurance-backed treatments, the conversation will increasingly turn to access: which countries can afford to import or license this technology, and how health systems in the Global South can prepare for a coming wave of neuro-rehabilitation tools.

Whether or not this technology reaches Nigerian hospitals in the near term, the message is clear: the future of medicine is increasingly about the brain talking directly to machines — and that future has now, quite literally, begun.

text:
Every morning, many people wake up before 4:00am, prepare for work, enter traffic and spend most of their day doing jobs they no longer enjoy.

They complain about their salary, the workload, the management and the lack of growth. Then they return home, sleep and repeat the same routine the following day.

Disliking your job is understandable. But complaining about it without preparing for another option can keep you trapped for years.

I am not saying that you should resign tomorrow.

The job you dislike may still be paying for your food, rent, transportation, internet data and family responsibilities. Leaving it without savings, a reliable alternative or a proper plan may create a more difficult problem.

The wiser approach is to let your current job support you while you gradually build your next opportunity.

Of course, learning a new skill while working is not easy.

Many employees return home physically and mentally tired. Some have children or relatives to care for. Others do not know which skill to choose or are afraid of becoming beginners again.

Some expect quick results. When they do not start earning after watching a few tutorials, they become discouraged.

Social media can also make learning a skill look easier than it is. You see someone announce a new job, client or business success, but you do not see the months or years of learning, practice, rejection and improvement behind it.

Despite these challenges, developing a marketable skill can create possibilities your current job may not provide.

It could help you qualify for a better paying position, offer services to businesses, work as a freelancer, start a small side business, improve an existing business or build an additional source of income.

There are many useful skills you can learn: sales, digital marketing, copywriting, graphic design, video editing, data analysis, web development, data entry, customer service, etc.

You do not need to learn all of them.

Start by identifying the kind of opportunity you want. Then research the skills that are useful in that area. Choose one and commit to learning it properly.

Remember that watching tutorials alone does not make you skilled.

A skill becomes valuable when you can use it to solve a real problem, produce quality work and show evidence of what you can do.

Create a realistic weekly learning schedule. Practise through small personal projects. Build a simple portfolio. Offer to help a few individuals or businesses, collect honest feedback and improve your work.

You must also learn how to communicate, market and sell your ability. Being good at something is important, but people need to know what you can do and how it can help them.

Imagine a Nigerian employee who returns home every evening feeling exhausted. They say they have no time to learn, yet they spend two hours scrolling through social media to relax.

What if they redirected just 45 minutes of that time into learning one skill?

Over several months, those 45 minute sessions could produce useful knowledge, completed projects and the beginning of a portfolio. It would not guarantee employment or income, but it would put them in a stronger position than months of scrolling and complaining.

Learning a valuable skill requires sacrifice.

You may need to reduce entertainment, wake up earlier, use part of your weekend wisely or spend money on reliable training and internet data. You may also need to continue practising when progress feels slow.

Motivation will not always be available. That is why you need a manageable routine. Forty five focused minutes you can maintain is often more useful than studying for six hours once and abandoning the process.

As you improve, begin testing your skill in the real world. Speak to potential clients, apply for relevant opportunities, attend useful events and build genuine professional relationships.

Do not resign simply because you earned money once from a side hustle.

Before leaving your job, consider whether the income is consistent. Think about your emergency savings, dependants, healthcare, debt and monthly living expenses. One successful month is not always evidence of a stable business.

Learning a skill does not guarantee instant success. Not every skill will automatically produce income.

Results depend on demand, competence, consistent practice, visibility, relationships and your ability to solve problems people are willing to pay to have solved.

Employment is not failure, and keeping your job while preparing for something better is not cowardice. Your salary can become part of the support system that funds your learning and gives you time to make thoughtful decisions.

But do not spend years complaining about a job you hate while refusing to prepare for the life you want.

Keep your job if you still need it but start building your next option.

text:
PULSE BIOSCIENCES $PLSE FUNDS ITSELF BY SELLING SHARES INTO ITS OWN RALLY:

The Momentum Len5 is watching Pulse Biosciences at $53.24, -$1.47 / -2.69% on Friday. US markets are shut Monday, September 7 for Labor Day, so that is the latest price on both names here. The Hayward, California company is developing devices that treat an irregular heartbeat with very short bursts of electricity rather than heat or cold, disabling the small patches of heart tissue that carry the faulty signal.

The verdict: this is the name this Len5 rates first, and the emptiest business behind any climb on it. Pulse sold $434,000 of product in three months and is worth about $3.8B. Everything in that gap is two clinical trials - and the rally is what pays for them.

The June quarter, reported August 7:

- Product revenue - money from selling devices and the single-use parts that go with them - $434k, against $0 in the same quarter last year
- Net loss $24.7M, wider than the $19.2M a year earlier; $0.36 a share against $0.28
- Research and development $17.0M; selling and administrative costs $8.5M
- Cash $101.6M at June 30, on 70.8M shares outstanding

Now the line that explains how a company losing $24.7M in three months still holds $101.6M. A year earlier the balance was $106.3M. Twelve months on, it is down $4.7M. Selling stock covered the rest: $46.8M net through an at-the-market program in the June quarter alone - new shares fed into the open market a few at a time, at whatever price the day offers - plus $10.7M more since, with a fresh $75M facility behind it.

So the share price here is not a scoreboard. It is an input. On May 12 Pulse disclosed that co-chairman Robert Duggan and chief executive Paul LaViolette had bought 675,233 shares through that same program for about $13.3M, roughly $19.70 each; the stock rose $4.22 / +22.1% that session, $19.08 to $23.30. At the $12.66 this settled at on November 20, its lowest close of the past year, that same $13.3M would have cost owners about 1.6 times as many shares. A higher price makes the money cheaper, and this company needs a great deal more of it.

What the money buys is a patient count. The catheter study, NANOPULSE-AF, is past halfway at more than 82 patients across 12 sites; Pulse raised its own target to 164 and expects to finish enrolling early in the fourth quarter. The surgical study, NANOCLAMP-AF, is the first pulsed-field trial the FDA has cleared for a heart-surgery ablation device used alongside another operation, and its US enrolling is mapped to finish by the middle of 2027.

Six styles, one company:

- MOMENTUM - STRONG, and why it sits here. Wants a price near its own twelve-month best with the one-, three- and six-month stretches all pointing the same way. They do, without argument: +39.2% from the $38.24 of August 6, +110.2% from the $25.33 of June 5, +193.5% from the $18.14 of March 6, and Friday closed 2.7% under the $54.71 of September 3, its best in a year. CHANGE IT: a close back under the $41.51 of August 10, where this month started.

- HYPERGROWTH - PARTIAL, and the halves split cleanly. Wants a business early as well as fast. Early is beyond argument. Fast cannot be measured yet - $434k against $0 is a beginning, not a growth rate, and Pulse calls this a limited release. CHANGE IT: a quarter where product sales are large enough that a percentage means something.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Wants real expansion nobody has already overpaid for. Overpaid is settled by the two figures above, and the expansion has not started. CHANGE IT: an approved product selling at a scale that turns the price into a multiple of something.

- QUALITY-VALUE - NOT A FIT. Wants a hard-to-copy business at a fair price. The technology has a real claim - the cardiac surgery system won the FDA's Breakthrough Device Designation in July 2024, a status that speeds review of devices with no good alternative - but a patent position is not yet a business, and no measure available makes this price a fair one. CHANGE IT: approval, then customers buying the disposable parts a second and a third time.

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - NOT A FIT, and the nearest in shape. Wants a good business marked down after something visible went wrong. The event half is genuine and dated. The markdown half does not exist at +252.3% over twelve months. CHANGE IT: a disappointing trial reading, the only route by which this style ever gets a look here.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT, furthest off. Wants cash genuinely reaching owners, funded by the business. It runs backwards: no dividend, no buyback, and owners handed the company $46.8M in the June quarter and $10.7M since, rather than collecting anything. CHANGE IT: nothing realistic for years.

AtriCure at $51.52, -$0.94 / -1.79% on Friday is the finished version of this idea, and it sits on the same Momentum Len5 on a climb that holds across every stretch. The Mason, Ohio company makes the tools heart surgeons already use on an irregular heartbeat; its own June quarter, reported July 23, brought revenue of $153.6M, +12.8%, and $9M of profit. Nearly the same share price, and about $2.6B of market value against Pulse's $3.8B - the company that sells the product is worth less than the company still testing one.

The strongest fact against Friday's close is not the loss. Of the four brokerages that set a target on this stock in recent weeks - Oppenheimer $35 on July 28, Canaccord Genuity $43 and Mizuho $45 on August 10, Needham $58 on August 17 - three sit below where it finished.

Nobody buying this on Friday was buying $434,000 of product. They were buying a headcount at twelve hospitals, and that count is meant to be complete within weeks. The risk sits where the reward does: the money funding those trials comes out of the share price, so a fall makes the next raise dearer just when it would be hardest to skip. Pulse has not dated its third-quarter report; last year's landed November 5.

Not investment advice.

text:
A guy I know started dating a lady he met through a mutual friend. 

Everything was going well.

They talked every day, went on dates, and after a few weeks, she started spending weekends at his place.

One Saturday, he came back from the market with foodstuff.

Rice. Chicken. Vegetables. Everything.

He dropped the bags in the kitchen and went to take a shower. When he came back, the lady was sitting in the living room scrolling through her phone.📱 

Then he asked casually: “Babe, have you eaten?” She said, “No.”

He looked towards the kitchen. “You didn’t cook?”

She replied: “I don’t cook for men. I’m not your wife.”

He laughed because he thought she was joking. But She wasn’t.

He said, “That’s fine. You could have just told me you don’t like cooking. I can respect that.”

She replied: “Exactly. And I’m not using my money to feed you either. If you want to eat, order for yourself.”

That evening, she ordered food for herself.

He ordered his own.

The next morning, the same thing happened.

She made breakfast for herself but didn’t offer him anything.

He didn’t argue.
He simply observed.

A few days later, he sat her down.

He told her: “I’m not looking for a woman to serve me. But I’m also not looking for someone who thinks every act of consideration in a relationship is oppression.”

She said: “I’m setting boundaries.”

He replied: “Boundaries are okay. But there’s a difference between having a boundary and deliberately withholding basic consideration from someone you’re claiming to build a relationship with.”

They eventually ended things. 

Safe to say they don’t deserve each other. 😫

Defence division president Steve Parker said the drone is meant to fly with crewed fighters, share sensor data and extend their reach. Airbus is also weighing an entry as U.S., European and Japanese firms compete.

Australia had eight Block 1 aircraft by late 2024, with more than 100 flight-test hours and live weapons drops. Nine Block 2 jets are in build; Block 3 is planned with an internal bay and longer range.

Boeing teamed with Rheinmetall to offer the type to Germany. The drone flew at Valiant Shield 2026 from the Marianas and completed Point Mugu tests with an IRST nose sensor.

Japan awarded Boeing about ¥155 million ($997,000) in 2025 for manned-unmanned teaming simulations linked to its next-generation fighter with the UK and Italy. Tokyo has also joined the U.S. Collaborative Combat Aircraft effort.

text:
Why do you hate Bremer? The truth is I do not hate Bremer at all, nor do I have any personal issue with him. My grievance is purely tactical, analyzing football strictly from a Juventus standpoint.

The whole story began when De Ligt was sold for €85 million, and Juventus management directed €60 million into signing Bremer. Bremer was outstanding at Torino, but he played as a central sweeper in a back three. Andrea Agnelli went overboard on the transfer fee. Marotta at Inter offered €35 million, but Agnelli pushed it to €55 million just to hijack the deal.

The objective was to sign a defender capable of covering two positions: Bonucci's role and Chiellini's left-sided role whenever needed. That was the tactical mistake that cost Juventus dearly in transfer fee and a massive salary, currently reaching €11 million gross for a contract tied down until 2029.

What is the difference between Gatti and Bremer? In simple analytical terms, Gatti is superior in 1v1 duels, ball recoveries, and aerial power. Bremer offers better mobility and speed alongside solid defensive quality.

Both have very weak left feet and face tactical difficulties playing as a left-sided center-back. Therefore, both are competing for the exact same spot: either right center-back or central sweeper.

So I neither love Bremer nor hate him. The entire issue stems from his long contract and bloated salary. Management is living on the fantasy of selling him, but Obviously no club will step up to match those outrageous wages.

The outcome is persistent injustice toward Gatti, attempting to sell him for €30 million to minimize financial losses, while rotating Kalulu with Bremer or signing a youth prospect for €10 million on a €1.5 million salary. That is the reality.

That is the issue. I am not against Bremer; I am against treating Gatti unfairly to the detriment of Juventus.

You are benching the squad's best ball-winner, an extra target on corner kicks, a player who embodies the true Juventus spirit, and a leader on the pitch, all to justify a flawed financial decision. That is the root problem. By the way, to anyone defending Bremer, if a decent offer arrived tomorrow morning, he would be sold immediately.

The only aspect where Bremer holds an edge over Gatti is mobility. But as a pure defender, when speaking about interceptions, physical duels, and aerial strength, let us be realistic: Gatti belongs in conversations with Van Dijk and Rúben Dias, not defenders like Bremer.
