text:
Russia–Brazil: Strategic Reach Meets Structural Limits - Russia and Brazil are deepening an established strategic partnership, but the verified record does not support the conclusion that Brazil is entering a Russian geopolitical sphere.
Bilateral trade reached a reported US$12.4 billion in 2024, yet its concentration—especially Brazilian imports of Russian fertilisers—creates interdependence rather than a diversified strategic-economic bloc.
Local-currency settlement is a declared objective, not an operational bilateral regime. Trade imbalance, banking exposure, liquidity and sanctions-compliance risks remain decisive constraints.
The 2025 BRICS declaration advanced technical work on payment-system interoperability; it did not establish a common currency or a completed BRICS payment system.
Brazilian participation in a Russian security forum and reported interest in examining Russian defence products do not establish procurement, technology transfer, testing or fielded capability.
Moscow gains diplomatic legitimacy and commercial resilience from Brasília; Brazil gains fertiliser security, negotiating leverage and strategic optionality.
The most defensible outlook is selective expansion without alliance: stronger institutional dialogue and practical trade mechanisms, but limited defence penetration and no demonstrated Brazilian abandonment of strategic autonomy.

Brazil and Russia: Partnership Without Alignment
Brazil and Russia have built a relationship that is politically useful, commercially substantial and strategically constrained. Their cooperation operates through BRICS, the G20 and the United Nations; bilateral trade reached US$10.9 billion in 2025; and a defence agreement permits military exchanges, exercises and technical cooperation. Yet the architecture remains asymmetric. Brazilian agriculture depends on Russian fertilisers and diesel, while Russia absorbs comparatively few Brazilian exports. National-currency settlement cannot correct that imbalance. Defence contacts offer access to Russian technology but expose any procurement to sanctions, export controls and uncertain lifecycle support. The decisive question is therefore not whether Brasília and Moscow can deepen relations. It is whether they can convert diplomatic proximity into durable economic and technological capacity without compromising Brazil’s strategic autonomy.

Strategic Distance
The defining feature of the relationship is cooperation without geopolitical alignment. Vladimir Putin and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva share an interest in a more distributed international system, stronger representation for emerging economies and institutional coordination outside exclusively Western frameworks. This creates diplomatic convergence, but not a common security policy.

Brazil’s position is anchored in sovereign decision-making, peaceful dispute settlement and freedom to maintain multiple partnerships. Its defence doctrine identifies national sovereignty, territorial integrity and protection against external interference as central objectives, while calling for investment in domestic capabilities and military readiness. Livro Branco de Defesa Nacional — Ministry of Defence of Brazil — 2024

Moscow consequently offers Brasília an additional channel of influence, not an alliance. Russia benefits from engagement with the largest economy in Latin America and from demonstrating that Western pressure has not produced universal diplomatic isolation. Brazil gains negotiating latitude across BRICS and the G20 while preserving relations with the United States, Europe and China. Neither side, however, has accepted obligations of mutual defence, coordinated deterrence or foreign-policy discipline.

That distinction is essential. A strategic partnership describes the breadth of dialogue; it does not establish identity of interests.

The Weight of Trade
The commercial relationship is large enough to matter but too concentrated to rebalance the partnership. Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies reported that bilateral merchandise trade reached US$10.9 billion in 2025. Brazilian exports accounted for US$1.5 billion, while imports from Russia reached US$9.4 billion, principally fertilisers and diesel. Rússia quer retomar cooperação parlamentar e levar missão a Moscou — Chamber of Deputies of Brazil — Mar 2026

Calculated from those official figures, Russian goods represented 86.2% of the bilateral flow, leaving Brazil with a merchandise deficit of US$7.9 billion. For every dollar of Brazilian goods sold to Russia, Brazil purchased approximately US$6.27 from it.

This is not balanced interdependence. Russia supplies inputs that affect Brazilian agricultural yields, freight costs and food-price formation; Brazil’s exports to Russia do not exercise comparable leverage over the Russian economy. The relationship’s political visibility therefore exceeds its commercial diversification.

The imbalance also explains why bilateral ambitions have repeatedly turned toward new Brazilian exports, investment and industrial cooperation. Without broader Russian demand for Brazilian food, manufactured goods, machinery, services and technology, higher trade volumes can deepen concentration rather than create resilience.

Fertiliser as Infrastructure
Fertiliser is commonly classified as a traded commodity. For Brazil, it is more accurately understood as production infrastructure. Its availability affects planting decisions, yields, rural credit, export income, transport utilisation and food inflation. Russian supply therefore connects the bilateral relationship directly to Brazil’s fiscal, monetary and agricultural-policy environment.

This dependence gives Brasília a rational interest in preserving commercial channels with Moscow. It does not eliminate the case for diversification. A supply structure concentrated in a geopolitically exposed market transfers external shocks into domestic production costs. Shipping disruption, banking restrictions, insurance withdrawal or sanctions uncertainty can affect delivery even when agricultural trade itself is not formally prohibited.

US authorities have explicitly stated that their Russia sanctions are not designed to target agricultural trade. That protection is significant but not equivalent to frictionless commerce: banks and logistics companies still screen counterparties, ownership, vessels and payment routes. Fact Sheet: Russia Sanctions and Agricultural Trade — US Department of the Treasury — Jul 2022

Brazil’s strategic objective should therefore be continuity without exclusivity: maintain lawful Russian supplies while expanding domestic production, alternative sourcing, port flexibility and inventories. The relevant measure of sovereignty is not the nationality of the supplier but the system’s ability to withstand its interruption.

The Currency Illusion
The proposal to settle trade in reais and roubles has political appeal. It can reduce conversion costs in some transactions, limit direct reliance on dollar clearing and demonstrate the ability of emerging economies to construct additional payment channels. But currency denomination cannot solve an underlying shortage of reciprocal commercial flows.

With Brazil importing US$9.4 billion and exporting US$1.5 billion in 2025, Russian sellers would accumulate far more reais than Russian importers require for purchases from Brazil. A sustainable local-currency mechanism would need one or more balancing functions: deeper Russian demand for Brazilian goods; investment opportunities for accumulated reais; central-bank liquidity arrangements; currency swaps; or conversion through another internationally accepted asset.

Each mechanism introduces price, liquidity, convertibility or counterparty risk. Exporters ordinarily prefer currencies that can be used predictably to pay suppliers, service debt or preserve value. A payment system may move the transaction away from the dollar, but it cannot manufacture demand for the weaker side’s currency.

The same limit applies to BRICS financial initiatives. The bloc can expand settlement options and institutional experimentation, but a common political preference for monetary diversification is not a substitute for deep capital markets, transparent pricing, liquid hedging instruments and balanced trade. Currency substitution is an instrument of commerce—not a cure for its structure.

Defence Without Procurement
Brazil and Russia possess a formal defence framework. The agreement signed in Moscow on 14 December 2012 and approved by Brazil’s Congress on 25 May 2017 covers political-military consultations, peacekeeping experience, military education, maritime search and rescue, technical systems, delegation visits, exercises, training and visits by military aircraft and warships. The designated implementing authorities are the two defence ministries. Agreement between the Government of the Federative Republic of Brazil and the Government of the Russian Federation on Defence Cooperation — National Congress of Brazil — May 2017

The instrument creates access, not an acquisition mandate. A delegation may examine equipment, exchange operational experience or attend a security forum without generating a Brazilian requirement, budget appropriation or contract.

The historical record nevertheless shows that cooperation can reach operational level. Brazil acquired 12 Russian Mi-35M attack helicopters, designated AH-2 Sabre. In April 2020, the Brazilian Air Force reported that the aircraft had arrived in four lots and accumulated more than 8,000 flight hours. Há 10 anos, helicóptero AH-2 Sabre era incorporado à Força Aérea Brasileira — Brazilian Air Force — Apr 2020

Brazil’s Ministry of Defence also records officer exchanges, cyber and space working groups, aviation cooperation and negotiations concerning Igla and Pantsir-S1 air-defence systems. Crucially, the official wording distinguishes the completed helicopter acquisition from air-defence negotiations; it does not record a completed Pantsir-S1 purchase. Parcerias e acordos em Defesa — Ministry of Defence of Brazil — current institutional record

The Sanctions Perimeter
The central obstacle to a new Russian weapons acquisition is not diplomatic access. It is transaction execution and support over the equipment’s full service life.

US sanctions apply through designated Russian manufacturers, banks and intermediaries, while US export controls can affect US-origin and specified foreign-produced components, software and technology. The US Treasury warns that persons outside Russia can face exposure for significant transactions or material support involving Russia’s military-industrial base, designated entities or sanctions-evasion structures. Frequently Asked Questions—Recently Updated — Office of Foreign Assets Control — current record The broader legal architecture includes the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act and successive Russia-related executive orders, regulations, directives and designations. Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act-Related Sanctions — Office of Foreign Assets Control — current record

European exposure is equally relevant. Regulation (EU) 2021/821 controls exports, brokering, transit and technical assistance involving dual-use goods, software and technology. It applies throughout the Union, with national enforcement in Italy, France, Germany and the other member states. Exporting dual-use items — European Commission — current record The United Kingdom operates a separate sanctions and export-licensing regime.

These rules are not automatically Brazilian prohibitions. Their reach arises through suppliers, controlled content, banks, insurers, shipping companies, software licences and maintenance providers under the relevant jurisdictions. Paying in roubles or reais does not release a controlled semiconductor, authorise a blocked counterparty or persuade an insurer to accept prohibited exposure.

The Lifecycle Test
The decisive evaluation of Russian equipment is therefore not its catalogue performance or acquisition price. It is whether Brazil can finance, integrate and maintain the system through 2031.

A credible programme would require verified access to technical data, diagnostic equipment, spare parts, munitions, software updates and depot-level maintenance. Brazil would need authority to integrate national communications, sensors and weapons; lawful access to every material third-country component; and contractual protection against supply interruption.

Technology transfer must also be measured precisely. Assembly is not design authority. Training is not control of source code. A domestic maintenance facility is not strategic autonomy if critical modules must still return to Russia or depend on components whose export can be denied.

This is where industrial policy and sanctions converge. A purchase intended to diversify Brazil’s suppliers can reproduce dependency in a less transparent and more politically exposed form. Conversely, a narrowly defined cooperation project with genuine Brazilian intellectual property, local production and replaceable inputs might improve autonomy even if Russian technology participates in it. The determining variable is control over the lifecycle.

The 2031 Balance
The most defensible trajectory is continued political dialogue, commercial interdependence and selective defence contact without a major geopolitical realignment. Brazil has incentives to protect fertiliser and energy flows, expand exports, preserve BRICS coordination and examine technologies from multiple suppliers. Russia has incentives to retain a major non-Western partner with global diplomatic weight.

Yet structural limits will remain. Trade concentration restricts the economic case for national-currency settlement. Sanctions and export controls raise the cost of defence procurement. Brazil’s existing industrial relationships require interoperability across non-Russian systems. Most importantly, Brasília’s concept of autonomy is incompatible with replacing one external dependence with another.

A different outcome would require visible official evidence: a published Brazilian capability requirement, budget authority, procurement instrument, named suppliers, tested configurations, licensed components, an executable payment channel and a sovereign maintenance plan. Until those elements appear, diplomatic warmth should be read as strategic optionality—not as the prelude to alignment.

Brazil and Russia can broaden their partnership by 2031. Its durability, however, will be decided less in summit language than in fertiliser terminals, payment ledgers, export licences, production lines and maintenance hangars. Those are the places where sovereignty becomes measurable. - https://t.co/1y5A1Akqzw via @https://debuglies.com

#ISPR
Official Press Release 

Pakistan Air Force observed 7th September as Martyrs’ Day at all PAF Bases across the country to honour the supreme sacrifices of its martyrs and pay homage to their courage, valour and devotion to duty. 

The day commenced with a special Du’aa and Quran Khawani for the Shuhada of the 1965 and 1971 Wars, the brave martyrs of Marka-e-Haq and all PAF personnel who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty since the inception of Pakistan.

Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu, NI (M), HJ, Chief of the Air Staff, Pakistan Air Force, was the Chief Guest at the Martyrs’ Day ceremony held at Air Headquarters, Islamabad. The Air Chief paid rich tribute to PAF martyrs, underscoring that their sacrifices constitute the foundation of PAF’s proud legacy of courage, professionalism and unwavering commitment to the defence of the motherland. He said that the valiant deeds of our forefathers are not merely chapters of history but a living legacy that places a profound responsibility upon the present generation. 

Paying homage to the martyrs, Chief of the Air Staff said, “Our Shuhada are enduring symbols of courage, sacrifice and national resolve. Their legacy reminds us that the defence of our motherland is a sacred trust, which we shall continue to uphold with steadfast commitment.”

Later, the Air Chief laid a floral wreath at the Martyrs’ Monument and offered Fateha in solemn remembrance of the gallant martyrs of PAF.

text:
Write about: Follow Jesus’ emotions. Read looking only for moments when Jesus shows compassion, grief, anger, joy, tenderness, urgency, or anguish. Ask, “What moved His heart?”

A powerful way to read the Gospels is to stop for a while from asking only, “What did Jesus teach?” and begin asking, “What moved Jesus?”Read slowly and watch His heart.Notice when compassion interrupts His journey. Notice when grief brings Him to tears. Notice when anger rises against hardness, hypocrisy, exploitation, or the misuse of holy things. Notice His tenderness toward children, the ashamed, the sick, the grieving, and those others overlooked. Notice His joy when people receive the truth. Notice His urgency when crowds are wandering without a shepherd. Notice His anguish as the cross approaches.Then ask:What moved His heart?Compassion — suffering moved Him
Again and again, Jesus does more than observe suffering. He is moved by it.When He sees crowds who are “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd,” He has compassion on them (Matthew 9:36).When a widow is walking behind the coffin of her only son, Jesus sees her grief and says, “Don’t cry.” Then He acts (Luke 7:13–15).When hungry people have remained with Him for days, He does not dismiss their physical need. He says, “I have compassion for these people.” (Mark 8:2 NIV)Following Jesus’ emotions reveals something important: human misery was never an abstraction to Him.He noticed faces.He noticed hunger.He noticed loneliness.He noticed bewilderment.He noticed people crushed by sickness, sin, grief, oppression, and spiritual confusion.Ask yourself:Do the things that moved Jesus still move me?Grief — unbelief and death wounded Him
Jesus wept. At Lazarus’s tomb, surrounded by grieving people, “Jesus wept.” (John 11:35 NIV)He knew resurrection was moments away, and still He entered their sorrow.That tells us something profound about God.Knowing the ending does not make grief meaningless.Jesus also wept over Jerusalem:“As he approached Jerusalem and saw the city, he wept over it.” (Luke 19:41 NIV)He was grieving more than architecture or politics.He saw people resisting the peace God was offering them.Jesus’ tears reveal what His heart values.Death grieves Him.
Unbelief grieves Him.
People refusing the life God offers grieves Him.Anger — hardened hearts and corrupted worship provoked Him
Jesus was not emotionally indifferent toward evil. In Mark 3, religious leaders watched to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath so they could accuse Him.Jesus looked at them “in anger and, deeply distressed at their stubborn hearts” (Mark 3:5 NIV).Notice the combination:anger and grief.His anger was not petty irritation.Their hardness prevented them from rejoicing over mercy.His cleansing of the temple also shows fierce zeal. A place intended for prayer had been distorted by exploitation and commerce.Jesus’ anger asks us a searching question:What makes me angry?Personal inconvenience?Being contradicted?Losing status?Or the things that angered Jesus—hard hearts, injustice, hypocrisy, exploitation, and barriers placed between people and God?Tenderness — vulnerable people drew Him near
Jesus repeatedly moves toward people others might consider interruptions.Children.Lepers.Blind beggars.Women carrying shame. Tax collectors.The grieving.The socially unwanted.When people brought children to Him and the disciples tried to stop them, Jesus was indignant and said:“Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them.” (Mark 10:14 NIV)Then:“He took the children in his arms, placed his hands on them and blessed them.” (Mark 10:16 NIV)That is worth imagining slowly.The hands that would be pierced by nails were placed gently upon children.The King of heaven made room for those who possessed no status. Joy — Jesus rejoiced when God’s truth was received
Jesus was not perpetually solemn.Luke records an extraordinary moment:“At that time Jesus, full of joy through the Holy Spirit…” (Luke 10:21 NIV)What produced this joy?The Father was revealing His kingdom to humble people.Jesus delighted when ordinary people began seeing what God was doing.His joy reveals that salvation is not merely a theological transaction. God delights in redemption. You can read the Gospels asking:What made Jesus glad?Faith.Humility.Repentance.Truth received.Lost people found.The Father's purposes unfolding.Urgency — lost people mattered now
Jesus sometimes speaks with startling urgency.“As long as it is day, we must do the works of him who sent me.” (John 9:4 NIV)He sees the harvest and tells His disciples:“The harvest is plentiful but the workers are few.” (Matthew 9:37 NIV)His urgency was not frantic anxiety. It came from knowing that people mattered eternally.Jesus could spend long hours in prayer and still move through life with a powerful awareness:There are people who need the kingdom of God.Anguish — Gethsemane opens a window into His suffering
Few passages reveal Jesus’ inner life more deeply than Gethsemane.He tells His disciples:“My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death.” (Matthew 26:38 NIV)Jesus does not approach the cross emotionally untouched.He feels its horror.He prays.He agonizes.He submits Himself to the Father:“Yet not as I will, but as you will.” (Matthew 26:39 NIV)This is obedience at tremendous emotional cost.Following Jesus’ emotions prevents us from imagining holiness as emotional numbness.Jesus was perfectly holy and profoundly feeling.A revealing pattern appears
When you trace Jesus’ emotions through the Gospels, something striking emerges.He was tender toward broken sinners and severe toward hardened hypocrisy.He had compassion on crowds.He touched lepers.He welcomed children.He received repentant people.He wept with mourners.He grieved over cities.He confronted religious pride.He became angry when mercy was resisted.He anguished over the cross.And through everything, His heart remained aligned with the Father.That gives us a beautiful way to pray while reading:Jesus, teach me to love what You love.
Teach me to grieve over what grieves You.
Teach me to become angry at what dishonors God rather than what merely inconveniences me.
Give me compassion for suffering people.
Give me tenderness toward the weak.
Give me joy when sinners come home.
Give me urgency for people who are far from God.
Shape my heart until what moves Your heart begins to move mine.That may be one of the most transformative ways to read the Gospels:Don't merely follow Jesus' footsteps. Follow His heart.

text:
【意外と知らない 英語で読む建築と美術 ㊼ ― パラディオの《ヴィラ・ロトンダ》は、なぜ「四方向すべてが正面」なのか】

建築には普通、

front

「正面」

があります。

玄関があり、

そこから建物へ入る。

ところが、

Andrea Palladio

アンドレア・パラディオの、

Villa Rotonda

《ヴィラ・ロトンダ》

を見ると、

少し戸惑います。

四方向に、

ほぼ同じような神殿風の玄関がある。

つまり、

「正面はどこ？」

という問いが生まれる。

今回は、

symmetry

「対称性」

central plan

「集中式平面」

orientation

「方向づけ」

そして、

landscape

「風景」

から建築を見てみましょう。

まず、

facade。

「ファサード・建物の外観面」。

特に、

principal facade

「主要な正面」。

普通、

建物には、

正面と背面があります。

front facade

「正面」。

rear facade

「背面」。

しかし、

ヴィラ・ロトンダでは、

four facades

「四つの外観面」

が、

かなり似た構成になっています。

Each facade is treated almost like a principal facade.

「それぞれの外観面が、ほとんど主要正面のように扱われている。」

ここで、

treat A as B

「AをBとして扱う」。

非常に便利です。

そして、

portico

という建築英語。

「柱で支えられた玄関ポーチ」。

a columned portico

「列柱のあるポルティコ」。

Each side has a classical portico.

「それぞれの面に古典的なポルティコがある。」

ここで、

classical

「古典的な」。

古代ギリシャ・ローマ建築との関係を示します。

columns

「柱」。

pediment

「ペディメント・三角破風」。

temple front

「神殿風正面」。

つまり、

住宅なのに、

神殿のように見える。

ここで、

domestic architecture

「住宅建築」。

temple architecture

「神殿建築」。

Palladio applied elements of temple architecture to a domestic building.

「パラディオは神殿建築の要素を住宅に応用した。」

apply A to B

「AをBに応用する」。

英語学習でも重要な表現です。

では、

なぜ四方向に玄関があるのでしょうか。

ここで、

orientation。

「方向づけ・方位」。

Buildings are oriented toward something.

「建築は何かに向かって方向づけられる。」

道路。

広場。

海。

山。

庭。

都市。

建築は、

周囲との関係によって、

向きを持ちます。

しかし、

ヴィラ・ロトンダでは、

一方向だけが絶対的な正面ではない。

周囲には、

landscape

「風景」

が広がります。

そこで、

view。

「眺望」。

vista。

「遠くへ開ける眺望」。

The porticos frame views of the surrounding landscape.

「ポルティコは周囲の風景への眺望を枠取る。」

ここで、

frame。

前回も登場しました。

絵画の frame は、

世界を切り取ります。

建築も、

窓。

柱。

開口部。

玄関。

によって、

風景を frame することができます。

Architecture can frame the landscape like a picture.

「建築は絵のように風景を枠取ることができる。」

つまり、

建物だけを見るのではなく、

建物から外を見る。

これが重要です。

What can you see from the building?

「建物から何が見える？」

建築鑑賞では、

ぜひ覚えておきたい質問です。

そして、

plan

「平面計画」。

ヴィラ・ロトンダでは、

central plan

「集中式平面」

という考え方が重要です。

central

「中心の」。

center

「中心」。

建物の中央に、

特徴的な central hall

「中央ホール」

があります。

その上には、

dome

「ドーム」。

ここで、

axis

「軸」。

複数形は、

axes。

The plan is organized around intersecting axes.

「平面は交差する軸を中心に構成されている。」

intersect

「交差する」。

intersection

「交差」。

一本の軸だけではない。

複数方向が、

center

で交わる。

そこで、

centrality

「中心性」。

The design emphasizes centrality.

「この設計は中心性を強調している。」

では、

中心とは何でしょうか。

単に、

建物の真ん中？

それだけではありません。

中心があることで、

周囲の方向が整理されます。

north

「北」。

south

「南」。

east

「東」。

west

「西」。

center

と、

surroundings

「周囲」。

建物の内部に中心を作り、

そこから四方向へ世界を見る。

ここで、

radiate

という動詞。

「中心から放射する」。

Spaces appear to radiate from the center.

「空間が中心から放射しているように見える。」

そして、

symmetry。

「対称性」。

以前、

ルネサンス建築でも扱いました。

symmetrical

「左右対称の」。

bilateral symmetry

「左右対称」。

しかし、

ヴィラ・ロトンダでは、

一方向から見た左右対称だけでなく、

中心を軸にした秩序が強く感じられます。

ここで、

geometric order

「幾何学的秩序」。

The building is governed by a strong geometric order.

「建物は強い幾何学的秩序によって構成されている。」

govern

は、

「統治する」

だけではありません。

原理や規則が、

全体を支配する、

という意味にも使えます。

The composition is governed by symmetry.

「構成は対称性によって統御されている。」

そして、

proportion

「比例」。

パラディオ建築を語るとき、

重要な概念です。

room

「部屋」。

dimension

「寸法」。

ratio

「比率」。

relationship

「関係」。

Proportion creates relationships between parts.

「比例は部分同士の関係を作る。」

以前も出てきましたが、

proportion は、

単に「きれいな比率」

ではありません。

part

「部分」

と、

whole

「全体」

の関係です。

The parts are related to the whole.

「各部分が全体と関係づけられている。」

ここで、

coherence

という重要語があります。

「一貫性・まとまり」。

coherent

「一貫した・まとまりのある」。

The proportional system gives the building visual coherence.

「比例体系が建物に視覚的なまとまりを与えている。」

そして、

harmony

「調和」。

ただし、

harmony は、

何となく美しい、

という意味だけで使わない。

何と何が調和しているのかを見る。

geometry and landscape

「幾何学と風景」。

building and site

「建築と敷地」。

center and surroundings

「中心と周囲」。

interior and exterior

「内部と外部」。

ここで、

relationship。

建築を見るとき、

最も重要な言葉の一つです。

Architecture is about relationships.

「建築とは関係について考えることでもある。」

柱だけを見る。

窓だけを見る。

ドームだけを見る。

それでは、

建築全体は見えません。

柱と壁。

窓と光。

内部と外部。

建物と土地。

人間と空間。

その relationship を見る。

さらに、

approach

という言葉。

名詞なら、

「近づき方・アプローチ」。

動詞なら、

「近づく」。

How do you approach the building?

「あなたはどう建物へ近づく？」

これも、

建築を見る重要な質問です。

ヴィラ・ロトンダでは、

複数方向から建物へ接近できます。

すると、

arrival

「到着」

の経験も、

一つではありません。

The building offers multiple approaches.

「建物は複数のアプローチを提供する。」

offer

「提供する」。

つまり、

建築は、

一枚の正面写真だけでは理解できない。

歩く。

近づく。

階段を上る。

ポルティコを通る。

中央へ入る。

別の方向を見る。

外へ出る。

そこで、

sequence

「連続・一連の流れ」。

spatial sequence

「空間の連続」。

Architecture unfolds as a sequence of spaces.

「建築は空間の連続として展開する。」

unfold

「展開する」。

建築英語で覚えておくと、

とても便利です。

A view gradually unfolds.

「眺望が徐々に開けていく。」

A spatial sequence unfolds as we move.

「移動するにつれて空間の連続が展開する。」

つまり、

建築には、

time

「時間」

があります。

見る位置が変わる。

風景が変わる。

光が変わる。

正面が変わる。

絵画では、

基本的に作品の前に立つ。

建築では、

鑑賞者自身が移動する。

ここで、

movement

「移動」。

Architecture is understood through movement.

「建築は移動を通して理解される。」

そして、

site。

「敷地」。

建物は、

抽象的な白い空間に存在しているわけではありません。

地形。

方向。

眺望。

気候。

周辺環境。

これらと関係しています。

ここで、

site-specific

「場所固有の」。

respond to the site

「敷地に応答する」。

The building responds to views in different directions.

「建物は異なる方向の眺望に応答している。」

respond to

「〜に応答する」。

建築評論で頻出します。

安藤忠雄。

フランク・ロイド・ライト。

ガウディ。

でも使える表現です。

今回の重要語をまとめると、

facade
外観面・ファサード
principal facade
主要正面

portico
列柱玄関
columned
柱のある

pediment
三角破風
temple front
神殿風正面

domestic architecture
住宅建築
orientation
方向づけ

landscape
風景
view
眺望

vista
遠くへ開ける眺望
frame
枠取る

central plan
集中式平面
central hall
中央ホール

axis
軸
intersect
交差する

centrality
中心性
radiate
放射する

symmetry
対称性
geometric order
幾何学的秩序

proportion
比例
ratio
比率

coherence
まとまり・一貫性
relationship
関係

approach
建物への近づき方
arrival
到着

sequence
連続
spatial sequence
空間の連続

unfold
展開する
movement
移動

site
敷地
respond to
〜に応答する

です。
ヴィラ・ロトンダを見るとき、

正面写真だけを見ない。
How many possible fronts does the building have?

「この建物には、いくつの正面があり得る？」
Where is the center?

「中心はどこ？」
Which axes organize the plan?

「どんな軸が平面を構成している？」
What views are framed by each portico?

「それぞれのポルティコは、どんな風景を枠取っている？」
How does your experience change as you move around the building?

「建物の周囲を移動すると、体験はどう変化する？」
そして、

Does a building need to have only one front?
「建物には、本当に正面が一つしかなくてはいけないのか？」

ここまで考えると、
ヴィラ・ロトンダの四つの玄関は、

単なる反復ではなくなります。
The building has a center, but it faces many directions.

「建物には中心がある。しかし、多くの方向を向いている。」
これは、

面白い建築思想です。
強い中心を持つことと、

一方向だけを見ることは、
同じではない。

中心があるからこそ、
四方へ開くこともできる。

建築は、
世界から自分を切り離して中心を作ることもできる。

しかし、
その中心から、

再び周囲の世界へ視線を開くこともできる。

パラディオが設計したのは、

四つの正面を持つ家だけではありません。

「中心にいながら、世界を多方向から見る」

という、

一つの視点の構造だったのです。

是非フォローお願いします！

text:
The daily routine of an ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness) monk begins very early in the morning, typically between 3:00 AM and 4:30 AM, focusing heavily on intensive prayer, scripture study, and devotional service 
Early Morning (3:00 AM – 7:30 AM) 

• Waking & Bathing: Monks wake up during the Brahma-muhurta (an auspicious pre-dawn window), bathe to purify themselves, and wear clean traditional clothes (such as dhotis and kurta). 
• Mangala-āratī (4:30 AM – 5:15 AM): The first congregational worship ceremony of the day, featuring singing (kīrtana), dancing, and offering incense and lamps to the Deities. 
• Tulsi Puja & Japa (5:15 AM – 7:30 AM): Worship of the sacred Tulsi plant, followed by individual meditative chanting (japa) of the Hare Krishna Mahamantra on japa beads, fulfilling a daily commitment of a minimum of 16 rounds (approx. 1,728 repetitions).

Morning & Afternoon (7:30 AM – 4:00 PM) 

• Darshan & Guru Puja (7:30 AM – 8:15 AM): Greeting the newly dressed Deities when the altar curtains open, followed by honoring the spiritual master (Guru Puja). 
• Scripture Class (8:15 AM – 9:30 AM): Attending a lecture and discussion on sacred texts, primarily the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam or Bhagavad-gītā. 
• Prasādam (Breakfast & Lunch): Eating sanctified vegetarian food (prasādam) that has been formally offered to Krishna. 
• Practical Service (Seva): Engaging in temple duties from late morning through the afternoon. This includes book distribution (sankirtan), temple administration, cooking, cleaning, managing community outreach, or maintaining temple grounds.

Evening & Night (4:00 PM – 9:30 PM) 

• Evening Services & Arati: Participating in evening devotional gatherings, further chanting, and attending classes or local outreach programs. 
• Dinner Prasādam & Rest: A light evening meal followed by final personal prayers, scriptural reading, and retiring to shared monastic quarters by around 9:30 PM to prepare for the early morning rise. 💯EOD

text:
Late Dr. Yugal Kishore Vashistha, my tauji, comes from Nohar, a small town in Rajasthan. The way he thought, lived, or looked at the world, however, was so big and vast. 

Immensely curious and yet having a deeper affection for life in all its forms, his love for animals was reflected in every step he would take towards saving and nurturing them. 

Being particularly fond of white pigeons, he would often bring them home all the way from Delhi. Once he even got snakes rescued from a sapera (snake-charmer) and released them into the jungle. When the snakes somehow found their way back home, not at all frightened, he rather began keeping them.

This speaks of a fundamental quality in him—his fearlessness. A constant sense of wonder and ability to see beyond what most people won’t even consider was him. A compassionate being whose caring acts extended far beyond his immediate circle. 

Gogamedi Mela is an annual fair in Rajasthan. When Tauji visited it for the first time and found people there without proper access to drinking water, he immediately took action. Joining hands with a few friends, he began supplying water. The water initiative gradually expanded into providing food and eventually a medical camp as well. 

When the Rajasthan government saw their dedication to the cause, it offered them land near the Gogamedi temple, where they built a dharmshala that eventually became associated with the Nohar Relief Society and grew into a larger community initiative.

The Nohar Relief Society is perhaps one of the strongest connections I can make between Tauji’s life and my own. His intent to serve the community, to notice and fulfill their needs, has travelled through generations, including being in my genes.

Interestingly, Tauji, besides doing tons of things, also cherished the art of expression, being deeply involved in language and music. He spoke Hindi, English, Marwari, Marathi and Gujarati, and could play the banjo and mouth organ remarkably well. There was an effortless versatility about him—making his way through languages, music, people, and ideas.

A pro-technology person, given the time and the environment he lived in. Whenever a new gadget arrived in the market, he went for it. He would call us after buying, and ask us to teach him its applications. There was no hesitation about learning and trying what’s new, no confining beliefs that technology was “for the younger generation.” He was curious enough to keep learning throughout his life. And that is something that stays with me.

It's almost a decade now; he is no longer with us, but the way he lived remains, not only as fragments of memories, but as a quiet direction-giving light in my life.

By profession, Tauji was a doctor, and by action, a kind and generous human being. 

A life so radiant as his and so committed to serving humanity that leaves deep imprints in our thoughts and imagination. This is perhaps how our involvement in life leaves traces behind that people can easily see.

Today marks his death anniversary. I simply wanted to share a few memories of Tauji - not just to remember him, but to reflect on the many ways in which the life he lived continues to stay with me. Some people leave behind memories; some leave behind a way of looking at life. For me, Tauji did both.

[Pic from his 50th wedding anniversary celebration at  Gogamedi]

text:
LONG READ ALERT ABOUT HINDUTVA 🚨

Bengal is a riverine land of the east. Here it is customary to offer whatever is finest to the worshipped deity, whether hilsa or shol fish from the riverbanks of Birbhum. If someone has been telling me since yesterday to eat paneer every day, that does not mean I will offer palak corn every day. My religion has also taught me to offer a goat sacrifice, in the manner of Gopal Mukhopadhyay. And my religion has taught me to honour the Vaishnavas in a sattvic spirit.

We do not eat vegetarian food on all the days of Durga Puja. In our family it is not eaten—this is our custom, our habit, the tradition of our home. If someone comes from outside, plays a microphone, gives sermons, and tells me what I must eat and must not eat, that does not mean my dietary habits will change.

My Hinduism has not taught me to practise religion only in one fixed mould. It has introduced me to the soil of Bengal, to its Shakta heritage, to its tantric sadhana.

My Hinduism has taught me of Tarapith, where the worship of the Goddess is not confined to flowers, garlands, and vegetarian offerings. There the cremation ground, Bhairava, Bhairavi, tantra, and Shakti have created another world of sadhana. It has taught me of that Bengal where, in many streams of Shakta practice, non-vegetarian food, fish, meat, liquor, sacrifice, and other tantric rites have become part of religious ceremony.

My Hinduism is that of Krishnananda Agamavagisha. It is of Bhairava and Bhairavi. It belongs to that long Shakta-tantric lineage, which cannot be understood through a few simplified food rules.

Our Hinduism will remain ours. The land in which I was born, the soil in which my religious consciousness and pride in Hindu identity have awakened, is the soil of Shakti. This Bengal is not only the Bengal of Durga Puja—it is a deep and many-layered land of Shakta sadhana. In the religious history of this region there are many traces of the Dashamahavidya, Shakta tantra, Buddhist tantra, Nath sadhana, and the worship of Bhairava and Bhairavi.

In the temple of Lord Jagannath in Puri there is Mother Bimala. The relationship of Jagannath’s Bhairava doctrine with this Shakta lineage is also a remarkable example of the religious consciousness of eastern India. If Vaishnava and Shakta are always seen as opposite poles, a large part of history is left out.

I do not deny Vaishnava doctrine.
I do not deny Shaiva doctrine.
I do not deny Shakta doctrine.
I do not deny the historical influence of Buddhist tantra either.

All of it is mine. But that does not mean one person will impose their method of worship upon another. Diversity is not weakness. One of the strengths of Hinduism is that it does not make a single path compulsory for all, but allows many paths to coexist.

text:
I hear this quite often from bureacrats, politicans and opinions makes on X. Our smartest people are busy delivering Dhaniya and vada pav in ten minutes, or deciding which ad you should watch. 

The argument is too shallow and disappointing, let me explain.

First of all respect for the problem - Nobody anywhere in the world has made this work at this scale and made a real business out of it. Not the US, not Europe. India is the probably first country to do it, and we haven't even bothered to claim the title. 

Think about what has to happen inside those ten minutes. Before you even opened the app, the system had already decided that a store 2 km from your house should be holding that exact SKU, in that quantity, on a Tuesday evening when it's raining and there's a match on. Each store carries between 8,000 and 45,000 SKUs for a 2-3 km radius. Inventory accuracy has to be near perfect, because in a ten-minute window nobody has time to call you and offer a substitute. Riders have to be positioned before the demand arrives, not after it. Assignment, batching, routing, packing, payments, fraud - all settled in a few hundred milliseconds, a few million times a day. Roughly million times a day across 6,000+ dark stores, actually.

And the engineering is only half of it. The harder half is making it a business - on a ₹500 basket, with a delivery cost that has to stay in single digits of that, in a country where an address is a landmark and not a pin code. Getting it to work once is a demo. Getting it to work profitably, every day, in hundreds of cities, is the part that took a decade of the best product and engineering talent this country has.

If you have never built software at that scale, none of this is visible to you. What you see is a boy on a bike.

Now the part that I think the narrative misses completely.

There was a time when the best minds in the world were working on getting you a cab on time (Uber). And on bringing the shopping mall to your door (Amazon). Nobody called those noble problems either. They looked like conveniences for people who wouldn't walk to a corner shop.

Look at what came out of them. The company that sold books online built AWS, and a large part of the world's software now runs on it. The company that ranked web pages and matched ads gave us the paper that today's entire AI industry is built on. And look at where those founders went next - Bezos is building rockets and putting things into orbit. Even Elon built the paypal first. The ordinary-looking consumer problem is what funds the infrastructure, and more importantly, it is what trains the people. Capability first, application after.

That is already happening here. Look at who is founding/investing India's space, defence, semiconductor and AI companies today. A lot of them learnt to build inside consumer internet.

And then the part nobody wants to discuss - the counterfactual. If we don't have hard engineering problem right now thats being solved, ambitious people don't become less ambitious. They just leave. That mind ends up in investment bank, hedge fund or showing ads to billions. I would much rather it stays here and builds the logistics spine for 1.4 billion people, even if version one of that spine delivers Dhaniya.

You don't build a ship on day one. Before the ship there are thousands of steps that look nothing like a ship.

So my request is simple. Before dismissing it tomorrow, read this and decide yourself.

"The Alternative for Germany (AfD) under lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund is vying to win power for the first time in closely watched elections in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday.
Under Germany's federal system, state ​governments sit in the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, and also have wide ‌powers in education, domestic security and culture.
The party has laid out its plans in its "Vision 2026" election manifesto.

IMMIGRATION
Based on the manifesto, an AfD-led Saxony-Anhalt would launch a state-level deportation offensive and establish a task force to coordinate quicker deportations, in echoes ​of the United States' efforts to crack down on migration.
The party said it would encourage small- and ​medium-sized businesses to adopt artificial intelligence and digitalise their processes through incentives rather ⁠than turn to skilled migrant workers from what it called "culturally alien" backgrounds.

The AfD, which seeks closer ties to ​Russia, would also advocate for removing war refugee status for Ukrainians in Germany as long as the conflict ​remains concentrated in eastern Ukraine, arguing they should seek refuge in western Ukraine.

SCHOOLS, RELIGION AND CULTURE
Under the AfD, the children of refugees would be placed in separate classes to convey the message that "their stay in Germany is merely temporary" and prevent "various ​stresses" on the other children from being around different cultures.

Children with disabilities would also no longer be ​taught in the same classroom as those without, instead being sent to special schools.
Schools would be banned from flying rainbow flags, ‌with the ⁠German national flag raised daily instead. The national anthem should be sung by students and staff at school celebrations.
The government would also "exhaust all legal avenues" to limit Islamic expression, including banning the call to prayer and stipulating how mosques are decorated.

It would make major changes to the school curriculum with a "patriotic cultural policy", ​focusing more closely on medieval ​rulers and 19th-century giants ⁠of German history such as the "Iron Chancellor", Otto von Bismarck. Social and psychological support and integration measures would be scrapped.
It has also pledged to dismantle the ​current structure of the public broadcasting system in the state and withdraw state ​funding from ⁠some cultural institutions.

FAMILY
To tackle Germany's ageing population, the party rejects attempts to attract more immigrants and would instead offer financial incentives to German citizens to bear children.
It says greater acceptance of "sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles" has contributed to ⁠sinking ​birth rates and promises to aggressively promote "traditional" family structures consisting of ​a mother, father and children.
The AfD would also push to restrict access to puberty blockers and gender-affirming hormone therapies for children and ​adolescents to counteract what it calls an increasing "trend" towards gender dysphoria."

text:
🚨🚨
The last LeDeR report is out. They’re not doing another one.
People with a learning disability still die 19 years younger than everyone else. More than half die before 65. Avoidable deaths are still about twice the general rate. Pneumonia. Heart disease. Epilepsy. Things that should have been treated.
That report existed because families had to prove their relatives were dying from neglect, not from “having a learning disability.” Now the government says this is the last national academic report. The data goes into a quieter dataset. Reviews continue, they say. Independent public scrutiny does not.
At the same time they want an assisted suicide law.
Aktion T4 did not begin with a public announcement that disabled people should be wiped out. It began with the language of mercy, burden and cost. “Lives unworthy of life.” Doctors filled in forms. Institutions made lists. Officially about 70,000 people were murdered in the first phase. By the end of the war the killing of disabled people ran to around a quarter of a million. The gas chambers used later on Jews were first tested on people with disabilities.
Britain had its own respectable version of that idea long before Hitler. In 1910 George Bernard Shaw told the Eugenics Education Society that eugenic politics would land us in “an extensive use of the lethal chamber,” because “a great many people would have to be put out of existence simply because it wastes other people’s time to look after them.” He also said: if they are fit to live, give them decent conditions; if they are not, kill them in a decent human way.
That is the logic you have to kill first: some lives are too expensive, too inconvenient, too much trouble.
Look at Canada if you want the modern version without the black uniforms. Medical assistance in dying started as a tightly framed terminal-illness law. Then it expanded to people who were not dying. Disability advocates there now say the same thing, over and over: it can be easier to get death than housing, home care, pain clinics or mental-health support. Veterans offered MAID instead of services. People in poverty and isolation approved on Track 2. A man with pressure sores getting an assisted death after the hospital failed him. Inclusion Canada’s line is simple: no one should find assisted suicide easier to access than the supports needed to live with dignity.
The UK bill is not T4. It is not yet Canada’s Track 2. It is still sold as six months, capacity, two doctors, a panel, extra training and an advocate for learning disability and autism.
That is not the point.
The point is the order of operations. You do not bury the only national report that still shows how people with learning disabilities actually die — 19 years too young, still dying of treatable illness — while you legalise a state-assisted death and tell us the safeguards will be fine. You do not cut specialist nursing, lose independent scrutiny, leave annual health checks and reasonable adjustments half-done, and then offer a new “choice” at the end.
Shaw’s sentence is the tell. The lethal chamber arrives when looking after people is treated as a waste of other people’s time.
If this government valued those lives, the last LeDeR report would not be the last, Canada would be a warning not a roadmap, and an assisted dying bill would not be coming before the care.
What is the real motive — better data, or less sunlight on a group it has already decided is too expensive to keep alive properly?

text:
🚨🧠🔎 EDUCATION AND FACTS. FIRST FEAR, THEN THE “THIRD WORLD,” AND FINALLY AfD AS THE “LAST HOPE.” THIS IS HOW PROPAGANDA IS BUILT IN JUST A FEW SENTENCES.

“This is not the Kremlin introducing these transformational migration policies that are destroying Europe as we know it. AfD is Germany’s last hope of avoiding becoming some kind of Third World hell.” One could simply shrug and move on. Just another post on X: a few grand words, no data, plenty of emotion. The problem is that this is precisely how the boundaries of normal political debate are shifted. You do not persuade people with an argument. First you give them fear. Then you give them an enemy. Finally, you present one political party as the only possible salvation. Everything else is supposed to follow automatically.

Germany genuinely does have a migration problem. And that is exactly why it deserves a serious discussion rather than a fairy tale for adults about an impending civilizational apocalypse. I have no intention of pretending that German migration policy over the past decade has been an uninterrupted success story. It has not. The decisions of 2015 left consequences that remain visible today. There were failures in controlling inflows, problems deporting people with no legal right to remain, and municipalities left carrying costs they were never prepared to absorb. There are districts where integration works badly. There are culturally isolated communities. Foreign nationals do commit crimes, and some groups are overrepresented in parts of the police statistics. If someone commits rape, robbery or murder, they must be held accountable. If someone has no right to remain and the legal conditions for removal are met, the state should be capable of carrying out that removal. A national border cannot be merely decorative. All of that is true.

But something else is also true, and you will not learn it from a post about a “Third World hell.” Net migration to Germany did not increase in 2025. It fell to around 235,000 people — roughly 45 percent lower than in 2024. Final Destatis figures indicate around 1.48 million arrivals and 1.245 million departures. A year earlier the net balance was roughly 430,000. That is not the opinion of the left, the CDU, AfD or the European Commission. It is the official statistical record of Germany’s federal authorities. The picture becomes even more interesting when we look at the population as a whole. Germany ended 2025 with roughly 83.5 million inhabitants, around 100,000 fewer than a year earlier. Why? Because Germany’s problem is not migration alone. Germany is ageing. For years, significantly more people have died than have been born, and in 2025 the gap between births and deaths again exceeded 300,000. Migration was not even large enough to offset that demographic loss.

That already undermines the simplistic story of a country being endlessly “flooded” by an ever-growing wave. It does not mean that net migration of 235,000 is insignificant. It is not. Schools, housing, healthcare, security, integration and municipal budgets all matter. But when someone claims that Germany is currently experiencing an ever-accelerating migration surge while the net figure has fallen by 45 percent, it is worth asking what exactly they are describing: reality, or their own emotions?

The same applies to people seeking protection. At the end of 2025, Germany had around 3.236 million people classified as seeking or receiving protection, roughly 3.9 percent of the country’s total population. A substantial number. Yet compared with the end of 2024, that figure fell by around 68,000, or 2.1 percent. The number of people newly entering that category during 2025 fell by almost half. Moreover, the largest group among newly arrived people seeking protection were Ukrainians — around 93,000 out of approximately 155,000. Again, one may consider that figure too high. One may demand tighter controls. One may argue for different asylum criteria. But why pretend that the data say the opposite of what they actually say?

Across the European Union, the number of first-time asylum applications fell to around 669,400 in 2025, down about 27 percent year on year. Germany was no longer even the EU country receiving the highest number of first applications; Spain, Italy and France were ahead of it. Yet the most grotesque element of the phrase “Third World hell” lies elsewhere. At the end of 2025, approximately 14.07 million foreign nationals were registered in Germany’s Central Register of Foreigners. That sounds dramatic if you stop there. But about five million were citizens of other European Union countries, and a further roughly 4.6 million were citizens of other European states. In other words, more than two-thirds of registered foreigners in Germany were European nationals. Only around one-third came from other continents, were stateless, or fell into other categories.

So is a Pole who has worked in Hamburg for twenty years part of this supposed “Third World”? A Frenchman in Berlin? A Dutch citizen in Munich? A Czech woman in Saxony? A Spaniard in Cologne? Statistically, they are all foreigners. The average foreign national registered in Germany has lived there for around 14.8 years, while roughly 1.7 million foreign nationals were themselves born in Germany.

And this is where one of the simplest tricks of migration propaganda begins. First, every meaningful category is removed. A legal worker, a war refugee, someone under temporary protection, an EU citizen, a student, a scientist, a person residing illegally and a criminal all get thrown into one bag. Then the label “migrants” is stuck on the bag. A moment later it becomes “the Third World.” Once the audience has been frightened sufficiently, you can sell them the solution: the “last hope.”

That is not how the rule of law works. The entire reason a state governed by law has statutes, procedures, public authorities, courts, police and border controls is precisely so that it can distinguish between different situations. Someone who legally arrived for work is not the same as someone with no right to remain. A refugee entitled to international protection is not the same as an irregular economic migrant. A suspect is not a convicted offender. An Afghan does not bear collective responsibility for a crime committed by another Afghan, just as a Pole living in Berlin does not answer for every Polish citizen arrested by German police. Simple? It should be. Collective blame, however, is far more politically effective than boring legal distinctions.

Then, inevitably, comes the argument about crime. Here there is no point doing what some people on the opposite side of the debate do and pretending the issue does not exist. It does. German police statistics show a high proportion of suspects without German citizenship. That is a fact and should be analysed rather than shouted down. But “a suspect without German citizenship” does not automatically mean “refugee,” “Muslim,” “African” or “illegal migrant.” That category also contains EU citizens, tourists, temporary residents, workers, people who have lived in Germany for many years and people whose asylum claims are still being processed. Demography matters as well. The migrant population is on average younger and contains a higher proportion of young men than Germany’s ageing native population, and young men — regardless of nationality — are statistically much more likely to be involved in crime than women or elderly people.

Does any of this excuse crime? No. Nothing does. If a foreign national commits rape, that person should stand trial. If convicted, and if the law subsequently permits deportation, the state should carry it out. Neither racism nor sentimentalism is required. What is required is a functioning criminal justice system.

At the same time, there is another side to the balance sheet that almost never appears in memes about the “Third World.” Germany’s Federal Employment Agency stated plainly in July 2026 that since 2024, employment growth in Germany has been driven entirely by foreign workers. Between 2014 and 2024, the number of working-age people with German citizenship fell by approximately 3.9 million, while the number of working-age foreign nationals rose by around 3.4 million. The Agency does not mince words: without migration, Germany’s labour-market potential would already be considerably smaller. The share of foreign workers in shortage occupations has roughly doubled over a decade, from around 7 to around 14 percent. In parts of eastern Germany, employment growth today is almost entirely linked to foreign workers.

And that is Germany’s real problem. Not a meme. How do you simultaneously reduce uncontrolled and illegal migration, deport more effectively those who have no right to remain, improve security and integration, and avoid crippling an economy that, because of its demographic structure, needs hundreds of thousands of workers? That is a question for the government. For the CDU. For the SPD. And for AfD. Yes, AfD is entitled to offer its own answer. If voters regard it as the best one, they are entitled to vote for AfD.

Yesterday’s result in Saxony-Anhalt shows that a very large number of voters did exactly that. AfD achieved a historic victory, winning roughly 44 percent according to the initial results and more than doubling its 2021 performance. That is a political earthquake. Pretending nothing happened would be absurd. But democracy has one small characteristic that politicians sometimes forget: an election decides who receives a mandate to govern. It does not decide whether a statement is true. If 80 percent of voters tomorrow become convinced that net migration has risen by 50 percent while the statistics show that it fell by 45 percent, the statistics do not magically change. Elections can be won on fear. They can be won on anger. They can be won because previous governments ignored genuine problems. A ballot paper does not, however, come with a licence to rewrite the statistical record.

And this is exactly where Russia enters the discussion. The author begins with the dramatic claim that “the Kremlin is not introducing Germany’s migration policy.” Well, obviously not. Putin does not sit in the Bundestag. Lavrov does not draft German asylum law. The Russian Foreign Ministry does not issue German residence permits. But no serious analyst claims that this is how Russian influence operations work. An influence operation does not need to create a problem from nothing. It is much easier to exploit a problem that already exists. Migration, energy prices, war, Ukraine, crime, the pandemic, housing shortages and minority rights are all genuine issues. Russian propaganda does not need to invent an alternative planet. It merely needs to distort the proportions until citizens stop seeing a problem that can be solved and start seeing their own state as the enemy.

That distinction matters. You do not have to convince a German that Putin is a hero. It is enough to convince him that Berlin is a greater threat than Moscow. You do not have to tell a French citizen that Russia is right. It is enough to persuade him that his democracy is corrupt and useless. You do not need to turn a Pole into a supporter of Russian imperialism. It is enough to convince him that Ukraine is his principal enemy, NATO is exploiting him, the EU is robbing him and isolation is the only authentic national policy. After that, the rest becomes much easier.

AfD’s support for rebuilding political and economic relations with Russia and ending or sharply reducing German support for Ukraine is not some hidden secret. It is part of the party’s public political position and one of the central areas of controversy surrounding it in Germany. Does that prove that every AfD voter is a “Russian agent”? Of course not. Does it prove that the author of this post works for the Kremlin? I have no such evidence and I am not going to manufacture it. The person may be writing entirely from personal conviction. They may genuinely fear migration. They may have voted AfD for years. They may never have had the slightest contact with any Russian influence operation. But one can still observe that the narrative “stop looking at Russia; your real enemies are migrants and your own government” fits perfectly into the logic of operations designed to deepen existing divisions.

AfD itself should also be assessed precisely rather than giving its opponents the gift of sloppy exaggeration. In 2025 Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classified the party as right-wing extremist, but on 26 February 2026 a court in Cologne temporarily blocked the use of that classification for AfD as a whole pending final resolution of the dispute. The court simultaneously pointed to serious indications of anti-constitutional tendencies within the party, but concluded that the available evidence did not yet justify extending that assessment sufficiently to the entire organisation. That is the current legal position. It is therefore inaccurate to state without qualification that AfD as a whole is currently and finally classified as an extremist organisation. If we claim to oppose propaganda, we cannot answer it with propaganda of our own.

Which brings us back to the phrase that reveals more about the original post than anything else: “Third World hell.” This is not a legal concept. It is not a statistical category. It is not an economic category. It describes no immigration status whatsoever. It is pure emotional imagery. It is designed to invoke dirt, chaos, violence, alien people and a civilisation under siege. It does not ask who a person is. Where they come from is enough. An Indian IT specialist? Third World. A Syrian doctor? Third World. An Afghan girl fleeing the Taliban? Third World. A care-home worker? Third World. A scientist? Third World. A criminal? Third World as well. Convenient, isn’t it? No distinction is required anymore. And once we stop distinguishing between people, it becomes much easier to stop distinguishing between their rights.

That is how a language develops in which a person’s responsibility no longer depends on what they have done but on the group into which we have placed them. The European rule of law was built precisely against that mechanism. Not so that borders would cease to exist. Not so that everybody would have to be admitted. Not so that crime should be tolerated. It was built so that the state acts according to law rather than collective hostility.

A country can pursue a very tough migration policy while maintaining individual responsibility. There is no contradiction whatsoever. You can deport someone with no right to remain without describing every foreigner as a threat. You can restrict asylum and still protect someone who faces torture or death if returned. You can prevent illegal border crossings while creating legal routes for nurses or engineers whom the economy genuinely needs. That is what governing a state looks like. Complicated. Sometimes politically thankless. Impossible to compress into a single sentence. Which is precisely why it loses so easily to a meme.

“AfD is the last hope.” That phrase is not accidental either. Not “AfD has a better migration policy.” Not “AfD proposes solutions I support.” Not “the other parties have failed.” The last hope. That is a different category of communication. It removes the possibility of alternatives. If something is the “last” hope, then everything outside it becomes part of the catastrophe. The political opponent is no longer simply an opponent. He becomes someone obstructing the rescue of the nation.

This language is worth recognising. First, an extraordinary sense of danger is created. Then people are persuaded that ordinary institutions have stopped working. Next, they are told that every established political party is complicit. Finally, one single solution appears. History knows this mechanism very well.

And that is why the answer to this kind of post cannot be the equally idiotic claim that “migration is wonderful and causes no problems.” It does cause problems. Germany should deport people who have no right to remain more effectively. It should process asylum claims faster. It should control its borders. It should respond more forcefully to crime. It should demand integration. It should resist the formation of communities in which religious or clan rules are placed above the constitutional order. It should tailor labour migration to the needs of the economy. That is serious policy.

But serious politics begins precisely where collective hysteria ends. If we genuinely want a secure Europe, we need borders that work, police that work, courts that work, migration authorities that work, deportations that are actually carried out when there is a lawful basis for them, and legal migration where the state has decided it is necessary. We do not need stories about a “Third World hell.” Nor do we need yet another self-appointed “last salvation.”

The 2025 data do not show Germany accelerating towards unlimited migration. They show a 45 percent fall in net migration, a decline in the number of people seeking protection, a 27 percent fall in first-time asylum applications across the EU, and at the same time a country whose demographic structure means that without foreign workers its labour market would shrink even faster. That does not mean German migration policy is good. It means reality is considerably more complicated than a post on X.

AfD has just won a major regional election and will become an even stronger political force. That is a fact and should not be dismissed. If traditional parties want those voters back, they must stop responding to genuine anxieties with moral lectures. They need credible border control, public safety, effective deportations and a convincing integration policy. But AfD must also be assessed like any other party seeking power: by its programme, its people, its voting record, its public statements, its relationship to the constitution, its policy towards Russia and the economic consequences of its proposals. Not as a devil. And not as a saviour.

No democratic political party is the “last hope of a nation.” It is a political instrument that voters may choose, evaluate and later reject. And that is perhaps where the most important boundary between education and propaganda lies. Education says: check the numbers; separate legal migration from illegal migration; asylum from employment; a foreigner from a criminal; an individual offender from an entire ethnic group; AfD’s actual policies from our emotions about AfD; and a Russian influence operation from an accusation against a specific person for which we have no evidence. Propaganda says: “Hell. Third World. Last hope.” Three slogans. No analysis. Fear does the rest.

That is why I refuse to choose between two equally stupid extremes: “migration causes no problems” and “migrants are destroying Europe.” Both are forms of intellectual laziness. Europe must control migration. Europe must defend itself. Europe must protect its borders. Europe must remove people who have no right to remain when the law permits their removal. But Europe must also remain Europe precisely when circumstances become difficult: law instead of collective revenge, evidence instead of stereotypes, individual responsibility instead of ethnic responsibility.

Because if, in the name of “defending European civilisation,” we throw away precisely the principles that distinguish that civilisation from authoritarianism, Putin will not need to destroy Europe himself.

We will have done part of the job for him.

Facts are less spectacular than fear. But they have one decisive advantage: once checked, they are still facts.

"Iran expects an agreement establishing a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz to be signed in the coming days, but will not commit to fully reopening the strategic waterway unless the United States halts attacks and other hostile actions, the country’s top security official said on Sunday.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told state TV that entry and exit through the planned corridor would be managed by Tehran.

Iran and Oman have been negotiating arrangements for a temporary shipping corridor through the strait, with sections of the route running through Iranian and Omani waters. The talks are part of diplomatic efforts to restore maritime traffic through a waterway that carried roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February.

Rezaei said Tehran would only guarantee that the strait remained open if the US refrained from attacks and what he described as acts of sabotage.

He said the main problem with the US-Iran memorandum of understanding, signed in June to end the war and establish a framework for a broader agreement, was the lack of guarantees, adding that mediators had been unable to ensure its implementation.

Under the deal, Washington was to lift its naval blockade of Iran while Tehran was to facilitate the safe passage of commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. The agreement later unraveled amid disputes over its implementation.

Despite discussions over the new corridor, Rezaei insisted that the Strait of Hormuz was currently “completely closed.”

He said no more than seven or eight ships were passing through the waterway each day, with five or six carrying essential goods for Iran.

Rezaei claimed US forces occasionally facilitated the passage of five or six vessels through waters near Oman, but said those ships were typically targeted and did not pass through unharmed. He said that such movements did not amount to a reopening of the strait.

Shipping through Hormuz has been severely disrupted since the outbreak of the war, while Washington and Tehran have offered conflicting accounts of the extent to which the waterway is open.

Rezaei also said Iran would soon declare a restricted zone around the strait, warning that vessels entering the area would be placed on an Iranian sanctions list and would subsequently be unable to transit Hormuz without Tehran’s approval.

He said Iran was tightening restrictions in the waterway and claimed the impact of Tehran’s sanctions there would ultimately be greater than that of its missile attacks.

On the military front, Rezaei said Iran had for the first time tested a domestically produced destroyer-launched missile against a US naval vessel 48 hours earlier.

His comments came amid renewed maritime clashes between the two countries. US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Saturday that American forces struck three Iranian crude oil tankers after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles toward two US Navy warships.

Rezaei also sought to play down the economic impact of the confrontation on Iran, saying the country had sufficient stocks of food and other essential goods and continued to sell oil and receive payment for its exports.

His comments come as a US naval blockade targeting vessels entering and leaving Iranian ports has sharply curtailed Tehran’s oil exports, a key source of government revenue and foreign currency."

text:
PAYCOM $PAYC SHRANK ITS SHARE COUNT 20% THIS YEAR. FRIDAY IT STILL FELL 3.7%:

Paycom Software PAYC at $231.67 Friday, -$8.85 / -3.68%. Markets are shut Monday, September 7 for Labor Day, so Friday is the latest quote for every name below. The Oklahoma City company sells the software that lets an employee handle their own paycheck, benefits, and time card from one app, instead of a payroll office doing it by hand.

Six Len5es, one Friday, and a real split in the numbers. The picks funded by cash a business is already collecting - a bank's loan book, a shipping company's dividend - closed higher. The picks still priced mainly on a growth story that has not fully arrived yet - and Paycom, up almost 100% since spring, is the loudest of those - mostly fell. All on the day a much-hotter-than-expected jobs report made the Federal Reserve's September 16 decision look like a real coin flip tilted toward a rate increase, not the cut markets had been leaning on.

Paycom is the Momentum Len5's pick, and for months it has been the cleanest version of what that style hunts: a price near its own best level, with the short run and the long run agreeing. They agreed all the way up. The stock closed at $120.26 on April 1 and $239.10 on August 31 - a roughly 99% gain in five months - and touched a fresh 52-week high above $244 in early September. Behind it: an August 5 second-quarter report that beat on every line - revenue $531 million, up 10%; GAAP profit $2.34 a share, up 20%; adjusted cash profit margin 44.2%, up more than 3 points - plus a raised full-year forecast. The company also spent $1.4 billion buying back its own stock in the first half of the year, cutting shares outstanding by roughly 20%. Fewer shares means the same profit splits fewer ways, which is most of why per-share earnings grew twice as fast as the business itself did.

Then Friday: -3.68%, pulling the stock about 5% off that new high. Management has called its own buying "opportunistic" against what it termed a "valuation disconnect" - company language for a stock trading above where its own numbers alone would put it. Two brokerages raised targets in the week before the drop - UBS to $285 on September 1, JPMorgan to $264 on August 25 - chasing a price that had already passed the average target analysts were using in August. WATCH: whether bookings keep growing fast enough to catch up to the price, or whether Friday was the first crack in a rally built mostly on a shrinking share count. Paycom has not yet set a date for third-quarter results.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
- McDonald's, ticker MCD, at $255.69, -$3.94 / -1.52% Friday, near its lowest price of the past year. The Chicago company owns the real estate under most of its restaurants and collects rent plus a cut of every franchisee's sales, so it barely runs a grill itself - a business that gets paid whether or not a given restaurant is having a good month, which is exactly what this Len5 hunts. The August 4 quarter showed both halves of the argument: revenue of $7.10 billion came in a touch under the roughly $7.13 billion expected, while adjusted profit of $3.38 a share beat the $3.32 modeled. Global comparable sales - sales at restaurants open at least a year - rose 1.3%; in the US, just 0.8%. Real growth, barely. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: that US number turning negative, which would say the royalty stream itself is shrinking rather than simply growing slowly.

DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
- Intercontinental Exchange, ticker ICE, at $161.26, -$3.33 / -2.02% Friday. The Atlanta company owns the New York Stock Exchange, runs futures and options markets, and sells mortgage-processing software to banks. This Len5 is watching a specific, dated event: on July 30, the same day it reported second-quarter results, ICE agreed to buy MarketAxess, a bond-trading platform, for about $167 a share in cash - a 33% premium, roughly $6.0 billion, funded entirely with new debt rather than new stock. The mortgage-software business is the other half of the case: it earned $45 million on paper last quarter, an 8% margin, but $239 million and a 43% margin once the accounting cost of past acquisitions is stripped back out - the gap between what the business reports and what it actually keeps. Friday's drop gave back part of a 3.2% jump three days earlier, when ICE reported August trading volumes up 14% from a year ago and record activity in its agriculture, metals, and financial-futures markets. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: regulators taking longer than the deal's own first-half-2027 target to clear the purchase, which would leave ICE carrying new debt without the business it borrowed to buy.

GROWTH LEN5:
- Ameris Bancorp, ticker ABCB, at $86.05, +$0.22 / +0.26% Friday. The Atlanta bank lends to businesses and households across the Southeast. This Len5 wants real expansion the market has not already paid up for, and the expansion here is in the loan book, not yet in per-share profit: new loan commitments reached $2.4 billion in the second quarter, up 24% from a year earlier, while the gap between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits widened to 3.88%. The reported profit line told a messier story - net income of $0.77 a share, down from $1.60 a year ago - because a jury verdict in a California employment case forced an $82.5 million legal charge onto the quarter. Strip that one item back out and adjusted profit was $1.60 a share, flat with a year ago and a few cents under the roughly $1.66 expected. The stock trades near 15.6 times the past year's earnings. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: that 24% loan growth finally showing up as per-share profit growth once the legal charge is a year behind it, instead of staying stuck at flat.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
- Wise Group, ticker WSE, at $12.78, -$0.42 / -3.18% Friday. The London company moves money across borders for individuals and businesses, and increasingly rents that same payment network to other banks and financial platforms that want to offer it inside their own apps. This Len5 is watching where it is, not just how fast it is growing: Wise only began trading on Nasdaq on May 11 this year, keeping its original London listing as the secondary one, and is still building the US attention a company its size would normally carry. The growth underneath is real - the fiscal year ended March 31 brought net revenue of $2.5 billion, up 19%, at a 26% profit margin that came in above the company's own target range, and the quarter reported July 16 grew net revenue 25% to $714 million with active customers up 21% to 11.9 million. More than half of that revenue no longer comes from the classic cross-border transfer business, a sign the company is spreading into new ground rather than just moving more of the same money. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: growth settling at the low end of Wise's own 15%-20% medium-term target once the newer, non-transfer businesses stop scaling faster than the core one.

INCOME LEN5:
- Teekay Corporation, ticker TK, at $13.63, +$0.16 / +1.19% Friday. The Bermuda-based company holds a controlling stake in a fleet of Suezmax and Aframax oil tankers that carry crude around the world. This Len5 wants cash that genuinely reaches owners and is funded by the business, and both halves are unusually clean here: a $0.25-a-share regular quarterly dividend - a full year of which is $1.00 - plus a $1.00-a-share special dividend paid in June add up to roughly a 14.7% trailing yield, sitting on a parent-company balance sheet with no debt and about $1.2 billion of cash. The second quarter, its best on record, brought revenue of $379.1 million and net income of $69.5 million, or $0.79 a share, as its larger tankers earned an average of $109,200 a day and its smaller ones $74,100 a day - both near the top of their own historical range. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: tanker rates coming back down to earth, which is the only thing standing between this dividend and a much smaller one - the special portion carries no guarantee the way the $0.25 base payment does.

Line the six up and Friday reads less like noise and more like a preference. The two names getting paid today closed green. The four still mostly being paid on a promise - Paycom's loudest of all, a stock that erased a fifth of its own share count and still could not hold a week-old high - closed red, on the one day this month that promise got a little more expensive to keep.

Not investment advice.
