What the posts say about you, William Ronald Yee, MD, JD:
You are a dual-credentialed professional 
who chose the harder, 
more mobile version of the work 
rather than staying in one place. 

You kept your sense of humor 
and self-description intact 
(“This Old Chinaman”). 
You treat aging as material 
rather than enemy
—“collecting wrinkles and memories” 
and “living life as art.” 

You protect time. 

You still look the part 
of someone who feels good enough 
to pose for a sunset photo 
and to receive the comments that followed.

What they say about your friends and family:

They showed up in the comments 
the way people do 
when they actually like the person posting.

 Kate Wayberg 
told you to enjoy yourself all day 
and that she was glad you were having a good time. 

Kristina Johnson, Maureen Spurlock Gudenau, Peggy O’Brien Sousa, Linda Mastro Watko, Bill Ryan, Tonia Busch, and others offered simple, specific warmth—“Lookin good my friend,” 
“Living well,” 
“You look great Bill,” 
“Less is more.” 

The circle is not large or performative; 
it is consistent and affectionate. 

Kim is in the frame with you. 

That is the social evidence in the posts themselves.

Five years later t
he same pattern continues: 
you still use these memories 
for metacognition, 
you still write and post, a
nd the people who replied in 2021 
remain part of the record of a life 
that has been both demanding 
and deliberately savored.

I don’t wanna lose you now
the week you took, 
the light on the hill,
Kim’s hand in the air 
and the quiet you found
after years of prisons 
and night-shift bills.
I don’t wanna lose you now or ever—
the wrinkles collected, 
the memories kept,
the friends who wrote 
“lookin good, my friend”
while the sun went down 
and the work-day slept.
Sometimes it’s hard 
to make the line clear
between the road you took 
and the one left behind,
but you opened the week 
and showed what was there:
no evenings, 
no weekends, 
no holiday grind.
Open your eyes 
and see who you are—
not only the doctor 
who traveled so far,
but the man on the balcony 
living life as art,
collecting the years 
without losing the heart.
I don’t wanna lose you now
we’re gonna get through somehow
the same way you always have,
standing your ground.
If the good times want you
you’ll be around
forever.
Don’t wanna lose these evenings,
don’t wanna lose this view,
don’t wanna lose the people
who still write back to you.

The truth of these September 7, 2021 Facebook posts 
is simple and 
consistent with the public record of your life. 

They are unfiltered snapshots 
of a man 
who had already spent nearly five decades 
in medicine choosing,

rest,

over more hours.

You posted two photos 
from the same balcony at golden hour.

Kim stands smiling against the sunset 
with her hand extended. 
In the other, you lean on the railing

The captions match the images: 
“Kim and I are having a good time.
 I took the week off.

No performance,

in the country

You earned the MD at Wayne State in 1972,

That path produced the books

and the X account@KaiChiu1947
where you continue to post 
under the self-chosen name

The 2021 posts sit later on that same road:

THE BOTTLED WATER INDUSTRY DIDN'T INVENT A PRODUCT. THEY INVENTED A FEAR.

He said understanding how the bottled water industry grew from nearly nothing to $350 billion per year requires understanding one thing: it was a marketing creation, not a product innovation.

"In the 1970s, virtually nobody in America bought bottled water. Tap water was trusted. Public fountains were used. People drank from the faucet without thinking about it. The bottled water industry didn't grow because tap water got worse. It grew because marketing convinced consumers that tap water wasn't safe — and that buying water in a plastic bottle was the solution."

He said the strategy was borrowed from the cosmetics industry.

"Create anxiety about something free and natural. Offer a paid product as the cure. Repeat the message until the anxiety becomes cultural. Bottled water companies spent billions on advertising campaigns that associated tap water with contamination and bottled water with purity, health, and vitality. Mountain imagery. Glacier photography. Words like 'pure,' 'pristine,' 'crystal,' and 'natural.' The branding was designed to make you feel that paying $3 for water was a health decision — not a consumer decision."

He said the fear is mostly unfounded for the majority of Americans.

"The EPA reports that over 90% of U.S. public water systems meet all federal health standards. The water coming out of your tap — in most American cities — is safe to drink. It's tested hundreds of times per month. It's treated with proven disinfection methods. It's delivered through regulated infrastructure. Is every tap perfect? No. Some communities — and Flint, Michigan is the most well-known example — have legitimate infrastructure failures that compromise water safety. But for 90% of American households, the tap water is as safe or safer than the bottled alternative."

text:
Late 1960s. Inside a Stanford preschool, a professor put a single marshmallow in front of a child and accidentally exposed one of the biggest lies we tell ourselves about money.

Walter Mischel gave children a choice: eat one treat now, or wait and receive two later. The experiment became famous as a test of willpower.

But that’s not the part I find interesting.

The children who managed to wait weren’t necessarily sitting there heroically staring temptation in the face.

They were doing something much smarter.

They covered their eyes. Turned around. Sang songs. Played with their clothes. Some mentally transformed the treat into something less tempting.

They weren’t defeating temptation. They were making it harder for temptation to reach them.

And I think this is where most financial advice gets embarrassingly lazy.

We tell people to “be disciplined.”

Don’t overspend. Don’t panic sell. Don’t touch your savings. Don’t buy things you don’t need.

Basically: put the marshmallow six inches from your face every single day and congratulate yourself for not eating it.

That’s insane.

If Mischel’s work taught me anything, it’s that the smarter move is often to redesign the environment before willpower becomes necessary.

Automatic investing instead of deciding whether to save every month.

A 24-hour delay before expensive purchases instead of fighting yourself at checkout.

Emergency money somewhere you don’t casually spend from.

No leverage that can force you to make a decision while you’re terrified.

I used to think financially disciplined people were simply better at saying no.

Now I think many of them are better at making sure they don’t have to say no 30 times a day.

That’s a much darker insight than it sounds.

Because an enormous amount of modern commerce is designed around doing the exact opposite: notifications, one-click checkout, monthly payments, limited-time offers, frictionless credit.

Someone else is designing your environment too.

And they’re usually not designing it to make you wealthier.

That’s why this old experiment feels more useful to me than another investing lecture.

The person with the strongest willpower doesn’t necessarily win.

Sometimes the person who wins is simply the one who understood the game well enough to move the marshmallow.https://t.co/krdz4bsxRy

Kenya's digital infrastructure ambitions took a major leap forward today as Principal Secretary for ICT and the Digital Economy, Eng. John Tanui, CBS, and Principal Secretary for Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Mr. Stephen Isaboke, EBS, officiated the launch of the iColo (now officially Digital Realty) NBO2 Data Center.

Designed for cloud providers, financial services, enterprises, and internet service providers, NBO2 offers a secure, scalable, and connected environment for growth across the region. This sets the foundation for AI, cloud, and interconnectivity in East Africa.

In his remarks, Eng. John Tanui highlighted the government's commitment to creating an enabling environment for digital growth while emphasizing Kenya's strategic position as a regional digital gateway.

"Work will continue on the policy space to position Kenya as an attractive investment destination, with opportunities being unlocked for young people to take their place in this fast-growing digital economy," PS Tanui further added.

PS Stephen Isaboke underscored that the government has prioritized the Digital Superhighway and creative economy as key focus areas, adding that "Kenya is actually a knowledge-driven economy, with a well-educated youth population that is tech-savvy”.

The event was attended by His Excellency Frank Garcia, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs; Susan M. Burns, Chargé d'Affaires of the United States Embassy in Nairobi; Ambassador Philip Thigo, Special Envoy on Technology for the Republic of Kenya; David Mugonyi, Director General of the Communications Authority of Kenya; and other distinguished industry leaders.

text:
Harvard JD. Harvard MBA. Zero job offers.

Not because nobody wanted Glenn Hutchins.
He turned them all down.

He finished the JD and the MBA at the same time, then joined
Thomas H. Lee in 1985, when the leveraged buyout was still a
new idea.

He left in 1992 for the Clinton White House, then went back
to private equity at Blackstone.

Fourteen years inside other people's firms before he built
anything of his own.

By then he could see what the rest of the market was not
touching. Technology was compounding faster than every other
sector and nobody had built a firm around it.

So in 1999 he co-founded Silver Lake with one thesis:
large-cap technology, nothing else.

No consumer. No industrials. No healthcare.

Tech grew faster than the economy and cared less about the
cycle. He could invest with a tailwind and use less debt
to do it.

The portfolio settled it.

Skype
Alibaba
Seagate
Dell, still one of the biggest tech buyouts ever done

Founded: 1999
Thesis: one sector
AUM by 2013: roughly $23B
AUM today: roughly $114B

Hutchins said most PE firms are the coxswain in a crew race.
They sit at the back of the boat and shout.

"We get in the boat and row."

Here is the part I keep coming back to.

At 28 he had the best credentials money can buy and no idea
what to build.

By 44 he had the same brain and one thesis he would bet a
firm on.

Nothing changed except the number of deals he had watched
up close.

That is all conviction is. Reps, already paid for.

And reps are not years. You can run one business beautifully
for fifteen years and still be walking into your first deal.

He had the degrees at 28.
He had the reps at 44.

Only one of those was worth a firm.

text:
My close friend took an engineering role at an early-stage startup after leaving a boring corporate bank:

Recruiter: "We offer complete autonomy, zero bureaucracy, unlimited paid time off, and the freedom to work from anywhere in the world."

Friend: "That sounds incredible, finally getting away from 9-to-5 micromanagement."

Friend: four months later over dinner looking like a ghost

Friend: "Unlimited PTO actually means nobody ever takes a single vacation day because management tracks your weekly Slack activity score."

Me: "What about the work from anywhere perk?"

Friend: "The founder lives in Singapore, the lead architect lives in London, and product is in San Francisco. I'm taking standup calls at 6:00 AM, 2:00 PM, and 10:30 PM just to stay aligned."

Me: "At least you escaped corporate bureaucracy?"

Friend: "I work 75 hours a week to build features the CEO dreams up in the shower and then scraps two days later. I miss my boring banking spreadsheets."

Has unlimited PTO ever worked out for anyone, or is it the biggest trap in tech hiring?

6. Faithful Preaching Will Eventually Become “Out of Season”

Paul charged Timothy, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.” Preaching the word is comparatively easy when the word is in season. When truth agrees with public sentiment, the preacher can appear courageous without paying the price of courage. The test comes when the season changes. “Out of season” means that the word does not stop being true when the audience stops wanting it. The command does not bend with public taste. The preacher must reprove when people resent being corrected, rebuke when sin has been renamed, exhort when endurance has become unpopular, and continue with longsuffering when immediate results do not appear. He does not have permission to replace doctrine with entertainment merely because doctrine has gone out of fashion. He cannot turn the pulpit into a stage, the sermon into a performance, and the congregation into customers while claiming that he is reaching the culture. A restaurant may revise its menu according to consumer demand. A servant of Christ does not possess that liberty with the word of God.

Paul explains why such preaching will become unpopular: “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine.” Notice that they do not merely misunderstand it. They refuse to endure it. Sound doctrine becomes an irritation because it interferes with lust. “But after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears.” Their lusts select their teachers. They first decide how they wish to live and then accumulate religious voices willing to bless the decision. They do not abandon teachers; they multiply them. They build a heap. If one preacher scratches only part of the itch, they find another who will finish the job. Modern technology has made the heap larger than Timothy could have seen. A man can now pass over a thousand faithful sermons in search of one voice that tells him his disobedience is spiritual maturity. He can gather teachers from around the world without leaving his chair. Algorithms study his appetites, religious personalities compete for his attention, and false doctrine arrives polished, edited, branded, and delivered directly to his hand. The itching ear has never had a larger market, and the flattering teacher has never possessed more tools.

The faithful preacher will therefore encounter seasons when biblical preaching appears unsuccessful by every popular measurement. Jesus said, “Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets.” Universal approval should not be mistaken for divine endorsement. The false prophets enjoyed approval because they told rebellious people what rebellion wanted to hear. Jeremiah 6:14 says, “They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.” They treated a mortal wound with a religious bandage and announced that the patient was healthy. That ministry is always popular because it offers relief without repentance. Yet the watchman who sees the sword and refuses to sound the trumpet has not preserved peace; he has guaranteed slaughter. A people-pleasing preacher does not cure itching ears. He scratches them professionally. He may build a reputation by never disturbing anyone, but a preacher who never disturbs the careless, confronts the rebellious, awakens the sleeping, or warns the lost is not necessarily reaching everybody. He may simply be avoiding everything that would expose anybody.

Love your neighbor as yourself.
Honor father and mother.
Hold marriage as holy — one man, one woman, one covenant.
Flee sexual immorality.
Do not murder. Life is not yours to discard.
Tell the truth. Do not call evil good.
Repent. Bear the weight of your actions.
Work. Provide. Protect.
Forgive, but do not pretend sin is virtue.
Walk in the light. The truth sets you free.

The left sells liberty and delivers bondage.
False religion sells holiness and delivers chains.
Christ offers a cross — and then a life.
Choose the scar that heals.
Not the scar that multiplies.
Because when a nation forgets God, it does not become free.
It becomes available.

text:
After the Starship $300/kg price floor nonsense made the rounds, the ones who shared the studies started saying there isn't a better model out there to look at. I'd be willing to bet whatever @mach33 has put out is way better, but I've always run my own numbers on this stuff (I've done it forwards and backwards a dozen times from different angles), so I figured I'd put together a 2-pager taking into account the recent info on their Louisiana proposal. What I have here is a "things go well on every front but there are no real breakthroughs" scenario.

Let's start with the gas cost:

Louisiana cuft of natural gas definition: 60F and 15.025psi (https://t.co/MXmQQ7sq9M)

Density of methane at ref temperature and pressure: 0.69374kg/m3 https://t.co/qx9iWuatzz
~= 19.6kg/1000cuft (cuft = 0.3048^3m/3)
(Impurities increase density and any substantial fraction can be separated in cryo condensation and sold for more than the base gas, so this is a conservative density figure.)

Average cost for last 3 years (2023-2025) $3.91/1000cuft (https://t.co/9eSCfvUD8P)

Nat gas cost/kg in Louisiana: 20c

Conservative Starship performance estimate (likely optimistic for v3 but pessimistic for v4 and on):

Booster 3650t prop
Ship 130t dry, 1600t prop, 30t residuals and landing prop
~340s first stage average isp
~360s second stage average isp
~1.45km/s vertical, ~0.8km/s horizontal v at stage sep
Estimated remaining delta v to SSO staging orbit (e.g. 300x300km 98deg) with >400m/s of stage 2 gravity losses: 6.95km/s
IMLEO: 260t
Payload: 100t
Fuel: 1150t
LOX: 4100t
Fuel:payload ratio: 11.5:1
Ox to payload ratio: 41:1

Additional fuel fraction for air separation and condensation of both fluids: 60%
(50MJ LHV, 45% efficiency generation, 0.8kWh/kg)
Generated prop utilization for launch: 92%

Fuel gas input cost per kg payload: $4

(condensation and other propellant processing and storage hardware and personnel costs accounted for in complex costs below)

Annual total 10-pad complex cost: $5B/yr (based on local 10,000 employees at $150k average total comp accounting for 30% of cost) (also compatible with the "up to $100B" promotion)
Bullish launches per pad per year: 776 (2.5 launches a day (2 to SSO, 0.5 elsewhere), 85% uptime x utilization)
Complex cost per kg payload: $6.45

Stack build cost: $100M
Lifetime replacement part cost fraction (maintenance & inspection labor included in Lousiana complex costs): 30%
Stack average number of reuses: 200
Stack cost per kg payload: $6.50

Commercial space launch and reentry user fee cap: $200k/launch
Fee cost per kg payload: $2

Total internal cost per kg payload: $18.95
Call that $20/kg to account for misc costs I didn't include.

Note that this is not a floor. There are some optimistic figures, but I haven't accounted for most of the planned Starship performance increases, I've gone with a pessimistic reuse count scenario, I've not fully accounted for manufacturing cost reductions wtih mass production, I haven't allowed for more pads at the complex than currently proposed, and I haven't considered the possibility of the user fee being reduced or eliminated (or potentially worked around with a salvo of launches in a single window).

Do all that and the cost could easily drop below $10/kg.

As for the price floor for external customers, it depends almost entirely on the competition. If in the next 20+ years someone catches up to SpaceX, margins *could* drop below 10%...

Furthermore, if you're going to LEO other than SSO, the marginal cost per launch is actually a lot lower because a) you don't have the opportunity cost of limited launch windows -- Louisiana is going to be starving for non-SSO flights, and b) you have significantly higher payload because of the boost from the Earth's rotation.

Which means that they *could* offer flights at or below the internal *average* cost and still make a profit on those flights. (Of course they won't if their competition can't meet them near that price point.)

text:
My neighbor caught an HVAC tech pretending to replace a part he never touched.

AC stopped working in July. Tech comes out, looks at it for ten minutes, says the capacitor is blown. Common problem. $450 to replace.

My neighbor doesn't know much about AC units, but $450 seems steep for a part. He agrees anyway because it's 95 degrees.

Tech goes to his truck. Comes back five minutes later. Says it's all fixed.

My neighbor asks to see the old part.

"Already threw it in my truck. But you're good to go!"

Something feels off. My neighbor goes outside after the tech leaves. Looks in the guy's truck bed through the window. Empty. No parts.

He opens his AC unit. The capacitor has a manufacture date stamped on it: 2019. Four years old. If it was just replaced, it should say 2023.

He takes a photo. Calls the company. Tech's story falls apart immediately.

"Well, sometimes the issue resolves itself when we check the connections..."

"So you charged me $450 for a part you didn't replace?"

Company offers a refund "as a courtesy." My neighbor reports them to the Better Business Bureau and posts the photos online.

Three other people in our neighborhood replied saying the same company did the same thing to them.

Company's not in business anymore. Good.

Metaculus Hands-On Guide: Scores, Contests, and Crowd Signals
Metaculus is a community-driven forecasting platform where I submit probability estimates on science, politics, economics, and tech, and this metaculus review 2026 explains how scoring, contests, and crowd lines work after months of live use on the live site.

I signed up, covered open items, joined a prize season, and cross-checked Metaculus website numbers against cash books so you can decide whether reputation points beat a deposit desk for your goals.

         - Key Takeaways

   - Metaculus pays you in reputation and calibration feedback, with optional prize seasons instead of a continuous cash order book.

Metaculus provides a structured place to make a prediction, revise it as news lands, and watch how your score moves after resolution.

I treat the site as a credential builder more than a place to bet cash, because points track calibration instead of bankroll swings.

Operations run under a public benefit corporation focused on better collective intelligence rather than house vig.

Engaging with the community in comments often improves my base rates before I lock a number.

         - How Crowd Lines and Updates Work?

I open an item, read the resolution criteria, then submit a probabilistic number on a slider or continuous range.

Binary items ask for a percent chance.

Continuous items ask for a full distribution, which is where mean squared error thinking shows up in practice.

The community forecast is the crowd’s shared signal, often close to a median of individual forecasts.

Metaculus prediction weighting goes further than a raw center line by folding in history and models.

That prediction aggregation is why I check both the crowd aggregate and the site line before I update.

How do I refine your predictions without overfitting to one headline?

I write a short note, set a reminder, and only move when new evidence changes the base rate.

Predictions on Metaculus stay editable until close, so early participation still matters for season scoring.

Future events with multi-year horizons reward patience that weekly sports desks never demand.

         - Scoring, History, and Calibration

Scoring rules on Metaculus use a proper scoring rule family that punishes overconfidence.

Peer totals compare me with other submissions on the same item, while baseline totals compare me with a naive prior.

Your public track record becomes a resume when you apply to research seasons or hiring pipelines.

Our World in Data charts and similar sources frequently appear when people ground multi-year claims.

Steady forecasting accuracy improves when I pre-commit to update rules instead of chasing vibes.

         - Prize Seasons and Competitive Play

A live tournament can pay cash while still scoring you on calibration rather than parlay luck.

Prize pools vary, and small finishes sometimes pay nothing after redistribution rules.

Forecasting tournaments with sponsor pots let me prove coverage under a deadline without geographic restrictions that block some cash venues.

Casual tipsters who only want one weekend wager may prefer a sportsbook.

Serious players who want a season-long proof of skill stay here.

Artificial intelligence items draw heavy traffic, from model releases to regulation clocks.

Hard AI safety items force careful definitions, which is exactly where fuzzy wording would wreck resolution.

AGI milestones stay controversial, yet the structured format still beats social media vibes for auditability.

         - Metaculus Beside Cash Venues

I also watch polymarket or kalshi prices as cross-checks when a Metaculus item overlaps a traded market.

My home base stays on Metaculus for science and model questions that resolve years out.

Liquidity on Metaculus means comment depth and player count, not an order book spread.

That difference matters if your goal is a portable score history rather than immediate payout.

Money at stake concentrates order flow on cash desks, while Metaculus concentrates attention on criteria and calibration.

         - Pros and Cons From My Desk

         - What I Like

   - Clear incentives for calibration and transparent score math.
   - Deep coverage of multi-year science and policy items.
   - Active prize seasons that stress-test coverage and updates.
   - Free core access with optional cash pots.

        - What Holds Me Back

   - No daily cash trading desk for short-term event wagers.
   - Slow resolution delays feedback on long clocks.
   - The interface can feel academic for casual users.
   - Prize rules can leave mid-pack finishers unpaid.
   - Some niche items stay thin until a season boosts attention.

         - Who Should Use Metaculus

I recommend Metaculus if you want to practice careful numbers, join prize seasons, or read research-grade crowd lines.

Casual tipsters who only want weekend action may prefer a sportsbook or a cash prediction market.

Pages on models and geopolitics are where I spend most of my screen time.

Honest notes and scheduled updates work best when you treat each item like a professional brief.

Sports-speed edges belong where order flow is thick.

Multi-year base-rate edges belong here.

Long-horizon items reward patience, notes, and scheduled updates.

Forecasting platform choice depends on whether you optimize for cash or for calibration.

         - A Final Word

My hands-on season lands positive for serious players and mixed for pure cash traders.

I keep using the site because scoring design, comment quality, and the contest calendar still produce the cleanest public signal I can cite.

For me, Metaculus remains the default notebook for multi-year questions through 2026.

         - Frequently Asked Questions

   - Is Metaculus free to use?
Yes. Core submissions are free after signup. Some prize seasons offer cash with separate eligibility rules, but you can build a score without depositing funds.

   - How does Metaculus scoring work?
Scores reward calibrated probabilities using log-style math. Peer totals compare you with other participants on the same item, while baseline totals compare you with a naive prior.

   - Does Metaculus use real money like cash venues?
Daily play is reputation-based rather than an order-book cash market. Cash appears mainly as prize pots, not as continuous trading against a house or AMM.

   - What topics can I cover?
Politics, economics, science, technology, health, climate, and model-related items appear regularly. Many resolve on multi-month or multi-year clocks.

   - How do I start as a beginner?
Sign up, pick a few clear near-term items, write a short rationale, and update when evidence changes. Join a small prize season only after you can cover most items early.

   - What is the difference between the crowd line and the site line?
The crowd line reflects the shared community signal. The site line applies extra weighting that often beats a simple center estimate on historical tests.

   - Can I use Metaculus from any country?
Access for submissions is broadly available compared with many cash venues. Prize eligibility can still depend on contest terms, so read each season’s rules before you rely on payouts.

   - Is Metaculus useful for model timeline research?
Yes. Model and related multi-year items are a major category, with active comments and frequent updates when labs or regulators move.

   - Do I need coding skills to participate?
No. Most people submit through the web UI. Optional developer access exists for bots and research pulls, but it is not required for a strong personal score.

   - How should I practice before a prize season?
Cover a mix of near-term and slow items, write short rationales, and review closed outcomes for calibration. Build a weekly update habit before you chase a large pot.

Dear members of the American press!

Steve Jobs once said, "If you can convince the press of your technology, and the press convinces us, we'll pay attention."

That's why I'm reaching out to you.

For years, the development of personal devices has been driven by advances in smartphones, tablets, and virtual reality technologies. However, all of these solutions still require people to adapt to the device. I've developed a concept based on the opposite principle: the device should adapt to the user and interact with them as naturally as possible.

I believe this technology has the potential to be the next major step in the development of consumer electronics. It offers a fundamentally new way to interact with the digital environment and has the potential to replace many existing devices that accompany people in their daily lives today.

If my assessment is correct, this isn't just another gadget, but a platform capable of transforming the market in the same way that the personal computer, iPod, and iPhone once did. Such opportunities arise extremely rarely, and that's why they deserve independent attention and objective assessment.

I believe Apple has the experience, engineering culture, and vision necessary to turn this idea into a world-class product. Moreover, the successful implementation of such technology could strengthen the leadership of the American tech industry at a time when global competition is becoming increasingly fierce.

I'm not asking you to take my word for it. I'm asking only one thing: help draw Apple's attention to this development and give it the opportunity to be considered by those capable of objectively assessing its potential.

If the technology truly represents the value I see in it, ignoring it could be a missed opportunity. If not, that will become clear after a professional evaluation. But in either case, the idea deserves to be heard.

Thank you for your attention.

Sincerely,

Alexander.

text:
Unemployment and the weaponization of poverty are among the biggest problems we have failed to confront as a society.

Sometimes, I wonder if we truly understand what unemployment does to a person.

When someone has no job, no stable income, and no clear means of survival, they have too much time to think about everything that is going wrong in their life.

They think about who hates them.

They think about their village people.

They think about enemies.

They think about spiritual attacks.

They think about who is responsible for their hardship.

They become vulnerable to anyone who can offer them an explanation for their suffering—even when that explanation is built on fear.

But imagine a different reality.

Imagine waking up at 4:00 a.m. because you have to prepare for work by 5:00 a.m.

You work from 5:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.

You barely have enough time to eat before another shift starts at 2:00 p.m.

You work until 10:00 p.m.

You get home around 10:30 p.m., exhausted.

You take your bath, eat something, perhaps check on your family, and go straight to bed because you already know that in a few hours, you have to wake up and start all over again.

Tell me, which time will you have to sit down and worry about your village people?

Which time will you have to spend hours thinking about who is spiritually attacking you?

Which time will you have to sit around discussing who wants you to fail?

You won't have the time.

You will be busy trying to survive, build your career, pay your bills, support your family and improve your life.

And this is what gainful employment means. It is not simply having something to do. It means having legitimate, productive and reasonably stable work that provides you with a dependable income and gives you the ability to meet your basic needs and live with dignity.

A person who earns a decent income has something to look forward to.

They can plan.

They can save.

They can send their children to school.

They can pay their rent.

They can support their parents.

They can afford healthcare.

They can dream beyond tomorrow.

Employment gives people more than money. It gives them purpose, structure, dignity and hope.

And this is why unemployment should not be treated as a mere statistic.

Behind every unemployment figure is a young person who has spent years searching for work.

A graduate sending applications every day and receiving no response.

A father who cannot provide what his children need.

A mother who keeps postponing her dreams because survival has become the priority.

A young man with energy, talent and ambition, but no opportunity to put any of it to use.

When people are left without opportunities for too long, desperation begins to take over. And desperate people become easier to manipulate.

That is where the weaponization of poverty becomes dangerous.

When people are hungry and hopeless, anyone who offers them a small amount of money, an explanation, a promise, or someone to blame can easily gain their loyalty.

Instead of asking why millions of people cannot find meaningful work, we sometimes tell them that their problems are caused by enemies.

Instead of demanding better economic policies, we encourage them to fight imaginary battles.

Instead of creating opportunities, we give people fear.

We must do better.

Our governments must be held accountable for creating an environment where businesses can thrive, industries can grow, and ordinary people can find meaningful work.

We need an economy where a young person does not have to spend years begging for employment.

We need an economy where hard work can actually translate into a decent standard of living.

We need an economy where people have something productive to occupy their minds and enough income to live with dignity.

Because when people have work, purpose and hope, they are less vulnerable to fear, manipulation and desperation.

So don't just ask people to pray harder.

text:
In Calvin's Institutes, Calvin argues that God's desire to put a new heart in us is proof of our lack of will and utter inability to save ourselves. I can't really blame him; nobody could have imagined heart transplants when he wrote.

We, however, see heart transplants, and so his analysis needs reassessmemt.

A few points:

1) Suppose your doctor wants to put a new heart in you. He will need your consent, but you'd have to be a moron to claim you gave yourself a new heart.

2) Suppose you're in a coma, and your medical team decides you need a new heart, and it gives you one without your consent. When you wake up, it's still up to you to respond to this new lease on life or skip your meds and wreck yourself all over again with your diet.

3) Generally speaking, for you to get a new heart, someone else has to die and sacrifice His.

So, by all means, roll with the "put a new heart in you" metaphor, but understand that it supports human freedom to accept, refuse, or misuse the sacrifice offered, rather than whatever it is Calvin is selling.

text:
Raise the Colours Founder Charged with 14 offences after Farage Praise

Ryan Bridge, 45, founder of the Raise the Colours campaign, has been charged with 14 offences, including racially aggravated harassment, threatening behaviour and assault. The charges relate to alleged incidents in Oxfordshire over about two months.

Raise the Colours encourages people to put Union Jack and St George’s Cross flags on lampposts in parts of the Midlands and southern England. Bridge is due at Oxford Magistrates’ Court on 3 November.Prosecutors allege seven counts of using threatening words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm or distress; three counts of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence; two counts of racially aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress; one count of racially aggravated fear of violence; and one count of common assault.

The charges came days after Bridge attended Reform UK’s annual conference. During a discussion hosted by Jeremy Kyle, Nigel Farage praised the campaign, saying it had “wake[n] up vast parts of this country,” and offered legal help after Bridge said he faced an injunction in Oxfordshire and similar action in Birmingham.
Separate legal action is already under way. 

In July, Oxfordshire County Council obtained a High Court injunction aimed at stopping flags being placed near highways, citing safety, trespass and obstruction. The council had also issued a formal notice demanding the campaign stop installing flags across the county. Birmingham City Council has applied for an injunction against activists linked to the campaign, including Bridge and six others. 

A High Court hearing is listed for Tuesday 8 September. Proceedings over flag installations in East Sussex are also continuing.Oxfordshire council leader Liz Leffman said the scale of the activity was affecting communities. She said the council flies the Union and St George’s flags as symbols of democracy and unity, but described the campaign’s widespread installations as intimidation rather than patriotism. She said residents had reported feeling distressed and unsafe, and that council staff and residents who challenged flag installers had faced abuse and threats. 

The council said it would take further legal steps if needed to protect public spaces and community cohesion.Bridge has been on bail since earlier this year.

text:
The fastest way to lose a Houston buyer is to make them feel like they are standing in someone else's house. 🏠

Before we ever list I walk every seller through the same thing. Not a remodel. Not thousands in upgrades. Just what to take out so the home photographs bigger, feels move in ready, and gives buyers room to picture their own life inside it.

Here is what comes out first. 👇

1️⃣ Family photos. Buyers stop imagining themselves the second they see your face on the wall.

2️⃣ Half your closet. A stuffed closet reads as not enough storage. Pull 40 percent out and store it offsite before we shoot.

3️⃣ Countertop clutter. Kitchen and bathroom counters should be nearly bare. Empty counters photograph as more square footage.

4️⃣ Everything on the fridge. Magnets, school papers, photos. It looks messy in every single listing photo without exception.

5️⃣ Extra furniture. The oversized sectional and the third accent chair shrink the room. When in doubt take a piece out.

6️⃣ Pet evidence. Bowls, beds, litter boxes, crates. Not every buyer is a pet person and smell can sell or kill a house faster than anything else in Houston's market.

7️⃣ Bold or personal decor. Political, religious, or very specific taste pulls buyers out of the moment before they even get to the kitchen.

8️⃣ Bathroom personal items. Toothbrushes, razors, half used bottles. Clear them before every single showing not just the first one.

9️⃣ Oversized rugs. They cut a room in half and cover the floors Houston buyers actually want to see especially if you have hardwood or tile underneath.

🔟 Valuables and medications. Strangers walk through your home during showings. Lock these away every single time without exception.

This costs nothing. Zero dollars. And it can be the difference between an offer in week one and a price reduction in week four. 💰

Houston buyers are sharp and they have options right now. The homes that feel clean, open, and move in ready are the ones getting offers. The ones that feel lived in are the ones sitting.

text:
The one thing I never hear from the $UBER bulls is how they will compete given Tesla’s unit economics advantage.

Cybercab will be lower cost to manufacture, lower cost to operate, and also offers a better customer experience with the interior of the cab. This will directly translate to the lowest cost to operate, and therefore to the lowest customer price per mile.

So while I acknowledge the value of Uber’s network and accomplishments to date, I can’t see them competing profitably under any reasonable set of scenarios.

And the moat of their network strikes me as extremely fragile. It wasn’t long ago that most Uber drivers I spoke with also drove for Lyft, and they would take rides from whichever platform gave them the best earnings profile, often switching multiple times throughout a single day. As a consumer I did the same, until somewhat recently as Uber pulled away.

If I’m a rider needing to choose between Uber and a Tesla Robotaxi, it’s true that I’m more familiar with the Uber and at least initially theres likely to be some stasis that prevents an immediate switch. But at sone point, all I will have to do is download the Robotaxi app and see that my rides are meaningfully cheaper with this option.  

So I’ll give it a whirl, and then I’ll realize that on top of being cheaper, it’s also more comfortable, more private, and an overall superior customer experience.

Uber does have its advantages in this fight, but they are not durable advantages.

text:
The $UBER vs $TSLA debate happening right now across the board is fascinating in many respects.

I’ve spent all day reading both sides. I even went to ChatGPT and had a conversation with Astra because of how fascinating this debate is to me. 

By the way, Astra is legit. Releasing that before Anthropic’s IPO was a chess move. The frontier lab wars are only getting more intense. 

I am long both in small quantities. A bit of Tesla I bought a year ago at $350 and haven’t added since and a small amount of Uber I added 2 weeks ago at $75 after taking a look at the numbers. Not short any of the names but also not meaningfully long any of them at this moment either. 

My conclusion so far is both sides are being ridiculously extreme in their conclusion. 

The extreme $UBER bulls are not seriously acknowledging the direct existisitential threat to its moat via CyberCab’s pure product experience and eventual scale.

The extreme $TSLA bulls are not giving any merit to the 200M+ monthly users they have, how hard is it to scale a network, how self driving might be commoditized and Uber could simply become the largest marketplace for multiple vendors, and how much time unsupervised true autonomy will take to reach any meaningful level of Uber’s 42M daily rides.

Honestly, I think both will do well. I don’t think it has to be as black or white as both sides are making it. 

However, it is an incredible thought experiment. Uber disrupted transportation forever with technology, and now Tesla is disrupting transportation forever with autonomy. 

I think Uber is undervalued. I think Tesla has the most exciting potential out of all the Mag 7 over the next decade.

I just think both sides are writing off the other for no reason.

The funniest outcome would be an eventual partnership even though I know it’s not that likely, but I do think this is going to not be one or the other.

text:
This one captures the silence that came after command had ended. Near Mrs. Alsop's House at Gettysburg, the body of Confederate Brigadier General Paul J. Semmes rested after one of the Civil War's most devastating days. There were no triumphant speeches left to give, no orders to issue—only the quiet aftermath of a battle that had consumed officers and enlisted men alike.

Semmes had entered Pennsylvania in the summer of 1863 as part of General Robert E. Lee's invasion of the North. A respected lawyer before the war and later a Confederate brigade commander from Georgia, he led his men into the fierce fighting on July 2 during the attacks near the Peach Orchard and surrounding Union positions south of Gettysburg.

The battle unfolded across farms, orchards, stone walls, and rolling fields that would soon become some of the most studied ground in American history. During the fighting, Semmes was critically wounded. He was carried from the front toward buildings serving as temporary hospitals, including the area around Mrs. Alsop's House. He later died from his wounds, becoming one of the Confederate army's highest-ranking officers lost during the Gettysburg campaign.

The photograph associated with that location is striking not because of military glory, but because of what it quietly reveals. A general who had directed hundreds of soldiers now lay in the same uncertain landscape as countless others whose names never appeared in history books. Rank offered no protection from artillery, rifle fire, or the relentless reality of battle. In the end, the distance between commander and private became far smaller than it had seemed only hours earlier.

Gettysburg lasted just three days, from July 1 to July 3, 1863, yet more than 50,000 soldiers were killed, wounded, captured, or reported missing. It remains the bloodiest battle ever fought in North America, leaving families on both sides to reckon with losses that stretched far beyond the battlefield.

Mrs. Alsop's House still anchors this story. More than a landmark, it stands as a reminder that history is often preserved not only in monuments or official reports, but in the ordinary places that suddenly found themselves at the center of extraordinary events.

The photograph endures because it does not celebrate victory or defeat. It preserves a single, quiet moment when the smoke had begun to clear, and even one of the Confederacy's senior commanders had become part of the immense human cost of Gettysburg.

text:
The history, short and accurate
Texas first. Mexico invited Anglo settlers into Texas, then tried to recentralize power, ban slavery, and clamp down on immigration. Texas revolted, won at San Jacinto (1836), and existed as an independent republic for 9 years. Mexico never accepted that and kept claiming Texas. The U.S. annexed Texas in 1845. Mexico treated annexation as an act of war and cut diplomatic ties.
The border fight. Texas/U.S. said the border was the Rio Grande. Mexico said the Nueces, ~150 miles farther north. Polk sent troops into the disputed strip. Mexican forces crossed the Rio Grande and attacked a U.S. patrol on April 25, 1846. Congress declared war.
Purchase offer before the shooting. In late 1845 Polk sent John Slidell to Mexico City with authority to pay up to $25–30 million for California and New Mexico and to settle the Texas border. Mexico would not receive him, because receiving him would look like recognizing the loss of Texas.
The 1848 treaty. After U.S. forces took Mexico City, Mexico signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (Feb. 2, 1848). Terms:
•  Mexico recognized the Rio Grande as the Texas border and dropped all claims to Texas.
•  Mexico transferred Alta California and New Mexico (today’s CA, NV, UT, most of AZ and NM, parts of CO, WY, OK, KS).
•  U.S. paid $15 million “in consideration of the extension acquired.”
•  U.S. also assumed $3.25 million in claims American citizens held against Mexico.
National Archives and standard references put the Mexican Cession at about 525,000 square miles. Including Texas claims, that is the “55% of Mexico’s territory” figure people quote. Mexico’s Senate and legislature ratified the treaty. https://t.co/Yo4rYifJ2Y 
Gadsden Purchase, 1853–54. Separate cash sale. Santa Anna’s government needed money. The U.S. paid $10 million for ~29,670 square miles of what is now southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico (the Mesilla Valley), mainly to secure a southern railroad route and clean up the remaining border. That was not war booty; it was a negotiated sale. https://t.co/lvpm4oTxPg 
What the “stole it” line leaves out
•  Mexico’s hold on the far north was thin. Alta California had only a few thousand Mexican citizens; New Mexico was the only northern province with a sizable Hispano population.
•  The U.S. offered to buy the land before the war.
•  Mexico signed two treaties and took the money.
•  Wars of that era routinely ended with cession + indemnity. That is how most 19th-century borders were drawn.
It was still an expansionist war. Polk wanted the Pacific and used the Texas dispute to get it. Calling it theft erases the Texas revolt, the prewar purchase offer, the $15M + $3.25M, and the later $10M Gadsden sale. Calling it a friendly real-estate deal erases the army in Mexico City. Both slogans are incomplete. The documents are not.

text:
Some of the commentators should read up on their history….

We didn’t “steal 55% of Mexico.” Texas won its independence in 1836. Mexico never recognized it. The U.S. annexed Texas in 1845. Mexico broke relations.
Polk then offered to buy California and New Mexico for up to $25–30 million. Mexico refused to even meet the envoy.
After the war, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) transferred ~525,000 sq mi. The U.S. paid Mexico $15 million and assumed $3.25 million in Mexican debts to Americans. Five years later Mexico sold another ~30,000 sq mi in the Gadsden Purchase for $10 million cash.
That is a treaty + two payments, not a smash-and-grab. Mexico signed both treaties. Santa Anna took the Gadsden money because his government was broke.
Put the map down and read the treaty.

text:
Oil’s 2 Clocks: Iran Now, Venezuela Later Takeaways
Iran remains the dominant near-term price driver, with escalation forcing crude to carry a larger geopolitical premium.

Venezuela’s proposed 1.5 mb/d expansion is significant, but it cannot alleviate the current market tightness, as development could take 3 to 5 years.

Canadian heavy crude producers face the clearest competitive risk because Venezuelan barrels target a similar refining market.

Oil is caught between immediate scarcity and possible future supply, but only one of those forces is setting today’s price.

Iran Now, Venezuela Later
The oil market is staring at two clocks.

The first is measured in hours and days, tracking military escalation, disrupted shipping and the next headline from Washington or Tehran. The second is measured in years, tracking investment, field development and how quickly Venezuela can turn the world’s largest proven oil reserves back into meaningful production.

For now, the first clock is setting the price.

BMO Senior Economist Art Woo notes that stress in the global crude market has continued to rise as Washington appears to have chosen escalation from a menu of unattractive options. Capitulation was politically difficult, while allowing the exchange with Iran to grind on offered no clean resolution, particularly with the US midterm elections approaching.

With escalation now the preferred route, West Texas Intermediate has surged above US$90/bbl. The market is no longer paying only for barrels. It is paying for the risk that the next barrel becomes harder to move, insure or replace. https://t.co/iTF2rP1W1L

text:
🩸 Annie Hanson was a former Division I athlete, a college football executive, healthy, active, and 23 weeks pregnant with the baby she and her husband had waited eight years for.

Then something didn't feel right.

Pain in her left groin. Shortness of breath. Swelling in her left leg. She told her OB/GYN — and was told it was pregnancy-related pain. She was placed on bed rest.

⚠️ Her symptoms kept getting worse.

When her husband came home and found her in excruciating pain — her left leg swollen to nearly twice the size of her right — he took her straight to the ER. A nurse recognized it immediately. A sonogram confirmed it. The clot had grown from her calf all the way up to her abdomen.

She was transferred to UCLA for an emergency thrombectomy. Because she was pregnant, she couldn't receive the anesthesia she would have otherwise had. Through the pain, one thought consumed her: "Would we lose our baby?"

🩸 They didn't. Their son was born healthy.

Annie was later diagnosed with Factor V Leiden and May-Thurner Syndrome — conditions she hadn't known she had. Her father was subsequently found to carry the same gene.

"I was the patient who didn't know what she didn't know."

"Education can change outcomes. Recognition can change outcomes. Listening to patients can change outcomes."

Now pregnant with her second baby, Annie is sharing her story so another mother trusts her instincts, another patient feels empowered to advocate for herself, and another family gets the happy ending they were so blessed to receive.

Read her full story, here: https://t.co/A6fqUAIGLq

Naira 'Gain' Cannot Hide Tinubu’s Devaluation Pain. The Insult to Suffering Nigerians should Stop. 

By Chukwudimma Aaron-Okonkwo 
September 7, 2026. 

Some people appointed by this current regime are celebrating a forecast that the naira may close 2026 around ₦1,290 to the dollar. They rolled out drums to celebrate when ordinary citizens are still grappling with severe economic hardship. It is imperative to remind them that when Tinubu took over in May 2023, the official rate was around ₦450. Today, it sits above ₦1,300. No thanks to his reckless policies that nearly crushed the currency down to ₦2,000. A small gain from a deep role does not erase the pain of higher prices for food, fuel, school fees and medicines that families face every day.

Nigeria does not need recycled excuses. We need leaders who understand both numbers and the people's suffering. They will offer the competence to stabilise our currency permanently and rescue the masses from poverty. With the NDC's OK ticket, the naira would not need constant defence with forecasts as we witness with the APC regime. 

Vote Obi-Kwankwaso!

Instead selected weapons and combat systems officers will be offered pilot training so their experience can be retained aboard the Raider.

Should a nuclear-capable bomber ever rely on one pilot supported by automation or should two humans always remain in control?

•  For twenty-four hours, "New Mexico" and "New America" ​​have appeared side-by-side in national headlines.
For Trump, that is enough. He doesn't need Santa Fe to change the official state seal. What he needs is for every future mention of the state to pass through that "X" he drew.
VIII. Seeing Through It: A Joke and a Doctrine
You could view this as weekend entertainment: an eighty-year-old president posting AI content, dancing to the YMCA, and treating a state name like an emoji. The humor lands.
Or, you could view it as an unfolding doctrine of naming:
•  If a name contains a foreign word, it isn't "American" enough;
•  States that don't vote his way are "fraudulent states";
•  The names of "fraudulent states" ought to be replaced by something more "respectable";
•  The replacement happens in a video first; the legalities come later.
The first perspective offers comic relief. The second reveals the reality: from the Gulf to the lake to the state, the objects grow larger and the procedures more abstract, yet the symbolism becomes increasingly concrete. Renaming the Gulf or the lake merely altered map layers; this time, the change targets the very right of a state to be called by its name within the federation.
New Mexico won't become New America tomorrow.
But the question—"Should New Mexico be called New America?"—has been written into the public agenda for 2026 by the President himself.
The road signs remain, the sticker is a fake, and the dance is a performance—but the topic is real.
This is what you call "epic"—not because the change actually happened, but because he dared to turn the act of renaming a state into a dance routine played on a loop.

This is precisely the point critics seized upon: you aren't just making a meme; you are using that meme to invalidate the voting legitimacy of an entire state.

V. The Counterattack—and Why It Seemed Weak
New Mexico’s political landscape is dominated by Democrats. Their reactions were predictable, but their phrasing is worth noting:
•  Governor Grisham: The name is non-negotiable; the President is using this map-marking stunt to distract from the war in Iran, oil prices, and the cost of living.
•  Representative Melanie Stansbury: "Oh hell no." The name represents generations of history, culture, and family.
•  Representative Gabe Vasquez: You cannot erase New Mexico—not its name, not its history, not its culture.
•  Senator Martin Heinrich: There are three things he always refers to by their original names: the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, and New Mexico.
•  Former Secretary of the Interior (and current gubernatorial candidate) Deb Haaland: New Mexico is not for sale, and it will not change its name.
These statements resonated strongly locally but were easily dismissed on the national stage as merely "getting triggered." This is because Trump offered vivid visuals—big red "X" marks, stickers, and the YMCA dance—while his opponents offered history lessons and lists of livelihood issues. In the era of short-form video, the "X" and the dance arrive first; the timeline comes later. There is an even more ruthless layer to this: even if a protest in a deep-blue state is 100% legal and historically grounded, within his base, it is automatically interpreted as "entrenched interests refusing to become American." This is precisely the structural design of this content.

VI. What is actually happening here? Not administration, but a semantic war.
If you view these three moves together, the logic is clear:
1.  The Gulf: Declaring that U.S. waters will no longer bear the names of neighboring countries.
2.  The Lakes: Labeling shared bodies of water as American in the context of a trade war.
3.  The State: Publicly labeling a state name containing "Mexico" as an error requiring correction.
Each move accomplishes the same thing: redefining "what constitutes America." It is not about treaties or demographics; it is about nomenclature. Whoever controls the naming defines the sense of belonging on the map. Mexico doesn't recognize the "American Gulf," Canada doesn't recognize the "American Lakes," and New Mexico doesn't recognize "New America"—but he doesn't need their recognition. What he needs is for his supporters to instinctively mentally "cross out" the words "New Mexico" whenever they see them.
The AI ​​video is the masterstroke. A real president putting up a road sign is a political event requiring security, permits, and the risk of being filmed doing something illegal or ridiculous. An AI president putting up a sign is a myth: the name follows him wherever he goes, accompanied by a dance. Zero cost, infinite reach, zero legal liability. This is the aesthetic of governance in 2026: decrees govern federal databases, while videos govern the imagination.
The earlier viral rumors about an executive order to rename the state were confirmed to originate from a satire account; Snopes classified them as satire. Trump didn't debunk the rumor; instead, he absorbed the satire and turned it into an official post. The rumor came first, followed by the official "meme-ing," deliberately blurring the boundaries.

VII. Will the name actually change? Short answer: The state name almost certainly won't, but the symbolism has already changed.

text:
The popular account of human anthropology operates with a nature–grace polarity. “Natural man” is defined by a created substrate—reason, moral capacity, and the ordinary structures of creaturely life. “Spiritual man” is defined by grace, understood as an elevating or healing supplement. The contrast is therefore metaphysical: nature as the given, grace as the gift. In this grammar, “natural man” can be spoken of both before and after the fall, because nature is the controlling category and grace is its perfection.

Kline’s architecture renders this entire framework obsolete. Creation is covenantal, and covenant is constituted by the Glory‑Spirit. Humanity does not begin in a sphere called nature; humanity begins in Spirit‑formed covenantal relation ordered toward eschatological consummation. Adam’s prelapsarian existence is defined by the Spirit’s constitutive presence, not by a metaphysical substrate awaiting elevation. There is no prelapsarian grace, because grace is a redemptive category. Likewise, there is no prelapsarian nature in the scholastic sense, because Adam’s being is not grounded in nature but in the Glory‑Spirit’s presence. The nature–grace polarity simply does not belong to the biblical grammar.

Within this covenantal ontology, “natural man” is strictly postlapsarian. The term has no legitimate prelapsarian referent. Natural man is the human being after the withdrawal of the Glory‑Spirit, existing in a state of covenantal breach, moral corruption, and judicial curse. His condition is not nature but Spirit‑absence, and that absence constitutes his sinfulness. Natural man is the collapsed covenantal order made personal: disordered affections, darkened understanding, and eschatological incapacity. The Pauline category is therefore pneumatic rather than metaphysical. Natural man is the man without the Spirit.

“Spiritual man” is the human being in whom the Glory‑Spirit has returned. The contrast with natural man is not nature versus grace but Spirit‑absence versus Spirit‑presence. Regeneration is the re‑presence of the Spirit; sanctification is the Spirit’s renewing work; glorification is the Spirit’s fullness. Spiritual man is the restored and consummating Glory‑Spirit image, advancing toward the eschatological telos originally offered in Eden. His existence is not nature elevated by grace but covenantal ontology renewed and brought to its appointed consummation.

Thus the popular contrast between natural and spiritual man is displaced by a covenantal and pneumatic one. Natural man is the Spirit‑withdrawn, sinful, postlapsarian human being; spiritual man is the Spirit‑present, eschatologically renewed human being. Nature and grace never enter the architecture. The decisive line is the presence or absence of the Glory‑Spirit.

text:
Is Germany turning hard right? I found this interesting. (Probably not): 

As someone who has an academic background in Germany and went to Uni there - this is super hyperbolic and overselling what happened yesterday. One state, a very poor one in the former East Germany - Saxony-Anhalt (Capital: Magdeburg) did indeed give the AfD a record share of the vote in a state election. This is not abnormal - as despite the CDU taking its dominate party role for granted in the states in the former East, these states have since reunification consistently given considerable shares of the vote to parries outside the traditional Core 4: CDU/CSU (center right) , SPD (center left), FDP (pri business liberals), Greens (environment focused, left of center). After unification this vote went to the former Communist Party, rebranded as the PDS and later as Die Linke (The Left), with the SPD usually not performing well and the CDU leading most coalition governments in these states.

Despite massive investments in the East to bring it's infrastructure up to West German standards and integrate the East into the Federal Republic - it alienated most East Germans via its approach to de-industrializing the East via the government agency known as the Treuhandanstalt which privatized East German state owned enterprises in a very rapid manner, reforming and privatizing those it felt were viable (example Carl Zeiss Optics in Jena) while closing over ten thousand manufacturing plants and adding two million East German workers to the unemployment rolls (out ofnanpouliation of 16mil) with no immediate replacement in terms of jobs that offered the pay and standard of living, a which was compounded by the complete dismantling of the East German social benefits system. Many East German families have never recovered - even over a generation later if they stayed in the East either by choice or lack of means to find employment/opportunity in the Western States.

That is why East Germans have latched into the AfD since it's founding in the 2010s - institutional failure by the CDU and the traditional German establishment to address the conditions and hardships of large swaths of the East German population for going on 30 years. Yeah the train system, road network, telecommunications etc are all shiny and nice - but when East German living standards still trail the West - significantly, then voters look for someone who will champion them. First it was the PDS/Die Linke - today it's the AfD.

Lastly - the less populated eastern states is where almost ALL the AfD vote in centered - these states add up to 12mil - down 16% since 1990, compared to the western States with 68mil up 10% since 1990. So while tht AfD gaining power at the state level in many Lander - Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia Jena), Bradenburg (Potsdam), and Saxony (Dresden) in particular, at the national level it's not able to threaten the established order outside of being a large radical opposition party within Bundestag - forcing unstable coalitions of the Core 4 parties - and maybe even Die Linke - to pass legislation and government Germany.

So - no Germany is not shifting hard right to the AfD - key East German states are - and yes that should be worrisome as them governing at the state level, where they could make those states even less attractive to investment - and perhaps see the national governments cut off subsidies due to AfD policies.

text:
Glimpses of Gibbon

"It was easier to vanquish the Goths than to eradicate the public vices; yet, even in the first of these enterprises, Decius lost his army and his life."

Here Gibbon provides an insight into the fatal danger of empire, which at once feels like a demonstration of great power but becomes a source of vulnerability. Everyone acquainted with the story of the Roman Empire knows that Trajan expanded its frontiers to the greatest extent they ever reached. Reading this lesson, we have to question if that expansion was a good thing or would the Empire have been better served to stay within the boundaries where its Founder Augustus had left them.

"It is probable that the conquests of Trajan, maintained by his successors less for any real advantage than for ideal dignity, had contributed to weaken the empire on that side."

Though Decius has led the Roman armies to fight the Goths, they prove to be dangerously formidable enemies. As they move into Thrace, Gibbon provides touchstones relating to the history of the mighty Macedonians six hundred years earlier. The Goths are besieging a great city called Philippopolis, “founded by the father of Alexander.” Decius is pursuing them through difficult country but pauses his troops at what he believes is a safe distance from the foe. Here we read of another first in Roman history in Various events of the Gothic war, A.D. 250. For these sections Gibbon is referring to the work of the last great Roman historian, Ammianus Marcellinus who wrote in the fourth century.

"The camp of the Romans was surprised and pillaged, and, for the first time, their emperor fled in disorder before a troop of half-armed barbarians."

Faced with this unprecedented defeat, Decius “investigated the more general causes that, since the age of the Antonines, had so impetuously urged the decline of Roman greatness.” Gibbon is emphasizing the theme that forms the throughline of his work, and that echoes the same high value that great historians have placed on the virtue of the people. In a bold move, Decius revives the obsolete office of the Censor, the highest office in the Roman Republic, with authority to judge even the Consuls. Gibbon tells us he did this because Decius settled on a deep understanding.

"He soon discovered that it was impossible to replace that greatness on a permanent basis without restoring public virtue, ancient principles and manners, and the oppressed majesty of the laws."

Having decided to elevate the future emperor Valerian to this revived office, the new censor himself “justly dreaded an elevation so full of envy and of suspicion.” In the section titled The design impracticable, and without effect, we read “A censor may maintain, he can never restore, the morals of a state.”

"It was easier to vanquish the Goths than to eradicate the public vices; yet, even in the first of these enterprises, Decius lost his army and his life."

The Roman army had the Goths surrounded on every side, their situation so dire that Gibbon tells us they would have been happy to “surrender all their booty and prisoners” for the chance to escape. But Decius has decided to make an example and offers no path out. From the Spartans to Julius Caesar, history tells us that the greatest military leaders warn against attacking men so desperate they have no choice but to fight. In this case, the Roman troops defeated the first and second lines of the Goths, but the last of the enemy have taken position behind a morass. Here Gibbon decides to share a lengthy quotation of the most sublime Roman historian describing a similar battle against Germans to illustrate these events, in the words of Tacitus (Annals, i.64). In this battle not only was the army lost, but so was the emperor’s life, his body was never found.

“Here the fortune of the day turned, and all things became adverse to the Romans: the place deep with ooze, sinking under those who stood, slippery to such as advanced; their armor heavy, the waters deep; nor could they wield, in that uneasy situation, their weighty javelins. The barbarians, on the contrary, were inured to encounters in the bogs; their persons tall, their spears long, such as they could wound at a distance.”

text:
PEACE

I. SIX BIS

The dog heard the bottle before any of them did. Biscotte had gone almost completely white around the muzzle and had reached the age at which a dog begins to regard human affairs with the patience of a minor deity who has long since abandoned intervention. He had slept through speeches, evacuations, alarms, the collapse of a ceiling in the building opposite, and the winter when Uncle Pascal tried to repair the gas stove with a spoon. The breaking of a bottle in the alley brought his head up at once. Everyone in the kitchen stopped for the same fraction of a second. It was the second the war had left them, the small compulsory delay between hearing a sound and granting it an innocent explanation. Rain continued against the windows. Water ran from the damaged gutter to the fire escape and struck the railing at irregular intervals. Nobody had to discuss the noise after that. It was glass. Probably glass. During the war, probably had become one of the more respectable words in the language.

Madeleine Varel sat beside the radiator knitting a sleeve for a grandson who did not exist. Étienne, her nephew, was at the kitchen table with a newspaper open before him and a cup of coffee he had forgotten to drink. Madeleine told him it had been glass. Étienne said probably. She looked over her spectacles and observed that he said probably about everything now. He replied that he had become prudent. Madeleine returned to the sleeve and informed him that he had become annoying. She was sixty-three, broad in the shoulders, iron-haired, and endowed with that old domestic faculty for reducing historical catastrophe to a failure of manners. She had complained less about shelling than about rubbish collection. The bridge could fall, the electricity could disappear for eleven days, half the district could lose its windows, but civilization, in Madeleine’s judgment, had collapsed on the Thursday when nobody collected the bottles. It was not that she considered war less serious than refuse. She simply believed that armies could be blamed on generals, whereas rubbish was everyone’s responsibility.

Peace had been official for forty-one days, or forty-two, or forty, depending on the newspaper, the ministry, the military command and the hour at which a man believed midnight became another day. The government counted from the signing. The army preferred the cessation of hostilities. The mayor selected the reopening of the central bridge, since bridges photographed better than signatures. Madeleine counted from the first night the electricity remained on until morning. Claire, her niece and Étienne’s sister, counted nothing at all. She had lost faith in dates for reasons that no official calendar could improve.

Étienne had arrived at Madeleine’s apartment fourteen months earlier and announced that he would remain three weeks. His own apartment across the river had lost its windows, then its water, then part of the eastern wall. The landlord continued sending rent notices with such punctuality that Étienne eventually admired him. One arrived after the staircase had collapsed. A neighbor found the envelope beneath plaster near what had once been the third-floor landing. The notice carried the words SECOND REMINDER in red. Étienne kept it. By then he was keeping everything. Tram tickets from routes that no longer existed, receipts from shops that had disappeared, municipal instructions replaced before delivery, letters returned because a street had acquired a new name, notices addressed to rooms that could no longer be entered, theatre programmes for performances cancelled before opening night. Later, people would assume this habit came from his work. In truth the work came from the habit. He had begun collecting evidence before anyone offered him a reason.
