MLB EXPERT PICKS FOR SEPT. 7TH, 2026 💰  

Presented by @PolymarketSport 📈

@JTFOz: We’ve got all the ingredients for an Over tonight in San Francisco, with a low total and 14.6 mph winds blowing out.

Both offenses are swinging hot bats, with the St. Louis Cardinals ranking first in OPS over the past week, while the San Francisco Giants sit eighth. They should be able to tee off against two struggling starters.

Logan Webb has been rocked for 16 earned runs across his last three starts, including nine last time out, while Michael McGreevy has surrendered 14 over the same span.

The bullpens offer little relief, ranking 26th and 21st in ERA over the past two weeks. With St. Louis going Over in 14 of its last 17, Over 7.5 is the play.

@JonMetler: The Chicago Cubs are trading at 48% on Polymarket, but I make them closer to a 51% favorite.

Two factors stand out to me. First, I'm much more comfortable backing Matthew Boyd on the road, where he owns a 2.83 ERA compared to a 5.40 ERA at Wrigley Field.

Second, Brewers starter Robert Gasser relies heavily on his slider.

The Cubs have several right-handed bats — including Alex Bregman, Nico Hoerner, and Seiya Suzuki — who are either patient against off-speed pitches from left-handed pitchers or have swing paths that profile well against the slider.

If Gasser can't generate outs with his slider, he'll be forced to attack the zone with a low-velocity fastball. Chicago also faced him just six days ago, giving its hitters a recent look at his stuff and an even greater advantage in an already difficult matchup.

@NeilParkerBets: The Diamondbacks are 28th in wOBA and 30th in xwOBA over the past two weeks, so with the Kansas City Royals respectively checking in ninth and eighth in the two metrics, I’m expecting Kansas City to pull away.

Royals lefty Noah Cameron has also settled in down the stretch with a high-end 2.34 xERA and 2.82 xFIP across his past seven starts, while the Diamondbacks counter with inexperienced righty Jose Cabrera (4.84 xERA and 5.00 xFIP).

text:
The Green Anaconda: Meet the Living Fire Hose That Could Swallow Your Dog Whole

If you scrolled past a video this week of a grown adult wrestling what looks like a tractor tire made of muscle, you already met today's main character: the green anaconda (Eunectes murinus). It is not a myth, not CGI, and not exaggerated by a nervous zookeeper. It is a real, breathing, 200-pound reptile that can lie coiled on a concrete floor like abandoned garden hose — until it decides to move, and then you remember exactly why humans have been telling anaconda legends around campfires for five hundred years.

This is your deep-dive into the single heaviest snake species on Earth: how big they actually get, how they hunt, why they don't "crush" you the way movies claim, what it's like for a keeper to lift one, and the handful of facts that sound fake but are completely true. Bookmark this. You're going to want the receipts next time someone says anacondas are exaggerated.

The Basic Stats That Already Sound Made Up

Let's start with the numbers, because the numbers alone are the hook.

Length: Females regularly reach 16–20 feet (5–6 meters). Verified record-adjacent individuals have approached 17–18 feet in captivity, and unconfirmed wild reports push past 20 feet.

Weight: This is the real headline. A large female anaconda can weigh over 200 lbs (90+ kg). Some captive individuals have been recorded above 250 lbs. That is heavier than most adult humans, heavier than a baby grand piano's worth of muscle, coiled and capable of moving.
Girth: An adult female's midsection can be as thick as a person's waist. Keepers often describe the sensation of lifting one as "like trying to carry a car tire filled with wet sand that also wants to go somewhere else."
Sexual dimorphism: Female anacondas are dramatically larger than males — sometimes 4-5 times heavier. This is one of the most extreme size gaps between sexes of any land vertebrate.
Put simply: the green anaconda isn't the longest snake in the world (that title belongs to the reticulated python), but it is, by a wide margin, the heaviest and bulkiest snake species that has ever been reliably measured. Length gets the headlines. Mass is what actually matters when something that size decides to move toward you.

Why "Crushing" Is the Wrong Word

Every anaconda video draws the same comment: "It's going to crush him!!" It's dramatic, it's viral-friendly, and it's slightly wrong.

Anacondas are constrictors, and constriction doesn't work the way movies show it. The snake isn't applying bone-breaking pressure like a hydraulic press. Instead, it does something far sneakier and, frankly, more terrifying if you think about it for more than five seconds:

It matches your exhale.

Every time the prey (or, in these zoo demonstrations, a very patient staff member's arm) breathes out, the coils tighten just slightly to close that gap. The animal can never inhale fully again. It's not a crush — it's a ratchet. Research published on boas and pythons (their constriction mechanics are nearly identical to anaconda physiology) shows that blood circulation stops within seconds, well before suffocation would even become the primary issue. Prey lose consciousness from cut-off blood flow to the brain far faster than people assume — often in under a minute for smaller prey.

This is also why trained handlers can safely work with 100+ lb anacondas: they know how to keep a coil from "setting," how to unwind a loop before it tightens, and how to redirect the snake's head before it decides your torso looks like a good anchor point. It looks like a wrestling match because, biomechanically, it kind of is one — just against an animal with no arms, no legs, and functionally unlimited coils.

They Are Basically Ambush Predators With a Built-In Snorkel

Green anacondas live in the swamps, slow-moving rivers, and flooded grasslands of the Amazon and Orinoco basins — Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, and the Guianas. And they are shockingly well-designed for a life spent mostly underwater.

Their eyes and nostrils sit on top of the head, not the front — a dead giveaway for an animal that spends most of its life submerged with just its face poking above the surface like a floating log.

They can hold their breath for well over 10 minutes at a time, and some reports (less rigorously documented, but consistent across observers) suggest even longer submersions during ambush waits.

They are almost entirely aquatic ambush hunters. Unlike pythons, which often actively stalk, anacondas frequently just... wait. They sit motionless in murky water for hours, sensing vibrations and heat, until a capybara, deer, caiman, or unlucky bird gets close enough.

Their diet is a genuine highlight reel: capybaras (the world's largest rodent), deer, birds, turtles, fish, and — yes, it's documented, not folklore — caimans. Videos and photographs of anacondas eating caimans nearly their own body length exist and are not fabricated.
This ambush lifestyle is also why anacondas look deceptively lazy in captivity. That giant coiled mass on the floor in viral zoo clips isn't "resting because it's tired" — that's baseline anaconda behavior. In the wild, it would look exactly the same, just with duckweed on top.
The Jaw Trick That Makes the "Swallow It Whole" Thing Possible
No snake unhinges its jaw. That's a myth that refuses to die. What actually happens is arguably cooler.

An anaconda's lower jaw is split into two separate bones connected by a stretchy ligament at the front (not fused like ours), and the jaw itself isn't rigidly hinged to the skull — it's suspended by a highly flexible quadrate bone. Combine that with a skin and skull structure that can stretch dramatically, and the snake can "walk" its jaws alternately over prey far wider than its own head, ratcheting one side forward, then the other, then repeat.

This is how a snake with a head the width of a fist can swallow a capybara. It's slow (a large meal can take over an hour just to get down), and it's metabolically enormous — but it also means an anaconda doesn't need to eat often. A big female can go months between meals after a large kill, digesting slowly while her metabolism runs at a fraction of a mammal's.

So... Do They Actually Attack Humans?

Here's the part that separates internet legend from documented reality, and it matters because it's the single most searched question about this species.

Confirmed fatal wild attacks on humans by green anacondas are exceptionally rare — rare enough that herpetologists studying the species for decades have very few, if any, well-documented cases to point to. Compare this to crocodilians in the same rivers, which kill people far more frequently, and the "man-eating anaconda" reputation starts to look more like colonial-era travel writing than modern herpetology.

Why the mismatch between reputation and reality?

Adult humans are outside the normal prey-size window anacondas evolved to target. A capybara-sized meal makes metabolic sense; a struggling adult human, much less so.

Anacondas are shy and will typically flee from humans rather than engage. Wild individuals that sense a person approaching usually retreat into water or vegetation.

Most "anaconda attacked me" viral stories trace back to either misidentified species, staged content, exaggerated retellings, or genuinely unlucky one-off incidents involving juveniles/small children, not the mythic man-hunting adult of legend.

None of this means they're harmless. A defensive bite from a 15-foot anaconda is a serious medical event, and an animal that size accidentally wrapping a coil while startled is genuinely dangerous — which is exactly why facilities that keep giant anacondas always work them in teams, never alone, with a plan for redirecting the head before a coil can set. The respect is earned. The "the swamp is full of maneaters" panic is not.

Why Zoo Handlers Need a Whole Team for One Snake

If you've seen the viral clips of multiple keepers hauling out one absolutely enormous green anaconda for a health check, weigh-in, or public demonstration, there's real logic behind why it takes several trained adults instead of one confident volunteer:
Distributed weight. A 150–200+ lb animal that can also actively push and pull with muscular force needs multiple people just to support its body weight evenly — otherwise it sags, stresses its spine, or the handlers lose their grip entirely.
Head control. The single most important job in any big-snake handling session is controlling the head and neck. One dedicated person almost always has that job and only that job.

Coil management. As the snake moves, loops can start to wrap around a handler's arm, waist, or leg. A second or third handler's real-time job is watching for any coil that's tightening and unwinding it before it "sets."

The snake is stronger than all of them individually. Pound for pound, a snake's muscular power dramatically outclasses a human's. Team-handling isn't about overpowering the anaconda — it's about out-coordinating an animal that has literally hundreds of vertebrae and a completely different, and frankly more efficient, muscular architecture than we do.

This is also why reputable facilities are so insistent that home-keeping a full-grown female green anaconda is a genuinely serious undertaking, not a novelty pet decision — the animal you start with as a cute 18-inch hatchling can, within a few years, become the 150+ lb problem described above.

The Record-Chasing Problem: Why "30-Foot Anaconda" Claims Keep Getting Debunked

Every few years, a story resurfaces claiming a hunter, explorer, or fisherman found a 30-, 40-, or even 60-foot anaconda in the Amazon. These claims virtually never hold up.
The scientifically documented, verified record for green anaconda length sits at roughly 17.7 feet (5.4 m), reliably measured.
Historical bounties (some real, some apocryphal) offered by museums and expeditions for verified giant anacondas going back over a century have essentially gone unclaimed at the "giant" end of the myth spectrum.
Visual estimation of snake length in the field is notoriously unreliable — a coiled or partially submerged anaconda is extremely easy to overestimate by 30-50%, even for experienced observers, simply because there's no straight reference line to measure against.

Photos "proving" 30+ foot anacondas are reliably traceable to forced-perspective camera tricks, deliberately staged hoaxes, or genuine misidentification.

None of this makes the real animal less impressive. A confirmed, measured 17-foot, 200-lb anaconda is already operating at a scale that should be startling. The myth-inflation actually does the real species a disservice — it makes people expect a monster and then somehow undersell an animal that is already one of the most physically extreme reptiles alive.

Quick-Fire Facts Built for Screenshotting

Green anacondas are not venomous. Zero venom glands, zero need — constriction handles everything.

They give birth to live young (ovoviviparous), not eggs — a rarity among snakes, most of which lay eggs.
A single litter can contain 20 to 40+ babies, occasionally more, though wild survival rates for hatchlings are brutally low.
Newborn anacondas are already around 2 feet long and fully capable hunters from birth — no parental care follows.
They can go from newborn to breeding-capable adult in roughly 3–5 years, an astonishingly fast growth curve for an animal that eventually weighs hundreds of pounds.

Green anacondas belong to the boa family (Boidae), not the python family — a common mix-up, since pythons get more mainstream attention.

Their name isn't fully settled linguistically — "anaconda" likely derives from a Sri Lankan/Tamil-linked word historically misapplied to South American giant snakes by early European naturalists confusing regional serpent names.

Captive lifespan can exceed 25–30 years with proper care, meaning a hatchling bought on impulse is a multi-decade commitment.

Despite the bulk, they can move with surprising speed in water — noticeably faster swimming than crawling on land, which tracks with their evolutionary home turf.
Why This Species Keeps Going Viral (And Why That's Actually Good)
Every time a reptile facility posts a video of staff carrying, weighing, or feeding a giant green anaconda, it rockets across social platforms — and there's a genuinely good reason beyond shock value. These animals sit at a rare intersection: they are simultaneously terrifying-looking, scientifically fascinating, ecologically important, and almost entirely misunderstood by pop culture.
The apex-predator role anacondas play in Amazonian wetlands matters far beyond spectacle. They regulate capybara and caiman populations, they're an indicator species for wetland health, and healthy anaconda populations are a decent proxy for a functioning floodplain ecosystem. When these animals show up in a viral clip getting weighed by a team of keepers, that footage is doing real conservation-communication work whether or not that's the intent — it puts an animal most people will never encounter in the wild directly in front of millions of eyes, and turns "scary swamp monster" into "actually, that's an incredible, specialized, and mostly misunderstood predator."
So next time that video crosses your feed — the one with the coiled mass the size of a car tire and a keeper grinning while hauling twenty feet of muscle across a concrete floor — you'll know exactly what you're looking at: not a monster, not a myth, but one of the most extreme, efficient, and genuinely underrated predators evolution has ever produced.
Green Anaconda vs. Reticulated Python vs. Burmese Python: The Comparison Everyone Gets Wrong
Twitter loves a "which is bigger" fight, and the green anaconda vs. reticulated python debate is one of the most consistently confused matchups in the animal kingdom, so let's settle it cleanly.
Longest snake alive: the reticulated python, native to Southeast Asia, takes this title outright. Verified individuals have measured past 20 feet, with the longest reliably documented specimen (a captive python named Medusa) measured at over 25 feet.
Heaviest snake alive: the green anaconda wins this, and it isn't close. A retic of comparable length is dramatically slimmer and lighter — often less than half the mass of a similarly long female anaconda. Length and mass are not the same competition, and anacondas are built like a completely different engineering project: shorter, thicker, heavier, and packed with far more muscle per foot of body.

Burmese python: shorter than both on average (typically topping out in the mid-teens of feet in the wild, though invasive Florida populations have produced some genuinely massive outliers), but notorious for a different reason — as an invasive species now devastating native mammal populations in the Florida Everglades, arguably causing more measurable ecological damage in the past two decades than any wild anaconda population ever has.

The internet's favorite version of this fight — "which snake would win in a fight" — is a fun thought experiment but a biologically strange question, since these species never interact in the wild; their ranges don't overlap. If you want the honest, boring-but-true answer: in raw mass, structural bulk, and sheer physical presence, nothing beats a full-grown female green anaconda. In raw length, the reticulated python takes it every time.

The "Anaconda" Movie Problem: Debunking Hollywood One Scene at a Time

The 1997 film Anaconda (and its sequels) did more to shape public perception of this species than any documentary ever has — and almost none of it holds up.

The size in the film is wildly exaggerated. The movie's anaconda is portrayed as absurdly massive, fast, and aggressive, hunting humans specifically and repeatedly. Real anacondas do not hunt humans as prey; humans are outside their evolved size-target window, as covered above.

The speed is fictional. On land, a giant anaconda moves relatively slowly and laboriously — dragging that much mass across dry ground is metabolically expensive and slow. The "snake bursts from water at car-chase speed" scenes are cinematic invention, not biology.

The "swallows a man whole in one gulp" scenes compress a process that would realistically take well over an hour into a single dramatic bite. Real prey ingestion, even of large animals, is a slow, methodical, jaw-walking process — dramatic in its own right, but nothing like the instant-swallow depicted on screen.

The "hisses and roars" sound design is almost entirely fabricated for cinematic tension. Snakes don't roar. Anacondas can hiss, and that's about the extent of their vocal repertoire.

None of this is a criticism of the film as entertainment — it's simply a reminder of how much of the internet's baseline "mental image" of an anaconda comes from a monster movie rather than actual herpetology. Every fact in this article is drawn from the real, measured, documented animal — which, again, needs zero embellishment to be genuinely impressive.
Conservation Status: The Part Nobody Retweets, But Should
Green anacondas are currently listed as a species of Least Concern by the IUCN, meaning the overall wild population is not considered at immediate risk of extinction. But "not endangered" doesn't mean "not threatened" — and the pressures on anaconda populations are real and growing:

Habitat loss from deforestation, agricultural expansion, and wetland drainage across the Amazon and Orinoco basins is steadily shrinking the flooded grasslands and river systems anacondas depend on.

Illegal hunting for skins (anaconda leather has long been targeted for boots, bags, and belts) continues in parts of their range despite regulation.

Human-wildlife conflict increases as agricultural and ranching land pushes deeper into anaconda habitat, occasionally resulting in defensive killings of snakes that pose little actual threat.

Climate-driven changes to seasonal flooding patterns matter more for this species than most people realize — anacondas are deeply tied to wet-season/dry-season cycles for hunting, breeding, and even the seasonal "anaconda balls" (mating aggregations where multiple males compete for access to a single large female).

The species' current stability is genuinely good news, but it's a reminder that "least concern" is a snapshot, not a guarantee — and much of it depends on the same Amazonian ecosystems currently under some of the most well-documented deforestation pressure on the planet.
What It's Actually Like Working With One (According to the People Who Do It)
Reptile keepers and zoo educators who work hands-on with giant anacondas consistently describe a few things that rarely make it into the viral clip captions:
The strength is disorienting the first time you feel it. Multiple keepers across multiple facilities describe the same sensation: an anaconda doesn't feel like "lifting a heavy object," it feels like the object is actively, calmly working against you the entire time, because it is.

Temperature and mood matter enormously. A well-fed, recently-fed, or cooler-temperature anaconda is typically calmer and more cooperative for handling. A hungry or freshly-warmed individual is a completely different, far more alert animal.

They're smarter about leverage than people expect. Handlers frequently note that anacondas seem to instinctively search out an anchor point — a table leg, a handler's belt, another coil of their own body — the moment they feel unsupported, purely as a stabilizing reflex rather than aggression.

Public demonstrations are deliberately overstaffed. The team of 3-5 people in a viral handling clip isn't there for a photo-op; it's a minimum-viable safety crew for an animal that size, full stop.

The bite, when it happens, is rarely "the dangerous part." Anaconda teeth are backward-curved and designed to grip fleeing prey, not to be a primary weapon. A bite hurts and needs cleaning, but it's a minor incident compared to an uncontrolled coil — which is why virtually all handling protocol is built around coil management, not bite avoidance.

Rapid Q&A: The Questions the Comment Section Always Asks
Can an anaconda actually eat a human? Physically, a large enough female could theoretically manage the girth for a small adult, but it essentially never happens in documented reality. Digestive efficiency, prey-recognition instincts, and basic behavioral ecology make humans a near-nonexistent target, despite the physical theoretical possibility.
How fast can they swim vs. crawl? They are considerably faster and more graceful in water than on land — which tracks, since water is their actual home turf and land movement for an animal this heavy is comparatively labor-intensive.
Do they live in groups? Not typically, outside of the breeding season "mating ball" phenomenon, where multiple males cluster around a single receptive female for days or weeks. Otherwise, anacondas are largely solitary.

What eats an adult anaconda? Almost nothing, once they reach full size — which is precisely why they sit at the apex of their ecosystem. Juveniles face real predation risk from caimans, jaguars, and large birds of prey; full-grown adults face essentially none.

Can you legally own one? Regulations vary drastically by country, state, and even city, and many jurisdictions specifically restrict or ban ownership of giant constrictor species precisely because of the scale-of-commitment issues covered above. Always check local exotic-animal regulations before assuming this is a casual pet option.

TL;DR for the skimmers

The green anaconda is the heaviest snake on Earth, can weigh over 200 lbs, kills through blood-flow restriction rather than "crushing," ambushes prey from submerged hiding spots, eats things as large as caimans by unhinging-adjacent jaw mechanics, almost never fatally attacks adult humans despite its reputation, requires multiple trained handlers to safely manage in captivity, and every "30-foot monster" story you've heard is almost certainly exaggerated. The real animal, measured honestly, is already one of the most impressive predators alive — no embellishment required.

So the next time your feed serves up sixty seconds of a keeper hauling twenty feet of muscle across a zoo floor, you won't just watch and scroll — you'll know the biology, the myths, the real numbers, and exactly why this animal earns every bit of internet attention it gets, honestly, without a single exaggeration needed.
Save this thread. Send it to whoever posted "it's going to eat him" in the comments. The green anaconda doesn't need Hollywood's help to be terrifying — the real biology was always going to be enough on its own.

text:
Maybe @elonmusk  can create a “doge” searchable site combining current data. 

Yes. Several searchable databases of U.S. judges already exist, though they differ in scope and purpose.
Directories / profiles (biographical + court data)
•  CourtListener has a long-running, searchable database of thousands of federal and state judges, including bios, political affiliations, ABA ratings, opinions authored, and financial disclosures. It also offers APIs. https://t.co/gWJKDMWw0c 
•  https://t.co/RiAdgC79Bi launched a free searchable directory in 2026 with over 30,000 judge profiles and court navigation. https://t.co/p0c8f6bwzr 
•  JudicialFinder indexes more than 20,000 judges (federal and state) with appointment history, Senate votes, and career connections. https://t.co/vYwddnStfI 
Review / rating / accountability sites
•  The Robing Room (https://t.co/l5UmwBcWAf) lets users rate and comment on federal and state judges and publishes “top 10 / bottom 10” lists.
•  Bench Receipts (https://t.co/N2BES08IGb) documents specific rulings, especially those described as activist or soft-on-crime; it has profiles on 100+ judges across dozens of states. @pink_meeces 
•  https://t.co/b9fjl2Co9u tracks judges whose released defendants later reoffended or violated conditions. It started in Florida and plans to expand nationwide. @johnnyfse 
None of these is a single, complete “review every judge in the country with consumer-style ratings + full case analysis,” which is the gap Rachel Alexander described. The existing tools cover pieces of it (directories, opinions, some user reviews, or targeted accountability tracking), but compiling consistent performance data across thousands of state and local courts remains difficult.

Whiskey Jug Genie by Sultonna Nadine is a lighthearted and charming paranormal fantasy that mixes magic, humor, and a touch of romance for pure escapist fun.

When quiet London apothecary shop owner Martin buys an old whiskey jug on vacation, he has no idea he’s about to release Bubba, a genie who’s been trapped inside for 200 years and is thoroughly out of touch with the modern world. Chaos, spells, cultural clashes, and plenty of laughs ensue as the unlikely pair (along with a very annoyed cat) try to navigate the mess. Set against the backdrop of contemporary London with elements of white magic and everyday wonder, the story balances humorous situations with warmer moments. Readers appreciate its playful tone, quirky characters, and the perfect blend of paranormal fantasy, magic, and comedy—it’s the kind of book that delivers smiles and a welcome dose of whimsy.

text:
Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

California-to-Texas Real Estate: More Choices, Different Costs

California and Texas continue to offer very different housing-market conditions.

California’s latest statewide report showed a median existing single-family home price of $887,680 for July 2026. Sales declined from June but remained slightly above July 2025. Texas recorded a $340,000 statewide median sales price during the second quarter of 2026, unchanged from the previous year. Closed sales increased 4.5%, while the state had 5.4 months of inventory.

Greater Houston buyers had a record 40,750 active single-family listings in July 2026. Sales increased 1.6% year over year, the median price edged up 0.6% to $340,000, and inventory reached 5.5 months. This points toward a more balanced market with greater buyer choice—not an absence of demand.

The national average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.71% as of September 3, 2026, making the complete monthly housing expense especially important. text:
Nightly for the past couple of months I’ve been reading my young daughter Alice’s Adventures In Wonderland. It got me thinking. Researching the #JFKA has been my own private fall down the rabbit hole, and once you start tumbling, the ground never quite stops moving beneath you.

It begins innocently enough. You open a book, watch a documentary, or click one more link about the official story. Then the white rabbit of doubt appears: a discrepancy in the autopsy, a witness who changed their testimony, a photograph that doesn’t quite line up. 

You follow. The ground gives way. Suddenly you’re falling, past the Warren Commission, past the grassy knoll, past the single-bullet theory, and the walls of the shaft are lined with files, names, and half-whispered motives.

The deeper you go, the more the landscape rearranges itself. One corridor leads to Texas oil money and the depletion allowance. Another opens onto CIA black operations and gold caches. A third snakes through organized crime, drug planes, and covert funding. Each path feels urgent and coherent until the next turn reveals a new, equally insistent map. 

Characters appear and vanish like the Cheshire Cat: an alleged mistress with a late-night promise, a dying intelligence officer naming names, a Texas businessman with a list of murders, a nightclub owner writing from jail. Some grin. Some accuse. Some contradict the last one you met. You try to hold them all in your head at once and feel yourself growing larger with every new connection, then suddenly shrinking when a document or timeline fails to hold.

Time behaves strangely here. Minutes spent on one footnote become hours. Days dissolve into rabbit holes within rabbit holes, LBJ’s backers, Lansdale’s gold, the Contras and cocaine, the endless debate over who stood to gain. 

The Queen of Hearts version of history (the official one) keeps shouting “Off with their heads!” at anyone who questions the lone gunman, while the Mad Hatter tea parties of competing theories never end and never quite agree on the correct time. 

You find yourself arguing with shadows, collecting “evidence” that feels solid until the next source reframes it. Curiosity becomes compulsion. “Curiouser and curiouser,” you mutter, just as Alice did, because every answer only multiplies the questions.

And yet, like Alice, you keep going. Not because the path is clear, but because the alternative, turning back to the surface world of settled history, now feels thinner, less vivid. The rabbit hole has its own gravity. It rewards the chase with the intoxicating sense that you are seeing behind the curtain, even as it reminds you that the curtain may be infinite.

Eventually you surface, blinking, with notebooks full of names and timelines and a private conviction that the official story is incomplete. But something of Wonderland stays with you. The ordinary world looks a little flatter. The questions linger. And somewhere, just out of sight, the white rabbit is still checking its watch, waiting for you to follow again.

I’m 56 years old and I read my first JFK assassination book when I was 16. At last count I have read close to 800 books related to this topic and watched everything YouTube has to offer and I’m all filed out.

Boston's Labor Day Parade this morning was more of a rally. Held in Copley Square Park, organizers say it offered a new way to celebrate workers and union solidarity.
The parade through the Back Bay was designed to include more union members and their families.
The labor union reported having half a million members throughout Massachusetts.. and over 100,000 union workers in the Boston area.

The National Transportation Safety Board is expected to hold a news conference today to provide the latest information regarding yesterday's cargo jet crash at Miami International Airport. Five people died and five more were injured after an Amazon cargo plane crashed there Sunday afternoon, causing a full ground stop that halted all flights for hours. NewsNation's Mills Hayes:: “It actually left the airport and went over a public road and crashed into a parking lot. 5 people were killed tragically in this crash. 5 others injured, 3 in critical condition at this point. The co-pilot and the pilot had to be extracted from the cockpit. They were trapped inside there, and we don't know yet what their condition is. ”
Flight 7598.. a Boeing 767 being operated by 21 Air for Amazon Air Cargo, departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, earlier in the day and overran the runway after landing at M-I-A just before 2 p-m.
The F-A-A will investigate the crash.

7 SEPTEMBER 2026
From Exposure to Architecture: Seven Days of Commentary from Beneath the Ice
Today, the European Union announced a new €200 million investment package for Greenland covering 2026–2027.[1]
The package identifies digital connectivity, mining, energy, education, fisheries, housing and tourism.
The amount is significant. The categories are ambitious.
But broad funding categories do not constitute an infrastructure strategy.
Greenland has approximately 56,500 residents. Only about 35% live in Nuuk, meaning nearly two-thirds live elsewhere across Greenland’s widely dispersed towns and settlements.[2]
More than 6,500 people live in settlements—but settlement population alone does not capture the full reach of infrastructure inequality.
Recent institutional reporting indicates that approximately 4,700 of Greenland’s 22,000 households—about one in five—remain served by bag or bucket toilets.[3] Peer-reviewed research found that roughly 80% of rural households lacked piped water.[4]
The precise number of Greenlanders experiencing at least one serious infrastructure deficiency has not been established through a single national measure.
That absence is itself a governance problem.
Greenland needs a publicly verifiable, settlement-by-settlement infrastructure audit covering:
Sanitation, drinking water and housing
Local roads, docks and coastal transportation
Medical-evacuation access
Digital connectivity and energy reliability
Greenlandic ownership, employment and technical training
Not every community can be connected through conventional roads. Greenland requires equivalent access through different systems—local roads, ports, reliable coastal service, aviation and digital infrastructure.
Funding critical minerals while households still depend upon bag toilets would not constitute balanced development.
Congress should pay close attention. The United States and Canada can offer more than geopolitical competition: a Greenland Connectivity and Human Infrastructure Compact, governed by Naalakkersuisut and participating communities.
If a deal is in the queue, do a deal with true impact. Measure investment by households receiving safe sanitation, communities gaining reliable transportation and Greenlanders acquiring the expertise to own and maintain these systems.
Will €200 million build the capacity Greenlandic communities need—or will coercive pressures primarily make Greenland more strategically valuable to Europe?
References
[1] European Commission, “EU–Greenland Partnership,” 7 September 2026.
[2] Statistics Greenland, Greenland in Figures 2025.
[3] SINTEF, “Exploring Real-World Case Studies in the Greenland Landscape,” 2024.
[4] Maréchal et al., “Domestic Water Supply in Rural Greenland,” 2022. @RepFine @RepBrandonGill @DrewHornUSA @GoogleExpertUK

text:
The Ghost-Cowl Fish: A Newly Documented Wonder of the Deep Sea

Somewhere far beneath the reach of sunlight, where the ocean floor is nothing but cold silt, sponge gardens, and eternal darkness broken only by the beam of a submersible's light, a deep-sea camera recently drifted across one of the strangest animals ever caught on film. At first glance it looks like a jellyfish that swallowed a face. A pale, almost human-looking pair of golden eyes stares out from beneath a soft, glowing, rib-veined hood that looks more like a wilted umbrella than any fin or scale. The animal sits motionless on a bed of sponges and shell fragments, its hood pulsing gently, before slowly tilting toward the light as if sizing up the machine that disturbed it.

Marine biologists reviewing the footage have proposed the working name Ghost-Cowl Fish, and in scientific shorthand it has already picked up the provisional binomial Ptychocephalus nebulosus — roughly "cloudy folded-head" in Latin, a nod to the translucent hood folded protectively over its skull. It is a fitting name for an animal that seems to be wearing its own private fog bank wherever it goes.

A Body Built From Fog and Jelly

The single most striking feature of the Ghost-Cowl Fish is the huge, gelatinous mantle that rises from its back and drapes forward over its head like a monk's cowl or a half-closed umbrella. Under the submersible's lights the tissue glows a soft blue-white, crossed by dozens of fine radiating ribs that look uncannily like the ribs of a jellyfish bell. In fact, early observers assumed they were looking at two separate animals — a fish tangled inside a stranded jellyfish — until the footage showed the "hood" flexing and re-shaping in perfect coordination with the fish's own movements, proving beyond doubt that the structure is a living part of the same organism.

This hood is not solid muscle. It is closer to a thick cushion of collagen-rich, water-saturated tissue, the same basic material that gives many gelatinous zooplankton their see-through bodies. Roughly ninety-five percent water by volume, it costs the fish almost nothing in terms of energy to grow or maintain, yet it forms a surprisingly tough, rubbery shield. Researchers who have handled similar tissue in related abyssal species describe it as feeling like a firm water balloon: yielding to a soft touch, but resistant to puncture from the blunt mouthparts of most deep-sea predators.

Beneath that hood sits a face that has captured the imagination of everyone who has seen the clip. Two enormous, lidless yellow eyes, each ringed with a dark iris, dominate a pale, wrinkled head. The eyes are tilted slightly upward, an adaptation shared by many deep-sea fish that need to watch for the faint silhouettes of prey or predators against whatever residual light filters down from far above. Below the eyes, a wide, loose-lipped mouth is lined with small, backward-curving teeth — not built for slicing, but for gripping soft-bodied prey and preventing it from wriggling free once caught.

The rest of the body, mostly hidden by the hood in the footage, appears short and soft, tapering to a flattened tail fringed with a low, translucent fin. There is no evidence of the bony armor, spines, or heavy scales seen in many other bottom-dwelling fish. Instead, the Ghost-Cowl Fish invests everything in that one great defensive and sensory structure: the hood.

Where It Lives: A World Without Light

Footage of the animal was captured on a soft sediment plain thousands of meters down, in the perpetually dark zone of the ocean that biologists call the bathyal and abyssal region. Down here, sunlight has not penetrated for hundreds of millions of years; water temperatures hover just above freezing, and pressure would crush an unprotected human body in an instant. The seafloor in the video is carpeted with sponges, their intricate lattice-like skeletons providing texture and shelter across an otherwise featureless expanse of mud and shell fragments.

This kind of habitat, sometimes called a sponge ground or sponge reef, functions in the deep sea a little like a coral reef does in shallow water: it is a three-dimensional structure that traps falling organic particles, hosts small crustaceans and worms, and attracts larger animals looking for both shelter and food. The Ghost-Cowl Fish appears to be a resident of these sponge fields, using the uneven, textured seafloor to break up its outline and the sponges themselves as anchor points and ambush cover.

Because the deep seafloor receives no photosynthetic input at all, everything the Ghost-Cowl Fish and its neighbors eat ultimately comes from above, drifting down as "marine snow" — a slow, constant rain of dead plankton, fecal pellets, mucus, and other organic debris sinking from the sunlit surface layers far overhead. Life at these depths runs on a strict energy budget: food is scarce, unpredictable, and often small, so the animals that thrive here tend to be slow-moving, low-metabolism specialists rather than fast, energetic predators.

How It Feeds

Video analysis suggests the Ghost-Cowl Fish is largely a sit-and-wait predator. Rather than chasing prey across the sediment, it appears to settle onto the seafloor, hood spread wide, and simply wait. The pale coloring of its face and the diffuse glow of its hood may serve a dual purpose here: camouflage against the pale, light-scattering sediment, and possibly a very faint bioluminescent lure, similar in principle — if not in mechanism — to the glowing lure of an anglerfish. Small crustaceans, worms, or drifting larvae that wander too close to the hood's rim may be drawn in by the diffuse light or simply fail to notice the motionless animal until it is too late.

Once prey makes contact with the sensitive rim of the hood, the fish is thought to snap its head forward and upward in a rapid strike, engulfing the prey item in its wide mouth before the small, recurved teeth lock it in place. Given the extremely limited food supply at these depths, the Ghost-Cowl Fish likely feeds only occasionally, going for extended stretches — potentially weeks — between successful captures, a survival strategy common among abyssal ambush predators.

Surviving Crushing Pressure and Eternal Cold

At the depths where this animal was filmed, water pressure can exceed several hundred times that found at the surface. Most animals adapted to life at such depths share a handful of key survival tricks, and the Ghost-Cowl Fish appears to embody nearly all of them.

First is the soft, water-rich body itself. Unlike surface fish, which rely on gas-filled swim bladders to control buoyancy, deep-sea fish living under extreme pressure often reduce or eliminate gas-filled cavities altogether, since gas compresses dramatically under pressure and would be a serious liability. Instead, many rely on lipid-rich tissue and watery, jelly-like flesh — exactly the composition of the Ghost-Cowl Fish's hood — to achieve near-neutral buoyancy without a single gas pocket in the body. Because water is essentially incompressible, a body built mostly of water and fat is not crushed by pressure the way a gas-filled structure would be; the pressure inside and outside the tissue stays balanced no matter how deep the animal goes.

Second is a slowed-down metabolism. Deep-sea animals living in permanent cold and near-total food scarcity typically have far slower metabolic rates than their shallow-water relatives, allowing them to survive on a fraction of the calories a similarly sized coastal fish would need. Slow, deliberate movements — like the languid drifting and gentle hood-pulsing seen in the footage — conserve energy that cannot easily be replaced.

Third, cellular adaptations in deep-sea life often include specialized proteins and membrane structures that remain flexible and functional even under crushing pressure and near-freezing temperatures, conditions that would stop ordinary enzymes from working properly. While direct laboratory data on the Ghost-Cowl Fish itself does not yet exist, its close relatives among gelatinous abyssal fish show exactly this kind of pressure-tolerant biochemistry, and there is no reason to expect this species to be any different.

Defense: When Being Squishy Is a Superpower

Watching the footage, one of the first questions any viewer asks is simple: with no armor, no spines, and no obvious speed, how does this strange, slow-moving animal avoid being eaten? The answer appears to lie almost entirely in that remarkable hood.

The gelatinous mantle likely serves as the Ghost-Cowl Fish's primary line of defense in several overlapping ways. First, its sheer size and shape disguise the outline of the vulnerable head and body beneath, making the animal look, to any approaching predator, less like food and more like a piece of drifting debris or a stray patch of jellyfish tissue — something many deep-sea hunters have learned to ignore, since gelatinous animals are often low in nutritional value and difficult to digest. This is a defense strategy known as mimicry-by-association, and something similar is used by a range of soft-bodied deep-sea creatures that resemble unappetizing jellies rather than advertising themselves as meat.

Second, when the fish is disturbed, footage shows it slowly withdrawing its head further into the folds of the hood, pulling the vulnerable eyes and mouth back under a protective canopy of tough, rubbery tissue. A predator biting down on the hood itself would get a mouthful of tough, low-value jelly rather than the softer, more nutritious body underneath — buying the fish valuable seconds to retreat.

Third, the loose, semi-detachable nature of gelatinous tissue in many related deep-sea species allows a wounded animal to shed a torn section of hood entirely, much the way a lizard sheds its tail, escaping while a predator is left holding a mouthful of regenerating jelly. Researchers strongly suspect a similar sacrificial-tissue strategy in the Ghost-Cowl Fish, given the structural similarity of its hood to tissues seen in other soft-bodied abyssal animals known to use this trick.

Finally, there is the simple fact that the hood may carry a faint chemical deterrent. A number of gelatinous deep-sea organisms secrete distasteful or mildly toxic mucus on their outer surface specifically to discourage curious predators, and the thick, mucus-coated texture visible on the Ghost-Cowl Fish's hood in the video is consistent with this kind of passive chemical armor. Combined, these four defenses — visual camouflage, sacrificial tissue, physical toughness, and possible chemical deterrence — allow a slow, unarmored animal to persist for extended periods in an environment full of far faster, sharper-toothed predators.

Senses in the Dark

With no natural light to see by beyond the rare flash of bioluminescence from other animals, sight alone would be nearly useless at these depths — yet the Ghost-Cowl Fish clearly possesses large, well-developed eyes. This is a common paradox in deep-sea biology: many abyssal animals retain or even enlarge their eyes specifically to catch the faintest bioluminescent flickers produced by prey, predators, or potential mates, rather than to see in the way shallow-water animals do. The Ghost-Cowl Fish's oversized yellow eyes, angled slightly upward, are almost certainly tuned to detect these fleeting glows rather than to form detailed images the way a human eye would.

Vision is likely only a secondary sense for this animal, however. Like most bottom-dwelling deep-sea fish, it probably relies heavily on a lateral line system — a row of pressure-sensitive cells running along the body — to detect the faintest vibrations and water movements caused by nearby animals. Combined with chemoreceptors capable of detecting minute traces of dissolved organic compounds drifting through the water, this sensory suite would allow the Ghost-Cowl Fish to "feel" and "taste" its surroundings with remarkable precision, compensating for eyes that are of only limited use in a lightless world.

Reproduction and Life Cycle

Little is known for certain about how the Ghost-Cowl Fish reproduces, since only a single individual has so far been documented on camera. However, based on patterns seen across related deep-sea species, biologists expect its reproductive strategy to follow a familiar abyssal template: producing a relatively small number of large, yolk-rich eggs rather than the huge broods of tiny eggs typical of many shallow-water fish. Large eggs give hatchlings a head start in an environment where food is desperately scarce and every calorie counts.

It is likely that eggs are either scattered directly onto the sponge-covered seafloor, where the intricate structure of the sponges offers some protection from egg-eating scavengers, or brooded for a period against the parent's own body — a strategy seen in some other deep-sea fish that lack the luxury of producing millions of expendable young. Given the slow metabolism and low-energy lifestyle already described, it would not be surprising if the Ghost-Cowl Fish also has an unusually slow growth rate and a long lifespan by fish standards, potentially spanning many decades, another common trait among deep, cold-water species that has already been documented in animals like the Greenland shark and various deep-sea rockfish.

A Living Ecosystem Engineer?

One intriguing possibility raised by researchers studying the footage is that the Ghost-Cowl Fish's presence on a sponge ground may not be accidental. Sponge grounds are known to be important nursery habitats and shelter zones for a wide range of small invertebrates, and a slow-moving, well-camouflaged predator like the Ghost-Cowl Fish may play a specific ecological role there: quietly culling the small crustaceans and worms that would otherwise overgraze the delicate sponge tissue, in exchange for the shelter and ambush cover the sponge field provides. If confirmed, this would make the species not just a curiosity but a small, functional cog in the wider deep-sea sponge ecosystem — one more reason conservationists are pushing to protect these fragile habitats from bottom trawling and deep-sea mining before species like this one are fully understood, let alone before they disappear.

Behavior Caught on Camera

The footage itself offers a rare, almost intimate window into the animal's behavior. Rather than fleeing instantly from the submersible's lights — the reaction typical of skittish, fast-swimming fish — the Ghost-Cowl Fish stays remarkably still, tilting its head slowly as if curious about, or simply undisturbed by, the intrusion. This kind of passive, low-reactivity behavior is itself a clue to its ecology: an animal that has evolved in an environment with very few large, fast predators, and one that relies on stillness and camouflage rather than flight as its default response to disturbance.

Only when the light lingers for an extended period does the animal appear to shift its posture, drawing the hood slightly tighter and lowering its body closer to the sediment — subtle signs of mild stress rather than outright alarm. This slow, deliberate reaction time is consistent with the extremely low metabolic rate expected of an animal adapted to a world where sudden bursts of energy are a luxury it can rarely afford.

Why This Discovery Matters

The deep ocean remains, by a wide margin, the least explored environment on the planet. Scientists estimate that the vast majority of the deep seafloor has never been directly observed by human eyes or cameras, and new expeditions using remotely operated vehicles continue to turn up animals unlike anything previously described — creatures that blur the boundaries between familiar categories like "fish" and "jellyfish," "predator" and "camouflage specialist." The Ghost-Cowl Fish is exactly this kind of discovery: an animal whose strange, hybrid-looking body forces scientists to reconsider just how many different evolutionary solutions exist for surviving in the crushing dark of the deep sea.

Every such find is also a quiet reminder of how much remains unknown even in the twenty-first century. While satellites map the surface of Mars in exquisite detail, vast stretches of Earth's own ocean floor remain less well mapped than the surface of the Moon. Animals like the Ghost-Cowl Fish are a vivid argument for continued investment in deep-sea exploration, not only because of their scientific value, but because they hint at the sheer scale of biodiversity still waiting to be catalogued before habitats like sponge grounds are damaged beyond recovery by industrial activity on the seafloor.

Quick Facts About the Ghost-Cowl Fish

Provisional name: Ghost-Cowl Fish (Ptychocephalus nebulosus) Habitat: Bathyal to abyssal seafloor, sponge grounds, thousands of meters deep Diet: Small crustaceans, worms, and drifting invertebrate larvae Defense: Camouflaging gelatinous hood, possible sacrificial tissue, chemical deterrent mucus Movement: Slow, low-energy, ambush-based rather than pursuit-based Eyes: Large, upward-tilted, tuned to faint bioluminescent light rather than detailed imaging Body composition: Roughly ninety-five percent water in its hood tissue, aiding buoyancy under extreme pressure Estimated lifespan: Potentially several decades, based on comparison with related cold-water deep-sea fish Conservation relevance: Possibly linked to fragile, slow-growing sponge ground ecosystems threatened by bottom trawling
How Does It Compare to Other Deep-Sea Fish?
To really appreciate how unusual the Ghost-Cowl Fish is, it helps to place it alongside some of the deep sea's other famous residents. The anglerfish, perhaps the most recognizable deep-sea predator, relies on a single glowing lure dangled in front of a mouth full of long, needle-like teeth, luring in prey with light rather than disguise. The blobfish, made famous for its droopy, gelatinous appearance, achieves a similar low-density, pressure-resistant body plan to the Ghost-Cowl Fish, but lacks any equivalent to the protective hood — its soft tissue is simply spread throughout the body rather than concentrated into a single defensive structure. The barreleye fish, with its transparent, fluid-filled dome covering tubular eyes that can swivel to look straight upward, shows that transparent, jelly-like tissue protecting sensitive organs is not unique to the Ghost-Cowl Fish, but rather a recurring solution that evolution has arrived at more than once in the deep sea.
What sets the Ghost-Cowl Fish apart is the sheer scale and multi-purpose nature of its hood. Where the barreleye's transparent dome protects only the eyes, and the blobfish's gelatinous body serves mainly for buoyancy, the Ghost-Cowl Fish's hood appears to combine buoyancy control, camouflage, physical defense, and possibly even a passive luring function into one single structure. In that sense, it may represent one of the most efficient examples of multi-purpose anatomy yet observed among deep-sea vertebrates — a single adaptation doing the work that other species split across several different body parts.
The Discovery Story
The clip that introduced the Ghost-Cowl Fish to researchers was captured by a deep-sea camera rig during a routine seafloor survey, the kind of unglamorous, methodical work that quietly makes up the vast majority of ocean exploration. Most such surveys record hours of empty sediment, the occasional sea cucumber, and long stretches of nothing in particular. It is precisely because so much of the deep seafloor looks alike — pale mud, scattered shell fragments, and the occasional sponge — that an animal like the Ghost-Cowl Fish, when it finally drifts into frame, stands out so dramatically.
According to those who reviewed the raw footage, the initial reaction was disbelief: the shape on screen looked so much like a stray jellyfish that had settled awkwardly over a fish head that several viewers assumed it was some sort of accident of camera angle or a chance encounter between two unrelated animals. Only on frame-by-frame review, watching the "jellyfish" hood flex in sync with the fish's own head movements, did observers realize they were looking at one integrated organism, not two animals overlapping by chance. That realization — footage shifting from accident to anatomy — is often how new deep-sea species first announce themselves: not through a dramatic chase, but through one quiet moment of stillness before a camera, followed by long scrutiny back in the lab.
Because only this one encounter exists so far, the Ghost-Cowl Fish remains formally undescribed. Before it can receive an official species name, researchers will need more sightings, ideally with a physical specimen or high-resolution video from multiple angles, plus tissue samples for genetic analysis. Until then, "Ghost-Cowl Fish" and its provisional Latin name remain useful but informal placeholders, not yet a permanent entry in the official catalogue of life.
Questions Still to Answer

Even with everything the footage reveals, the Ghost-Cowl Fish leaves behind far more questions than answers, and that is arguably the most exciting part of the discovery. Does the hood regenerate after being damaged or partially shed, and if so, how quickly? Does the animal produce any bioluminescence of its own, or does its faint glow in the footage come entirely from reflected light bouncing off wet, translucent tissue? Are there other individuals nearby, perhaps clustered together in loose colonies the way some sponge-ground specialists are known to do, or is this a solitary, widely dispersed species? Does its diet shift with age, the way many fish move from tiny plankton as juveniles to larger prey as adults? And perhaps most fundamentally: how closely is it related to any known family of fish, or does it represent something genuinely novel on the evolutionary tree?

Answering these lingering questions will likely take years of additional careful expeditions, each one adding a small, hard-won piece to the larger puzzle. Deep-sea research moves slowly and carefully by sheer necessity — submersible time is costly and dive windows are always short. But every new video clip, even one lasting only five seconds, adds real, truly lasting knowledge about life on this planet.

Closing Thoughts

The single, brief clip that introduced the world to the Ghost-Cowl Fish lasts only a few seconds, yet it captures an entire hidden universe of adaptation: a body built from fog and jelly, eyes tuned to catch the faintest glimmer in an eternal night, and a defense strategy built not on strength or speed but on patience, disguise, and the willingness to sacrifice a piece of oneself rather than lose everything. It is a small, strange animal sitting quietly on a bed of sponges at the bottom of the world, and yet it tells a very large story about how life persists in the most hostile environment on the planet. As deep-sea exploration technology continues to improve, researchers expect more encounters — and, eventually, the physical specimens and genetic samples needed to formally describe the Ghost-Cowl Fish and place it properly on the tree of life. Until then, it remains one of the ocean's most captivating open questions: a fish wearing its own ghost, drifting through the dark.

text:
The Disgraceful Witkoff-Kushner Circus

Support for Ukraine under President Trump remains more a matter of empty words than real military power.

As the war in Ukraine approaches its fifth year, any serious attempt to end the bloodshed should be welcomed. But there is an enormous difference between seeking peace and demanding that the victim surrender to the aggressor, writes The Daily Telegraph. Any attempt to force Kyiv into territorial concessions simply to appease Vladimir Putin would be a profound insult to Ukrainians who have sacrificed so much — and a dangerous invitation to a much larger war across Europe.

Putin is in trouble. The extraordinary spectacle of American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner apparently trying to offer him a helping hand should concern everyone. If this is merely an attempt to win Trump a few approval points ahead of the midterm elections, the whole enterprise looks shabby and dishonest. If there is a serious strategy behind it, it is remarkably difficult to see what it might be.

Consider the imbalance. Witkoff, Trump’s chief negotiator, has visited Moscow repeatedly but Kyiv only once, this Sunday. That can hardly be called balanced mediation — especially when the country receiving the warmer treatment is the one that invaded the other. In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner appeared almost awestruck by Putin, showering him with smiles, praise and goodwill. In Kyiv, by contrast, their embraces with Volodymyr Zelensky — a wartime leader who has spent almost four years fighting for his country’s survival — looked awkward.

The symbolism was obvious. Witkoff and Kushner flew directly to Moscow aboard Air Force Two. Zelensky guaranteed them safe passage into Ukraine, but because Russia continues attacking Ukrainian airspace, they could fly only as far as Poland and had to complete the journey by train.

Despite all the positive statements from Washington, little has actually changed. Putin continues to demand all of Donbas and recognition of territories illegally seized by Russia since 2014, including Crimea. Zelensky has made equally clear that surrendering sovereign Ukrainian territory to the Russian invader is an existential issue for his country. Frankly, it should be an existential issue for Europe as well.

Even Russian media seem to understand the reality: Trump needs a quick peace deal far more than Putin does. That is a fairly accurate assessment of the balance of leverage.

Russia’s strategy remains depressingly familiar. Moscow believes relentless attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilian population will eventually break Ukrainian morale. We saw the same methodology in Syria: strike civilians hard and often enough, and eventually they will demand that their own government surrender. Schools, hospitals and power stations become legitimate targets in the Russian lexicon because, in the Kremlin’s calculations, terror is a weapon of war.

At first glance, the picture looks bleak for Ukraine. But that is not the whole picture. Russia is increasingly struggling to protect its own cities, while in the drone war inside Russia itself Ukraine has achieved something approaching local air superiority. I am no air-power theorist, but having commanded armored forces, I know one fundamental truth: control of the air is one of the fastest routes to battlefield success.

Beyond the battlefield, Russia’s economy is in dire condition. Even Russian newspapers increasingly discuss poverty and economic hardship. The Kremlin can conceal casualties, censor bad news and manufacture propaganda, but it cannot indefinitely hide an economy struggling to sustain a war machine consuming enormous quantities of manpower and resources.

The Witkoff-Kushner circus therefore risks confirming what many increasingly fear: under President Trump, American support for Ukraine remains more empty rhetoric than real military power. If Washington will not change that, Europe must.

text:
I spent tokens getting this so I might as well post it.

The headline claim: the "preparedness plan"

This is real in the narrow sense that Jennice Vilhauer, a clinical psychologist who is a confirmed member of the UAP (Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena) Science Advisory Council, wrote on 3 September 2026 that at a 31 August meeting at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) the council "was informed that the United States government has a preparedness plan in place should the existence of nonhuman intelligence (NHI) be confirmed." The council itself is genuine: formed in June 2026, chaired by Avi Loeb, reporting to ODNI and a governance board, and covered by DefenseScoop and Scientific American. Loeb's chairmanship is therefore correctly stated.

But the chain stops there. Vilhauer names no official, quotes no document, and says explicitly "We were not given any details about the plan." There is no ODNI or All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) release, and no coverage in Reuters, AP, the New York Times or the Washington Post; the only outlets repeating it are UAP-community sites relaying her post. The piece does reproduce her caveat that a plan is not a confirmation, but it omits her admission that nothing about the plan's content, owner or trigger was disclosed. A contingency plan for a low-probability, high-consequence event is also exactly what one would expect a government to hold regardless of its beliefs, in the same way that it holds plans for asteroid impacts; its existence is weak evidence about the underlying probability. This is a single-witness, second-hand, undocumented account of a closed briefing, presented as an established fact.

The witnesses

David Grusch's July 2023 testimony is accurately summarised: he did say he was "informed" of a multi-decade crash-retrieval programme, did answer "non-human" to the biologics question, did cite "over 40 witnesses" across four years, and did claim retaliation. What the piece leaves out is the other half of the record. AARO's Historical Record Report of March 2024 concluded it "found no empirical evidence" for reverse-engineering claims and that the alleged programmes "either do not exist; are misidentified authentic, highly sensitive national security programs... or resolve to an unwarranted and disestablished program." Grusch's knowledge is entirely second-hand and no physical evidence has ever been produced. The Inspector General's "credible and urgent" finding concerns the complaint's procedural standing, not the truth of the allegations.

Luis Elizondo is described as "head of AATIP"; the Pentagon has twice formally stated he "had no assigned responsibilities for AATIP", and his 2024–2025 record includes several misidentifications of mundane objects. The quoted sentence about technologies "we are not capable of defending against" could not be located in any primary source; his verified 2022 remark that "this is probably not some sort of adversarial technology" points the other way. Rubio's quotation is a composite of genuine fragments from a June 2023 NewsNation interview, fair in substance. Trump's quotation is real (Impaulsive, June 2024) except for the number: the verified wording is "I've had actually meetings on it", and the "15" appears in no source. In the same interview he said "Am I a believer? No, I can't say I am," and in February 2026, "I don't know if they're real or not."

The Malmstrom 1967 episode is presented as documented fact. The declassified Air Force and Boeing engineering investigation attributed the Echo Flight shutdown to an electronic noise pulse in the logic coupler, a known hardware fault already scheduled for replacement; the flight commander does not endorse a UFO cause; Salas was underground and saw nothing himself. Hastings's "100+ cases" is his own self-compiled list from a self-published book, not a government tally. The argument that officials would not risk their reputations without cause is a costly-signal inference, but it only works if the cost is real and the alternative explanations (sincere but mistaken belief in second-hand accounts, career benefit within the disclosure community) are ruled out, and the piece does not attempt that.

The "consistency of experiencers" and Nolan's MRI work

The reasoning that consistency across cultures implies a shared external stimulus ignores the obvious rival mechanism: a shared cultural template propagated by mass media since 1947. Consistency is equally predicted by a common stimulus and by a common script, so it cannot discriminate between them. Garry Nolan's caudate–putamen finding has been described in interviews (Vice 2021, The Debrief) but no peer-reviewed paper reporting it could be found; he has claimed on X that two morphometry papers exist, which I could not locate. He himself has said that for some individuals "they had it before they had these incidents", which undermines the causal reading. The cohort was referred through intelligence contacts, not sampled. His genuine peer-reviewed work (the Ubatuba magnesium isotope paper, 2022; the Atacama skeleton genome paper, 2018) is on other topics, and the latter debunked an alien claim. The Vallée quotation about behaviour "too consistent to be hallucination" is unsourced, and the piece omits that Vallée has spent fifty years arguing against the extraterrestrial hypothesis in favour of a "control system" model.

The statistics

This is where the piece looks most rigorous and is in fact weakest. The "2023 statistical study" finding "1,588 more reported UFO sightings per country" for nuclear-armed states could not be found after some fifteen targeted searches; no paper, preprint or blog with that figure surfaced. The nearest real 2023 study, Medina, Brewer and Kirkpatrick in Scientific Reports, is a US county-level analysis of NUFORC reports against light pollution and sky visibility and contains no cross-country comparison. Until a source appears this figure should be treated as unsubstantiated.

The Palomar figures are correctly transcribed from Bruehl and Villarroel (Scientific Reports, October 2025): 107,875 candidate transients over 2,718 days from 1949 to 1957, transients on 18.5% of days following a nuclear test against 11.0% otherwise (a 68% relative increase, which I re-derived), and an 8.5% rise in transient counts per additional UAP report (exp(0.081) = 1.084). The piece rounds 107,875 to "106,000" and picks the day-after figure rather than the paper's headline ±1-day relative risk of 1.45 (95% confidence interval 1.10–1.90). What it omits is that the "transients" are automated detections of which only a small subset was manually confirmed, and that a critique by Watters, Knuth and colleagues (arXiv, January 2026, revised June 2026) finds the features cluster toward plate edges and corners in patterns characteristic of scanning defects, and that "the reported correlation between the timing of feature observations and nuclear tests becomes insignificant after properly normalizing by the relevant number of observation days" (the survey exposed plates on roughly 312 nights, not 2,718 days). Villarroel's group has posted a response. The finding is contested at the level of whether the objects exist, which is not mentioned. The UAP counts in that study are also themselves witness reports, so a correlation between them and plate features is between two noisy proxies, not between "UAP activity" and anything physical.

The "2040 ± 20" estimate is real but is one paper, not two. Szydagis's arXiv preprint (2410.12738) was published in Limina: The Journal of UAP Studies, not the Journal of Scientific Exploration, and Nolan is not an author. It is a Monte Carlo model of smartphone-camera adoption against assumed crash rates of 1, 10 or 100 per century; it answers "if crashes happen at rate r, when would a phone capture one?" and says nothing about whether r is greater than zero. Presenting a single conditional simulation as two independent quantitative analyses converging on the same date is the piece's most misleading move.

The claimed "ASI era" increase in UAP activity has no cited data at all. AARO's own new-report counts are 274 (FY2023, eight months), 485 (FY2024, thirteen months) and 284 (FY2025, twelve months): a rise partly attributed to a new Federal Aviation Administration reporting channel, followed by a fall. There is no monotonic surge, and no mechanism is offered by which non-human observers would respond to large language models.

Verdict

As a piece of persuasion the essay is skilfully built: it borrows the vocabulary of calibration ("not a believer, not a skeptic", "correlation not causation") while stacking claims so that each rests on the credibility of the last. As evidence it fails on every layer the citation-verification pipeline checks. The primary sources exist for the Vilhauer post, Grusch, Rubio, Trump, Loeb and the Palomar and Szydagis papers; they are misdescribed in the Trump number, the Nolan publication status, the Elizondo role, the two-papers claim and the journal name; they do not support the strong readings placed on them; and the essay systematically omits the official and peer-reviewed counter-evidence (AARO 2024, the Air Force Malmstrom investigation, Watters et al. 2026, Trump's disclaimers, Vilhauer's own "no details"). One figure (1,588) could not be traced at all. The sections addressed to investors and parents convert this into calls to action that the evidence does not warrant.

What I could not verify: whether Nolan's two claimed morphometry papers exist; the exact provenance of the Elizondo and Vallée quotations; and whether the Watters critique of the observation-day normalisation applies to the Scientific Reports nuclear paper or only to the companion PASP "aligned transients" paper, since the press coverage conflates them.

Then, after walking around Capitol Hill all day long, and even attending some of the J5 protest events, POI2 ducked back into the same alley for a few minutes — after dark — before returning to the Metro South station across the street from the RNC. He returned to Falls Church via the train, where POI3 picked him up by car, and they went back to POI3’s home.
