text:
Cruelty

The following scene is a dramatization — but every physical detail in it is drawn from sworn testimony you’ll read a few paragraphs down.

The leather strap came across her back hard. Her screams filled the small room, echoing off the walls, but the blows did not stop. The searing sting from the first strike was replaced almost immediately with a subsequent strike, tearing her soft flesh. A trickle of blood appeared, but this wasn’t enough to stop the assault upon her. A last, frenzied strike made her legs wobble. She fell forward onto the floor. Her screams had been replaced by wracking sobs and her pitiful voice begging for her assailant to stop.

While shaking uncontrollably in pain and shame, only then was she allowed to put her clothing back on. Her assailant left her in the room alone. Shaking and in pain, she gingerly slipped her clothing back onto her small, battered body, careful not to cause any more injury to her split flesh. She’d have liked to have attended to the injury, but she didn’t want to incur any more wrath. Better to just deal with it later.

In 1780, Mary Rogers, a widow, was given charge of an abandoned Pequot girl named Hannah Ocuish. Rogers, a strict adherent of a fringe religious sect called the Rogerines, routinely whipped little Hannah, calling her a “devil-child.” Whipping Hannah was, in Mary Rogers’ opinion, the only way to chase the devil out of her.

The whippings were so constant and severe that after little Hannah was arrested for the murder of a neighbor girl, Eunice Bolles, Mary Rogers was facing possible indictment herself as a co-defendant due to her abuse of the little girl. Nearly everyone in New London who knew of Hannah, knew of her abuse by the Widow Rogers. It wasn’t a well-kept secret. In the end, the stern arm of justice fell solely on Hannah, and she alone was executed for the murder. The mitigating factors were regarded as irrelevant.

We look upon the abuse of a child as described above and shake our head. How could anyone be so cruel? What is to be gained by crushing a child’s spirit in such a manner? Wouldn’t they understand that a beaten child might lash out themselves, and do so to someone even weaker than they?

We pride ourselves on the fact that we’ve “evolved” over the centuries — that we wouldn’t do such a horrific thing to an abused girl. Yes, she took a life, but couldn’t it be argued that her life had also been taken from her? Abandoned. Abused. Neglected and unwanted. Where else is a child supposed to go?

Here’s the reveal: the account of the abused girl that opened this article was not an accounting of Hannah Ocuish’s abuse by Mary Rogers. It could have been. I researched Hannah’s life over seven years and hold a copy of an original document containing a deposition list with the names of Mary Rogers, as well as those of four of her seven children, leading up to Hannah’s murder trial. Mary Rogers was very much in danger of standing upon that gallows alongside Hannah, but the court opted not to go that far.

No — the account above belongs to Christa Gail Pike. She is, as of this writing, still alive, but sits awaiting execution at the hand of Tennessee Governor William Byron Lee.

Here is the relevant passage from her 2010 appeal:

Mr. Pike stated that he would use either his hand or a belt to discipline the Petitioner. At most, he struck her with the belt three or four times in the same day. Mr. Pike denied that he ever made the Petitioner remove her clothing for the spankings and stated that any scars on the Petitioner’s back were not the result of any spankings he gave her. (Page 25 of her appeal.)

What is telling is that Emil Glenn Pike, Christa’s father, offers information not asked. Why would he point out that he didn’t require his daughter — 12 years old at the time — to remove her clothing before he took a belt to her?

And how, exactly, would a father know his 11- or 12-year-old daughter, a girl entering puberty, had scars on her back from whippings? In some households, modesty might not be an issue, but Christa didn’t enjoy a normal household situation. Her home life was sexualized and abusive. Her parents divorced twice. The second time they divorced, Christa was still very young. She had no real agency.

Christa was shuttled between her father’s house and her mother’s. Glenn Pike remarried, and his new wife didn’t like Christa, later accusing her of abusing her daughter.

Again from Christa’s appeal:

Mr. Pike testified that he later married Kathleen Almond and that they had two children together. He confirmed that there had been an allegation that the Petitioner had sexually abused his younger daughter. Mr. Pike stated that his wife had told the therapist she was seeing that his younger daughter had reported that the Petitioner had “licked her” and had pointed “towards her belly or towards her genitals and said, ‘There?’“ The therapist told Mr. Pike’s wife that the Petitioner was not to be around the younger daughter. The Petitioner denied any wrongdoing, and Mr. Pike stated that he had never observed any inappropriate behavior between the Petitioner and his other children. He stated that he did not believe the Petitioner had molested his younger daughter.

Children often will engage in versions of “show me” with other children, but sexualization is learned behavior. Christa was first molested at age two by her grandmother’s boyfriend. She suffered subsequent sexual abuse by her mother’s various boyfriends. Based upon Glenn Pike’s need to clarify he had never whipped his daughter while she was naked, one is only left to contemplate the worst.

Glenn Pike removed his daughter from his household in West Virginia, depositing Christa at her mother’s in North Carolina. All of this happened shortly after Christa’s beloved grandmother, the only real stable force in her life, died of cancer. Christa once again found herself abandoned and neglected. There is no record of Christa ever having had therapy for her sexual or physical abuse.

Both Hannah Ocuish and Christa Pike suffered from Fetal Alcohol Syndrome. While Christa was officially diagnosed, Hannah’s is speculative. Obviously, Colonial New England had no understanding of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome, but it can be inferred from her behavior and the observations made by others.

Hannah was described as having a mental deficiency. She had difficulty with concentration, impulse control, acting out unnaturally or expressing indifference in situations that most would expect some sort of normal reaction. She was called a devil child and a feral savage, due to her sometimes explosive temper. These are all markers of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome. Hannah’s mother was a known drunk.

Likewise for Christa. She suffered seizures as an infant and toddler due to the effects of FAS. Her mother was a heavy drinker all throughout her pregnancy. Christa was described by those around her as a “fireball.” Judge Mary Beth Leibowitz was irritated that Christa seemed unconcerned throughout her murder trial, even flirting with reporters. Hannah was similarly observed acting the same way during her October 1786 trial. Again, hallmarks of FAS.

It could be understood that Judge Richard Law would have had no idea why Hannah reacted with such indifference at her trial, even knowing that conviction meant the death penalty. That Mary Beth Leibowitz was similarly ignorant of the effects of FAS is stunning, and one would think such a dearth of basic medical knowledge by a judge in a capital murder case would warrant a dismissal of the charges, and even judicial review.

However, none of that happened. The subsequent appeals were hampered by legal procedure rather than facts. Strickland v. Washington (1984) set the standard federal courts use to evaluate claims that a defendant’s trial counsel was constitutionally ineffective — requiring a petitioner to prove not just that counsel’s performance was deficient, but that the deficiency changed the outcome of the trial. It’s a brutal standard to clear, and combined with procedural rules that limit what new evidence can be introduced on appeal, it meant that mitigating facts about Christa’s life and diagnosis that weren’t fully developed at her original 1996 trial had little path back into the record.

Leibowitz, who had presided over the original conviction, was the same judge reviewing her own prior ruling on Christa’s 2010 appeal — a conflict of interest built into the process itself, whatever her personal intentions. And so the conviction stood as originally rendered.

Cruelty.

Here is a definition from the American Heritage Dictionary, 5th Edition:

1. Something, such as a cruel act or remark, that causes pain or suffering.

2. The intentional infliction of physical or mental distress, especially when considered as a basis for granting a divorce.

3. The attribute or quality of being cruel; a disposition to give unnecessary pain or suffering to others; inhumanity; barbarity.

Christa Pike murdered Colleen Slemmer on the night of January 12th, 1995, in a wooded park not far from the Holiday Inn motel that acted as their dormitory while they attended courses through the Knoxville, Tennessee Job Corps program.

Christa’s reasoning was simple. She believed Colleen wanted to steal her boyfriend, 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp. She didn’t, but to Christa, that wasn’t even close to being a good enough reason. Again, victims of FAS do not process information the way you and I do. We would have seen Christa’s fixation on Colleen as silly. After all, it started because Colleen merely waved to Tadaryl in the hallway of the dorms and said hi to him. But Christa witnessed this exchange and flagged it as an existential threat. Once again, someone was trying to take from her what little she had. She needed Tadaryl. Losing him wasn’t an option. The threat had to be eliminated.

Here is another fact: Christa could not have murdered Colleen on her own. She lacked the strength and ability. Colleen was taller and faster. One on one, Colleen, despite Christa’s explosive behavior, would have emerged alive. Perhaps bruised, but alive. Christa needed muscle. She enlisted Tadaryl and another friend, Shadolla Peterson — three against one.

When Colleen did break free from the assault, it was Tadaryl who chased her down, tackled her, and dragged her back to be beaten and stabbed to death.

All three were caught the next day. There was no effort to hide the crime. Christa bragged to certain friends, showing them a piece of Colleen’s skull. The three were arrested and charged with first-degree murder. This is where it went awry for Christa.

Shadolla Peterson, who acted as a lookout and had no physical role in Colleen’s murder, testified for the prosecution and wound up being given probation. Tadaryl Shipp, though he actively participated in Colleen’s murder, was only 17 at the time of the crime. He was given life with the possibility of parole after 25 years.

The hammer fell hardest on Christa. Her attorney, William Talman, turned down a plea deal that would have spared her a death sentence for life in prison — without telling her. Kelly Gleason, Christa’s post-conviction attorney, has said publicly, on the 2025 podcast Unrestorable, that Talman never told Christa about the rejected plea deal, and that Talman has since acknowledged this and expressed regret. Gleason has also stated that Talman pursued the rights to Christa’s story; a trial, rather than a quiet plea, made for a more marketable narrative. That Mary Beth Leibowitz didn’t remove him and refer him to the DA for prosecution is a wonder to me.

But the things that buried Christa were multi-fold. First, she took a piece of Colleen’s skull. Second, the murder happened at the height of the “Satanic Panic” era. The prosecution called a supposed expert on occult behavior, a man who took a one-day course on Satanism, and testified with conclusions that have since been thoroughly debunked. Lastly and most crucially, Christa was 18 years old. That meant the electric chair for her.

I am not excusing what Christa Pike did to Colleen Slemmer. I am not advocating for Christa’s release from prison. At this point, she would be lost on the outside. She’s had no real therapy for any of the trauma she suffered as a child; she has barely been cared for with respect to her medical maladies. She went years being misdiagnosed and given drugs that caused severe behavioral issues. On top of that, she is the only woman on death row in Tennessee. Male inmates can mix with one another. They aren’t alone. Christa, being a woman, had no one. She was held in virtual solitary for more than 25 years. She had to sue to get any contact.

Imagine being locked up 23 hours a day for 25 years. Most people couldn’t last 25 days.

Christa has all but exhausted her appeals. On September 30th, 2026, she will be strapped down to a gurney, and they will violate her body with an IV line. They will then pump pentobarbital into her veins, which will stop her heart. This, they will assert, is justice.

But is it? Thirty-one years of being less than human. Thirty-one years of being little more than regarded as the walking dead. Thirty-one years of trying to understand a justice system that allows killers like Dennis Rader (the BTK Killer), Gary Ridgway (the Green River Killer), Richard Allen Davis (killer of Polly Klaas), Richard Ramirez (the Night Stalker), and Jeffrey Dahmer (the Milwaukee Cannibal Killer), and many more, to live out their lives. Both Ramirez and Dahmer died in prison — Ramirez died of lymphoma in 2013, while Dahmer was beaten to death by two fellow inmates in the shower in 1994.

Christa’s only real hope lies with Governor Bill Lee. While Lee would have you believe otherwise, he does have the absolute power to commute Christa’s death sentence. The question is, will he?

In his two terms in office, Bill Lee has not ever commuted a death sentence. He has killed — and I say that because it is absolutely true — eight human beings. He attempted to kill nine, but Tony Carruthers’s execution was botched. Lee opted to grant him a one-year reprieve, leaving his fate to the subsequent governor.

The recent execution of Darrell Hines shows Lee’s lack of humanity. Hines, 66 years old and unable to walk, was already in poor health. Without being executed, it was likely that death would find him shortly in any event. Lee didn’t want to wait. This is not anything new for Lee. His fourth victim was a man who was legally blind. Nicholas Todd Sutton opted to be executed by the electric chair — a method he was entitled to use but was no longer the standard method since 2000. His hand had to be guided by his attorney to sign the waiver form to be put to death by electrocution rather than lethal injection.

Cruelty.

In the indifferent manner Bill Lee has carried out these nine executions, it is evident he had to “other” those whose lives have been entrusted to him by the God he claims to worship. To authorize nine executions without once exercising clemency requires a degree of moral distance that I struggle to reconcile with Christ’s command to love one’s neighbor. His religious teachings are largely responsible for this view.

Bill Lee, like myself, was raised in the Southern Baptist tradition and today identifies as a non-denominational evangelical Christian. I know this world because I came from it. For years, I accepted many of the same assumptions about civil authority, justice, and punishment.

Meet Tom F.!

Tom's grandfather was a railroader, and Tom got his start in the industry thanks in part to Todd at North Shore Railroads (watch our profile -- we're talking more about that later).

As an engineer and conductor at Winchester & Western Railroad, Tom is part of a team that serves 15 customers over 53 miles of track. That smaller footprint means Tom spends a lot of time interacting with customers. He sees the direct impact his railroad has on the community, especially when major (rail-served) industries come to town, bringing with them jobs and opportunity.

Working at the Winchester & Western offers Tom the best of many worlds. He's been able to settle in Virginia, enjoys a good work-life balance and is part of a small, tightly knit team that enjoys working together.

And, when he's out moving from customer to customer, Tom loves seeing kids watching as they pass. Their sense of wonder reminds him of the not-too-distant past, when he was a kid, standing outside, watching in awe as a big freight train passed by.

Thank you, Tom, for being one of our amazing #FacesofFreight!

"A democracy cannot exist as a permanent form of government. It can only exist until the voters discover that they can vote themselves largesse from the public treasury. For those who want to see our country last longer than the average empire, we want elected leaders who understand the above principle and will help prevent us from falling in to the same pitfall that undid all of the previous empires.

text:
CHAPTER 8

1861–1865 — Poles in the American Civil War

An estimated 4,000–5,000 Poles fought for the Union, while roughly 1,000–1,500 fought for the Confederacy.

Among the best-known Polish commanders was Włodzimierz Krzyżanowski, who organized the Polish Legion and later became a Union general. Polish immigrants and political exiles joined the Union cause for different reasons, including opposition to slavery, support for the Union, and their own traditions of fighting for national freedom.

The Union victory in 1865 led to the abolition of slavery in the United States through the 13th Amendment.

For Poles who had experienced the loss of their own state, the American Civil War offered another struggle in which the ideas of freedom, national unity and human liberty were at stake.

Fellow-citizens,
A man may speak his hatred of Zion, of Israel, of the Jew, from the housetop and the printing-press, and the law will not gag him. That is liberty of speech.
But when he opens a house of public entertainment — a coffee-house, an inn, a shop — and says to a father and a child, “You wear the star of David; you are a Jew; get out,” he has left the field of speech and entered the field of exclusion. He has made a public place a private ghetto. That is not liberty. That is a license to unmake the common right of every man to buy his bread where it is offered for sale.
We did not fight a great war that one class of citizens should be turned from the door because of the God they worship or the nation from which they sprang. A house divided against itself cannot stand; neither can a republic in which the public table is open to all except the Jew.
Let the man print his “Iced Intifada.” Let him name his drink after a murderer. The Constitution will bear it. It will not bear the turning out of a child because his father’s cap is a Jewish star.
Freedom is not the right of the strong to shut the door. Freedom is the law that keeps the door open.
A. Lincoln

Some ads hit.
Some die.

But you’re probably not magically 2-3xing ROAS just by making more creatives (I assume you guys the best at this 🧙🏻‍♂️)

The bigger lever is where you send the traffic.

Think of creatives like ducks in a bath lol.

Raise the water level = all the ducks rise with it.

Same thing here.

Better funnel performance raises the average performance of the creatives you’re already running.

I’d break it down like this:

D tier = donating money to Zuck
C tier = breakeven
B tier = finding winning pages + running your first real tests
A tier = multiple angled LPs, listicles, offers, constant testing, actual scaling

If you’re in D tier, you can have good creatives and still get absolutely cooked.

- Improve CVR.
- Build better angled LPs.
- Test different funnel formats.
- Test offers.

Suddenly the exact same traffic becomes way more valuable.

Which means you can effectively scale.

Pretty simple.

And no, brands like RYZE or Lemme aren’t building 20 completely new funnels every week.

They treat funnels like different kind of creatives.

But the idea is pretty similar

We talk nonstop about creative testing.

Probably need to talk way more about funnel testing too.

Fix your funnels.

My deepest sympathies and condolences are with the families who have lost their loved ones in the tragic incident in Delhi. No family should ever have to endure such unimaginable pain. But at the same time, one cannot help but ask: why does our system wake up only after lives are lost?

We have seen political leaders, senior bureaucrats and prominent media houses rushing to the site of the tragedy. Statements will be made, visits will happen, officials may be suspended, compensation may be announced, and there will be the usual rounds of rona-dhona before the cameras. But the question remains will any of this bring back the lives that have been lost?

Are we waiting for the same tragedy to happen in the Genocide Survivors' Camps in Jammu, where thousands of displaced Kashmiri Pandits continue to live in ageing and unsafe structures?

Yes, the Government has approved funds for repair and renovation of these camps, and that is certainly welcome. But repair on paper is not enough. These buildings need urgent structural assessment, comprehensive rehabilitation and, wherever necessary, reconstruction. They cannot be treated merely as old structures requiring cosmetic repairs when human lives are at stake.

I sincerely hope that the Union Home Minister, the Chief Minister, the Lieutenant Governor, the Chief Secretary and the concerned authorities do not wait for a building to collapse and innocent lives to be lost before visiting these camps and taking action. Please don't wait for a tragedy to create headlines.

The genocide survivors have already lost their homes, their homeland and decades of their lives to displacement. They should not be made to live with the additional fear that the very roof over their heads could become a death trap.

Government action should be preventive, not reactive.

Because once a tragedy happens, suspending officials, announcing compensation and expressing grief before television cameras serves very little purpose. A life saved before the tragedy is worth far more than a condolence offered after it. The Government must act now before we are forced to mourn another avoidable tragedy.

DEVELOP A SPIRIT OF THANKSGIVING

I will praise You, O Lord my God, with all my heart,
and I will glorify Your name forever.
For great is Your love toward me,
and You have delivered my soul
from the depths of the grave.
(Psalm 86:12–13)

Through Jesus, I will continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise,
that is, the fruit of lips that give thanks to His name.
(Hebrews 13:15)

A grandmother is on the beach with her only grandson. As she watches him playing in the surf, a huge wave comes up and carries him away. In a panic, she desperately pleads to God for his return: “Take me instead—he’s my whole life, my only reason for living. Do anything—just save him!” Miraculously, a second huge wave appears and deposits the child at her feet unharmed. She inspects him briefly, raises her hands toward heaven and loudly proclaims, “He had a hat!”

Nothing ages more quickly than gratitude. As we take the many blessings of our lives for granted, the grace of God degenerates into entitlement. As my friend Ed Dudley used to put it, if we were born on third base, we wake up believing we just hit a triple.

If we are wise, we will not leave gratitude to spontaneous moments, but cultivate a spirit of thanksgiving for all God has done in our past (Deuteronomy 8:2–3, 11–18), contentment with what He is doing in our present (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18), and joyful hope for what He has promised for our future in Christ.  (1 Peter 1:3–4; 5:10).

text:
@AwakenWithJP this is not accurate. Lindsay Clancy did not confess quilt. Why do many make the assumption she did? Why is Reddington’s 2 pleas for bifurcation being largely ignored?

Grok: “**Lindsay Clancy pleaded not guilty and did not give a formal written or recorded confession introduced as such at trial.** The defense has never treated the killings as a contested “who did it” issue, which is why many people treat her as having admitted guilt.

Her lawyers do not dispute that she caused the deaths of Cora, Dawson, and Callan. They offered a written stipulation conceding her involvement so the case could focus on the only live question they wanted the jury to decide: whether the Commonwealth could prove she was *criminally responsible* under Massachusetts law (the *McHoul* standard—whether a mental disease or defect left her substantially unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of her conduct or conform it to the law). She never took the stand. Jurors instead heard second-hand accounts of what she later told her then-husband, psychologists, and others about a male voice and the events of January 24, 2023.

That combination produces the widespread assumption. Media coverage and public discussion routinely collapse “defense does not contest the act” into “she admitted she killed them” or “she confessed.” In an insanity/lack-of-criminal-responsibility case the defense *must* effectively concede the physical acts to reach the mental-state issue; otherwise the defendant cannot raise the defense without undercutting it. People hearing only the shorthand version reasonably (if imprecisely) treat that as a confession of guilt. The graphic details of the deaths, the 911 call, and the focus on postpartum psychosis versus calculated planning further reinforce the impression that the “did she do it?” question was already settled.

### The two bifurcation requests

Kevin Reddington asked the court twice to separate the issues:

- First motion (filed February 2026): Split the trial into a guilt phase (did she commit the killings?) followed by a criminal-responsibility phase. Judge William Sullivan denied it on March 30 / April 3. He found the issues overlapping, the evidence impossible to cleanly divide, testimony likely duplicative, and a single trial more efficient and less confusing for the jury. There was no other defense besides lack of criminal responsibility.
- Motion for reconsideration (April 2026): The defense offered a formal written stipulation to her involvement in the deaths so the first phase could be skipped or collapsed and the trial limited to criminal responsibility. Sullivan denied reconsideration on April 22/26 for the same reasons—overlapping evidence, lengthy expert testimony that would be repeated, and no gain in judicial economy. Prosecutors also refused the stipulation; they wanted to present their full theory of premeditation, planning, and extreme atrocity.

These rulings received relatively little sustained public attention because they were pretrial procedural decisions. Coverage and online discussion centered on the human tragedy, postpartum mental health, competing expert diagnoses, and later the 11-1 deadlock and mistrial. Once the judge refused to restructure the case, the trial simply proceeded as a conventional single-phase proceeding in which the act itself was treated as essentially uncontested. That framing stuck.

Bifurcation of this kind is uncommon in Massachusetts murder cases. The court treated the act and the mental state as too intertwined (sending her husband out, the method used, later statements, medical records) to separate cleanly without repeating large amounts of evidence. The result is the situation the question describes: no formal confession of *guilt*, a practical concession of the *acts*, two rejected attempts to isolate the responsibility question, and a public conversation that often treats those distinctions as already resolved.”

text:
🚨A Hood County, Texas, constable personally disconnected and bagged every automated license plate reader the county itself operated. 

The step was not a rogue protest. County leaders had already approved it.

On August 11, the Hood County Commissioners Court voted unanimously to cover and power down the three county-controlled Flock Safety cameras until the company retrieved its hardware. 

Precinct 2 Constable John D. Shirley then carried out that order. He later shared photos of the covered units and wrote that privacy is not optional and that mass surveillance is not how the county does business. He also told Flock Safety Systems to come collect its equipment.

The physical shutdown followed an earlier vote to cancel the county’s contract with Flock. Officials pointed to privacy worries and what they called the company’s failure to meet its contractual duties. 

The county is seeking a $126,000 refund and reportedly declined Flock’s offer of account credit instead.

Flock’s readers photograph vehicles as they pass and log license plates, vehicle traits, location, and time.

Partner agencies can search those records during investigations. 

Supporters say the systems help recover stolen cars, find missing people, and identify suspects. 

Critics say large, linked networks can map ordinary travel without individualized suspicion or a warrant.

The county’s action covers only its three cameras in unincorporated areas. Granbury, a separate city inside Hood County, still runs its own Flock cameras.

Shirley’s photos made the decision look dramatic. The larger fight—over whether these networks belong in local law enforcement at all—is still unfolding well beyond Hood County.

❓How are officials where you live navigating the Flock debate: public safety, or warrantless tracking?

“I sneaked into Messi’s dad’s hotel about four years ago in Barcelona for a meeting with him. Obviously, at that point, we weren’t ready to bring him and he wasn’t ready to come.

But I turned around to his dad and said: ‘We want your son. We want him to come to Miami when he’s ready.’

His dad had called us that week and said: ‘Leo’s going to make an announcement.’

text:
Russia Slams Deployment of Long-Range US Missile Launcher to Norway

@LibertarianInst 

The US has moved a launcher into Norway capable of firing Tomahawk missiles. The deployment drew a strong rebuke from Moscow.

“A US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III delivers a US Navy Containerized Launching System (CLS) to Trondheim, Norway, Aug. 27, 2026, to participate in Operation Atlantic City 26,” a Department of War statement published on Tuesday explained.

The CLS is a containerized derivative of the Mk-41 vertical launch system and is capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles

On Monday, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova slammed the CLS deployment. “We regard the deployment in Europe of US systems capable of launching intermediate- and shorter-range missiles as yet another step in the never-ending series of highly destabilizing actions by NATO countries,” she said. “Thus, these missile systems can be used in aggressive actions by NATO countries against our country to solve strategic problems.”

Zakharova went on to warn that the CLS deployment would interfere with any US and Russian talks on new nuclear weapons agreements and would be factored into future deterrence planning in Moscow. “Steps such as the deployment in Europe of US ground-based intermediate- and shorter-range missile systems that threaten Russia will, to put it mildly, ‘zero out’ the prerequisites for constructive talks with the US on strategic issues,” she added.

Since the end of the Cold War, Washington has withdrawn from several major arms control agreements with Moscow . President George W Bush withdrew from the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty, while President Donald Trump voided the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) treaty and the Open Skies pact.

Additionally, New START expired in February after Trump declined Russia’s offer to continue observing the treaty’s limits for another year. Trump has called for replacing New START with a new agreement that includes China.

The issues between Russia and Norway are not limited to the CLS  deployment. Norway seized a Russian ship in the Arctic after a court ruled that it should be used to compensate Ukraine.

The ship was seized while docked in Barentsburg on Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, where Russia maintains a longstanding presence centered around a state-owned coal mining operation.

text:
Israel has broken the taboo. President @Abdirahmanirro is now in Washington. From Berbera and the Abraham Accords to China, the Houthis, Congress and American investment, a rare convergence of strategic forces has brought Somaliland closer to possible U.S. recognition than at any time in its post-1991 history.

The President of the Republic of #Somaliland, H.E. Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro arrived in Washington on September 5 with a senior delegation for his first U.S. working visit since taking office for a diplomatic mission that centers on diplomatic relations, security and economic cooperation, investment and international support for recognition.

The timing is exceptional. Israel’s December 2025 recognition of Somaliland removed a three-decade international taboo and reshaped geopolitical dynamics along the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

Washington has heard that case for many and is well aware of Somaliland’s historical, legal, political and geopolitical case.years. The decisive task for president Irro is to persuade the Trump administration that recognition would advance identifiable #US interests strongly enough to justify departing from the longstanding policy of treating Somaliland within Somalia’s internationally recognized borders.

For the Trump White House, the strongest case is likely to be transactional and strategic. Somaliland must be presented not as a diplomatic burden requiring American generosity, but as a partner offering access, geography, security cooperation, commercial opportunity and political alignment in a highly contested maritime theater.

Senator Ted Cruz has already supplied much of this framework. In an August 2025 letter to Trump, Cruz urged formal recognition and highlighted Somaliland’s position on the Gulf of Aden, counterterrorism role, ties with Taiwan, support for Israel and the Abraham Accords, openness to a U.S. military presence, and potential critical-minerals cooperation. This is not about a senator who supports recognition. This is a significant argument translated into the language of American national security.

Berbera is Somaliland’s most important strategic card. But geography alone does not produce recognition. The delegation’s task is to turn Berbera from a point on a map into an operational proposition: maritime surveillance, logistics, contingency access, counterterrorism cooperation, search and rescue, intelligence sharing, aviation support and redundancy for U.S. operations around the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

If the Pentagon looks at Berbera only as useful, recognition can remain optional. If American defense planners conclude that a structured relationship with Somaliland materially improves force protection, maritime awareness or operational flexibility, the diplomatic calculus changes. Recognition then becomes connected to a security requirement rather than a symbolic political request.

The most important new security development may be the reported deepening relationship between Yemen’s Houthis and Al-Shabaab. A September 2026 Wall Street Journal investigation described weapons transfers, training, direct exchanges and efforts to expand maritime monitoring. The report cited U.S. military intelligence and other officials and said at least 100 Al-Shabaab fighters had traveled to Yemen for training.

This is a wake up call for Washington which historically treated Al-Shabab and the Houthis as separate geographical theaters. Yemen lies across the Gulf of Aden from Somaliland; Al-Shabaab operates in Somalia; global shipping passes through the Bab el-Mandeb corridor. If U.S. planners begin to see a single cross-Gulf security system involving drones, weapons smuggling, radar, militant training and maritime surveillance, Somaliland’s location becomes more valuable now.

A further escalation—especially credible evidence of advanced Houthi systems being transferred to Al-Shabaab or of coordinated attempts to threaten shipping—could become a recognition accelerator. It would sharpen the question of whether Washington can afford to leave a comparatively stable and strategically located Somaliland outside its formal security architecture.

Israel’s recognition did more than create a new bilateral relationship. It demonstrated that a state could recognize Somaliland and absorb the diplomatic backlash. It also gave Hargeisa an ally with direct access to Trump and to influential American political networks.

The Washington Institute has argued that Israel’s move creates new Red Sea dynamics and could encourage other governments, including the United States, to reconsider their positions. The strategic logic is straightforward: Israel sees the Red Sea and the approaches to Bab el-Mandeb as a national security theater increasingly shaped by the Houthis and Iran.

For Somaliland, the next diplomatic step is to convert Israeli recognition into coalition-building. If Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or other senior Israeli officials actively encourage Washington to follow, the political cost of recognition falls while its security rationale becomes easier to explain inside the Trump administration.

Recognition becomes more politically attractive if it can be packaged as part of a larger Trump foreign-policy achievement. Somaliland’s declared intention to join the Abraham Accords provides exactly such a vehicle. The Knesset’s June 2026 account explicitly records Irro’s commitment to join the framework.

Instead of presenting recognition as a technical reversal of Somalia policy, the White House could present it as part of an expanded peace, security and commercial architecture linking a Muslim-majority Somaliland with Israel and American partners around the Red Sea. That would give Trump something presidents value: a recognizable diplomatic event with a clear claim of authorship.

No publicly available source has yet confirmed an Oval Office meeting. But if one occurs, it could become the most consequential event of the visit because presidential recognition is ultimately an executive foreign-policy decision.

Therefore, President Irro’s strongest presentation should be short, concise and upto the point: Somaliland is stable; it controls strategic infrastructure; it is prepared to cooperate with the United States; it has aligned with Israel and Taiwan despite political pressure; and it seeks investment rather than permanent dependency. The Somaliland Recognition Case should support that argument, not overwhelm it.

Congressional support has moved beyond informal sympathy. H.R. 3992, the Republic of Somaliland Independence Act, was introduced in the 119th Congress to recognize Somaliland as a separate independent country. Senator Cruz has separately urged Trump to act.

Such measures short of immediate recognition are helpful and can make a big difference: Separate reporting requirements, direct security cooperation, a representative office in Hargeisa, Berbera feasibility studies, differentiated travel guidance or distinct commercial treatment are progressively institutionalizing the reality on the ground that Washington already deals with Somaliland differently from Somalia.

That incremental separation is already creating a contradiction in the US policy of “One Somalia” doctrine: if the United States treats Somaliland as a separate partner across security, trade, diplomacy and investment, why preserve a formal policy that denies the political reality underlying those relationships?

Somaliland’s relationship with Taiwan is not a side issue. It is evidence that Somaliland has accepted political costs in order to maintain a relationship opposed by China. Cruz’s recognition letter specifically cited Chinese coercion against Somaliland because of its Taiwan ties.

For China hawks in Washington, recognition can therefore be framed as support for a government that resisted Beijing rather than accommodated it. Berbera also offers strategic diversification in a region where China already maintains a military base in Djibouti.

Somaliland has promoted its mineral potential, and U.S. officials have shown increasing interest in supply-chain security. But this is an area where exaggeration would be damaging. Geological claims must be supported by credible surveys, commercial grades, licensing rules, infrastructure plans and transparent investment protections.

The same applies to hydrocarbons. Oil and gas potential can attract attention, but prospective geology is not equivalent to a bankable commercial discovery. The delegation will gain more credibility by presenting verified opportunities and clearly identifying what potentially remains exploratory.

#Israel broke the international taboo. An African government could break the continental one. Ethiopia remains the most consequential candidate because of its geography, security weight and long relationship with Somaliland. Somaliland’s Washington campaign therefore cannot be separated from its diplomacy with Ethiopia and other African capitals.

Opponents will portray recognition as encouragement for separatism across Africa. Somaliland’s response should emphasize the specificity of its history. The U.S. State Department’s own historical record states that the former British protectorate of Somaliland became independent on June 26, 1960, before joining the former Italian-administered territory in the Somali Republic on July 1. U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian A contemporaneous State Department historical note likewise records Somaliland’s June 26 independence.

This does not by itself settle the modern recognition question. It does, however, give Somaliland a distinctive legal and historical argument: Hargeisa can frame its claim as restoration of a previously independent territorial unit rather than the arbitrary creation of a new border.

Somaliland’s electoral record is strategically useful because it distinguishes Hargeisa from much of the surrounding region. The peaceful 2024 transfer of presidential power strengthened the argument that, unlike many African states, Somaliland’s institutions can survive political handover of power to the opposition.

@realDonaldTrump may place greater emphasis on security and transactions than on democracy promotion, but Congress, State Department professionals, think tanks, human rights watch groups, and potential investors will still assess institutional durability. Democratic continuity therefore remains part of the coalition-building case for recognition.

Republican sponsorship is indispensable under a Trump administration, but recognition will be more durable if Somaliland avoids becoming a partisan project. Irro’s delegation should cultivate Democrats as well as Republicans and present Somaliland through several overlapping frames: Red Sea security, democratic self-government, China competition, commercial opportunity, counterterrorism and regional stability.

A bipartisan foundation would also reduce the risk that recognition—or the policies leading toward it—becomes vulnerable to the next change of administration.

Recognition decisions rarely occur because every argument is resolved. They usually require a catalytic event that allows a president to act. For Somaliland, the most plausible triggers include a successful Trump–Irro meeting; a Pentagon recommendation for structured access to Berbera; a U.S.–Somaliland security agreement; formal movement toward the Abraham Accords; active Israeli lobbying; a second recognition by an African state; a major American investment package; or a sharp deterioration in the Houthi–Al-Shabaab maritime threat.

Somaliland is closer to a serious U.S. recognition debate than it has been at any point in its post-1991 history.  What has changed is the convergence of forces. Israel has recognized Somaliland. The Abraham Accords offer a political vehicle. Red Sea insecurity has raised the value of Berbera. Houthi–Al-Shabaab cooperation is making the Gulf of Aden a more integrated security theater. Taiwan gives Somaliland credibility with China hawks. Congress now contains an organized recognition constituency. American investors are being courted. And President Irro has arrived in Washington with enough time to work across government, Congress, think tanks, business and the diaspora.

The strategic objective should therefore be precise: make continued non-recognition appear less useful to the United States than recognition.

text:
September 7, 1191. Richard the Lionheart destroyed Saladin's reputation, and he did it by refusing to fight for eleven straight days.

Five days ago I posted the Treaty of Jaffa, the deal that ended the Third Crusade. This is the battle that made that deal possible.

After taking Acre, Richard had to march south down the coast to Jaffa. Saladin's plan was simple and had worked before. Swarm the column with horse archers, kill the horses, goad the knights into charging, break the formation, then destroy the pieces on open ground.

That is essentially how the crusader kingdom had been annihilated at Hattin four years earlier. Richard knew it.

So he built a marching machine.

He moved only in the mornings to stay out of the worst heat. He kept the fleet alongside on the coast carrying supplies and taking off wounded. He arranged the column as a shell, infantry on the landward flank, crossbowmen shooting outward, knights inside where they were protected, and he rotated the infantry units so the men absorbing the worst of it got relieved.

And he told them that under any provocation whatsoever, they were not to charge.

For eleven days Saladin's archers poured arrows into that column and it simply kept walking. Muslim accounts describe shooting at them from every side to annoy them, and failing. There are descriptions of crusader infantry walking on with arrows standing out of their padded armour like quills, still in formation, still in step.

Horses were being killed the entire time, which for a knight is close to unbearable. They absorbed it for eleven days.

On September 7, near Arsuf, the rearguard was the Hospitallers, and the rearguard always takes the worst of this. Their master asked Richard twice for permission to charge. Richard said not yet, because he wanted the enemy fully committed first.

Then a knight named Baldwin le Carron and the Hospitallers went anyway, shouting for Saint George. Whether that was outright insubordination or a signal misunderstood is still debated.

Richard had about two seconds to decide whether to let them die alone or commit everything he had.

He committed everything.

The entire crusader cavalry went in on an enemy that had dismounted and worked in close among the infantry, which is the single worst place horse archers can be caught. Saladin's right wing came apart.

And then Richard did the genuinely difficult thing. He stopped after about a mile, reformed, and only then charged again. Twice more. A pursuit that does not degenerate into a scattered chase is the rarest thing in medieval warfare, and it is the reason this was a victory rather than a mess.

Christian chroniclers claimed 7,000 Ayyubid dead, which is a chronicler's number and should be treated as one. Crusader losses were around 700, and the only notable leader killed was James d'Avesnes.

The real damage was not the casualty list. It was that Saladin had been beaten in open battle in front of his own army, and since Hattin his men had believed that could not happen to him.

He never offered Richard another general engagement. He pulled back and demolished his own fortresses at Ascalon, Gaza, Lydda and Ramla rather than let Richard take them, which is what a commander does when he has stopped expecting to hold ground.

Fourteen months later they signed the truce at Jaffa.

Battle of Arsuf, 7 September 1191.

text:
Nobody warns you about this before you make your first million.

They warn you about taxes. About lawsuits. About bad partners in business. About leverage, about liquidity, about the market eating you alive on a Tuesday morning when you least expect it.

Nobody warns you about what happens to your relationships once you actually win.

I've spent a decade around traders, founders, and operators who built real wealth — not "look at my car" wealth, but the kind that changes how rooms react when you walk into them. And I've watched almost all of them make the exact same mistake in the one area of life that money can't fix with a wire transfer.

They think love is a reward for winning.

It's not. It's a completely different game, with different rules, and most high performers are playing it on hard mode without even knowing it — because everything that made them rich is actively working against them here.

Let me break this down, because if you're building something real — a fund, a company, a book of clients, a portfolio that keeps you up at 3am watching futures — you need to hear this before you learn it the hard way, at 40, divorced, rich, and completely alone in a beautiful apartment you can't remember buying furniture for.

The instinct that makes you rich is the instinct that will make you lonely.

Traders are trained to be skeptical of everything. Question the narrative. Assume the crowd is wrong. Don't trust the headline, read the filing. That instinct is priceless in markets and poisonous in relationships. You start running due diligence on people. You start looking for the exit before you've even committed to entering. You treat vulnerability like a bad trade thesis — something to hedge against instead of something to sit inside of.

The people who love you best are not spreadsheets. They will never make sense on paper the way a good setup does. If you keep waiting for a relationship to "confirm the trade" before you go all in, you will die rich and alone, and I mean that literally, not as a figure of speech.

Money buys you access to more people and worse judgment about which ones matter.

This is the part nobody tells you. Once you have money, your dating pool doesn't get better. It gets bigger and much, much murkier. Everyone becomes interested. Attention stops being a signal. The girl who wants you and the girl who wants your bank balance say the exact same words in the exact same tone at the exact same restaurant.

Broke you had a brutal filter built in — nobody stuck around who didn't actually want to be there. Rich you loses that filter completely and has to build a new one from scratch, usually after getting burned two or three times by someone whose interest evaporated the second the market turned against you for six months.

You confuse being desired with being known.

Desired is easy when you're successful. People will desire the version of you that shows up in a good blazer with a good story and a good bank account. Known is a different animal entirely. Known means someone has seen you at 4am when the position went against you and you couldn't sleep and you weren't impressive at all — you were scared, and quiet, and human.

Most successful men have an army of people who desire them and almost nobody who actually knows them. That gap is where the loneliness lives. It doesn't matter how many people are in the room at your party. If none of them know the real one, you're still by yourself.

You start treating relationships like positions instead of people.

This one is subtle and brutal. Traders manage risk. It's what we do all day. So without noticing, you start managing risk in love too — never fully in, always with a mental stop-loss, always keeping one foot near the exit "just in case." You call it being smart. It's actually just fear wearing a suit.

The problem is love doesn't respond to risk management the way markets do. You can't size your emotional position at 2% and expect a real connection to form. People can feel when you're hedged. They feel the half-commitment even when you never say it out loud, and they either leave or they shrink to match the smallness of what you're offering.

Your calendar is a confession.

Look at where your time actually goes, not where you say your priorities are. Most high performers will tell you their family and their partner come first, then their calendar tells a completely different story — sixty, seventy, eighty hours a week on the business, and whatever scraps of energy are left over get thrown at the relationship like a tip left on a bar.

You cannot build a real connection on scraps. You will not fix this by buying something expensive to compensate for the time you didn't give. Gifts are not a substitute for presence, and deep down, everyone knows the difference between a man who is there and a man who sent something because he wasn't.

You've optimized every part of your life except the one part that can't be optimized alone.

You optimized your morning routine. Your macros. Your portfolio allocation. Your calendar, your sleep, your supplements, your workouts. You are, in almost every measurable way, running at elite level.

And then you get to the one domain where optimization requires a second, fully autonomous human being with her own needs, her own history, her own bad days — and you try to run the same playbook. It doesn't work. She is not a variable you can control for. The moment you understand this, actually understand it, not just nod along to it, everything about how you show up changes.

Status doesn't heal what status broke.

If you grew up without security — financial or emotional — there's a real chance that some part of the drive to build wealth is actually a drive to finally feel safe. That's not a bad reason to build something. But wealth alone doesn't heal that wound. It just gives the wound a much nicer apartment to live in.

I've watched men hit numbers that would have made 22-year-old them scream with joy, and feel absolutely nothing when they got there, because the thing they were actually chasing was never the number. It was the feeling underneath the number — being wanted, being safe, being enough — and no amount of zeros in an account fixes that if you never deal with it directly.

The right woman is not a trophy. She's a force multiplier, or she's a leak.

There is no neutral partner. Every relationship either compounds your life or drains it, and there's very little in between once you're operating at a high level. A partner who genuinely gets what you're building, who has her own fire, her own standards, her own life — she doesn't slow you down, she extends your range. She becomes the reason the wins feel like something instead of just numbers on a screen.

The wrong partner does the opposite. She becomes a second job. Every win gets smaller because you have to manage her reaction to it. Every stress at work becomes two stresses because now you're also managing the relationship stress it's creating. Choosing who sits across the table from you for the next twenty years is, without exaggeration, the single highest-leverage decision most successful men make carelessly.

You will meet women who love the lifestyle and women who love you, and for a while they will look identical.

This is the trap. In the beginning, both types say the same things, do the same things, seem equally into you. The difference only shows up under pressure — during a drawdown, during a slow year, during a health scare, during the version of you that isn't winning. One of them disappears the moment the winning stops. The other one stays and somehow makes the losing period feel survivable.

You cannot tell them apart at the champagne stage. You can only tell them apart in the dark. Which is exactly why so many successful men get burned — they're making a twenty-year decision using data from the best six months of someone's behavior.

Real intimacy requires the one thing you've trained yourself never to do: lose control.

Every skill that built your net worth is a control skill. Control your emotions during volatility. Control your risk. Control your reactions. Control the narrative. Real closeness with another person requires the opposite — a willingness to be out of control, to be affected, to let someone else's presence actually move you.

This terrifies high performers more than any market crash ever could, because a market crash is just money. Losing control in front of another human being feels like exposure. But that exposure is the entire price of admission for real love. There is no version of deep intimacy that doesn't require you to occasionally not be the smartest, calmest, most composed person in the room.

Loneliness at the top isn't a myth. It's a design flaw in how success is built.

The higher you climb, the fewer people are positioned to relate to you, challenge you honestly, or love you without an agenda. Your circle gets smaller not because you're becoming worse, but because success filters people — some drop away out of envy, some drop away because they can't relate anymore, and some stay for reasons that have nothing to do with actually caring about you.

This is why the relationship you build with a life partner matters exponentially more the more successful you become. She might end up being one of the only people left in your life who isn't there for what you can do for them. That's not romantic language. That's a structural fact about what happens to social circles at the top.

You keep waiting for the "right time" to prioritize this. There isn't one.

There will never be a year where the business is calm enough, the fund is stable enough, the deal flow is light enough to finally give a relationship the attention you keep promising it. That year doesn't exist. If you're waiting for the workload to shrink before you show up fully for someone, you will wait until you're sixty and wonder where the last three decades of Tuesdays went.

The people who actually build both — the empire and the relationship — didn't wait for balance to arrive on its own. They decided the relationship was a non-negotiable line item, not a leftover, and they protected it with the same discipline they protect a core position.

You are terrified of being loved for the wrong reasons, so you end up loved for none at all.

This is a strange, specific fear that almost nobody talks about. Successful men are so afraid of being a walking bank account to someone that they overcorrect into emotional unavailability, testing people, pushing people away, sabotaging good things early just to prove to themselves that "she'd still be here if I had nothing." It's an understandable instinct. It's also a great way to end up isolated by your own hand, protecting yourself from a wound nobody was actually about to inflict.

At some point you have to accept that you cannot fully verify anyone's motives with certainty, the same way you can never be 100% certain about a trade before you take it. You manage the risk. You watch the signals. And eventually, you have to actually place the position, because standing on the sidelines forever isn't safety — it's just a slower, quieter kind of loss.

The quietest moments are the ones that actually tell you the truth about a relationship.

Not the vacations. Not the dinners. Not the version of the relationship that performs well in public. The truth shows up in the silence — in the car, at the end of a long day, when nobody's talking and nobody's performing and there's nothing to distract from just being two people in a space together.

That silence either feels like peace or it feels like distance, and successful men, addicted to noise, motion, and constant stimulation, are usually the last to notice which one they're actually sitting in.

Everything I just said means nothing until you've actually felt it.

You can read all fourteen points above, nod at every single one, screenshot this, agree with it completely — and still go right back to the same patterns tomorrow, because insight and behavior change are two entirely different things. Understanding the game intellectually has never been the hard part for people like us. We're good at understanding games. The hard part is sitting still long enough, quiet enough, present enough, to actually feel what you've been avoiding feeling this whole time.

Some moments do that work for you without any effort at all. A view. A silence. Someone next to you who isn't asking you for anything, who isn't impressed by your last trade, who is simply there — and for a few seconds the noise in your head that never stops actually stops, and you remember, briefly, what all of this was supposed to be for in the first place.

I'm not going to describe what that looks like. Some things you have to actually watch to feel.

Below is one of those moments.

—

But let me go deeper, because if you've read this far, you're not looking for a motivational quote. You're looking for the parts nobody says out loud in your circles, at your dinners, in your group chats full of guys who all seem fine and are all, statistically, not fine.

The first year of real money is the most dangerous year of your relationships.

Not your relationship with a partner necessarily — your relationships with everyone. Money changes the physics of every interaction you have. Old friends start acting strange around you, either overly deferential or quietly resentful, and you can feel it even when nobody says it. New people show up who never would have found you before, and you have no calibration for reading them because you've never had to before.

This is the year most men either build a bunker or build a filter. The bunker version withdraws, trusts nobody, becomes cold and suspicious of everyone including people who genuinely cared before the money showed up. The filter version does the harder work — staying open while getting sharper, learning to read intention instead of just performance, keeping the door unlocked while still checking who's actually walking through it. One of these paths leads to a rich, connected life. The other leads to a rich, hollow one.

You will be tested by people who don't even know they're testing you.

Every date, every new friend, every person who enters your orbit after you've made it is running an unconscious test, whether they intend to or not: does this person's attention on me change if I stop being impressed by them? Does this person still show up if I'm inconvenient, tired, unglamorous, difficult on a random Tuesday?

Most people fail this test without even realizing there was one. The interesting thing is, you're being tested too — by the people around you, watching to see if success turned you into someone who only respects people who are also winning, or whether you can still be decent to someone who has nothing to offer you strategically. Character isn't what you do at the top of a great year. It's what you do on the boring Tuesdays when nobody's measuring.

Your nervous system doesn't know the difference between a market crash and a fight with someone you love.

This is physiological, not philosophical. If your body spends all day regulating stress from volatility, positions, deal risk, client pressure — it comes home already dysregulated, already primed for threat. Then a small disagreement at home, something that should be a five-minute conversation, gets processed by a nervous system that's still half-convinced it's under attack from the market close three hours ago.

This is why so many high performers seem "fine" all day and then completely overreact to something tiny at home. It was never about the tiny thing. It was about carrying an entire day of unprocessed stress into a room with someone who deserved your calibrated self, not your leftover self. Nobody teaches traders and founders how to actually come down from that state before walking through their own front door. Almost nobody does the work to learn it. The ones who do are the ones whose relationships actually last.

The people who tell you "just focus on the money, relationships will follow" are selling you something, even if they don't know it.

This advice sounds tough-minded and disciplined. It is actually one of the most expensive lies in success culture. Relationships are not a downstream reward of achievement. They're a completely separate skill tree that has to be trained in parallel, or it atrophies while you're busy getting stronger everywhere else.

I've met men worth nine figures who could not sit through a two-hour dinner without checking their phone eleven times, who could not tolerate silence with another person for longer than ninety seconds, who had literally forgotten how to be curious about someone without an angle. That's not a side effect of success. That's a skill that died from neglect while another skill was trained obsessively. You don't accidentally end up good at connection any more than you accidentally end up good at reading a chart. It has to be practiced, deliberately, the same way everything else you're good at was practiced.

Real partnership at this level looks less like romance and more like alliance, and that's not a downgrade — it's an upgrade almost nobody tells you about.

The Hollywood version of love is butterflies and grand gestures. The version that actually survives twenty years at the top looks more like two people who trust each other's judgment completely, who don't need to perform for one another, who can sit in a room in total silence and feel more at peace than they do anywhere else on earth. It's less cinematic. It's also the only version that has ever actually lasted for the men I respect most.

Alliance means she knows what you're building and wants it to succeed almost as much as you do, not because she benefits from it financially, but because she's genuinely invested in you as a human being achieving what you set out to achieve. Alliance means you know her ambitions the same way, in the same depth, and you protect them with the same intensity you protect your own portfolio. That kind of partnership compounds. It's the single biggest unlock most successful men never activate, because they're too busy looking for fireworks to notice they already have something sturdier and rarer sitting right in front of them.

Nobody becomes emotionally available by accident at 45. It's a decision you make earlier, or a wall you build that gets thicker every year you don't.

Every year you avoid vulnerability successfully — every year the strategy of staying guarded seems to "work" because you're still winning, still respected, still surrounded by people — the wall gets a little thicker and a little more load-bearing. By your mid-forties, for a lot of men, that wall isn't a defense mechanism anymore. It's the entire structure holding up their identity. Removing it doesn't feel like healing. It feels like collapse.

This is why the men who do the emotional work in their twenties and thirties, even when it feels unnecessary because everything looks fine on the surface, end up with something almost nobody else in their tax bracket has: the actual capacity to be close to someone, on purpose, without it costing them their sense of control. That capacity is worth more than most of the deals you'll ever close.

You are allowed to want both. Nobody actually has to choose between the empire and the person.

Somewhere along the way, a lot of driven men absorbed the idea that real ambition requires sacrificing real intimacy — that you can have the yacht or you can have the marriage, the fund or the family, but not both, because greatness demands total obsession and total obsession leaves no room for anyone else. This is one of the most convenient lies ever told, mostly by men who failed at the relationship part and needed a story that made the failure sound noble instead of avoidable.

The truth is less dramatic and more demanding: you can absolutely have both, but only if you treat the relationship with the same seriousness, the same planning, the same non-negotiable status you treat the business with. Nobody accidentally maintains a great marriage while running a great fund. It's built the same way the fund was built — with intention, with discipline, with actual scheduled attention instead of whatever's left over after everything else has been fed first.

The version of you that finally gets this right is usually not the version that made the first ten million. It's the version that survived losing something that mattered more.

This is the part almost nobody wants to hear, but it's true across nearly every man I've watched actually change: real understanding of what matters rarely comes from a win. It comes from a loss significant enough to shake the assumption that the money was ever going to be enough on its own. A relationship that ended. A parent who died before you finished proving something to them. A period alone in a very nice, very empty space that made the emptiness impossible to ignore any longer.

You don't have to wait for that loss to happen to you before you take this seriously. That's the entire point of everything above. The men who read something like this and actually change course before the loss forces them to are rarer than the ones who wait, and they are, without exception, the ones who end up with both the empire and the life to enjoy it in.

At some point, the quiet moments become the entire point, not the interruption.

For years, quiet moments feel like downtime between the real events — the closes, the launches, the milestones. Eventually, for the ones who actually figure this out, the order reverses completely. The milestones start to feel like the means. The quiet moments — the ones with almost nothing happening in them, just presence, just someone next to you who isn't asking anything of you, just a view that makes the noise in your skull go still for a second — those become the actual destination everything else was supposedly for.

If you're still early in the climb, you won't fully believe that yet, and that's fine. You don't have to believe it. Just don't be so busy chasing the next milestone that you miss every single one of those moments along the way, because they don't wait around for you to be ready. They happen once, quietly, and then they're gone, and no amount of money buys them back.

Everything above is a map. It's not the territory.

You can agree with every word of this and still not feel anything until you're actually standing in a moment like the one below — until the noise stops for a second and you're just there, with someone, looking at something bigger than both of you, and for once the number in your account has absolutely nothing to do with how good this feels.

That's the whole point. That's the entire thing money can't buy directly, only create the conditions for, if you're paying attention when it shows up.

I'm not going to explain what happens in the next eight seconds. I'm just going to tell you this: watch it, and notice what you feel before your brain starts analyzing it. That reaction, the one before the analysis kicks in — that's the part of you that's been waiting the longest to be let out.

One last thing, and then I'll let the video speak for itself.

If you've read this entire thing and your first thought was "this doesn't apply to me, I'm different, I actually have this handled" — sit with that reaction for a second before you dismiss it. That exact thought is the most common one in the room right before things fall apart, because certainty about your own emotional availability is usually inversely correlated with how emotionally available you actually are. The men who genuinely have this handled don't feel the need to insist on it. They just quietly have it, and it shows in the small, unremarkable moments nobody's grading them on.

And if instead your first thought was some version of recognition — a quiet, uncomfortable "yeah, that's me" — that's not a failure. That's the most useful thing that's happened to you all week. Insight like that is expensive to get and cheap to ignore, and most men who've built something real got there precisely because they don't ignore expensive information when it shows up, regardless of which domain it's coming from.

So don't ignore it here either.

Watch the video below. Not for the view. For the feeling that shows up before you have time to think about it.

THE CROWN PRINCE OF A COUNTRY THAT HAS NO THRONE: A WARNING TO SEYI TINUBU

Letters from Stockholm

Every week the Tinubu machine floods our timelines with another video of Seyi Tinubu. Seyi arriving. Seyi waving. Seyi in convoy with outriders, sirens and armed escorts, sweeping through a city where citizens cannot get a police response for a burglary. They post it as though nothing has changed. As though a federal judge in Washington is not sitting on their father's files. As though the world is not watching.

Let us be clear about one thing. Seyi Tinubu holds no office. He was elected to nothing. He was appointed to nothing. The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria knows no such position as the President's son. Yet he moves with the trappings of state power, paid for by the Nigerian taxpayer, and people who cross him have a habit of ending up in DSS custody.

That is not my invention. The former NANS president Atiku Isah told a Federal High Court in Abuja that he was beaten, stabbed and held by the DSS for over two weeks after refusing what he described as an offer from Seyi Tinubu to step aside, and he has sued Seyi Tinubu, the DSS and the NTA for thirty-eight billion naira. Only weeks ago a Lagos entertainer was picked up over a video about the President's son. His own lawyer went online begging the presidency for forgiveness. Forgiveness. For a video. This is how a republic learns to kneel.

Meanwhile Seyi sits on the board of CDK Integrated Industries, a Chagoury Group company, while his father's government hands Hitech Construction, another Chagoury Group company, the Lagos–Calabar coastal highway at an estimated thirteen billion dollars without competitive bidding. The presidency's defence is that he joined the board in 2018 and that a tiles factory has nothing to do with a highway. Any first-year student of corporate governance knows that conflict of interest is about the relationship, not the product line. In any serious country he would have resigned the day his father was sworn in. He did not, because in his mind the country is the family business.

And this is the moment he chooses to parade himself. His father is in a Washington courtroom fighting to keep sealed the records of a 1993 heroin-money forfeiture, and a sworn FBI declaration has now confirmed there was an investigation. My own conviction, which I have stated many times and state again as opinion, is that the reason those files are so dangerous is that they show what he gave the Americans to save himself, and whose names he gave. That is what he is fighting to bury. And his son is on Instagram in a motorcade.

I said this to Seyi directly once and I will say it in public now. Every siren, every outrider, every viral video is another knot in the noose around his own neck. The more he behaves like the crown prince of Nigeria, the more he makes himself the single most visible target for the sins of his father, his stepmother and himself. When the reckoning comes, and it always comes, the crowd does not look for the accountant. It looks for the face it was made to look at every day.

He should read his history. Isabel dos Santos was once the richest woman in Africa, untouchable, the daughter of a president who ruled Angola for thirty-eight years. Today her assets are frozen across three continents, she is charged at home and she cannot go back. Mohammed Abacha, son of a dictator who thought he owned Nigeria, spent years in detention after his father died, stood trial for murder, and watched the world spend two decades clawing back the family's loot from Switzerland, Jersey and the United States. Both of them believed the sirens would never stop. Both of them were wrong.

Power is a drug. Seyi Tinubu is plainly addicted to it, and like every addict he cannot see the day the supply runs out. That day is not far. The files will be released. The contracts will be examined. The people who were beaten in DSS cells will be called to testify. And a man who holds no office will find that he has no immunity.

Nigeria belongs to Nigerians. It does not belong to a family.

Kio Amachree
Worldview International, Stockholm

The 1993 Chicago matter was a civil forfeiture settlement, not a criminal conviction. Allegations concerning informant status, the coastal highway procurement and the treatment of detainees remain unproven in court and are stated here as matters of public record, pending litigation and the author's opinion.
