The best home sellers in America are dead. 2.8 million of them a year, and about 70% owned a house

Their kids live three states away, don't want it, and will thank you for taking it at 60 cents on the dollar. 70% of my deals come from exactly this. Here's the entire process, because it's public information and almost nobody uses it:

Why the house is cheap: when someone dies, their house goes into probate, a court process that takes 6-18 months to hand it to the heirs. During that time the kids are paying $500-$800 a month in taxes, insurance, and lawn for a house in a city they don't live in. Nobody's maintaining it. A small roof leak becomes water damage by month 4. Most realtors won't touch it because the timeline is a mess. The heirs don't want a project. They want a check and for it to be over

Step 1: Go to your county clerk or probate court website. Search "probate filings" or walk in and ask. Every case lists the deceased, the property address, the heirs' names, and the attorney handling the estate. It's public. It's free. It updates weekly

Step 2: Cross-check the address on Zillow. You want the ugly, dated, obviously-empty one. Overgrown yard on the street view is your tell

Step 3: Contact the attorney or the heir. Letter or call. This is the script, word for word:

"I buy houses for cash in [county]. I can close in 7-14 days. I'll handle the title work, the cleanout, and anything left in the house. You don't have to visit the property or spend a dollar. What number would make this easy for you?"

Step 4: Run your number. Fixed-up value × 0.65, minus repairs. A house worth $150,000 clean that needs $30,000 gets an offer around $67,000. They'll usually counter. Because their alternative is $800 a month for another year and a realtor who won't call back, the counter is closer to your number than you'd think

Step 5: Fund it without your money. Hard money covers 80% of the purchase and 100% of the renovation. Closing in 7-14 days is what makes you the best offer even when you're not the highest one

Step 6: Paint, floors, kitchen, bath. Rent it to a Section 8 tenant or sell it. Refinance, pull your cash back, keep the house

Real one: a woman in San Diego, mother passed 8 months earlier, house sitting empty in Ohio with $3,200 of back taxes and a burst pipe. She wanted $100,000. I offered $97,000 and she said yes within an hour because the funeral was still on a credit card. $31,000 renovation. Appraised at $205,000. Government pays the rent

"You took advantage of her"

I took a rotting house off her hands in 7 days when nobody else would return her call. She thanked me after closing. The neighborhood got a fixed house. A family off a 3-year waitlist got a home. Everyone did better than the day before I called

There is one of these on your street right now. Somebody's going to buy it. The records are open and the phone call takes 3 minutes

text:
Chapter 4: Why DeSoto?

Why DeSoto? Because we don’t take orders from politicians around here. And if y’all ever realize the power you actually have in the vote, you could be the ones giving the orders!

DeSoto County, which encompasses Senate District 1 and my old state representative District 28 and current Supervisor District 5, has become one of, if not the most, conservative voting blocs in the state of Mississippi. The establishment and special interest groups don’t like us constantly electing fighters to send to Jackson. They don’t like it when people “step out of line.” They prefer when people take orders. Let’s just say I know firsthand.

I know firsthand because in 2019 I “stepped out of line” and ran for governor against the heir to the throne. Why would I give up my position as a state representative to run for governor knowing the odds I’d lose handily? I was literally laughed at by many political insiders and told I wouldn’t even break 5%. I’d probably only get 3%.

I was even offered a spot in the lineup. A top donor called me and said he could host a fundraiser that could raise me six figures if I’d drop out of the governor’s race and run instead against the holdout Democrat Northern District Public Service Commissioner, Brandon Presley, or even against Delbert Hosemann for lieutenant governor. But those races weren’t my calling. It wasn’t about the odds of winning to me. It wasn’t about having or not having money. It was about being obedient and following my conviction. Every instinct told me not to run. The toil on my family and my business. The lack of a campaign war chest against one of the largest ever amassed in a Mississippi race — a $7 million campaign fund staring down at me. The lack of support from the GOP hierarchy. Against all of those odds I ran, because I had prayed and felt a deeper calling than I have ever felt before.

Here is how that war chest was built. Before 2018, Mississippi campaign-finance law let you spend campaign money on almost whatever you wanted, including personal expenses. Clothes. Boots. Cars. Groceries. When you left office you could even pocket what was left. In the 2017 session we finally passed a law to stop that. I was a state representative at that time. I’ll give credit where credit is due. Speaker Philip Gunn and Rep. Hank Zuber of Ocean Springs worked hard on that bill. Zuber had been pushing it for years. Tate Reeves was lieutenant governor. The new law did not take effect until January 1, 2018, and it came with a grandfather clause: money raised before that date could still be spent under the old rules. I know from inside knowledge, as a state representative sitting there when it happened, that Tate is one of the main ones who insisted on that clause in order to let the bill pass. Reeves had about $5.3 million sitting in that pre-2018 account. He went into 2019 with $6.7 million across his accounts. His Washington consultant called it $7 million in the bank.

How did he get all of this money built up, you ask? Pay to play is what it’s called in Jackson. The talk around the Capitol was if you wanted a meeting with the lieutenant governor you wrote a check. If you wanted a bill out of committee you wrote an even bigger check. And if you wanted a bill to pass, well, you get it. Not illegal, but definitely not what I would consider honorable.

I don’t believe he was planning on having to spend all that money on his campaign. He was planning to walk into the governor’s mansion with maybe one primary opponent. He knew he’d raise all he needed for the general election against the Democrat Party once he got the primary behind him, and he would never have to touch his little nest egg. I guess I ruined that plan by running, and many of You the people ruined it by voting for me. Good. 
1/3

text:
The war in Ukraine is entering a more dangerous phase of multilateral escalation, with few remaining guardrails. Ukrainian attacks are reaching deeper into Russia, Moscow is intensifying strikes on Ukraine and pressure on its maritime trade, and European support is becoming more directly connected to Kyiv’s capacity to strike Russian territory. Germany’s attribution of the attempted Leipzig airport attack to Moscow, alongside a succession of hybrid and other hostile incidents across Europe, has driven Russian-German relations into a new crisis and increased the risk of the confrontation spilling beyond Ukraine.

At the same time, Washington is making a new attempt to reopen negotiations, even though the positions of Moscow and Kyiv remain barely reconcilable.

Witkoff and Kushner returned to Moscow on 5 September after several months of work by Washington on a potential settlement framework. The disputed issues include territory, security guarantees, Ukraine’s future military capabilities, a possible international presence and the political conditions surrounding a settlement.

Russia’s fundamental terms have not changed, while Ukraine continues to signal that it is ready to keep fighting. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv appears prepared to make a strategic concession. The important questions are whether Putin continues to stand by earlier understandings and whether renewed contacts can produce more than another trilateral meeting.

The new R.Politik Bulletin assesses these questions alongside the military, maritime and Russian-European escalation now shaping the negotiating environment.

Russia’s domestic political system is also becoming less predictable as the first federal parliamentary campaign since the start of the war approaches. Yabloko was initially allowed to participate, only to be removed after the party began to look less politically manageable. The significance lies not simply in Yabloko’s electoral prospects, but in the reversal itself: was this a coherent policy shift, an improvised response to changing circumstances or the result of competing assessments of political risk? The bulletin examines the decision-making behind the party’s dismantling and the implications for the remaining boundaries of legal opposition.

Other developments raise similar questions about how wartime governance is changing. A new decree allows the state to place broadly defined critical infrastructure under temporary management without formally transferring ownership. Its practical application will determine whether it remains a security measure or develops into a wider instrument of corporate control.

The authorities have designated Pavel Durov an extremist while government bodies, businesses and election managers still rely on Telegram. This unresolved contradiction will become particularly important after the election, when the platform’s political utility may begin to change.

The prosecution of charity leader Lida Moniava tests how far social standing and institutional importance can influence the form of state pressure. In Udmurtia, an unexpected gubernatorial replacement offers a separate indication of the operational and personnel requirements emerging under wartime conditions.

Meanwhile, Russians continue to report relative personal stability while becoming markedly more pessimistic about the country’s future. Business confidence presents a similar picture: limited stabilisation, but at a persistently low level.

R.Politik Bulletin No. 15 (189) examines how these decisions are taken under pressure.

text:
On September 1, 2026, an American precision-guided missile slammed directly into a residential home in the small Iranian fishing town of Kuhestak, located in Sirik County along the strategic Strait of Hormuz. Inside, dozens of working-class families had gathered to celebrate the wedding of a local fisherman’s daughter. In a fraction of a second, an occasion of community joy was transformed into a horrific scene of devastation. Concrete walls collapsed, roofs caved in, and blood-soaked rugs, torn garlands, and children's shoes were left scattered among the rubble.

The strike killed at least five people, including four-year-old Amir-Ali Karimi, sixteen-year-old Mohammad Malahi, and twenty-two-year-old Fatemeh Taheri, who succumbed to her severe injuries in the hospital. Over sixty-eight others were wounded, predominantly women and children, because the U.S. missile struck the specific section of the home reserved for female guests.

As reported by Al Jazeera, heartbroken relatives buried four-year-old Amir-Ali while mourning families demanded international accountability. The Iranian Red Crescent immediately submitted a request to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate the strike as a war crime. Meanwhile, independent Spanish-language outlet Aporrea highlighted that Iranian authorities officially denounced the strike as a blatant violation of international law, executed during what Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei called "America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure" in its broader war against Iran.

To understand why a U.S. missile hit a civilian wedding party in Kuhestak, one must reject the convenient liberal mythology of the "tragic mistake" or "unfortunate collateral damage." The slaughter in Kuhestak was not an anomaly, a technical glitch, or an isolated oversight. It is the direct, predictable, and logical outcome of U.S. imperial doctrine—a doctrine defined by reckless military expansion, the ideological purging of internal military oversight, and an unwavering commitment to maintaining global Western hegemony at all costs.

Imperial Decay, Internal Purges, and the Dismantling of Civilian Protection
When pressed by reporters regarding the massacre, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins issued a canned response, insisting that the U.S. military was targeting nearby telecommunications equipment and claiming that "the U.S. military never targets civilians." Vice President JD Vance offered an even more callous dismissal, acknowledging an investigation while blithely noting that "sometimes things happen" during war.

Yet, as investigative analysis in The Cradle and reporting by weapons experts at Reuters revealed, physical evidence at the scene confirms the explosion was caused by a direct strike from a U.S. precision-guided munition. When a military equipped with the most advanced satellite surveillance and high-precision weaponry repeatedly strikes civilian homes, schools, and social gatherings, the excuse of "accidental targeting" completely crumbles.

The systemic nature of this recklessness is deeply linked to the political and ideological decay within the leadership of the U.S. war machine. On an episode of MSNOW, coverage centered on how U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth systematically gutted the Pentagon's civilian harm reduction program—an office specifically tasked with evaluating intelligence, setting operational safeguards, and minimizing non-combatant casualties during aerial bombardment. Hegseth executed these sweeping purges against the unanimous advice of senior military commanders, framing basic adherence to international humanitarian law as "woke bureaucracy" that stifled military aggression.

This internal stripping of operational oversight coincided with widespread purges of senior officers, escalating logistical chaos, and plummeting morale across the armed forces. As documented by the World Socialist Web Site (WSWS), the war against Iran—launched in late February 2026—has plunged the U.S. military into a severe structural crisis. The resignation of top military civilians, the firing of dozens of generals and admirals, and the exhaustion of naval crews deployed indefinitely aboard aircraft carriers like the USS Abraham Lincoln reflect an empire consuming itself from within. Deprived of clear strategic objectives and operating under commands that prioritize raw brutality over tactical precision, the imperial war machine strikes wildly at civilian infrastructure, converting working-class neighborhoods into free-fire zones.

A Quarter-Century Tradition: The Operational Feature of Western Hegemony
The massacre in Kuhestak must be viewed through a historical lens. Just thirty kilometers from Kuhestak lies the city of Minab, where, on the opening day of the war in February 2026, a U.S. airstrike targeted an elementary school, killing over 160 schoolgirls and teachers. In that instance, CENTCOM relied on outdated, decade-old targeting data that failed to recognize the building was no longer a military compound. The Pentagon completed an internal investigation into the Minab bombing in April 2026 but kept the findings strictly classified, refusing to release them to Congress or the public.

Furthermore, as Medea Benjamin detailed in Consortium News, the bombing of family celebrations is an established operational pattern of U.S. military intervention across the Global South. Over the past twenty-five years of the post-9/11 "War on Terror," American aircraft and drone strikes have bombed at least eight other wedding parties and wedding processions across Afghanistan, Iraq, and Yemen:

Uruzgan Province, Afghanistan (July 2002): A U.S. AC-130 gunship attacked a rural wedding celebration, killing dozens of civilians.

Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan (July 2008): A U.S. missile strike targeted a wedding party escorting a bride, killing forty-seven civilians, including the bride.

Rad'a, Yemen (December 2013): A U.S. drone fired four Hellfire missiles into an eleven-vehicle wedding procession, killing fifteen people and wounding fifteen others.

When a superpower repeatedly turns weddings into funerals across multiple decades and continents, civilian slaughter ceases to be an operational error—it reveals itself as a structural feature of imperial warfare. The fundamental premise of Western imperial strategy is that Global South populations are entirely expendable in the pursuit of geopolitical dominance, resource extraction, and regional control.

The Bipartisan War Consensus and Domestic Repression
While corporate media outlets occasionally frame foreign interventions around tactical disagreements between political factions, the reality is that U.S. imperialism is an entirely bipartisan enterprise. The war against Iran, the endless transfers of high-tech munitions, and the unquestioned support for regional escalation receive ironclad backing from both major capitalist parties in Washington.

As highlighted by the World Socialist Web Site (WSWS), both Democrats and Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives routinely pass stopgap spending bills that fund the Pentagon at staggering annual rates exceeding $839 billion. Even when opposition politicians offer mild tactical criticisms regarding how a war is conducted, they consistently vote to supply the capital, weapons, and logistical backing required to sustain the conflict.

This bipartisan consensus abroad requires relentless repression at home. To protect the war machine from domestic opposition, the political establishment actively criminalizes anti-war dissent. On the exact same day news broke of the Kuhestak wedding strike, lawmakers in Congress joined forces to pass legislation threatening higher education institutions with the loss of federal funding and tax-exempt status if they allow anti-war, anti-imperialist, or anti-Zionist boycotts on campus.

text:
The war in Ukraine is entering a more dangerous phase of multilateral escalation, with few remaining guardrails. Ukrainian attacks are reaching deeper into Russia, Moscow is intensifying strikes on Ukraine and pressure on its maritime trade, and European support is becoming more directly connected to Kyiv’s capacity to strike Russian territory. Germany’s attribution of the attempted Leipzig airport attack to Moscow, alongside a succession of hybrid and other hostile incidents across Europe, has driven Russian-German relations into a new crisis and increased the risk of the confrontation spilling beyond Ukraine.

At the same time, Washington is making a new attempt to reopen negotiations, even though the positions of Moscow and Kyiv remain barely reconcilable.

Witkoff and Kushner returned to Moscow on 5 September after several months of work by Washington on a potential settlement framework. The disputed issues include territory, security guarantees, Ukraine’s future military capabilities, a possible international presence and the political conditions surrounding a settlement.

Russia’s fundamental terms have not changed, while Ukraine continues to signal that it is ready to keep fighting. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv appears prepared to make a strategic concession. The important questions are whether Putin continues to stand by earlier understandings and whether renewed contacts can produce more than another trilateral meeting.

The new R.Politik Bulletin assesses these questions alongside the military, maritime and Russian-European escalation now shaping the negotiating environment.

Russia’s domestic political system is also becoming less predictable as the first federal parliamentary campaign since the start of the war approaches. Yabloko was initially allowed to participate, only to be removed after the party began to look less politically manageable. The significance lies not simply in Yabloko’s electoral prospects, but in the reversal itself: was this a coherent policy shift, an improvised response to changing circumstances or the result of competing assessments of political risk? The bulletin examines the decision-making behind the party’s dismantling and the implications for the remaining boundaries of legal opposition.

Other developments raise similar questions about how wartime governance is changing. A new decree allows the state to place broadly defined critical infrastructure under temporary management without formally transferring ownership. Its practical application will determine whether it remains a security measure or develops into a wider instrument of corporate control.

The authorities have designated Pavel Durov an extremist while government bodies, businesses and election managers still rely on Telegram. This unresolved contradiction will become particularly important after the election, when the platform’s political utility may begin to change.

The prosecution of charity leader Lida Moniava tests how far social standing and institutional importance can influence the form of state pressure. In Udmurtia, an unexpected gubernatorial replacement offers a separate indication of the operational and personnel requirements emerging under wartime conditions.

Meanwhile, Russians continue to report relative personal stability while becoming markedly more pessimistic about the country’s future. Business confidence presents a similar picture: limited stabilisation, but at a persistently low level.

R.Politik Bulletin No. 15 (189) examines how these decisions are taken under pressure.

GOVERNMENT-CONTROLLED HEALTH CARE, the government covers almost all medical care. Little or no bill at the doctor, if it sounds too good to be true, check who pays and how long you wait.

Employers and families pay premiums today

You see a bill or copay today. The bill is hidden. It does not disappear.
Insurers and patients ration with price
 Government rations with rules and queues.
“Free at the clinic” means the cash register moved to Washington.

Who still pays
Doctors, hospitals, nurses, and drug makers still get paid.
Under a full takeover
• Care looks free → people use more of it • Doctors and beds do not appear overnight • Coverage expands to everyone • The federal government picks up almost the entire tab

Extra federal cost in independent estimates: about $2.5 trillion to $4+ trillion more per year
 On the order of $30 trillion or more over 10 years

Today’s Medicaid + ACA slice is about $1.0–1.1 trillion — and that is not every working American. A full takeover is a different machine

How long you wait
Price at the door falls toward zero:
Demand jumps
Supply lags
The leftover is a waiting list

Canada, 2025: 28.6 weeks from family doctor to treatment. Almost 7 months. 208% longer than 1993. Neurosurgery 49.9 weeks. Orthopedics 48.6 weeks. 1.4 million people in line

UK NHS: huge public budget. Still long waits and staff shortages. A big appropriation does not erase the queue.

The tradeoff
Promise: care is free. Reality: taxes and borrowing replace premiums.
Promise: everyone is covered. Reality: demand outruns doctors and beds.
Promise: government controls costs. Reality: government controls access.
Promise: no more insurance companies. Reality: one insurer — the state.
Government-controlled care does not delete the bill. It collects it in taxes, debt, and time in line.
If the offer is “no bill at the doctor,” ask who writes the check — and how many weeks until the appointment.

Iran Eyes New Trade Routes as Sanctions Bite                   As Washington steps up its "maximum pressure" campaign, Tehran is quietly rethinking its trade strategy. Hadi Tizhoush Taban, head of the Iran-Russia Joint Chamber of Commerce, argues that a complete economic stranglehold is no longer feasible in a world where major powers pursue their own independent interests.

"The US can raise our transaction costs—that's the whole point," he said in an interview. Higher insurance premiums, shipping detours, and banking hurdles are all part of the design. But an absolute blockade? That, he insists, is another matter. With China, India, Russia, and Gulf states looking after their own commercial agendas, the global economy is too fragmented for total isolation.

Tizhoush Taban's prescription is straightforward: diversify or perish. Iran cannot rely on oil alone, nor on a single trade corridor. Northern routes through the Caucasus and Central Asia offer alternatives to southern ports, but no single path is a silver bullet. Competitive corridors—in cost and time—are the real priority.

Banking remains the Achilles' heel. Even if goods move, money often does not. The chamber chief warns that ditching the dollar is not a magic fix—it is the financial networks that matter. Regional payment systems and reciprocal accounts could help, but only if currency conversion costs, which can eat up to 25% of a deal, are reined in. "A fair exchange rate," he says, "is not a favor—it is a necessity."

The bottom line: sanctions are here to stay, but so is Iran's determination to find a way through. https://t.co/b8XB4WdZdC

text: The long weekend gave me a chance to enjoy Lawrence Lepard’s book THE BIG PRINT: What Happened to American and How Sound Money Will Fix It. It recounts one incident after another of monetary intervention by Washington and the Federal Reserve, the reckless behavior that got us into our $40 trillion sinkhole of unpayable debt. He does so not as a detached academic, but with more than 40 years of skin in the game on Wall Street and in venture capital. Just in this young millennium one calamity has cascaded into another. From the dotcom bubble that popped in 2000, pumped up by Alan Greenspan’s Fed money management, to his ferocious repression of interest rates when that bubble popped. Which gave way to… A bubble in the housing market. Which inevitably popped… Ushering in what became known as the Great Financial Crisis. The Fed and Congress rode to the rescue of their crony banks, exploding the Fed’s balance sheet from around $900 billion to $4.5 trillion. That represents money the Fed created out of thin air to buy things. But wait, as they say! There’s more!  Before long the Fed pumped up its assets to $9 trillion. That’s a lot of funny money. It also inflated the money supply by 42 percent. The result was the Biden inflation, the highest consumer price inflation in more than 40 years. The Covid interlude was another excuse for Washington to spend money it did not have. The government passed out checks promiscuously, dishing out trillions in stimulus checks and non-repayable loans. The Federal deficit in 2020 accordingly rose to $3.1 trillion. In 2021 it reached $2.8 trillion. And the red ink continues to gush! The result is massive, compounding Federal indebtedness, with interest on the national debt having quadrupled since 2000.  It is debt that cannot be repaid by any honest and ordinary means. It can only be repaid by debasing the dollar itself. That means digital money-printing. But if you think the past 20 years of political and financial dysfunction were chaotic, Lepard says “You need to buckle up – you haven’t seen anything yet!” It’s not a spoiler to reveal that he offers a fix that is both short and accurate: “If we fix the money, we fix the world.” Thanks for the book, Larry!
